pdf-item-equation-1-1.Breakdown.IsSmoothSolution: The equations in `IsSmoothSolution` are imposed at $t>0$; smoothness and the initial value extend to $t=0$. The predicate concerns a solution on the entire half-line. In Theorem 1.1 the constructed solution has these properties only up to, and not including, its singular time.

s1-viscosity.Breakdown.BreakdownOnSpace:
The inverse change is $u(t,x)=
u^{-1}	ilde u(t/
u,x)$ and $p(t,x)=
u^{-2}	ilde p(t/
u,x)$. The initial support is unchanged and $\|	ilde u(t)\|_2=
u\|u(
u t)\|_2$. Thus global existence with bounded energy for the datum $
u u_0$ at viscosity $
u$ would give global existence with bounded energy for $u_0$ at viscosity one.
s1-viscosity.Breakdown.BreakdownOnTorus: Only time and the values of the velocity and pressure are rescaled. Consequently a solution for $\nu u_0$ on the unit torus at viscosity $\nu$ would give one for $u_0$ on the same torus at viscosity one. The dilation to a torus of large period used in Section 6 is a different change of variables.

s1-domains.Breakdown.BreakdownOnSpace: The datum is chosen before the negation of global existence: for each $\nu>0$ there is one smooth compactly supported solenoidal $u_0$ for which no global smooth pair $(u,p)$ has $\sup_{t\ge0}\|u(t)\|_2^2<\infty$. In particular the claim concerns all global solutions from that datum.
s1-domains.Breakdown.BreakdownOnTorus: For periodic velocity the energy over a period cell is automatically finite at each time. The formal target imposes no uniform energy bound on the half-line and allows nonperiodic pressure. The moving-frame reduction in the proof removes the linear-in-space part of the pressure without changing the initial datum.

s1-headline.Breakdown.breakdownOnSpace_of_profile: Theorem 1.1 begins with a reference solution that becomes singular but need not have finite energy. The new datum is compactly supported; the new solution is constructed close to the reference in the gradient norm, not by truncating the solution at every time. The linked implication concludes global bounded-energy nonexistence from the stronger formal profile premise.
s1-headline.Breakdown.Periodic.breakdownOnTorus_of_p: The periodic statement requires more than taking the quotient of the whole-space velocity, which generally has no spatial period. The construction in Section 6 yields a periodic flow; the linked implication excludes global smooth periodic velocity from its datum. The singular time and quantitative approximation in (1.7) are not part of this implication's conclusion.

s1-fefferman.Breakdown.BreakdownOnSpace: Fefferman's condition (4) requires rapid decay of the datum and all its derivatives. Compact support is a sufficient way of meeting this condition. The formal conclusion excludes solutions satisfying the uniform energy bound (7), for zero force; it is thus the negation of (A) for the constructed datum and implies (C).
s1-fefferman.Breakdown.BreakdownOnTorus: The formal target excludes solutions with periodic velocity even when the pressure on the covering space is not required to be periodic. It therefore covers the periodic-pressure class in Fefferman's erratum as well. Choosing zero force gives the breakdown alternative (D) once this nonexistence is proved.

s1-profile-reduction.Breakdown.breakdownOnSpace_of_profile: The reference and the constructed solution need not be close in kinetic energy. Initial approximation in the gradient norm, followed by the finite-dimensional correction, suffices: the return map on this space is a compact perturbation of a contraction. The linked implication uses the stronger formal profile decay and concludes global bounded-energy nonexistence.
s1-profile-reduction.Breakdown.Periodic.breakdownOnTorus_of_p: The recurrence is an assumption on a field on $\mathbb R^3$, not on a spatially periodic solution. Theorem 1.1 uses that field to construct different data on the torus, with the cutoff error removed by a correction. `breakdownOnTorus_of_profile` proves the resulting nonexistence implication from the smooth, decaying profile hypothesis.

s1-finite-codimension-summary.Breakdown.DichotomyHolds: The stability is relative to the size of the singular solution: the error is required to decay in similarity variables. Lemmas 4.4–4.5 give a number $\Theta<1$ such that only finitely many spectral directions of the return map obstruct decay at the rate $\Theta^n$. Their initial components can be chosen; no bound less than one for the full return map is assumed.
s1-finite-codimension-summary.Breakdown.StepDataStatement: The finite-dimensional conditions are on a spectral projection of the datum. We may realize any prescribed value of this projection by a compactly supported solenoidal field (proof of Proposition 4.3). This is what permits the correction of a cutoff datum even when the exceptional spectral vectors themselves have no known spatial decay.

s1-certificate-summary.Breakdown.certificate_orbit: A small residual measures how nearly the approximate field solves the equation, not how near it is to any solution. Section 7 supplies the missing inverse estimate, then controls the quadratic error and selects a member of the family for which the auxiliary force can be removed. The linked theorem assumes a certificate with a rectangular parameter set and constructs a weak recurrent profile; the inequalities for the concrete numerical data are a separate task.

s1-profile-domain.Breakdown.PeriodicSimilarityProfileExist: The return fixes a time interval $S$, not necessarily a least period. Iteration gives $W(s+nS,y)=R^nW(s,R^{-n}y)$. In particular the $L^p$ and gradient norms on balls about the origin is periodic in $s$, although the velocity at a fixed point need not be. Even when $R^2$ is a rotation, it need not be the identity.

s1-profile-smoothness.Breakdown.PeriodicSimilarityProfileExist: Only the velocity must be nonzero somewhere, and only the velocity is required to recur. The equations do imply $\nabla q(s+S,y)=R\nabla q(s,R^{-1}y)$; thus a pressure normalized by $q(s,0)=0$ would have the corresponding return law. No such choice of gauge is needed in `PeriodicSimilarityProfileExists`.

pdf-item-equation-1-2.Breakdown.SimilarityResidual: With $\delta=T-t$, the identities $ds/dt=\delta^{-1}$ and $\partial_t y=y/(2\delta)$ give $\partial_t u=\delta^{-3/2}(\partial_sW+W/2+(y\cdot\nabla)W/2)$. The diffusion, advection and pressure gradient have the same factor $\delta^{-3/2}$. Dividing it out gives `SimilarityResidual`, including the positive signs of the two drift terms.
pdf-item-equation-1-2.Breakdown.IsSimilarityProfile: `IsSimilarityProfile` is the local equation-and-decay part of the profile hypothesis; neither recurrence nor nonvanishing is included. One constant $C$ controls the velocity and its first two spatial derivatives, with one more inverse power of $1+|y|$ at each differentiation, as well as $\nabla q$. The last bound is additional to (1.3) and Remark 1.2.
pdf-item-equation-1-2.Breakdown.PeriodicSimilarityProfileExist: The nonvanishing and the return law are conditions on the same smooth solution of the first two equations. The last two clauses of `PeriodicSimilarityProfileExists` also require decay of the Hessian and of the pressure gradient. These are hypotheses of the formal localization theorem, not conclusions from the definition of a profile.
pdf-item-equation-1-2.Breakdown.pushForward: The action on velocities is $\rho_R W(y)=R W(R^{-1}y)$. Its derivative is $R(\nabla W)(R^{-1}y)R^{-1}$. Orthogonality preserves the matrix norm and the spatial volume element, so $\rho_R$ is an isometry of the gradient space. This is used in measuring each successive return.

pdf-item-equation-1-3.Breakdown.IsSimilarityProfile: At radius $r\ge1$, integrating (1.3) in spherical coordinates gives $\int_{|y|>r}|\nabla W|^2\lesssim\int_r^\infty\rho^{-2}d\rho=r^{-1}$, uniformly in phase. The corresponding sixth-power velocity tail is $O(r^{-3})$. These are the integrable tails of $X$; the square of the velocity bound has radial integral $\int_r^\infty d\rho$, so (1.3) gives no energy bound. The formal profile also has Hessian and pressure-gradient decay.
pdf-item-equation-1-3.Breakdown.PeriodicSimilarityProfileExist:
The additional formal bounds on $
abla^2W$ and $
abla q$ have the same exponent three as $(W\cdot
abla)W$. By (1.2) they imply $|\partial_sW+	frac12W+	frac12(y\cdot
abla)W|\lesssim(1+|y|)^{-3}$. The separate terms in this combination may decay only as $|y|^{-1}$. Their cancellation gives a square-integrable bound for the physical time derivative in the proof of Proposition 4.1.

pdf-item-equation-1-4.Breakdown.physicalField: For $T=1$ the phase in `physicalField W 0 t` is $-\log(1-t)$. With initial phase $s_0$ the same formula starts at $W(s_0)$ when $t=0$, a choice used to obtain the mild evolution from any slice of the profile. The classical change of variables is valid for $t<1$; the total Lean function need not describe a solution at or after one.
pdf-item-equation-1-4.Breakdown.MildFramework.selfSimilar: Write $D_\mu f(x)=\sqrt\mu f(\sqrt\mu x)$. Then `selfSimilar` reads (1.4) at $T=1$ as a curve in $X$: $D_{(1-t)^{-1}}w(s_0-\log(1-t))$. Inverting by $D_{1-t}$ recovers the slice $w$ at that phase; no choice of pointwise representative is needed for either operation.

s1-similarity-time.Breakdown.physicalTime: If $s=-\log(1-t)$, the physical times corresponding to $s$ and $s+S$ are $1-e^{-s}$ and $1-e^{-s-S}$. Their difference is $(1-t)(1-e^{-S})$. The fixed interval of similarity time therefore gives a sequence of shrinking physical intervals, which accumulate only at time one.
s1-similarity-time.Breakdown.physicalScale: The velocity scale and the reciprocal spatial length scale are both $a(t)=(1-t)^{-1/2}$. In `physicalScale` this is the factor applied to both $W$ and its spatial argument. The corresponding dilation parameter in (3.4) is $a(t)^2$, not $a(t)$.

s1-physical-pde.Breakdown.Periodic.selfSimilarSolves: Incompressibility is preserved because $\operatorname{div}_xu=\delta^{-1}\operatorname{div}_yW$. The momentum residual transforms by $\delta^{-3/2}$, with the pressure scaled by $\delta^{-1}$. The linked result uses a centre at the middle of the periodic cube, rather than zero; translation of the spatial argument leaves these local identities unchanged.
s1-physical-pde.Breakdown.physicalPressure: The pressure scaling is forced by the momentum equation. If $p=\delta^{-1}q(s,y)$, then $\nabla_xp=\delta^{-3/2}\nabla_yq$, just as $\Delta_xu$ scales by $\delta^{-3/2}$. A function of time may be added to $p$ without changing either equation. `physicalPressure` is the $T=1$ form.

pdf-item-equation-1-5.Breakdown.MildFramework.IsOrbit: With $\lambda=e^{-S}$, advancing the physical time to $t'=T-\lambda(T-t)$ adds $S$ to the similarity phase. It also changes the dilation by $D_{1/\lambda}$. The two effects commute, so the recurrence of `IsOrbit` gives $u^*(t')=\rho_R D_{1/\lambda}u^*(t)$ in $X$.
pdf-item-equation-1-5.Breakdown.physicalField: To see the inverse isometry in the argument, put $\delta=T-t$. At $t'=T-\lambda\delta$, (1.4) evaluates $W(s+S,x/\sqrt{\lambda\delta})$. Replace this by $RW(s,\lambda^{-1/2}R^{-1}x/\sqrt\delta)$ using (1.2), and take out the velocity factor $(\lambda\delta)^{-1/2}$. This gives the stated scaling law.

s1-eulerian-decay.Breakdown.IsSimilarityProfile: Each spatial derivative introduces another factor $\delta^{-1/2}$, for $\delta=T-t$. Thus $\delta^{-(j+1)/2}(1+|x|/\sqrt\delta)^{-(j+1)}=(\sqrt\delta+|x|)^{-(j+1)}$. The velocity and gradient estimates correspond to $j=0,1$; the extra formal Hessian estimate has the same transformation with $j=2$.
s1-eulerian-decay.Breakdown.physicalField: The physical bound is uniform on $|x|\ge r>0$, but nonvanishing and recurrence give an actual singularity at the origin: if $W(s_0,y_0)\ne0$, at $t_n=T(1-e^{-s_0-nS})$ the value at $x_n=\sqrt{T-t_n}R^ny_0$ has norm $(T-t_n)^{-1/2}|W(s_0,y_0)|$. The points tend to $(T,0)$.

s1-smooth-finite-interval.Breakdown.IsSmoothSolution: The half-open interval in the paper requires regularity at the initial time and every time strictly before $T$. No extension across $T$ is included. In contrast `IsSmoothSolution` is defined on the closed half-line $[0,\infty)$, the class excluded by the breakdown predicates.

s1-energy-definition.Breakdown.EnergyBoundedOn: `EnergyBoundedOn` uses a closed interval $[0,T]$ and a single upper bound for the squared $L^2$ norm. The paper uses the analogous bound on $[0,T)$. This places no bound on $\|\nabla u(t)\|_2$; in three dimensions the energy of a dilated finite-energy field scales as $\|D_\mu f\|_2^2=\mu^{-1/2}\|f\|_2^2$, whereas its squared gradient norm scales as $\mu^{1/2}$.
s1-energy-definition.Breakdown.BreakdownOnSpace: The negation in `BreakdownOnSpace` is over a pair of smooth fields and a single bound $C$ valid at every time. For a prescribed datum it is not enough to exclude solutions in a particular perturbative class; one must exclude all global smooth solutions of uniformly bounded energy. The uniqueness argument in Section 2.3 supplies that passage.

s1-periodic-definition.Breakdown.Periodic.IsPeriodic: `IsPeriodic` states the translation identity for each coordinate vector $e_i$. Iterating it (and using it at $x-e_i$) gives invariance under every translation in $\mathbb Z^3$. The velocity remains a function on $\mathbb R^3$, so its derivatives are the usual derivatives; the integral in its periodic Sobolev norm is taken over one cell.

s1-periodic-pressure.Breakdown.BreakdownOnTorus: Periodicity of $u$ implies periodicity of $\nabla p$ by the momentum equation. Thus $p(t,x+e_j)-p(t,x)=b_j(t)$ is independent of $x$. Choose $a''=-b$, $a(0)=a'(0)=0$. Then $u(t,x+a(t))-a'(t)$ solves the equation with pressure $p(t,x+a(t))+a''(t)\cdot x$, up to an additive function of time. The pressure increments are $b_j+a_j''=0$ and the initial velocity is unchanged.

s1-theorem-premise.Breakdown.breakdownOnSpace_of_profile: The input is an exact nonzero recurrent profile on $\mathbb R^3$. No approximate profile or compact support is assumed here. `breakdownOnSpace_of_profile` uses the stronger formal decay premise to deduce nonexistence of a global smooth bounded-energy flow from suitable compactly supported data; the numerical construction of a profile is a separate implication.
s1-theorem-premise.Breakdown.Periodic.breakdownOnTorus_of_p: The same whole-space premise is used for the periodic theorem. The cutoff of $u^*$ is not itself a solution of the equations on the torus; Section 6 removes its defect by transferring the whole-space right inverse and inverting a small error. The linked theorem concludes nonexistence of a global smooth periodic velocity from suitable data.

s1-theorem-space.Breakdown.breakdownOnSpace_of_profile: On the noncompact domain a smooth velocity need not have bounded global gradient norm merely by smoothness. The formal contradiction is local. Choose $B_r$ with $m=\|W(s_0)\|_{L^6(B_r)}>0$. At the recurrent phases the rescaled solution has norm at least $m-Ce^{-\kappa s}$ there. But continuity of a velocity through $(1,0)$ bounds $\sqrt{1-t}\,u(t,\sqrt{1-t}\,y)$ on $B_r$ by $O(\sqrt{1-t})$. Uniqueness identifies any global bounded-energy candidate with the constructed mild trajectory before time one.
s1-theorem-space.Breakdown.TransferHolds: The dense subspace in `TransferHolds` is chosen before the datum: take it to be the embedded smooth compactly supported solenoidal fields. The result finds a datum from this subspace within $\varepsilon$ of $W(0)$ in $X$ whose mild evolution satisfies the rescaled estimate. Density by itself gives the initial approximation but does not select a solution with that estimate; this is the role of the finite-dimensional correction.

pdf-item-equation-1-6.Breakdown.TransferHolds: Put $U(s)=D_{1-t}u(t)$ with $s=-\log(1-t)$. Since $D_{1-t}u^*(t)=W(s)$, the error is exactly $\|U(s)-W(s)\|_X=(1-t)^{1/4}\|u(t)-u^*(t)\|_X$. `TransferHolds` bounds the left-hand side by $Ce^{-\kappa s}$ for some $\kappa>0$. The physical error in (1.6) follows on dividing by $(1-t)^{1/4}$.
pdf-item-equation-1-6.Breakdown.orbitNorm: The lower estimate follows from $\big|(1-t)^{1/4}\|u(t)\|_X-\|W(s)\|_X\big|\le C(1-t)^\kappa$. The positive lower bound supplied by `orbitNorm` is uniform in $s$, so the error can be made smaller than half that bound. The compensated norm of $u$ approaches the periodic function $\|W(s)\|_X$; (1.6) does not require this function to be constant.
pdf-item-equation-1-6.Breakdown.orbitBound: Let $M_0=\max_{[0,S]}\|W(s)\|_X$. The norm is periodic even when $W$ returns with a nontrivial isometry, so $M_0$ bounds all phases. Consequently the reference gradient norm is at most $M_0(1-t)^{-1/4}$, to which the smaller gradient error in (1.6) can be added.

s1-theorem-periodic.Breakdown.Periodic.TorusBlowup: `TorusBlowup` gives smooth periodic data and a mild curve in $V$, the unit-period space with full $H^1$ norm (including the zero Fourier mode). A hypothetical global solution with periodic velocity can first be changed to one with periodic pressure and the same datum. Its curve in $V$ is continuous through $T$, hence bounded on $[0,T]$; mild uniqueness contradicts the unboundedness on $[0,T)$. The predicate does not itself retain the quantitative estimates of (1.7).

pdf-item-equation-1-7.Breakdown.Periodic.TorusBlowup: With $\delta=T-t$, the ball $B_{1/16}$ becomes $B_{1/(16\sqrt\delta)}$. Both the $L^6$ and gradient norms of the rescaled error acquire the factor $\delta^{1/4}$, so (1.7) bounds them there by $C\delta^\kappa$ (using Sobolev on the fixed physical ball for $L^6$). On each fixed similarity ball Hölder also bounds the $L^2$ error. Thus one obtains local $H^1$ convergence; the entire expanding-ball $L^2$ norm has a different scaling. The linked `TorusBlowup` asserts unboundedness in the full periodic $H^1$ norm, not these comparisons.

s1-unperturbed-rate.Breakdown.Freq.dilation_holds: A single dilation $D_\mu f(x)=\sqrt\mu f(\sqrt\mu x)$ multiplies the gradient by $\mu$ and changes the volume element by $\mu^{-3/2}$. The squared gradient norm thus acquires $\mu^{1/2}$, and its square root $\mu^{1/4}$. Taking $\mu=(T-t)^{-1}$ proves the power in the displayed identity; no information about the shape of $W$ enters this calculation.
s1-unperturbed-rate.Breakdown.orbitNorm: The norm of a recurrent slice is a continuous periodic function of $s$. If it vanished at some phase, the mild solution starting at that phase would have zero datum and would remain zero; recurrence would then make all earlier slices zero as well. Hence the minimum on a period is positive. `orbitNorm` obtains a stronger conclusion by excluding all slices below a positive small-data threshold for the mild theory.
s1-unperturbed-rate.Breakdown.orbitBound: Because the isometry preserves the norm, it is enough to take the maximum of the continuous map $s\mapsto\|\nabla W(s)\|_2$ on $[0,S]$. No supremum over increasingly singular physical slices is needed. The factor $(T-t)^{-1/4}$ accounts for all physical growth of the upper bound.

s1-rescaled-error.Breakdown.TransferHolds: The exponent $\kappa-1/4$ in physical variables can be negative. The relevant error is $(1-t)^{1/4}\|\nabla(u-u^*)\|_2\le C(1-t)^\kappa$, which tends to zero. The same weight divides out the growth of the reference, so the physical gradient error is small *relative* to its norm, even when it grows absolutely.

s1-nearby-data.Breakdown.ContractionStatement: Put $\chi=w_0-W(0)$ and let $J_0$ be the inverse of $P_{\mathrm u}|_E$. For the homogeneous linearized equation, the required decay is equivalent to $P_{\mathrm u}(\chi+\gamma)=0$, giving $\gamma=-J_0P_{\mathrm u}\chi$. The quadratic interaction adds a further, source-dependent term to the right side of this finite-dimensional equation; its contribution is found together with the trajectory by contraction.
s1-nearby-data.Breakdown.StepDataStatement: The space $E$ is fixed before $w_0$ is specified, and all its elements are smooth solenoidal fields supported in one fixed ball. Neither $w_0$ nor its correction is required to have the space-time symmetries of the reference profile. The proof uses the spectral decomposition on the whole divergence-free space $X$.
s1-nearby-data.Breakdown.TransferHolds: The quantifiers differ. `TransferHolds` is enough to find one datum in any prescribed dense linear subspace $C'\subset X$, arbitrarily close to $W(0)$. Proposition 2.1 also allows us to specify a particular $w_0$ in a fixed ball and to require that the tracking datum lie in the affine space $w_0+E$.

s1-remark-decay.Breakdown.IsSimilarityProfile: Let $\delta=T-t$ and $r=\tfrac12\max(|x|,\sqrt\delta)$. On the backward cylinder of radius $r$, either $|x'|\ge|x|/2$ or $T-t'\ge\delta$, according to which scale defines $r$. Hence $r|u^*|\lesssim C_W$ on that cylinder. Rescaling the interior derivative estimate back gives $|\nabla_x^j u^*(t,x)|\lesssim r^{-1-j}$ for $j=1,2$; converting to $y$ gives the two velocity derivative bounds. `IsSimilarityProfile` also assumes the pressure-gradient estimate, which is not supplied by this remark.

s1-minimal-profile-premise.Breakdown.PeriodicSimilarityProfileExist:
Remark 1.2 obtains $|
abla W|\lesssim(1+|y|)^{-2}$ and $|
abla^2W|\lesssim(1+|y|)^{-3}$ from the velocity bound and the local equations. The return law and nonvanishing remain assumptions. The formal profile predicate writes both derivative bounds explicitly and also assumes $|
abla q|\lesssim(1+|y|)^{-3}$; the latter is not part of the remark. The printed-to-formal bridges are separate open targets.

s1-certificate-assumes-profile.Breakdown.certificate_orbit: In Sections 4–6 the reference profile is already an exact solution, and the unknown correction changes the initial datum so that the new solution follows it toward blow-up. Here the problem is to construct that reference profile in the first place: the correction changes a periodic field and the parameter selects its period. The two corrections have different purposes; neither requires the reference velocity itself to have finite kinetic energy.

s1-certificate-family.Breakdown.certificate_orbit: There is one parameter for each forcing coefficient, and the period is a given function $S(\alpha)$ of these parameters. At fixed $\alpha$ the correction problem has unknowns $(v,\beta)$; the approximate velocity and its coefficients $\beta^{\mathrm a}(\alpha)$ are given. The remaining task is to find $\alpha$ with $\beta^{\mathrm a}(\alpha)+\beta=0$. The linked Lean theorem uses the earlier rectangular parameter set rather than the more general set (7.29).

s1-certificate-universal-estimates.Breakdown.certificate_orbit: In the inverse estimate (7.18) it is the given coefficient field that is represented by finitely many numbers. The unknown $v$ ranges over the whole class $\mathcal D_{S(\alpha)}^\Gamma$, with no truncation in space or frequency and no smallness condition. Appendix B must control the components not represented in the finite cell inequalities as well as the represented ones. Only when a small residual is inserted into this uniform estimate can one infer the smallness of a correction.

s1-certificate-numerical-inequalities.Breakdown.certificate_orbit: There are two kinds of numerical input. For a given field, such as $F_\alpha^{\mathrm a}$, one can enclose its norms and pairings directly. For the linear estimate one must instead establish a quadratic inequality for arbitrary perturbations. In Appendix B the finite matrix tests are accompanied by estimates for omitted polynomial coefficients, harmonics and the spatial exterior. Their purpose is to give the estimate on the whole domain, not just on the space used to compute the approximate solution.

s1-certificate-smooth-conclusion.Breakdown.certificate_orbit: The bound (7.38) concerns the selected member of the family: $v(\theta)=W(S(\alpha)\theta)-W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}(\theta)$. Thus it compares the velocities at corresponding phases and at the same period. At this parameter the change of force coefficients is $\beta=-\beta^{\mathrm a}(\alpha)$, which is why the squared norm of $\beta^{\mathrm a}(\alpha)$ appears beside the squared correction norm. The linked weak existence theorem does not retain these quantitative conclusions or prescribe the isometry to be $I$.

s1-symmetry-class.Breakdown.certificate_orbit: The perturbation is required to have the same space-time symmetries as the approximate field. Consequently the linearized and quadratic terms stay in that class, and the inverse estimate need only hold there. For instance, a rotation after half a period gives a half-period for the gradient energy, even when the velocity itself needs the full period; this improves (7.55).

s1-background-main-conclusion.Breakdown.breakdownOnSpace_of_profile: The distinction from the forced ancient-solution construction is the choice of datum. A small change in the gradient norm, followed by a finite-dimensional initial correction, suffices to track an exact unforced recurrent solution. No source is added to the evolution. The formal implication excludes global smooth bounded-energy solutions under its recurrent-profile premise.
s1-background-main-conclusion.Breakdown.Periodic.breakdownOnTorus_of_p: Periodizing an evolving cutoff produces a nonzero equation defect even though the original reference solves the unforced equation. Section 6 cancels that defect to obtain a genuinely unforced periodic solution; the linked theorem gives the resulting global nonexistence statement, not a forced singular solution.

s1-lyapunov-perron-method.Breakdown.StepDataStatement: The condition at infinite similarity time is a rate of decay, not an initial condition imposed on the evolution run backwards. Only the exterior projection is propagated backwards, where the period map is invertible. Its initial value must cancel the response to all the future inhomogeneous terms (4.14).
s1-lyapunov-perron-method.Breakdown.ContractionStatement: In the wave-map application described above, a change of blow-up time undoes the modification of the datum. Here the modification is kept: the reference field, its phase and singular time are fixed while the initial velocity is changed. The parameter in `ContractionStatement` is the coefficient of this change, not a parameter of the reference orbit.

s1-stable-convergence.Breakdown.TransferHolds: Apply $D_{1-t}$ to the difference in (1.6). Since $D_{1-t}u^*(t)=W(s)$ and $\|D_{1-t}f\|_X=(1-t)^{1/4}\|f\|_X$, this gives $\|D_{1-t}u(t)-W(s)\|_X\lesssim e^{-\kappa s}$. Convergence is to the same phase $s=-\log(1-t)$, not merely to the set of slices of the profile.

s1-unforced.Breakdown.IsSmoothSolution: The momentum equation in `IsSmoothSolution` has only viscosity and pressure on its right-hand side. There is no force that can be chosen to sustain the singularity. The auxiliary forces used in the certificate construction must therefore vanish at the selected parameters, and the periodic cutoff defect must be removed.

s1-outline-base-solution.Breakdown.Periodic.selfSimilarSolves: There is no residual when the uncut $u^*$ is substituted in the whole-space equation. Its momentum equation follows from the local rescaling calculation, not from recurrence. Recurrence enters when solving for the perturbation through successive shrinking intervals. The linked result proves the rescaled classical equations before the final time.
s1-outline-base-solution.Breakdown.TransferHolds: The free return map has norm at most $e^{-S/4}$, not one: the gain comes from undoing the spatial dilation. The interaction with the reference changes the return by a compact operator. Hence a spectral circle of radius $\Theta\in(e^{-S/4},1)$ off the spectrum leaves only a finite-dimensional exterior range, including multipliers of modulus below one which decay too slowly.

s1-outline-contraction.Breakdown.ContractionStatement: On $|v|,|w|\le r$ the difference $v^2-w^2=(v+w)(v-w)$ has size at most $2r|v-w|$, whereas the slope of $av$ is $a$ even at zero. That is the distinction the mild equation uses. Expanding the mild equation at the exact reference cancels its self-interaction and leaves the mixed term $2\mathcal B(u^*,v)$ and the quadratic term $\mathcal B(v,v)$. The first need not be small; it belongs to the equation to be inverted. It is the quadratic term, evaluated on a small error, that has a small Lipschitz constant.

s1-outline-space.Breakdown.Freq.X: The decay in (1.3) gives an integrable squared gradient, even if the velocity has infinite energy. In the Fourier realization the quantity stored is $g(\xi)=2\pi|\xi|\hat u(\xi)$, rather than $\hat u$ itself; $g\in L^2$, $g(-\xi)=\overline{g(\xi)}$ and $\xi\cdot g(\xi)=0$. Reconstruction of the physical velocity uses the Sobolev inequality of Subsection 3.1.
s1-outline-space.Breakdown.Freq.gradSixDecay: At infinity the radial integrals for $\|W(s)\|_6^6$ and $\|\nabla W(s)\|_2^2$ are bounded by constants times $\int_1^\infty r^{-4}\,dr$ and $\int_1^\infty r^{-2}\,dr$, respectively. The constants are independent of $s$ by (1.3). The same argument for $\|W(s)\|_2^2$ gives only $\int_1^\infty 1\,dr$. The linked Sobolev estimate is proved for the smooth solenoidal decay class containing these slices.

s1-outline-torus-space.Breakdown.Periodic.V: The mean-zero condition removes the constants, on which the gradient norm vanishes. On a cell of side $L$, Poincaré gives $\|u\|_2\le (L/2\pi)\|\nabla u\|_2$, but the Sobolev bound $\|u\|_6\lesssim\|\nabla u\|_2$ has a constant independent of $L$. The latter bound is needed for the contraction on large tori. In `V` the period is already one; the full $H^1$ norm is used and constants are allowed.

s1-outline-regularity.Breakdown.MildRegular: The local $H^1$ solution is also a mild solution in $\dot H^1_{\mathrm{div}}(\mathbb R^3)$, so uniqueness identifies it with the constructed solution while both exist. On each shorter closed interval the latter supplies a bounded gradient norm, and the energy inequality supplies the missing $L^2$ bound. `MildRegular` formulates the whole-space regularity property on such a closed interval; the periodic argument is separate.

s1-outline-similarity-equation.Breakdown.SimilarityResidual:
On substituting $U=W+V$ in (1.2), the terms containing only $W$ vanish. The linearized convection is $(W\cdot
abla)V+(V\cdot
abla)W$, and the only remaining quadratic term is $(V\cdot
abla)V$. The equations for $V$ have the free drift and diffusion of (1.2), but no prescribed return law. One seeks decay of $V$, not a second periodic orbit.
s1-outline-similarity-equation.Breakdown.physicalField: The physical and similarity descriptions use inverse dilations: $U(s)=D_{1-t}u(t)$ when $s=-\log(1-t)$. This is why the natural norm for the difference is the rescaled one, even when the physical gradient becomes large. `physicalField` is the forward transformation for the reference field.

s1-outline-target.Breakdown.MildFramework.IsOrbit: The target is $U(s)-W(s)\to0$ in $X$, so at successive returns $U(s+nS)$ approaches $\rho_R^nW(s)$. `IsOrbit` supplies the exact reference curve and its integral equation in similarity time. The constructed solution need not satisfy a return law of its own.
s1-outline-target.Breakdown.TransferHolds: The distinction is between finding one nearby datum and correcting any prescribed nearby datum. `TransferHolds` takes a dense linear subspace $C'$ and a tolerance, and finds one tracking datum in it. Proposition 2.1 fixes a finite-dimensional space $E$ first: each sufficiently close datum $w_0$ can be corrected within its affine space $w_0+E$. This stronger uniformity does not imply that uncorrected nearby data track the reference.

s1-outline-subcritical.Breakdown.dilateField: For $\mu>0$, $\nabla D_\mu f(x)=\mu\nabla f(\sqrt\mu x)$, whereas $dx=\mu^{-3/2}\,dy$ for $y=\sqrt\mu x$. Thus the squared gradient norm scales by $\mu^{1/2}$ and the norm by $\mu^{1/4}$. The definition of `dilateField` is the spatial part of the Navier–Stokes scaling.
s1-outline-subcritical.Breakdown.Freq.dilation_holds: With $\mu=e^{-S}$, the dilation has norm $e^{-S/4}$ on $\dot H^1_{\mathrm{div}}(\mathbb R^3)$. Composing it with the contractive heat flow and an orthogonal isometry therefore gives the bound $e^{-S/4}$ for the free return map in Subsection 4.3. The actual return map also contains the terms linearized about the profile.

s1-outline-free-flow.Breakdown.Freq.heat_holds: Heat alone gives a contraction of norm one in the gradient space: its Fourier multiplier approaches one at frequencies approaching zero. The strict bound for the free return is obtained from rescaling the heat-evolved field. This leaves a nontrivial interval of admissible spectral radii below one.
s1-outline-free-flow.Breakdown.Freq.dilation_holds: For $D_\mu f(x)=\sqrt\mu f(\sqrt\mu x)$ the gradient gains a factor $\mu$ and the volume element loses a factor $\mu^{3/2}$. Thus the squared gradient norm gains $\mu^{1/2}$ and the norm gains $\mu^{1/4}$. Setting $\mu=e^{-s}$ gives the factor $e^{-s/4}$ in the free similarity evolution.

s1-outline-monodromy.Breakdown.MonodromyStatement: The endpoint $h_\chi(t_1)$ is a physical velocity perturbation at the smaller spatial scale of the next period. Applying $D_\lambda$, with $\lambda=e^{-S}$, restores the original scale, and $\rho_R^{-1}$ restores the original orientation. Thus the output of the period map is in the same coordinates as its input; its powers describe successive normalized returns.

s1-outline-compactness.Breakdown.monodromy: It suffices to compare the returns at the last time of a period. Lemma 3.2 makes the mixed kernel compact at positive lag. If we omit the last $\varepsilon$ units of the integral, the omitted operator has norm $O(\varepsilon^{1/4})$, by (3.7) and the bounded local linear evolution. The compactness argument therefore needs no compact kernel at lag zero.

s1-outline-spectrum.Breakdown.MonodromyStatement: The free radius bounds the essential spectrum. Above any strictly larger radius there are only finitely many eigenvalues of finite algebraic multiplicity. In particular one can choose a circle below one that encloses all the essential spectrum and misses every eigenvalue; the full spectral radius need not be below one.
s1-outline-spectrum.Breakdown.DichotomyHolds: The formal theorem gives radii $e^{-S/4}<r_1<r_2<1$ with the same splitting for both. One can take $\Theta=(r_1+r_2)/2$. Forward evolution on the interior and inverse evolution on the exterior then have respective weighted ratios $r_1/\Theta$ and $\Theta/r_2$. These are the two numbers whose geometric series are used below.

s1-outline-no-spectrum-assumption.Breakdown.DichotomyHolds: An eigenvalue of modulus greater than one is neither assumed nor needed. If the exterior range is zero, the whole-space linear inverse can use $E=\{0\}$; otherwise $\dim E=\dim\operatorname{ran}P_{\mathrm u}$. The construction uses the existence of this finite-dimensional range without locating its spectrum.

s1-outline-finite-corrections.Breakdown.DichotomyHolds: For a scalar multiplier $a$ with $\Theta<|a|<1$, the sequence $a^nx_0$ decays but is not $O(\Theta^n)$ unless $x_0=0$. With forcing $f_n=F\Theta^n$, the admissible initial value is instead $-F/(a-\Theta)$, as substitution shows. The required cancellation is of a homogeneous coefficient, not of the forcing itself.
s1-outline-finite-corrections.Breakdown.StepDataStatement: One prescribes a component of the initial datum of the forced linearized equation. The eigenvalues of that equation are unchanged. A compact solenoidal lift of the prescribed component may introduce an additional interior homogeneous solution; the forward power estimate controls it at the same rate.

s1-outline-weighted-perturbations.Breakdown.StepDataStatement: A per-period factor $3/4$ gives decay, but it misses a target factor $1/2$. Relative to that target it grows like $(3/2)^n$. At $t_n=1-e^{-nS}$ the rescaled error norm is $e^{-nS/4}\|v(t_n)\|_X$. Condition (4.5) bounds it by $\Theta^n\|v\|_\kappa$, where $\Theta=e^{-\kappa S}$. In the subdivision into $k$ equal similarity-time steps, the corresponding weight is $\theta=\Theta^{1/k}$, so each complete period still costs a factor $\Theta$.

s1-outline-right-inverse.Breakdown.StepDataStatement: The right side of (4.8) is a continuous additive curve, with the same weight as $v$. Its value at zero can be nonzero. Consequently a prescribed change of datum $\chi$ can be included as the curve $e^{t\Delta}\chi$, along with any Duhamel term, while the unknown compact correction is still a separate heat datum.

s1-outline-dense-data.Breakdown.Freq.testDense_holds: The relevant density is in $\|\nabla\cdot\|_{L^2}$, so no $L^2$ approximation of the spectral vectors is required. Project compact solenoidal approximants of a vector in the exterior range. The projected test space is a dense linear subspace of a finite-dimensional space, hence equals that space.
s1-outline-dense-data.Breakdown.Freq.testSpan_holds: All finite combinations of the chosen basis lifts remain compactly supported and solenoidal; their supports are contained in the union of the finitely many original supports. `testSpan_holds` identifies the formal test subspace with fields of this class. In particular, the adjustment does not undo the compactness of the cutoff datum.
s1-outline-dense-data.Breakdown.SectionStatement: The construction in `exists_section` first projects onto $V=\operatorname{ran}P_{\mathrm u}$ and then lifts into the dense subspace. Its map on $X$ is thus $J_0P_{\mathrm u}$, where $P_{\mathrm u}J_0=I_V$. In particular $J_0P_{\mathrm u}$ is a projection onto $E$ along $\ker P_{\mathrm u}$, not the spectral projection onto $V$ itself.

s1-outline-contraction-nearby.Breakdown.ContractionStatement: The nonlinear interaction is quadratic in the error, which becomes small in similarity variables. If the normalized error on short interval $n$ is $\theta^nz_n$, division of its equation by $\theta^n$ leaves the mixed operator unchanged and gives the quadratic term $\theta^n N(z_n,z_n)$. A single bound for $z$ in the supremum norm therefore suffices for the contraction on all intervals.
s1-outline-contraction-nearby.Breakdown.TransferHolds: For the application to compact data, it is enough that the initial datum be in the dense subspace of compact solenoidal fields and close to $W(0)$. The paper proves the stronger assertion that one fixed $E$ works for all nearby prescribed data, including ones outside that subspace. The linked formal conclusion does not state this uniform affine-space prescription.

s1-outline-fixed-time.Breakdown.TransferHolds: For the recurrence $\chi_{n+1}=M\chi_n+f_n$, impose $\chi_n=O(\Theta^n)$ with $\Theta$ strictly inside the exterior spectral radii. Multiplying the projected recurrence by the backward powers and summing gives $P_u\chi_0=-\sum_{m\ge0}M_u^{-(m+1)}P_uf_m$. The initial correction changes the projection of the given discrepancy to this value. The source itself depends on the nonlinear error, so the correction is determined together with the trajectory; neither the singular time nor the phase is varied.

s1-outline-vector-potential.Breakdown.Periodic.homotopyPotential: At fixed $t$, integrate the field along the segment from $0$ to $x$. The identity $\operatorname{curl}_x[\sigma u^*(t,\sigma x)\times x]=\partial_\sigma[\sigma^2 u^*(t,\sigma x)]$ follows from zero divergence. Thus the curl of the integral is determined by its two endpoints, giving $u^*(t,x)$. The formula `homotopyPotential` also allows the centre of the segments to be translated.
s1-outline-vector-potential.Breakdown.Periodic.cutoffField: The constant flow $u=(1,0,0)$ has zero divergence. Multiplying it by a cutoff $\chi(x)$ gives divergence $\partial_1\chi$, supported where the cutoff changes. Take a vector potential $A$ with $\operatorname{curl}A=u$ and cut off $A$ first. `cutoffField` is $\operatorname{curl}(\chi A)=\chi u+\nabla\chi\times A$. Its divergence is zero, and it agrees with $u$ on the inner ball where $\chi=1$.
s1-outline-vector-potential.Breakdown.Periodic.cutoffDivergenceFree:
The cancellation in `cutoffDivergenceFree` is local: $\operatorname{div}(
abla\chi	imes A)=-
abla\chi\cdot\operatorname{curl}A=-
abla\chi\cdot u^*$. The divergence of $\chi u^*$ is the opposite term. No decay assumption is used for this identity.

s1-outline-cutoff-error.Breakdown.Periodic.approxFieldProperties: The cutoff has two useful properties: it leaves the field unchanged where the singularity forms, and it confines the interaction with a perturbation to the support ball (see (6.9)). In `approxFieldProperties_holds` the two radii are $1/16$ and $1/8$ about $a=(1/2,1/2,1/2)$; the support is strictly inside the unit cell. Neither property by itself estimates the change in the gradient norm.
s1-outline-cutoff-error.Breakdown.Periodic.cutoffGradientClose: The singular length is $\sqrt{T-t}$, whereas the physical cutoff radius stays fixed. Thus the transition annulus eventually lies outside every fixed ball in similarity variables. In `cutoffGradientClose` the squared gradient error is measured in those variables, with inner radius $1/(16\sqrt{T-t})$; taking $T$ small makes the error small at every subsequent time. The paper instead bounds the physical gradient error uniformly by $Cr^{-1/2}$.

s1-outline-datum-only.Breakdown.TransferHolds: With the exact reference, the defect $F^{\rm a}$ in Lemma 4.8 is identically zero. The cutoff changes the prescribed initial discrepancy $\chi=w_0-W(0)$, before the initial correction is chosen; it creates no time-dependent source in the evolution. Thus the resulting velocity satisfies the unforced equation.
s1-outline-datum-only.Breakdown.Periodic.cutoffField: Truncating the potential instead of the velocity preserves incompressibility: $\operatorname{curl}(\eta_r A)=\eta_r u^*+\nabla\eta_r\times A$. Lemma 5.1 gives $|A|\lesssim1$, $|\nabla A|\lesssim r^{-1}$ on the transition annulus, hence a gradient error $O(r^{-2})$ there. The annulus has volume $O(r^3)$, and the squared exterior gradient tail is $O(r^{-1})$. Thus the gradient error is $O(r^{-1/2})$; there is no corresponding claim of small kinetic-energy error.

s1-outline-torus-scaling.Breakdown.Periodic.selfSimilarSolves: There are two changes of variables here. The periodic dilation $u\mapsto Lu(L^2t,Lx)$ sends the cell of side $L$ and singular time one to the unit cell and singular time $L^{-2}$. `selfSimilarSolves` verifies the substitution (1.4) in the differential equation, in which all four terms of the momentum equation acquire the factor $(T-t)^{-3/2}$. It does not assert periodicity of that reference field.
s1-outline-torus-scaling.Breakdown.Periodic.TorusBlowup: The dilation identifies a large-period problem of duration one with a unit-period problem of duration $T=L^{-2}$. In the latter the initial similarity length is $\sqrt T$ and the support radius is $1/8$; their ratio is $L/8$, just as in the former. The linked `TorusBlowup` specifies an unbounded mild trajectory on the unit torus, without fixing its duration or its rate.

s1-outline-torus-approximation.Breakdown.Periodic.approxFieldProperties: Periodization preserves the gradient norm of a field supported in one cell. It also preserves zero mean for a compact solenoidal $f$, since $f_j=\sum_m\partial_m(x_j f_m)$ and the integral of the derivative vanishes. Thus both the cutoff and every compact field in the correction space can be inserted into the paper’s mean-zero space. `approxFieldProperties_holds` supplies the support and solenoidality of the cutoff at unit period.

s1-outline-kernel-decay.Breakdown.FarField.lerayKernelBound_hold: For $x\in Q_L$ and $x\prime\in B_{L/8}$, the distance to the translated source at $x\prime+Lj$ is at least $3L|j|_\infty/8$ for $j\ne0$. Consequently the sum of the noncentral heat responses is bounded by $CL^{-4}\|F\|_1$ and its gradient by $CL^{-5}\|F\|_1$, using (3.9) for derivatives of orders one and two. Taking the $L^6$ and gradient $L^2$ norms over the cell gives $CL^{-7/2}\|F\|_1$ in each case. The linked `lerayKernelBound_holds` supplies the first-derivative bound; the second is also needed for (6.2).

s1-outline-flow-comparison.Breakdown.Periodic.FreeHeatComparison: For a compact solenoidal datum $f$, writing $f=\operatorname{div}(x\otimes f)$ allows the use of the same decaying kernel as for the nonlinear term. The factor $\|x\otimes f\|_1\le (L/8)\|f\|_1$ changes $L^{-7/2}$ into $L^{-5/2}$ in (6.3). For $f=\bar u(0)$ the mass bound gives $\|f\|_1\lesssim L^2$, so the final error is $O(L^{-1/2})$. For the formal `FreeHeatComparison` the datum is a fixed test field; the comparison is local and includes lag zero, with no claimed power of $L$.
s1-outline-flow-comparison.Breakdown.Periodic.HeatDivFreeComparison: For the nonlinear term the tensor is $\bar u\otimes\bar u$, of $L^1$ norm $\|\bar u\|_2^2\lesssim L$. Hence (6.2) gives $O(L^{-5/2})$ before time integration. In Lean the source is a compactly supported $L^2$ vector field and the comparison is in the local velocity-and-gradient norm, bounded by $\delta\|A\|_{3/2}$ for normalized lags in $[\varepsilon,\varepsilon^{-1}]$. Uniformity over the supported sources is needed for an operator comparison; lags below $\varepsilon$ can be estimated by the separate integrable smoothing bound.

s1-outline-neumann.Breakdown.Periodic.rightInversePerturb: If applying the operator to a trial correction gives $3g/4$, the remainder is $g/4$. Applying the same procedure to the remainder leaves $g/16$. Let $D=I-\mathcal L\mathcal R^{\mathrm a}$. Solving for $g$ by $\mathcal R^{\mathrm a}$ leaves $Dg$ to be solved, and solving for that remainder leaves $D^2g$. Thus $\mathcal R^{\mathrm a}\sum_{j\ge0}D^j$ is a right inverse, with norm at most $2\|\mathcal R^{\mathrm a}\|$ when $\|D\|\le1/2$. In `rightInversePerturb` one starts with $AR=I$ and takes $D=-(A\prime-A)R$. Only the composition on the source space must be invertible; the linearized map itself need not be injective.

s1-outline-torus-final.Breakdown.Periodic.SeqPerturbation: The paper chooses $\kappa$ by the whole-space spectral argument. In the sequence construction let $\lambda=e^{-S/k}$ for $k$ subdivisions of a return, $\mu_n=T\lambda^n$ and $t_n=T-\mu_n$. The selected weight $\lambda^{1/4}<\theta<1$ can be written $\theta=\lambda^\kappa$ with $0<\kappa<1/4$. The normalized velocity is $U_n(s)=\mu_n^{1/4}u(t_n+\mu_ns)$, on $0\le s\le1-\lambda$. Writing $U_n=\bar U_n+\theta^n z_n$ with bounded $z_n$, endpoint matching forces $z_{n+1}(0)=(\lambda^{1/4}/\theta)z_n(1-\lambda)$. This ratio is less than one. The physical error is bounded by $C\mu_n^{-1/4}\theta^n=CT^{-\kappa}\mu_n^{\kappa-1/4}$, which has the rate of (4.5) since $\lambda\mu_n\le T-t\le\mu_n$.
s1-outline-torus-final.Breakdown.Periodic.TorusBlowup: For the final dilation $u_{\rm per}(t,x)=Lu(L^2t,Lx)$, the gradient gains $L^2$ and the square root of the cell volume contributes $L^{-3/2}$. Hence the gradient norm gains $L^{1/2}$, and $L^{1/2}(1-L^2t)^{-1/4}=(T-t)^{-1/4}$ for $T=L^{-2}$. The region of exact agreement of the approximate field with the reference field shrinks from $B_{L/16}$ to $B_{1/16}$. `TorusBlowup` retains the unboundedness conclusion, not the quantitative rate or the local comparison.

s1-outline-unforced-correction.Breakdown.Periodic.SeqPerturbation: The two errors are removed in order. Once the right inverse of $\mathcal L$ has been made exact, the equation for $u=u^{\mathrm a}+z$ is $\mathcal L(\gamma,z)=-F^{\mathrm a}+\mathcal B_{\mathbb T}(z,z)$. The term $-F^{\mathrm a}$ cancels the original mild residual; the mixed terms are already in $\mathcal L$. In `SeqPerturbation` the corresponding source on interval $n$ is $-\theta^{-n}\mathrm{res}_n+\theta^n\mathcal B_n(z_n,z_n)$, with an additional initial discrepancy $\xi$ on the first interval. The contraction makes the corrected mild equation exact. There is no external force in it, even though the cutoff field used in the construction has a differential residual.
s1-outline-unforced-correction.Breakdown.Periodic.breakdownOnTorus_of_p: `breakdownOnTorus_of_profile` is the implication from a recurrent nonzero similarity profile to periodic breakdown. Its profile hypotheses include bounds on $\nabla^2 W$ and $\nabla q$ in addition to (1.3). The proof first constructs an unbounded mild trajectory, then uses uniqueness to exclude a global smooth solution with the same periodic datum. The moving-frame reduction allows one to start with a hypothetical global solution whose velocity is periodic without assuming periodic pressure; the breakdown conclusion holds for every positive viscosity. Neither construction here supplies the profile itself; that is the separate certificate problem of Section 7.

s1-outline-certificate-time.Breakdown.certificate_orbit: For $\mathcal W(\theta,y)=W(S\theta,y)$ one has $\partial_s W(S\theta)=S^{-1}\partial_\theta\mathcal W(\theta)$. Thus $S$ appears in the coefficient of the time derivative, and the trial fields all have period one. In particular their residuals and constraints can be compared in a single period space when the parameter changes.

s1-outline-certificate-force.Breakdown.certificate_orbit: Every $w(s)=\cos(s+\phi)$ solves $w''+w=0$. Varying the phase gives a nonzero derivative that still solves the homogeneous equation. For a nonstationary time-periodic solution, translating its phase produces another solution: $\partial_s W$ is then a homogeneous solution of the linearized equation. A phase constraint and a corresponding force direction address this obstruction. Appendix C.4 explains why more such pairs can be useful: one chooses right-hand sides for which the discretized linearized equation has a large response, and constrains the correction in the corresponding response directions. The finite-dimensional computation chooses the fields; (7.18)–(7.21) and Proposition 7.8 establish invertibility on the full domain.

s1-outline-certificate-fixed-point.Breakdown.certificate_orbit: At a trial $(\alpha,g)$ solve the linear equation with $-F_\alpha^{\mathrm a}-g$ as right-hand side; replace $g$ by the resulting $(v\cdot\nabla)v$, and replace $\alpha$ by the projection onto $K$ of (7.30). The projection is needed at this stage because the adjoint estimates apply to the actual quadratic term, not to an independent trial $g$. The ball of trial fields is weakly compact in $\mathcal H$. At the joint fixed point $g=(v\cdot\nabla)v$, so the adjoint estimates make the projection redundant and force cancellation follows. Lean instead solves the constrained nonlinear equation before updating the parameter.

s1-outline-certificate-smoothing.Breakdown.certificate_orbit: Periodicity and the $\dot H^1$ bound give an Eulerian $L^6$ estimate of order $(1-t)^{-1/4}$. Proposition 7.11 uses the mild equation to improve this to $L^{12}$ and then to $L^\infty$, obtaining smoothness at each $t<1$. The separate theorem of Chae and Wolf uses exact backward discrete self-similarity to obtain spatial decay, which is not implied by boundedness alone. The linked certificate theorem stops at the weak recurrent field.

s1-conventions-final-time.Breakdown.physicalField: The normalization does not change the profile equation: $u_T^*(t,x)=T^{-1/2}u_1^*(t/T,x/\sqrt T)$, with the same phase $\log(T/(T-t))$. `physicalField` fixes the final time one and allows an initial phase. A spatial period constraint requires the separate torus dilation.
s1-conventions-final-time.Breakdown.Periodic.TorusBlowup: The parabolic dilation $u_{\rm per}(t,x)=Lu(L^2t,Lx)$ changes period $L$ to one and time one to $T=L^{-2}$. Its gradient norm on the cell gains the factor $L^{1/2}$, while its velocity $L^2$ norm gains $L^{-1/2}$. In particular $L^{1/2}(1-L^2t)^{-1/4}=(T-t)^{-1/4}$. `TorusBlowup` asserts an unbounded mild curve in the unit-period $H^1$ space without fixing this rate or time.

s1-conventions-gradient.Breakdown.matSq: Here $|\nabla f|$ is the Frobenius norm of $Df$, not its operator norm. For the latter, $\|Df\|_{\rm op}^2\le |\nabla f|^2\le 3\|Df\|_{\rm op}^2$. Thus a decay bound on the operator norm also gives the squared-gradient integrability required below, with a fixed dimensional factor.

s1-conventions-fourier.Breakdown.Freq.freqTrL2: With this convention $\partial_j$ has symbol $2\pi i\xi_j$ and $-\Delta$ has symbol $4\pi^2|\xi|^2$. `freqTrL2` is the unitary extension of the transform to $L^2$ classes; in particular the transform is available for $\partial_j u\in L^2$ even when $u\notin L^2$.

s1-conventions-fourier-series.Breakdown.Periodic.freqTrCoef: The Fourier coefficient of $\partial_j f$ is $2\pi i k_j\hat f(k)$; the gradient norm therefore involves $4\pi^2|k|^2$. In `freqTrCoef` the period is one. At period $L$ the allowed frequencies are $n/L$, $n\in\mathbb Z^3$, and the coefficient is the integral divided by $L^3$.

s1-conventions-projection.Breakdown.Periodic.divFree: For $k\ne0$ the condition for a solenoidal Fourier coefficient $c$ is $k\cdot c=0$. `divFree` subtracts $(k\cdot c)k/|k|^2$ and leaves $c$ unchanged at $k=0$. In particular the projection does not enforce mean zero; the mean of a divergence vanishes separately, as used for periodization and the nonlinear term in Section 6.

s1-formal-space-result.Breakdown.breakdownOnSpace_of_profile: The formal theorem excludes every global smooth solution in the bounded-energy class for the constructed datum. It does not give the finite-time solution together with its rate and profile error as in (1.6). This is still sufficient for Fefferman's whole-space nonexistence alternative, provided the profile hypothesis is supplied.
s1-formal-space-result.Breakdown.Periodic.breakdownOnTorus_of_p: The periodic formal implication similarly excludes all global smooth periodic velocities from some datum, even allowing a nonperiodic pressure. It does not identify a smooth trajectory with a prescribed recurrent profile. Neither this implication nor its whole-space counterpart supplies a concrete certificate instance.

s1-formal-weak-result.Breakdown.certificate_orbit: The weak result gives an exact recurrence and the momentum equation tested against compactly supported solenoidal fields. Passing to the smooth profile of (1.2)–(1.3) requires a separate regularity and decay argument. The link uses the earlier rectangular certificate, and neither its premise nor that of the extended theorem is an instantiated numerical certificate.
s1-formal-weak-result.Breakdown.WeakPeriodicSimilarityProfileE: The formal conclusion supplies a nonzero recurrent velocity with uniform spatial $L^6$ and gradient $L^2$ bounds at every phase, a square-integrable weak Hessian over a period, and the momentum identity against solenoidal tests. It does not exhibit a smooth pressure or a continuous map into $X$. To use this field as the input of Theorem 1.1, one must still establish the hypotheses and conclusion of Proposition 7.11, including the spatial decay and, for the linked formal localization theorem, the stronger derivative bounds.

s2-test-fields.Breakdown.IsTestField: The fields in $C_{c,\mathrm{div}}^\infty$ are solenoidal pointwise, not merely after projection. Finite linear combinations stay in this class, so a correction chosen in a finite-dimensional span of these fields changes neither compact support nor smoothness of the datum. Density of the class in $X$ is a separate result in Subsection 3.1.

s2-space.Breakdown.Freq.X: The Fourier coordinate used for $X$ is $g=2\pi|\xi|\hat u$. The conditions $g(-\xi)=\overline{g(\xi)}$ and $\xi\cdot g(\xi)=0$ enforce a real, divergence-free velocity, and the $L^2$ norm of $g$ measures the gradient. The identification with physical $L^6$ fields uses the reconstruction and density results, not the definition of the subspace alone.
s2-space.Breakdown.Freq.velocity: To recover the velocity from $g$, take compact smooth solenoidal approximants in the weighted Fourier norm. The Sobolev inequality makes their physical velocities Cauchy in $L^6$, so the limit defines a bounded real linear map $V:X\to L^6$. This is the map selected by `velocity`; its existence is proved in `velocity_holds`.

s2-energy-norm.Breakdown.Freq.embedNormLinear_holds: The squared norm of an embedded field is $\int_{\mathbb R^3}\sum_j|\partial_j u|^2\,dx$. In particular the norm equality applies to the profile slices and to the compact smooth corrections, all of which satisfy the decay hypotheses in `EmbedNorm`. No term $\|u\|_2^2$ is included, and this linked identity does not by itself cover the entire physical homogeneous space.

pdf-item-equation-2-1.Breakdown.FarField.heatConv: For $t>0$ the heat kernel $G_t(x)=(4\pi t)^{-3/2}e^{-|x|^2/(4t)}$ has mass one. It acts on each velocity component by convolution on $\mathbb R^3$, without any pressure projection. The linked definition is the positive-time integral; at $t=0$ one must instead use the identity operator as in the next sentence.
pdf-item-equation-2-1.Breakdown.FarField.HeatVelocity: The heat flow is represented on $X$ by multiplication of $g$ by $e^{-4\pi^2t|\xi|^2}$. `HeatVelocity` asks that reconstructing the velocity after this multiplication give the same $L^6$ field as convolving the reconstructed velocity with $G_t$, almost everywhere. It is the identification property for $X$, not a convolution theorem for every $L^p$.
pdf-item-equation-2-1.Breakdown.FarField.heatVelocity_of_heatC: The identity can be checked on $C_{c,\mathrm{div}}^\infty$ and then extended to $X$. For fixed $t>0$, Hölder bounds the pointwise difference of the convolutions by $\|G_t\|_{6/5}\|u_n-u\|_6$, while boundedness of heat flow and reconstruction gives convergence in $L^6$ on the Fourier side. The linked density argument assumes the Gaussian bounds and the test-field identity.

s2-heat-at-zero.Breakdown.Freq.heat_holds: At zero lag the heat multiplier is one. For a fixed state $g\in X$, dominated convergence gives $\|G(t)g-g\|_2\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$, even though there is no $L^1$ heat kernel at time zero. This is strong continuity on $X$, as needed for the initial value in (2.4).

pdf-item-equation-2-2.Breakdown.Freq.heatDivFree: In the weighted Fourier coordinate of $X$, the expression in (2.2) acquires the factor $2\pi|\xi|$. Thus `heatDivFree` takes a physical $L^2$ force, projects its weighted heat transform onto the solenoidal subspace, and returns an element of $X$. The paper's definition has the larger domain $L^1+L^2$; the $L^{3/2}$ estimate is a further step.

pdf-item-equation-2-3.Breakdown.Freq.bilinX: One can characterize the output without first constructing a projected force in physical space. Pair it in the gradient inner product against a solenoidal test state with physical velocity $w$; the pairing is $-\tfrac12\int[(u\cdot\nabla)v+(v\cdot\nabla)u]\cdot(-\Delta e^{\tau\Delta}w)$. `bilinX` selects the bounded bilinear operator with this pairing, whose existence for positive lag is established separately.
pdf-item-equation-2-3.Breakdown.Freq.bilinTestFormula_holds: When the first input is a compact smooth solenoidal field $\varphi$, both $\varphi\cdot\nabla v$ and $v\cdot\nabla\varphi$ belong to $L^2$: for the second use local $L^2$ control from $v\in L^6$. The linked identity then realizes (2.3) with the $L^2$ projected heat operator. It is this specialization that is useful in the compactness argument of Lemma 3.2, rather than an identification for every pair in $X$.

s2-holder.Breakdown.Freq.trilinear_holds: Hölder gives $1/6+1/2=2/3$. Splitting a force $f\in L^{3/2}$ into $|f|>1$ and $|f|\le1$ puts the first part in $L^1$ and the second in $L^2$. The linked formal estimate instead pairs the transport term against $w\in L^2\cap L^6$: $\|w\|_3\le\|w\|_2^{1/2}\|w\|_6^{1/2}$ supplies the third Hölder exponent, $1/3$.

s2-bilinear.Breakdown.Freq.bilinX: Symmetrization gives the continuous bilinear form whose diagonal is the quadratic Navier–Stokes term. In particular, for $u=v+h$, one has $K(u,u)-K(v,v)=2K(v,h)+K(h,h)$ at a fixed lag. These are the linear and quadratic perturbation terms used in Section 4; the bounded operator selected in `bilinX` is specified by the symmetric pairing.
s2-bilinear.Breakdown.Freq.bilinX_symm: Symmetry follows by interchanging the two transport terms in the pairing with each $\psi\in X$; equality of all such pairings gives equality in $X$. In particular $K(u,u)-K(v,v)=K(u+v,u-v)$, which turns the uniqueness argument for mild solutions into a linear equation for their difference (Lemma 3.5).

s2-bilinear-target.Breakdown.Freq.bilin_holds: The important point is not only that $K(\tau)(u,v)\in X$ for positive lag, but that the bound in (3.7) is integrable in $\tau$ near zero. In the formal construction a bounded scalar functional of the third, solenoidal argument is represented by an element of the Hilbert space $X$. The linked theorem gives the resulting bilinear bound, not the full linear assertion of Lemma 3.1.

s2-diagonal.Breakdown.Freq.bilinForm: Putting $v=u$ gives two copies of the same advection term, which cancel the factor $1/2$ in (2.3); the minus sign remains. In the formal dual expression this gives $-\int (u\cdot\nabla)u\cdot(-\Delta e^{\tau\Delta}w)$, the pairing against a state with velocity $w$. The definition of the form does not itself establish its boundedness.

pdf-item-equation-2-4.Breakdown.MildFramework.IsMildOn: The first term evolves the datum at $a$ by the heat flow. The integral evolves each contribution of the projected nonlinearity from its time $t'$ to the observation time $t$, so the lag is $t-t'$ and the sign of advection is already in $K$. `IsMildOn` requires continuity and Bochner integrability in $X$ and the equality at every $a\le t<b$; no pointwise pressure is needed at this stage.

s2-duhamel-convergence.Breakdown.VarConstIntegralStatement: Fix $t<b$ and let $M=\max_{[a,t]}\|u(t')\|_X$. By (3.7) the norm of the integrand is bounded by $C_K M^2(t-t')^{-3/4}$, with integral $4C_KM^2(t-a)^{1/4}$. The value assigned to $K(0)$ at the single endpoint does not affect the integral. The abstract statement in Lean also gives continuity of the integral, and states the quantitative bound for intervals of length at most one.

s2-closed-mild.Breakdown.MildFramework.IsMildOnIcc: On a closed interval the continuity and integral equation are required also at $b$. Every restriction of a mild solution on $[a,b)$ to $[a,b']$, $b'<b$, satisfies this closed-interval definition, but the original solution need not have an $X$ limit at $b$. This distinction is needed when the limiting time is the blow-up time.

s2-mild-convention.Breakdown.MildFramework.IsMildOn: A mild solution here is a continuous curve in $\dot H^1_{\mathrm{div}}(\mathbb R^3)$ satisfying (2.4), not a velocity already known to solve the differential equations pointwise. In particular no $L^2$ bound on the curve follows from its definition. The use of smooth compactly supported data in Lemma 2.3 is what permits a return to classical solutions.

s2-periodic-mild.Breakdown.Periodic.V: To represent a unit-period $H^1$ velocity, `V` uses the sequence $a(k)=\sqrt{1+4\pi^2|k|^2}\,\hat u(k)$ in $\ell^2$. The conditions $a(-k)=\overline{a(k)}$ and $k\cdot a(k)=0$ express reality and solenoidality. In particular at $k=0$ the first condition makes $a(0)$ real and the second is vacuous. The paper instead uses the mean-zero space with the homogeneous gradient norm.
s2-periodic-mild.Breakdown.Periodic.IsMildOn: In `IsMildOn`, the value at each $t\in[a,b)$ is the heat evolution of the datum at $a$ plus the integral of the bilinear kernel from $a$ to $t$. The integrability requirement is for each such $t$, and the trajectory is continuous in `V`. There is no condition of boundedness or continuity at $b$ itself. The paper uses the corresponding mean-zero homogeneous space.

s2-whole-space-proposition.Breakdown.TransferHolds: The input to Proposition 2.1 is the exact reference $u_1^*$ from the profile; its own datum is not required to have finite kinetic energy. The construction works entirely in $X$ and will eventually be applied to a compact solenoidal approximation of $W(0)$. The certificate construction is a separate existence question.

s2-finite-dimensional-data.Breakdown.StepDataStatement: The order of choice matters: fix the reference, the spectral circle and $E$; construct $\mathcal R$ with bound $C_{\mathcal R}$; then choose the neighborhood of $W(0)$. In Section 5.2 the two inequalities on its radius are $C_{\mathcal R}^2\varepsilon_0\le\varepsilon_1$ for contraction and $4C_{\mathcal R}\varepsilon_0\le c_*$ for the lower bound on the corrected solution.

s2-every-nearby-datum.Breakdown.TransferHolds: Here $w_0$ is arbitrary in a ball of $X$, not necessarily in $L^2$. Only the eventual choice of a compact cutoff requires finite energy. The formal transfer assertion quantifies over dense linear classes and finds one datum in the class, rather than selecting a correction for each specified $w_0$.
s2-every-nearby-datum.Breakdown.ContractionStatement: The heat curve of the prescribed displacement has norm $\|e^{t\Delta}\chi\|_\kappa=\|\chi\|_X$: (4.20) gives one inequality, and $t=0$ gives the other. Smallness of the datum is therefore precisely smallness of this particular source in the space on which the inverse acts.

pdf-item-equation-2-5.Breakdown.TransferHolds: The relative error in (2.5) is at most $(C/c_*)(1-t)^\kappa$, by the lower bound (4.4) for the reference. Thus the physical gradient of the error can become unbounded while its ratio to the reference gradient tends to zero. Both the tracking and the blow-up rate are expressed in the global $\dot H^1$ norm.
pdf-item-equation-2-5.Breakdown.orbitNorm: A zero slice of $W$ would, by uniqueness of the mild physical solution started at that phase, give zero at every later phase; recurrence then gives zero everywhere. Lean proves a stronger useful bound via small data: if $\|W(s)\|_X$ is below the small-data threshold, recurrence and bounded physical evolution give $\|W(s)\|_X\le 2e^{-nS/4}\|W(s)\|_X$ for every $n$. Taking $n$ large forces the slice to be zero.
pdf-item-equation-2-5.Breakdown.orbitBound: The orthogonal action on $W$ preserves $\|\nabla W\|_{L^2}$, even for an isometry with a reflection. Continuity on one closed period therefore gives an upper bound $M$ on all slices. Scaling gives the physical upper bound $M(1-t)^{-1/4}$; the tracking error is of smaller order.

s2-smooth-approximation.Breakdown.Freq.testDense_holds: Density is needed in the gradient norm, not the energy norm. In the formal proof one first approximates the weighted Fourier state away from zero frequency, constructs a Schwartz vector potential for the approximation, and takes the curl of a compact cutoff of that potential. The paper makes a particular cutoff of the profile in Subsection 5.1. The derivative of the cutoff contributes a term of the same order as the discarded gradient tail, so the error is $O(r^{-1/2})$ in $X$.
s2-smooth-approximation.Breakdown.Freq.testSpan_holds: A point of the dense test-field span is itself the image of one test field: combine the finitely many physical fields before embedding. This gives a genuine smooth, compactly supported, divergence-free datum at the required tolerance, once density has been used. It does not yet give the dynamically corrected datum $w_0+\gamma$.

s2-cutoff-choice.Breakdown.Periodic.cutoffGradientClose: The tolerance $\varepsilon_0$ is chosen from the right-inverse and contraction bounds before the cutoff radius. The choice $Cr^{-1/2}\le\varepsilon_0$ gives $w_0=\bar u(0)$ in the permitted ball; the correction $\gamma$ is then chosen in $E$ so that the trajectory has the required weighted decay. In the linked formal cutoff estimate, it is the initial similarity length that is made small while the physical radius is fixed.

s2-periodic-proposition.Breakdown.Periodic.TorusBlowup: The input of Proposition 2.2 is the whole-space profile; the conclusion is a different solution with periodic data. `TorusBlowup` specifies the existence of an unbounded mild trajectory on the unit torus from smooth periodic solenoidal data. Unlike (2.6), it does not prescribe a two-sided rate or a local comparison with $u_T^*$.

s2-periodic-existence.Breakdown.Periodic.TorusBlowup: In the paper the initial correction space $E$ is fixed by Proposition 4.3. Its finite dimension gives a common support radius $r_E$, and one chooses $L\ge8r_E$ before periodizing any of its elements. The formal assembly instead transplants a compact test approximant $\psi_0$ to $W(0)$ and a compact lift of the finite-dimensional correction, both at scale $\sqrt T$ in the unit cell. `TorusBlowup` records existence of their smooth solenoidal periodic sum, without fixing its formula.

pdf-item-equation-2-6.Breakdown.Periodic.TorusBlowup: The lower bound in (2.6) concerns the gradient over the whole cell. The approximation is stated only on $B_{1/16}$, where the reference is uncut. Changing variables $x=\sqrt{T-t}\,y$ in the latter estimate gives an error $O((T-t)^\kappa)$ in the similarity gradient norm on $B_{1/(16\sqrt{T-t})}$. These balls contain each fixed ball in similarity variables for all sufficiently late times. The conclusion of `TorusBlowup` asserts unboundedness in $H^1$, without these rates or spatial comparisons.
pdf-item-equation-2-6.Breakdown.Periodic.GlueUnbounded: The hypothesis of `GlueUnbounded` gives a positive lower bound for the normalized approximate velocity at every time of each interval. In fact the proof uses only its values at the left endpoints: $\|U_n(0)\|\ge c_0-\theta^n Z\ge c_0/2$ for large $n$. The physical norm at $t_n$ is at least $c_0(T\lambda^n)^{-1/4}/2$. Hence unboundedness follows along a sequence tending to $T$; the paper proves the stronger two-sided bound for all $t<T$.

s2-from-mild-to-smooth.Breakdown.mildRegular_realization: The purpose of Lemma 2.3 is to recover a smooth representative of the trajectory already constructed in $X$. In the formal proof the local symbol flow from the test datum is identified with that trajectory by mild uniqueness. Continuity of the latter on $[0,b]$ bounds its weighted Fourier norm, and hence bounds the homogeneous first-order norm of the symbol flow, allowing continuation through $b$. This is a whole-space result on closed intervals; the periodic assertion is separate.

s2-smooth-representative-definition.Breakdown.MildRegular: A value of the mild curve is an almost-everywhere class. Smoothness means that one jointly smooth velocity $U(t,x)$ and pressure $P(t,x)$ solve (1.1), with $U(0)$ the specified datum and $U(t)$ representing the mild value for each time. The formal property imposes these conditions on a closed interval and also asks for bounded energy and bounded velocity and spatial gradient there.

s2-smoothness-lemma.Breakdown.mildRegular_realization: Fix $b<T$. On $[0,b]$ the mild curve has bounded gradient norm by continuity. Local $H^1$ theory with the test datum gives a smooth evolution, and uniqueness in $X$ identifies it with the mild curve. Since its $L^2$ norm is bounded by the initial one, the full $H^1$ norm stays bounded and continuation gives smoothness through $b$. The linked formal theorem is the whole-space closed-interval version, with finite energy on that interval rather than the stated global energy inequality.
s2-smoothness-lemma.Breakdown.MildRegular: The formal regularity condition quantifies over every closed interval $[0,b]$ on which the curve is mild and starts at the embedded test field. It asks for smooth velocity and pressure, the equation at interior times, and equality of the reconstructed velocity with the smooth one almost everywhere at each time. Applying the property on all $b<T$ gives local smooth representatives; their velocities agree on overlaps, and the pressures agree up to functions of time. The linked declaration states this property; `mildRegular_realization` proves it.

s2-energy-nonincrease.Breakdown.EnergyBoundedOn: For the smooth local solution, pairing (1.1) with $u$ and integrating eliminates the transport and pressure terms by zero divergence and yields $\tfrac{d}{dt}\|u(t)\|_2^2=-2\|\nabla u(t)\|_2^2$. This yields the same bound for every $t<T$, even if the gradient diverges as $t\uparrow T$. `EnergyBoundedOn` only asks for some finite bound on a specified closed interval; it is not the dissipation identity.
s2-energy-nonincrease.Breakdown.mildRegular_realization: The initial energy bound in the paper is independent of the continuation interval. In the formal proof a different estimate is used for the stated energy conclusion: the continued symbol flow has a bounded inhomogeneous $H^3$ norm on the closed interval, which bounds the squared $L^2$ norm of its physical velocity by Plancherel. This proves finite energy there, not the sharper initial-energy bound displayed here.

s2-proof-choice.Breakdown.Freq.testDense_holds: The order of choices matters: Proposition 2.1 has already fixed $\varepsilon_0$, so one may now choose a cutoff radius large enough that $Cr^{-1/2}\le\varepsilon_0$. In Subsection 5.1 the cutoff is applied to a vector potential before taking its curl; cutting off the velocity itself would introduce divergence. The linked density theorem supplies existence of a test field at this tolerance but does not specify the radius or the correction selected by the period map.
s2-proof-choice.Breakdown.Freq.testSpan_holds: The finite span in `testSpan_holds` consists of embedded single test fields. This removes any distinction between approximating the profile by a linear combination of embedded fields and approximating it by one smooth compactly supported solenoidal field. The correction $\gamma$ is chosen after $w_0$, in the space $E$ fixed by Proposition 2.1.

s2-proof-correction.Breakdown.ContractionStatement: The cutoff gives a small displacement in $X$, but imposes no conditions on its exterior spectral projection. Inserting its heat evolution into the right inverse selects the correction needed for the linear problem. The same inverse is then evaluated on the heat curve plus the quadratic Duhamel term, so the corrected datum accounts for the nonlinear interaction as well.
s2-proof-correction.Breakdown.TransferHolds: Take $w_0=\bar u(0)$ with cutoff radius sufficiently large for (5.2). Both $w_0$ and each element of $E$ belong to $C^\infty_{c,\mathrm{div}}$, so $w_0+\gamma$ belongs to the same class. `TransferHolds` supplies the abstract mild tracking conclusion for data from the dense class; the subsequent regularity argument uses the concrete field.

s2-proof-initial-class.Breakdown.Freq.testSpan_holds: If $w_0$ is supported in $B_r$ and the finitely many generators of $E$ are supported in $B_{r_E}$, then $u_0$ is supported in $B_{\max(r,r_E)}$. Linearity preserves both smoothness and incompressibility. `testSpan_holds` checks the analogous closure under linear combinations in the Fourier realization; it does not construct the particular space $E$.

s2-proof-regularity.Breakdown.mildRegular_realization: For every $b<1$ the constructed mild curve has bounded gradient norm on $[0,b]$. The compactly supported datum $u_0$ also has finite energy, so Lemma 2.3 recovers a classical solution on these intervals. In the formal proof uniqueness identifies each local symbol flow with the prescribed curve before the continuation theorem is applied. The initial-energy inequality in the paper gives a single bound on the union $[0,1)$, rather than a possibly different bound on each closed interval.

s2-norm-identification.Breakdown.Freq.X: The norms in (2.5) are already the physical gradient norms once the representative is recovered. Hence the lower bound gives gradient divergence and the error divided by the reference gradient norm is $O((1-t)^\kappa)$. The definition of the Fourier space explains the norm being tracked; actual gradient norm identification uses `embedNormLinear_holds` and the realization of the smooth curve, not `X` alone.

s2-finite-codimension.Breakdown.ContractionStatement: For $x\in\ker P_{\mathrm u}$, take $w_0=W(0)+x$. The linear right inverse applied to $e^{t\Delta}x$ gives zero datum correction, since the homogeneous solution already has the required decay. Thus $\gamma=(\mathcal R\mathcal B(v,v))_1$ and $\|\gamma\|_X\lesssim\|x\|_X^2$ by (4.8), (4.19), (4.24). Over the interior space the selected data have the form $W(0)+x+O(\|x\|_X^2)$, giving the tangent space of the selected family at $W(0)$.
s2-finite-codimension.Breakdown.TransferHolds: Let $d=\dim E$. Prescribing a class near $[W(0)]$ in $X/E$ leaves exactly $d$ real coordinates to be chosen. The complement used by the proof is $\ker P_{\mathrm u}$; the correction is a graph over this complement. The statement does not classify all data that may blow up, or all data with slower convergence to this profile.

ns-s3-physical-completion.Breakdown.Freq.X: The ambient completion is obtained in the gradient norm; the $L^6$ condition selects the representative and excludes nonzero constants. The formal $X$ is instead the solenoidal weighted Fourier subspace. Its reconstruction and test-field density are the corresponding solenoidal results, not a theorem about the completion of arbitrary nonsolenoidal vector fields.

pdf-item-equation-3-1.Breakdown.Freq.gradSixDecay: The bound (3.1) allows a velocity to be estimated using just its gradient, which is what closes the transport estimate in Lemma 3.1. The linked theorem proves this bound for smooth divergence-free fields with velocity and first-derivative decay as in (1.3), with a constant independent of the decay constant. The paper uses the ambient Sobolev inequality without these pointwise hypotheses.
pdf-item-equation-3-1.Breakdown.Freq.velocity_holds: The Sobolev inequality on test fields makes the map $J\varphi\mapsto\varphi$ bounded from the gradient norm to $L^6$. By density it extends to the formal Hilbert space, yielding $\|Vg\|_6\le\|V\|\|g\|_2$. The linked existence theorem concerns this solenoidal reconstruction; (3.1) also applies to nonsolenoidal fields.

ns-s3-hilbert.Breakdown.Freq.isClosed_sig: In physical variables, convergence of gradients in $L^2$ and of velocities in $L^6$ preserves zero distributional divergence. In the Fourier construction, reality and zero longitudinal component are kernels of bounded real linear maps on $L^2$; their intersection is closed. This proves completeness of the frequency space with its real inner product, which is the one used in the Riesz representation of $K$.

ns-s3-test-density.Breakdown.Freq.testDense_holds: Density is used twice: to approximate the fixed argument of $K(\tau)(u,\cdot)$ by a compactly supported field in Lemma 3.2, and to choose test fields projecting onto the finite-dimensional exterior spectral subspace. The latter works since the image of a dense linear subspace under the spectral projection is dense, hence equal to the finite-dimensional range. The formal construction cuts off a Schwartz vector potential and takes its curl; it also gives graph-norm density for the negative Laplacian.
ns-s3-test-density.Breakdown.Freq.testSpan_holds: The dense set is described in Lean as a real linear span. Since a finite sum of compactly supported smooth solenoidal fields is again such a field, `testSpan_holds` identifies every point of the span with one physical test field. Thus the density result really does permit compact support, not merely a formal sum of frequency states.

pdf-item-equation-3-2.Breakdown.Freq.partial_holds: Writing $g=2\pi|\xi|\hat u$ gives $\widehat{\partial_j u}=i\xi_jg/|\xi|$. This multiplier is bounded, and the squared moduli of the three scalar multipliers sum to one off the origin.
