Lean uses the difference of the integrals of $z^{-n}(z-\mathcal M)^{-1}$ on a large circle and on $|z|=r_2$ in the gap. Both are bounded by a constant times $r_2^{-n}$, since the large radius exceeds $r_2$. Multiplication by $\Theta^n$ makes the series summable.

ns-s4-051.Breakdown.StepDataStatement: From $\Theta=\lambda^\kappa$ one has $\kappa=-\log\Theta/S$. The interval $\lambda^{1/4}<\Theta<1$ is exactly $0<\kappa<1/4$. If there are $k$ steps in one period, $\theta=\Theta^{1/k}$ is the decay weight per step and $\theta^k=\Theta$; one should not use the full-period weight on every short step.

ns-s4-052.Breakdown.PeriodicInverseStatement: The normalized reference on short interval $j$ is the physical solution started at phase $jS/k$. Recurrence changes this reference by $\rho_R$ after $k$ intervals, so the corresponding local endpoint maps are conjugate. Within one period their phases generally differ. At full-period boundaries one can undo the accumulated rotation, reducing all the homogeneous block updates to the same operator (4.10).

ns-s4-053.Breakdown.PeriodicInverseStatement: Apply the semigroup restart to the part of (4.12) which has a heat term and a Duhamel integral, namely $v-g$. The contribution of the earlier intervals is then the heat evolution of $(v-g)(t_n)$, and $g(t)$ is left unchanged. In particular the restarted datum is not $v(t_n)$ unless $g(t_n)=0$.

ns-s4-054.Breakdown.orbitSeq: The exponent $n$ in $D_{\lambda^n}$ removes the physical scale of the $n$th interval; the exponent $-n$ in $\rho_R^{-n}$ removes its orientation. After taking the difference of the two rescaled curves at zero one obtains $\chi_n$. The subsequent division by $\Theta^n$ is a decay normalization, distinct from both changes of coordinates.

ns-s4-055.Breakdown.orbitSeq: The forcing in the recurrence is obtained from the entire response $\mathcal U g_n$ after subtracting $g_n$ itself. For example, if $g_n$ is a heat curve then $(\mathcal U-I)g_n$ is the part of its evolution produced by the mixed term. This explains why (4.13) is not simply a rescaled value of $g$ at the next time.
ns-s4-055.Breakdown.PeriodicInverseStatement: Write $d_n=\operatorname{Ev}(I-A_n)^{-1}g_n$, $M_i=\operatorname{stepMap}(i)$ and $\Theta=\theta^k$. In the first block, iteration of $y_{i+1}=\theta^{-1}(M_i y_i+d_i)$ gives $y_k=\Theta^{-1}(M_{k-1}\cdots M_0y_0+\sum_{i<k}\theta^i M_{k-1}\cdots M_{i+1}d_i)$, with the empty product equal to $I$. The factors $\theta^i$ are needed because the local sources are already divided. Rotating back at block boundaries gives the constant monodromy in the divided recurrence.

ns-s4-056.Breakdown.StepDataStatement: The equality $1-t=\lambda^n(1-\sigma)$ gives the bound directly: $\|g_n(\sigma)\|_X\le\Theta^n(1-\sigma)^{\kappa-1/4}\|g\|_\kappa$. The largest phase factor is $\lambda^{\kappa-1/4}$, attained at the end of the period. The endpoint map of $(\mathcal U-I)g_n$ multiplies this by at most $\lambda^{1/4}(1+\|\mathcal U\|)$, independently of $n$.

ns-s4-057.Breakdown.orbitSeq: The key point of the second identity in (4.14) is that $f_n$ is independent of $\chi_0$. Thus the datum can be chosen using the entire sequence of $f_n$, computed from the prescribed $g$. For the nonlinear equation we first fix a trial quadratic source, apply this linear selection, then use the resulting trajectory to update the source.

ns-s4-058.Breakdown.MonodromyStatement: The local Volterra lemma gives a solution for any heat datum $\chi$ and source $g$ on every $[0,b]$, $b<1$. Uniqueness gives agreement on overlaps. Thus the remaining question is not existence on $[0,1)$ but whether the resulting curve has finite $\|\cdot\|_\kappa$. The spectral choice of the datum addresses exactly this question.

ns-s4-059.Breakdown.PeriodicInverseStatement: Splitting the integral at $t_n$ and using (3.12), the part before $t_n$ is the heat evolution of $2\mathcal B(u^*,v)(t_n)$. Adding the original heat term yields the heat evolution of $v(t_n)-g(t_n)$. The remaining integral begins at $t_n$; this is the exact restart identity even when $g$ has no time derivative.

ns-s4-060.Breakdown.Freq.DilationAlgebra: Writing $\mu=\lambda^n$, the identity $D_\mu e^{\mu\sigma\Delta}=e^{\sigma\Delta}D_\mu$ moves the normalized heat operator outside the change of coordinates. Together with commutation with the isometry, the incoming heat curve becomes $e^{\sigma\Delta}\chi_n$. There is no extra power of $\lambda$ in this term.

ns-s4-061.Breakdown.MildFramework.stepOp: Upon setting $t'=t_n+\lambda^n\sigma'$, the factor $dt'=\lambda^n d\sigma'$ cancels the inverse time-scaling factor of $K$. In formulas, for $\mu=\lambda^n$, $\mu D_\mu K(\mu\tau)(a,b)=K(\tau)(D_\mu a,D_\mu b)$. Isometry equivariance and (4.3) then return the mixed kernel to $K(\sigma-\sigma')(u^*(\sigma'),v_n(\sigma'))$.

ns-s4-062.Breakdown.stepMap: Linearity of $\mathcal U$ separates $v_n$ into the solution driven by the incoming heat datum and that driven by the local additive curve. The monodromy is obtained from the first part alone. The second part contributes the source response to the recurrence; it must not be included in the definition of the homogeneous step map.

ns-s4-063.Breakdown.orbitSeq: At the common physical endpoint of periods $n$ and $n+1$ the two normalized values differ by $\rho_R^{-1}D_\lambda$. Applying this map to $v_n(t_1)-g_n(t_1)$ gives $\chi_{n+1}$. With $v_n=h_{\chi_n}+\mathcal U g_n$, its homogeneous term is $\mathcal M\chi_n$ and its source is precisely the difference in (4.13).

ns-s4-064.Breakdown.Freq.DilationAlgebra: The largest possible source norm on period $n$ is estimated at the smaller remaining time $\lambda^{n+1}$, since $\kappa-1/4<0$. The dilation multiplies that bound by $\lambda^{n/4}$, leaving $\lambda^{\kappa-1/4}\Theta^n$. The extra factor is fixed once the period and exponent are fixed.
ns-s4-064.Breakdown.StepDataStatement: In terms of the fixed-period constants, $\|f_n\|_X\le\lambda^{1/4}(1+\|\mathcal U\|)\|g_n\|_\infty\lesssim\Theta^n\|g\|_\kappa$. Here the dilation costs a factor less than one and the inverse contributes the fixed bound for the first period. There is no accumulation of inverse norms in this estimate of a single forcing term.

ns-s4-065.Breakdown.SectionInternal.exists_preimag: Choose $c_j$ in the dense test subspace converging to an exterior vector $b$. Their projected images converge to $b$. The image of the test subspace is itself linear and finite-dimensional, hence closed, so $b$ is an exact image of a test field. The last inference is why finite rank is needed in addition to the density of compact solenoidal fields.

ns-s4-066.Breakdown.exists_section: The compact lifts are independent because their projections are a basis. Their span $E$ meets $\ker P_{\mathrm u}$ only at zero, and every $x\in X$ is the sum of the lift of $P_{\mathrm u}x$ and an element of $\ker P_{\mathrm u}$. The finite-dimensional inverse gives $\|\gamma\|_X\lesssim\|P_{\mathrm u}\gamma\|_X$ on $E$.

ns-s4-067.Breakdown.StepDataStatement: The quantities controlled by the inverse include the size of the initial correction and the entire trajectory. Both bounds may be large if the gap is narrow or the chosen compact lifts have large norms. Section 5 chooses the neighborhood only after these constants are fixed; Section 6 makes the cutoff error small relative to them by increasing the spatial period.

ns-s4-068.Breakdown.DiscreteDichotomyInternal.tail: Write the exterior recurrence from $0$ to $N$, then apply $\mathcal M_{\mathrm u}^{-N}$. It gives $P_{\mathrm u}\chi_0=\mathcal M_{\mathrm u}^{-N}P_{\mathrm u}\chi_N-\sum_{m<N}\mathcal M_{\mathrm u}^{-(m+1)}P_{\mathrm u}f_m$. The terminal term tends to zero for $\chi_N=O(\Theta^N)$. The exponent $m+1$ appears because $f_m$ first enters at time index $m+1$.
ns-s4-068.Breakdown.DiscreteDichotomyInternal.norm: If the forcing has norm at most $F\Theta^m$ at index $m$, and $\|\mathcal M_{\mathrm u}^{-j}P_{\mathrm u}\|\le A r_2^{-j}$, the first omitted term after $N$ indices has bound $AF r_2^{-1}(\Theta/r_2)^N$. The norm of the entire tail is at most $AF(\Theta/r_2)^N/(r_2-\Theta)$. At $N=0$ this gives the bound for the prescribed exterior datum, before lifting it into $E$.

ns-s4-069.Breakdown.DiscreteDichotomyInternal.step: Multiplication of the future sum at $n$ by $\mathcal M_{\mathrm u}$ gives a first term $-P_{\mathrm u}f_n$; adding the current forcing cancels it. All later summands have the exponents of the sum at $n+1$. This checks the recurrence itself, not only the bound on its solution.
ns-s4-069.Breakdown.DiscreteDichotomyInternal.rec_: The forward formula has a homogeneous term $\mathcal M^n(I-P_{\mathrm u})\gamma$ as well as the past sources. One must retain this term: the compact lift of the prescribed exterior datum need not itself lie in the exterior range. A source at index $m$ enters the state at $m+1$ and undergoes exactly $n-1-m$ further returns.

ns-s4-070.Breakdown.DiscreteDichotomyStatement: The estimate for past forcing is $KF\Theta^n/(\Theta-r_1)$, and that for future forcing is $AF\Theta^n/(r_2-\Theta)$, if $\|f_m\|\le F\Theta^m$ and the two projected power bounds have constants $K,A$. For the past sum the exponent of a power is $n-1-m$; for the future sum the inverse exponent is $m-n+1$. The remaining homogeneous term has norm at most $Kr_1^n\|\gamma\|$.

ns-s4-071.Breakdown.PeriodicInverseStatement: The decay of the endpoint $\chi_n$ must be converted to a bound on the whole normalized period. Use $v_n=\mathcal U(e^{\sigma\Delta}\chi_n+g_n)$ and heat contractivity to obtain $\|v_n\|_\infty\le\|\mathcal U\|(\|\chi_n\|+\|g_n\|_\infty)$. This step has one fixed constant for all periods, so it loses no decay rate.

ns-s4-072.Breakdown.MildFramework.gluePieces: Undoing the change of scale gives the exact norm relation $(1-t)^{1/4-\kappa}\|v(t)\|_X=(1-\sigma)^{1/4-\kappa}\Theta^{-n}\|v_n(\sigma)\|_X$. The phase factor is at most one and at least $\lambda^{1/4-\kappa}$ on a period. Thus bounded divided pieces give the claimed physical-time estimate, and conversely the physical-time estimate bounds all divided pieces.

ns-s4-073.Breakdown.StepDataStatement: For this fixed choice of $E$, the linear inverse (4.8) is in fact unique. The difference of two solutions has zero source and initial datum in $E$. Its exterior projection must vanish by the backward power bound, whence the datum is zero because $E\cap\ker P_{\mathrm u}=\{0\}$. Local uniqueness gives zero trajectory. The resulting linear map is bounded by the preceding estimates.
ns-s4-073.Breakdown.PeriodicInverseStatement: In the sequence inverse the first component is an exterior vector; applying the fixed lift makes it a physical datum correction. Its second component solves the local equations for arbitrary additive curves. Matching the full endpoints also requires the local sources to vanish at each noninitial left endpoint; the residual and quadratic Duhamel term have this property in the nonlinear application. Thus the gluing assertion concerns the corrected mild trajectory, not arbitrary inputs to the abstract inverse.

ns-s4-074.Breakdown.HeatBilinear: The estimates in this subsection use the heat semigroup and the symmetric kernel bound, not recurrence of the reference. The right inverse is now an assumption. Consequently the same contraction applies to the whole-space reference and to the localized periodic reference of Section 6.

ns-s4-075.Breakdown.Periodic.SeqPerturbation: The residual is the difference between the proposed curve and the mild formula with its own initial value. It is zero at the left endpoint whether or not the curve solves the equation. The sign in (4.17) is negative because the error must cancel this defect; in the piece version this also makes the residual contribution zero at each restart.

ns-s4-076.Breakdown.Periodic.SeqPerturbation: The defect in (4.16) is a mild-equation residual, so its norm is measured after the heat evolution and time integration, in the same space as the velocity error. This is the norm estimated in Lemma 6.2. In the formal sequence setting the analogous local defect is divided by $\theta^n$; its smallness is a bound uniform in $n$.

ns-s4-077.Breakdown.PiecePerturbationStatement: Expanding $\mathcal B(u^{\mathrm a}+v,u^{\mathrm a}+v)$ gives the reference term, two equal mixed terms and the quadratic error. Subtracting the heat input of the prescribed datum separates $F^{\mathrm a}$ and $\mathcal L(\gamma,v)$ from the remaining two terms. For an exact background this reduces to the compact-interval implication `PiecePerturbationStatement`.

ns-s4-078.Breakdown.Periodic.SeqPerturbation: On piece $n$ write the actual normalized error as $\theta^nz_n$. Its quadratic term after division is $\theta^n N_n(z_n,z_n)$, while the given residual is $-\theta^{-n}r_n$. The prescribed datum contributes a heat curve on piece zero only. Later heat curves are those of the propagated corrected endpoints, so the initial perturbation is not counted again.

ns-s4-079.Breakdown.PiecePerturbationStatement: At zero, (4.17) gives $v(0)=\chi+J\gamma$ because both the residual and the integrals vanish there. With $u^{\mathrm a}=u^*$ the residual vanishes identically; the corresponding local perturbation implication gives the exact corrected mild solution on a compact interval.
ns-s4-079.Breakdown.Periodic.SeqPerturbation: On the first piece no division is present, since $\theta^0=1$. Its initial displacement is $\xi+Je$. For later pieces the starting displacement comes from the preceding endpoint after dilation. The finite-dimensional adjustment is thus made once, at the initial time, not once per period.

ns-s4-080.Breakdown.ContractionInternal.exists_sma: The contraction treats $e^{t\Delta}\chi-F^{\mathrm a}$ as a known curve and $\mathcal B(v,v)$ as a trial-dependent one. A linear inverse bound $C_{\mathcal R}$ makes the trial ball of radius twice the norm bound for the known response. The quadratic term is small relative to this radius when the known source is sufficiently small; no smallness of the mixed term is assumed.

ns-s4-081.Breakdown.varConstIntegral: Write $r=1-t$ and $\tau=t-t'$. Then $1-t'=r+\tau$, and the change $\tau=r\theta$ yields the factor $r^{-3/4+\kappa-1/2+1}=r^{\kappa-1/4}$. The remaining dimensionless integral is bounded independently of $t$; this is precisely the factor canceled by the weight of $C_\kappa$.

ns-s4-082.Breakdown.varConstIntegral: The transformed integrand behaves as $\theta^{-3/4}$ at zero and $\theta^{\kappa-5/4}$ at infinity. The first singularity is integrable; the second is integrable exactly when $\kappa<1/4$. At equality the common estimate loses a logarithm as $t\uparrow1$; this concerns the mixed bound (4.21), not the estimate for two bounded inputs.

ns-s4-083.Breakdown.varConstIntegral: The two products have different time dependence: the quadratic product has exponent $2\kappa-1/2$, and the interaction of a bounded field with a $C_0$ field has exponent $-1/4$. On $0<1-t'\le1$ both are bounded by $(1-t')^{\kappa-1/2}$. The common integral (4.18) therefore controls both (4.19) and the cutoff estimate (4.21).
ns-s4-083.Breakdown.PieceOperatorStatement: On a compact interval the kernel estimate gives the factor $4C_KL^{1/4}$ times two ordinary supremum norms. These norms need not be bounded as the interval approaches time one. Substitution in (4.18) keeps the pointwise time-dependent input powers inside the integral and gives an output bound uniform in the weighted norm.

pdf-item-equation-4-19.Breakdown.PieceOperatorStatement: The estimate loses some of the decay of a product of two errors: their product has the power $(1-t')^{2\kappa-1/2}$. In fact (4.18) with $\eta$ in place of $\kappa$ bounds $\mathcal B(v,v')$ in $C_\eta$ whenever $\eta\le2\kappa$ and $0<\eta<1/4$. For the fixed point it is enough to take $\eta=\kappa$, without changing the spectral circle used for the inverse.

pdf-item-equation-4-20.Breakdown.HeatBilinear: By heat contractivity and $(1-t)^{1/4-\kappa}\le1$, the weighted norm of the heat curve is at most $\|\chi\|_X$. The value at $t=0$ attains this bound, so in fact equality holds. This is why smallness of the prescribed datum in $X$ suffices to make its heat input small in $C_\kappa$.

ns-s4-086.Breakdown.varConstIntegral: The bounded input in (4.21) need not decay in physical time. In Section 6 it is the difference $\bar u-u^*$, whose ordinary supremum norm is $O(L^{-1/2})$ by (6.4). The other factor is allowed the reference rate in $C_0$. This estimate makes their mixed Duhamel term small in the stronger $C_\kappa$ norm required by the inverse.

ns-s4-087.Breakdown.varConstIntegral: Fix $b<1$. Both inputs have finite ordinary supremum norms on $[0,b]$, so removing a lag shorter than $\varepsilon$ costs $O(\varepsilon^{1/4})$ uniformly there. The truncated integral varies continuously with its endpoint; passing to the limit proves continuity on $[0,b]$. Since $b$ is arbitrary, no field at time one is needed.

ns-s4-088.Breakdown.HeatBilinear: The lag $t-t'$ controls smoothing, while the time to the singularity $1-t'$ controls the size of the inputs. Their relation is $1-t'=(1-t)+(t-t')$. The substitution in (4.18) separates out the current remaining time $1-t$ and leaves a dimensionless integral, whose finiteness is what makes the bound uniform in $t$.

ns-s4-089.Breakdown.PieceOperatorStatement: At a fixed short interval the kernel gives a bound by $4C_K L^{1/4}$ times the two supremum norms. The global proof must instead keep the powers of $1-t'$ inside the time integral; a supremum over all physical times could be infinite. The rescaled piece proof handles the same issue by keeping the factor $\theta^n$ in its quadratic term.
ns-s4-089.Breakdown.HeatBilinear: Only the heat contraction and the singular bilinear kernel bound are used here. These are the relevant fields of `HeatBilinear`. No recurrence or compactness is required for the nonlinear estimates once a bounded right inverse has been supplied.

ns-s4-090.Breakdown.Periodic.SeqPerturbation: The lemma assumes a right inverse of the mixed equation about the chosen reference, whether or not the reference is exact. It does not need that reference to be small. In `SeqPerturbation` the analogous given inverse acts on divided pieces, and the residual and prescribed heat input are small together. The hard part on the torus is constructing that inverse, not proving a second contraction principle.
ns-s4-090.Breakdown.ContractionStatement: For an exact reference the residual is zero. The source of the sequence inverse is $\Gamma\xi$ on the first interval, plus $\theta^nN(z_n,z_n)$ on every interval. The heat effect of $\xi$ is carried into later intervals by the preceding endpoints. The approximate-reference theorem adds the negative divided residual on each interval.

pdf-item-equation-4-22.Breakdown.PeriodicInverseStatement: The inverse is applied to trial right-hand sides, and only its second component is iterated. The parameter space $E$ therefore needs no norm in Lemma 4.8. A bound for the parameter is available if the inverse has one, as in (4.8) or the bounded sequence inverse, and is needed for the Lipschitz estimate of the selected datum in Section 5.2.

ns-s4-092.Breakdown.Periodic.SeqPerturbation: Let $a=\|e^{t\Delta}\chi-F^{\mathrm a}\|_\kappa$. The radius is $\delta=2C_{\mathcal R}a$, and on this ball the Lipschitz constant of the inverse applied to the quadratic term is at most $2CC_{\mathcal R}\delta=4CC_{\mathcal R}^2a$. The square in (4.23) thus comes once from the size of the solution and once from applying the inverse to a difference.

ns-s4-093.Breakdown.Periodic.SeqPerturbation: With $a=\|e^{t\Delta}\chi-F^{\mathrm a}\|_\kappa$, (4.24) gives a trajectory of size at most $2C_{\mathcal R}a$. If the known input vanishes then the selected fixed point is zero. In the formal sequence estimate the bound is $2\|R\|(\rho+\|\xi\|)$ on the divided pieces; the actual normalized error has the additional factor $\theta^n$.

ns-s4-094.Breakdown.Periodic.SeqPerturbation: The endpoint condition in `SeqPerturbation` follows by evaluating the corrected mild formula at zero of each piece: the mixed and quadratic integrals and the local residual vanish there. Thus for $n>0$ the divided incoming error is $(c/\theta)z_{n-1}(L)$, where $c$ is the endpoint scaling. Multiplying by $\theta^n$ and adding the matching reference gives the required matching of corrected fields.

ns-s4-095.Breakdown.ContractionInternal.exists_sma: For the generic fixed-point lemma take $b=C_{\mathcal R}a$ and $K=CC_{\mathcal R}$, with $a=\|e^{t\Delta}\chi-F^{\mathrm a}\|_\kappa$. Its hypothesis $8Kb\le1$ is exactly (4.23) for $\varepsilon_1=(8C)^{-1}$. It gives a fixed point in the closed ball of radius $2b$.

ns-s4-096.Breakdown.ContractionInternal.exists_sma: For a trial velocity $v$ use the second component of $\mathcal R[e^{t\Delta}\chi-F^{\mathrm a}+\mathcal B(v,v)]$. If that component equals $v$, the first component of the same pair gives the datum parameter. There is no separate iteration of the datum, and no norm of the parameter is required to establish the contraction.

ns-s4-097.Breakdown.ContractionInternal.exists_sma: On the ball of radius $\delta$ the contribution of the known source is at most $\delta/2$ and that of the quadratic term at most $CC_{\mathcal R}\delta^2\le\delta/4$. Their sum is at most $3\delta/4$. The self-map property of the ball is thus established separately from the contraction estimate.

ns-s4-098.Breakdown.ContractionInternal.exists_sma: Bilinearity gives $\mathcal B(v',v')-\mathcal B(v'',v'')=\mathcal B(v'-v'',v')+\mathcal B(v'',v'-v'')$. Each term contains the difference once and an unchanged factor of norm at most $\delta$. With (4.19) and the bound for the inverse this gives Lipschitz constant $2CC_{\mathcal R}\delta\le1/2$.

ns-s4-099.Breakdown.ContractionInternal.exists_sma: The fixed-point equation alone is an equality of trajectories. Recovering $\gamma$ from the first component of the same inverse evaluation gives the whole pair satisfying (4.17). For a fixed inverse this choice is unique in the contraction ball; Lemma 4.8 does not assert uniqueness of corrections obtained from other inverses.
ns-s4-099.Breakdown.Periodic.SeqPerturbation: At the fixed point, adding the reference and error equations cancels the residual and produces the actual quadratic self-interaction of the corrected curve. The local version gives a mild solution on every piece and matching endpoints; the gluing theorem then gives one solution on the physical half-open interval.

ns5.purpose.Breakdown.TransferHolds: The quantifiers in Proposition 2.1 permit choosing a single $E$ once the reference and rate are fixed, then varying the prescribed $w_0$ in a small ball. `TransferHolds` only asks for one datum in each given dense subspace and tolerance. It suffices for choosing compactly supported data, but the assertion that every nearby test datum can be corrected by that same $E$ is additional.

ns5.cutoff.solenoidal.Breakdown.Periodic.cutoffDivergenceFree: Where the cutoff varies, $\operatorname{div}(\eta(\cdot/r)u^*)=r^{-1}\nabla\eta(\cdot/r)\cdot u^*$. The additional term from the curl has exactly the opposite divergence, by $\operatorname{curl}A=u^*$. `cutoffDivergenceFree` establishes this cancellation without estimating the size of the added term.

ns5.cutoff.scalar.Breakdown.Freq.Internal.NiceApprox.stdBu: The same bump is used at every radius, so the first and second spatial derivatives of $\eta(\cdot/r)$ cost $r^{-1}$ and $r^{-2}$. The formal `stdBump` has radii $1$ and $2$; its rescaling by $2/r$ gives the inner and outer radii $r/2$ and $r$.

pdf-item-equation-5-1.Breakdown.Periodic.homotopyPotential: The formula uses the field along the segment from the centre to $x$ at one fixed time, so it requires no solution of a spatial elliptic equation or boundary condition for the potential. The order $u^*(t,\sigma x)\times x$ gives $\operatorname{curl}A=u^*$, not its negative. `homotopyPotential` allows the centre to be translated, which is useful in placing the cutoff inside the unit cell.
pdf-item-equation-5-1.Breakdown.Periodic.cutoffField: In (5.1) the product rule gives $\bar u=\chi u^*+\nabla\chi\times A$, with $\chi=\eta(\cdot/r)$; this is the formula of `cutoffField`. Since $|A|\lesssim1$ and $|\nabla\chi|\lesssim r^{-1}$, the correction has the same order $r^{-1}$ as the velocity in the transition annulus. This is why enforcing zero divergence does not increase the order of the mass estimate.
pdf-item-equation-5-1.Breakdown.Freq.Internal.NiceApprox.cutof: The theorem `cutoff_isTestField` gives the three properties of the cutoff curl needed for membership of $C^\infty_{c,\mathrm{div}}$: smoothness, compact support and zero divergence. Its fixed bump at scale $r/2$ gives the paper's support radius. Equality with $u^*$ on the inner ball requires the separate curl identity for $A$.

ns5.cutoff.parameter.Breakdown.Periodic.cutoffField: The radius is held fixed during each evolution. On $\mathbb R^3$ the cutoff changes only the datum; on the torus it changes the reference at every time. In the latter case $r=L/8$ makes the support a fixed ball, which is why the entire mixed advection in (6.9) is determined by the perturbation restricted to that ball.

ns5.lemma5.1.geometry.Breakdown.Periodic.approxFieldProperties: Lean also localizes the pressure, in order to estimate the differential residual. Write $p_T^*(t,x)=(T-t)^{-1}q(s,(x-a)/\sqrt{T-t})$ for the physical pressure and $x_0$ for the fixed point of the transition annulus. The pressure used is $\chi(x)(p_T^*(t,x)-p_T^*(t,x_0))$. Its gradient agrees with the original gradient in the inner ball. The subtraction eliminates dependence on a time-dependent pressure gauge and allows the extra cutoff term to be bounded using differences of pressure, hence $\nabla p_T^*$.
ns5.lemma5.1.geometry.Breakdown.Freq.Internal.NiceApprox.cutof: The support and smoothness of the potential multiplied by a bump pass to its curl, and the divergence of a smooth curl vanishes. `cutoff_isTestField` packages these facts for each fixed nonzero scale. Neither equality on the inner ball nor a bound uniform in time follows from membership of the test-field class alone.
ns5.lemma5.1.geometry.Breakdown.Periodic.cutoffGradientClose: In similarity coordinates, $f(y)=\sqrt\ell\,\bar u(t,a+\sqrt\ell y)$, $\ell=T-t$, agrees with $W(s,y)$ on $B_{1/(16\sqrt\ell)}$. The identity $\|\nabla_y(f-W)\|_2^2=\sqrt\ell\,\|\bar u-u_T^*\|_{\dot H^1}^2$ is on the whole space before periodization. `cutoffGradientClose` chooses the threshold on $\ell$ uniformly in the phase. A choice of $T$ below that threshold works also at all later times.
ns5.lemma5.1.geometry.Breakdown.Periodic.cutoffMassBound: Increasing $r$ improves the gradient approximation but need not bound the mass uniformly in $r$: the radial integrals of the squared gradient bound outside $r$ and of the squared velocity bound inside $r$ are of orders $r^{-1}$ and $r$. In the formal cutoff the physical radius is fixed, so the latter growth occurs only in the similarity-coordinate mass; `cutoffMassBound` compensates it by the physical volume scaling.

pdf-item-equation-5-2.Breakdown.Periodic.cutoffGradientClose: The paper gives an explicit physical norm estimate for every $r>0$. With remaining time $\ell$ and fixed physical $r$, squaring and changing to similarity variables gives $\|\nabla(f-W)\|_2^2\lesssim\sqrt\ell/r$. `cutoffGradientClose` proves the needed smallness of the squared similarity gradient by an integrable majorant, with a weaker power of $\ell$ in its proof and a fixed physical radius. Its tolerance is a squared norm, not the norm in (5.2).
pdf-item-equation-5-2.Breakdown.Periodic.cutoffMassBound: The normalized inhomogeneous norm has two terms. If $\ell=T-t$, $f(y)=\sqrt\ell\,\bar u(t,a+\sqrt\ell y)$ and $\mu$ is the remaining time at the start of the current interval, its square is $(\mu/\ell)^{1/2}\|\nabla f\|_2^2+\sqrt{\mu\ell}\|f\|_2^2$. Here $\lambda\mu\le\ell\le\mu$ and `cutoffMassBound` bounds the second term by $K\sqrt\mu$. The gradient term is bounded above and away from zero by the first estimate of (5.2) and the profile norm bounds. This is why both estimates are used in `ApproxSizes`.

ns5.proof.uniformity.Breakdown.Periodic.cutoffGradientClose: The constants in the cutoff estimate do not deteriorate with time: outside $B_{r/2}$ the physical decay bounds of (4.1) have no singular time factor, and inside the potential integral the powers of $\sigma$ compensate the bounds at $\sigma x$. The corresponding `cutoffGradientClose` estimate is uniform in $T,t$ with $T>0$ and $T-t$ positive and sufficiently small.
ns5.proof.uniformity.Breakdown.Periodic.cutoffMassBound: In `cutoffMassBound` the squared similarity mass is at most $K/\sqrt{T-t}$ for $0<T-t\le1$. The physical squared mass is $\sqrt{T-t}$ times that integral. It is therefore at most $K$, with $K$ independent of the singular time as well as the current time; the growing similarity support has not introduced a growing physical mass bound.

ns5.proof.smoothness.Breakdown.Periodic.Cutoff.Internal.contD: At any time strictly before blow-up, the integrand is smooth also at $\sigma=0$: there the velocity is evaluated at the centre and multiplied by $\sigma$. Thus the radial integral is not an improper integral at its lower endpoint. `contDiff_potentialIntegrand` proves the joint smoothness in $\sigma$ and $x$ for a fixed smooth spatial field.
On a compact neighbourhood of any $(t,x)$ with $t<1$, the integrand and its derivatives are bounded on the product with $[0,1]$. This justifies differentiating the radial integral in time and space; no estimate uniform as $t\uparrow1$ is needed for smoothness. `contDiff_cutoffField_family` gives this conclusion for a globally smooth input family, with a local version used for the profile before blow-up.

ns5.proof.curlintegrand.Breakdown.Periodic.Cutoff.Internal.poten: For a smooth field $g$, differentiation gives $\operatorname{curl}_x[\sigma g(\sigma x)\times x]=2\sigma g(\sigma x)+\sigma^2 Dg(\sigma x)x-\sigma^2x\operatorname{div}g(\sigma x)$. The zero-divergence hypothesis eliminates the last term. The first two constitute a derivative in $\sigma$, so there is no spatial inversion left to perform. `potential_pointwise` proves the componentwise identity with a translated centre as well.

ns5.proof.curlpotential.Breakdown.Periodic.homotopyCurl: Integrate the preceding identity in $\sigma$. The upper endpoint is $u^*(t,x)$, while the lower endpoint is zero because of $\sigma^2$ and smoothness at the centre. `homotopyCurl` proves this identity and smoothness for any smooth solenoidal $g$, with no support or decay assumption.

ns5.proof.productformula.Breakdown.Periodic.cutoffField: Writing $\chi(x)=\eta(x/r)$, the two derivatives of the cutoff satisfy $|D\chi|\lesssim r^{-1}$ and $|D^2\chi|\lesssim r^{-2}$. Although only one derivative of $\bar u$ is to be bounded, it differentiates the term $\nabla\chi\times A$, and hence a second cutoff derivative is needed. `cutoffField` uses the gradient of the rescaled bump itself.

ns5.proof.support.Breakdown.Periodic.cutoffDivergenceFree: On $B_{r/2}$ the two terms are $u^*$ and zero; outside $B_r$ they are both zero. The curl identity and the cancellation in `cutoffDivergenceFree` give zero divergence everywhere, including the transition region. No separate correction at the boundary of the support is needed because the cutoff is smooth.
ns5.proof.support.Breakdown.Periodic.approxFieldProperties: In the formal construction the centre $a$ has distance $1/2$ from every face of the unit cube, while the support radius is $1/8$. The field vanishes on an open neighbourhood of the faces. Thus repeating the field in adjacent cells does not introduce a jump in the velocity or its derivatives. `approxFieldProperties_holds` proves the support and inner agreement used here.
ns5.proof.support.Breakdown.Freq.Internal.NiceApprox.cutof: `cutoff_isTestField` gives smoothness, compact support and zero divergence for the curl of the bumped potential. It gives membership of the test-field class used to approximate the homogeneous Sobolev space. Agreement with the uncut field on the inner ball uses the separate radial curl identity.

ns5.proof.differentiate.Breakdown.Periodic.Cutoff.Internal.parti: Differentiating in a unit direction $v$ gives $\sigma^2 Dg(\sigma x)v\times x+\sigma g(\sigma x)\times v$. Thus a derivative of $g$ is accompanied by two powers of $\sigma$, and the undifferentiated $g$ by one. The two inverse-distance bounds of (4.1) have precisely the powers that these factors cancel. `partialAt_potential` gives the coordinate version of the differentiation.
For $x\ne0$ and $\sigma>0$, the two differentiated integrands have sizes at most $C_W\sigma^2|x|/(\sigma|x|)^2$ and $C_W\sigma/(\sigma|x|)$, both equal to $C_W/|x|$. Integrating over $0<\sigma<1$ thus gives $2C_W/|x|$ for a directional derivative, without a logarithmic loss. The corresponding similarity-variable estimate is proved in `potential_deriv_bound`.

For $\sigma>0$, $\sigma|u^*(t,\sigma x)||x|\le C_W$, even near the lower endpoint. `norm_potential_le` uses the decay of $W$ to obtain a uniform bound on its radial potential $A_s$. In physical variables $A(t,x)=A_s(x/\sqrt{1-t})$: the velocity amplitude and the position factor in the cross product cancel.

The similarity potential satisfies $|D A_s(y)v|\le 2C/|y|$ for $|v|\le1$, by `potential_deriv_bound`. For $A(t,x)=A_s(x/\sqrt{1-t})$ the derivative contributes $(1-t)^{-1/2}$ and the bound at $y=x/\sqrt{1-t}$ contributes $\sqrt{1-t}/|x|$. They cancel; the sum over the coordinate directions only changes the constant. No bound at $x=0$ is needed here.

ns5.proof.errorformula.Breakdown.Periodic.cutoffField: In the gradient of $(\chi-1)u^*+\nabla\chi\times A$ there are four kinds of terms, involving $Du^*$, $(D\chi)u^*$, $(D^2\chi)A$ and $(D\chi)DA$. On the annulus their sizes are respectively $O(r^{-2})$, $O(r^{-1}r^{-1})$, $O(r^{-2})$ and $O(r^{-1}r^{-1})$. This is the point at which the vector-potential cutoff costs no more, in order of magnitude, than discarding the velocity tail.
At $x=a+\sqrt\ell y$, $\ell=T-t$, the velocity normalized by $\sqrt\ell$ is $f(y)=\chi(x)W(s,y)+\sqrt\ell\,\nabla\chi(x)\times A_s(y)$, as in `cutAt_formula`. The potential itself is unchanged in amplitude by the similarity transformation. The extra factor $\sqrt\ell$ in the cutoff term and the receding similarity annulus are the two features used to make its gradient small.

On the physical annulus the four bounds are $|\nabla u^*|$, $r^{-1}|u^*|$, $r^{-1}|\nabla A|$ and $r^{-2}|A|$, each $O(r^{-2})$. For the fixed radius in Lean, differentiation in $y$ and normalization of velocity together contribute a factor $\ell=T-t$. Indeed `fderiv_diff_mid` bounds a unit directional derivative of the error by $C(1+|y|)^{-2}+C_1\ell$, with $|y|\asymp\ell^{-1/2}$; both terms are $O(\ell)$ on that annulus.

Outside the cutoff support, the error is exactly $-u^*$, and differentiation introduces no terms from $\eta$ or $A$. The gradient bound follows at once from (4.1). `fderiv_diff_outer` gives the corresponding identity with the opposite sign for $D(W-f)$ beyond the scaled support radius; the boundary follows by continuity and the norm is insensitive to the sign.

The formal proof uses a common integrable majorant rather than evaluating the sharp radial tail. Outside the inner radius $1/(16\sqrt\ell)$ one has $(1+|y|)^{-1/2}\le4\ell^{1/4}$, so the squared tail bounded by $(1+|y|)^{-4}$ is at most $4\ell^{1/4}(1+|y|)^{-7/2}$. The remaining term of `grad_sum_le` is $O(\ell^2)$ on a ball of volume $O(\ell^{-3/2})$. Integration gives $O(\ell^{1/4}+\ell^{1/2})$, sufficient for the uniform smallness asserted below.
ns5.proof.energyintegral.Breakdown.Periodic.cutoffGradientClose: The annulus contributes $O(r^{-4}r^3)=O(r^{-1})$ to the squared gradient norm and the exterior contributes $4\pi C_W^2\int_r^\infty\rho^{-2}d\rho=4\pi C_W^2/r$. The norm error is therefore $O(r^{-1/2})$. In `cutoffGradientClose`, `gradEnergy` is a squared norm in similarity variables. To obtain a norm error at most $\varepsilon$, its tolerance must be $\varepsilon^2$.

On the annulus $r/2\le |x|\le r$, the bounded potential contributes at most $C/r\lesssim C/|x|$ to the velocity, so both terms obey the same inverse-distance bound. In similarity coordinates `cutAt_sq_le` controls the two squared terms by $2C^2/(1+|y|)^2+2\ell G^2C^2$ on the support, where $G$ bounds the physical cutoff gradient. The constant second term is integrated only over the cutoff ball.

The inverse-square velocity majorant has a radial integral proportional to the radius, since the Jacobian $\rho^2$ cancels $\rho^{-2}$. In `radial_bound` there is also a constant summand $b$ in $2(a/(1+|y|))^2+b$; its integral on $B_R$ has size $bR^3$. For the cutoff $R=1/(8\sqrt\ell)$ and $b=O(\ell)$, so $bR^3=O(R)$ as well. Both summands give the same order of squared mass.
ns5.proof.massintegral.Breakdown.Periodic.cutoffMassBound: At $r=L/8$ the mass bound gives $\|\bar u(t)\otimes\bar u(t)\|_1=\|\bar u(t)\|_2^2\lesssim L$, the quantity needed for the nonlinear heat comparison (6.2). Since its coefficient is $L^{-7/2}$, the image error is $O(L^{-5/2})$. In `cutoffMassBound` the physical radius stays fixed: multiplying the similarity squared mass bound $K/\sqrt\ell$ by the factor $\sqrt\ell$ from the change of variables gives a bound independent of time.

ns5.correction.data.Breakdown.StepDataStatement: The spectral circle, the space of compact corrections and the bound of the inverse have all been fixed before the nearby datum is chosen. The two smallness conditions serve distinct purposes: the first permits the nonlinear solve and the second leaves a positive lower bound for the physical solution. Shrinking the neighborhood changes neither the reference nor the correction space.
ns5.correction.data.Breakdown.orbitNorm: The paper obtains the lower reference bound by excluding zero slices and taking the minimum over one period. `orbitNorm` uses the small-data threshold: if a slice were sufficiently small, uniqueness would give a bounded physical solution from it. At its $n$th normalized return the norm is at most $2e^{-nS/4}$ times the initial norm, yet recurrence makes these norms equal. This forces the slice, and then the entire orbit, to vanish.
ns5.correction.data.Breakdown.ContractionStatement: A contraction about a reference yields a tracking trajectory, but does not of itself yield blow-up. The lower bound for the reference and the comparison $4C_{\mathcal R}\varepsilon_0\le c_*$ prevent the correction from canceling the singular norm. These are additional ingredients beyond `ContractionStatement`.

ns5.correction.smallness.Breakdown.ContractionInternal.exists_sma: The first smallness inequality gives $C_{\mathcal R}^2\|e^{t\Delta}\chi\|_\kappa\le\varepsilon_1$, allowing Lemma 4.8. Its error bound then has coefficient at most $2C_{\mathcal R}\varepsilon_0$. The second inequality makes this coefficient at most $c_*/2$, which is used in the reverse triangle inequality.

ns5.correction.initialdifference.Breakdown.physicalField: At time zero, $u^*(0)=W(0)$, so $\chi=w_0-W(0)$. Since $(1-t)^{1/4-\kappa}\le1$ and the heat flow is a contraction on $X$, the entire function $e^{t\Delta}\chi$ has $\|e^{t\Delta}\chi\|_\kappa\le\|\chi\|_X\le\varepsilon_0$. This is the small inhomogeneity to which the right inverse is applied, rather than a smallness condition on the reference itself.

ns5.correction.apply.Breakdown.contraction: On $\mathbb R^3$ the reference remains the exact $u^*$ and $F^{\mathrm a}=0$. The given input to the inverse is the heat curve of $\chi=w_0-W(0)$; the nonlinear input is the quadratic interaction of the error. In the formal recurrence the first is supplied only on the initial piece and the second on every piece with the factor $\theta^n$.

ns5.correction.zerodefect.Breakdown.orbitPhysical: The reference has no defect: $F^{\rm a}=u^*-e^{t\Delta}u^*(0)-B(u^*,u^*)=0$ by Proposition 4.1. Accordingly (4.17) has right-hand side $e^{t\Delta}\chi+B(v,v)$. The initial cutoff contributes only through $\chi$; there is no external force to cancel in the whole-space evolution.

ns5.correction.rightinverse.Breakdown.StepDataStatement: The linearized operator on $\mathbb R^3$ does not change when we replace the initial field by a cutoff: the reference in its coefficients is still $u^*$. The inverse (4.8) therefore applies directly. In Section 6 the reference in the coefficients is itself cut off and periodized; the original inverse must be transferred to that different operator before it can be used.

ns5.correction.heat.Breakdown.Freq.HeatSemigroup: In §5.2 the reference in Lemma 4.8 is $u^*$ itself, so $F^{\rm a}=0$ and the known source is the heat evolution of $\chi=w_0-W(0)$. The heat contraction gives $\|e^{t\Delta}\chi\|_\kappa\le\|\chi\|_X$ since $(1-t)^{1/4-\kappa}\le1$; equality holds at $t=0$. By (5.2), choosing $w_0=\bar u(0)$ with $r$ large makes this source small. No bound on the $L^2$ norm of $w_0$ is required in (4.23).
ns5.correction.heat.Breakdown.ContractionInternal.exists_sma: The cutoff controls the size of the known source; the right inverse of Proposition 4.3 handles the mixed interaction with the possibly large $u^*$. Applied to $e^{t\Delta}\chi+\mathcal B(v,v)$, its second component determines $v$ by a contraction, and its first gives $\gamma\in E$. At $t=0$ this yields $u(0)=w_0+\gamma$, still compact and solenoidal if $w_0=\bar u(0)$. The error estimate $\|v\|_\kappa\le2C_{\mathcal R}\varepsilon_0$ and the second restriction on $\varepsilon_0$ give $\|u(t)\|_X\ge c_*(1-t)^{-1/4}/2$. The linked fixed-point lemma is also used in the formal construction on rescaled time intervals.

ns5.correction.solution.Breakdown.ContractionStatement: At time zero the identity is $u(0)=u^*(0)+\chi+\gamma=w_0+\gamma$. The sequence version gives $\xi+Je$ as the initial displacement from the reference. The correction belongs to the fixed finite-dimensional image of the lift, while the later heat inputs are determined by propagation, not chosen freely.
ns5.correction.solution.Breakdown.TransferHolds: The adjustment leaves $[w_0]$ in $X/E$ unchanged. For a fixed choice of right inverse it gives a selected tracking datum with the same singular time and phase as $u^*$. The existence statement `TransferHolds` suffices for choosing one such datum in the test subspace, but does not state a selection for every affine class near $[W(0)]$.

ns5.correction.error.Breakdown.ContractionInternal.exists_sma: By (4.24), $\|v\|_\kappa\le2C_{\mathcal R}\|e^{t\Delta}\chi\|_\kappa\le2C_{\mathcal R}\varepsilon_0$. Undoing the norm weight gives the first bound. The second uses the independently chosen inequality $4C_{\mathcal R}\varepsilon_0\le c_*$, not any improvement of the contraction estimate.
ns5.correction.error.Breakdown.TransferHolds: Using (4.4), subtract the error estimate from the reference lower bound to obtain $\|u(t)\|_X\ge c_*(1-t)^{-1/4}[1-(1-t)^\kappa/2]$. The bracket is at least $1/2$ throughout the interval. This shows why the uniform comparison matters in addition to asymptotic convergence in similarity variables.

ns5.correction.blowupbounds.Breakdown.orbitNorm: The second smallness condition $4C_R\varepsilon_0\le c_*$ is exactly what is needed here. Lemma 4.8 gives $\|v\|_\kappa\le 2C_R\varepsilon_0$. Since $(1-t)^\kappa\le1$, the reverse triangle inequality with (4.4) gives $(1-t)^{1/4}\|u(t)\|_X\ge c_*-2C_R\varepsilon_0\ge c_*/2$ for every $t<1$. The upper bound follows by the ordinary triangle inequality.
ns5.correction.blowupbounds.Breakdown.TransferHolds: The norm of the right inverse $C_R$ is fixed before the tolerance is chosen. The bound $C_R^2\varepsilon_0\le\varepsilon_1$ makes the quadratic correction a contraction, and $4C_R\varepsilon_0\le c_*$ ensures that the resulting error is at most half the reference lower bound. Neither choice depends on the particular $w_0$ in the ball; Proposition 2.1 has this uniformity, while `TransferHolds` states the existence of one tracking datum for each tolerance.

ns5.correction.compactdata.Breakdown.Freq.testDense_holds: In the construction of Lemma 5.1, the gradient error squared is $O(r^{-1})$ but the squared $L^2$ norm of the truncated velocity is only bounded by $O(r)$. Increasing $r$ therefore makes the datum close to $W(0)$ in $X$ without requiring energy convergence. `testDense_holds` supplies this approximation abstractly in the gradient space; every approximant is still a finite-energy test field.
ns5.correction.compactdata.Breakdown.Freq.testSpan_holds: The dense subspace used in the transfer theorem is the span of the embedded test fields. `testSpan_holds` ensures that a datum in this span is itself the embedding of a single smooth compactly supported solenoidal field, since that class is closed under finite linear combinations. There is no limiting operation in the final choice of datum that could reintroduce a tail.

ns5.correction.radiuschoice.Breakdown.Periodic.cutoffGradientClose: The choice of $r$ comes after the choice of $\varepsilon_0$; no new inverse is needed for the cutoff datum. For comparison, `cutoffGradientClose` fixes the physical cutoff radius and uses $T-t$ as a small parameter. Its outer radius in similarity coordinates at $t=0$ is $1/(8\sqrt T)$, and its tolerance is for the squared gradient norm.
ns5.correction.radiuschoice.Breakdown.Freq.testDense_holds: Density alone would suffice in Section 5, since only the initial velocity is approximated there. In Section 6 one needs a compact approximation of the entire curve, with a common support ball and a mass bound uniform in time. Formula (5.1) supplies these additional properties. `testDense_holds` is the density assertion in $X$.
ns5.correction.radiuschoice.Breakdown.Freq.testSpan_holds: The closure argument in `testDense_holds` uses the span of the embedded test fields. To obtain a datum, rather than just an element of that span, take the same finite linear combination of the original test fields. `testSpan_holds` justifies this step; the combination retains smoothness, zero divergence and compact support.

ns6.intro-period.Breakdown.Periodic.V: Increasing $L$ separates the periodic copies from a reference flow whose singular time is fixed. Equivalently one can work on the unit torus and decrease $T=L^{-2}$. The paper uses the mean-zero gradient space because its Sobolev constant is independent of $L$; `V` works on the unit torus with the full $H^1$ norm and includes the zero Fourier mode.

ns6.intro-solution.Breakdown.Periodic.SeqPerturbation: The datum parameter $\gamma$ is an unknown in the equation, not a specified initial displacement. The choice of $E$ in Proposition 4.3 permits a correction in $C_\kappa$, whose growth is less than that of the reference. In the piece equation `SeqPerturbation`, the analogue of $\gamma$ enters at the first left endpoint only; subsequent initial values are determined by propagation.
ns6.intro-solution.Breakdown.Periodic.TorusBlowup: The approximate velocity is already smooth and solenoidal, with exactly the desired field on the inner ball. It does not generally solve the periodic equation. The correction must make the equation exact and retain the singular growth. `TorusBlowup` asks for smooth solenoidal data and an unbounded mild $H^1$ trajectory; it does not assert the rate or local approximation in (2.6).

ns6.intro-construction.Breakdown.Periodic.SeqPerturbation: The residual in Lemma 6.2 is attached to one curve. The right inverse in Lemma 6.3 must work for arbitrary inputs, since the source of the correction will be $-F^{\mathrm a}+\mathcal B_{\mathbb T}(z,z)$, with $z$ still unknown. `SeqPerturbation` starts after this linear problem has been solved, with the exact inverse on sequences as a hypothesis.

ns6.periodization.Breakdown.Periodic.transplantField: At a point of $Q_L$ only the central copy contributes, so $\Pi_L(fg)=(\Pi_L f)(\Pi_L g)$ for supported factors (componentwise for vector or tensor products). This identity does not extend to the heat evolutions of the factors. `transplantField` places the scaled field $\mu^{-1/2}f((x-a)/\sqrt\mu)$ about the center $a$ of the unit cell, with the same separation of its copies.

ns6.periodization-coefficients.Breakdown.Periodic.sourceCoefFormula: For $k\in L^{-1}\mathbb Z^3$, the exponential is unchanged on translating by $Lj$, so the Fourier integral unfolds to $L^{-3}\hat f(k)$. In `sourceCoefFormula` the source is $A((x-a)/\sqrt\mu)$ on the unit cell, without the velocity multiplier. Its coefficient is $\mu^{3/2}e^{-2\pi i k\cdot a}\hat A(\sqrt\mu k)$; the phase records the translation to the cell center.

pdf-item-equation-6-1.Breakdown.Periodic.TransplantNorm: The homogeneous norm is a norm on mean-zero fields. Compact solenoidal data have zero mean since each component is a compactly supported divergence, $f_j=\sum_m\partial_m(x_j f_m)$. In the formal space `V` the zero mode need not vanish, and `TransplantNorm` includes the mass term as well as the gradient term.
pdf-item-equation-6-1.Breakdown.Periodic.transplantSmooth: The support ball leaves a collar of width at least $3L/8$ at the faces. Periodization joins two zero fields there, including all derivatives. `transplantSmooth` requires $\sqrt\mu b\le1/8$ for a field supported in $\bar B_b$; the formula on the central ball of radius $1/4$ is therefore the unwrapped, dilated field.
pdf-item-equation-6-1.Breakdown.Periodic.transplantNorm:
For $f_\mu(x)=\mu^{-1/2}f((x-a)/\sqrt\mu)$ the volume element contributes $\mu^{3/2}$. Thus $\|
abla f_\mu\|_2^2=\mu^{-1/2}\|
abla f\|_2^2$ and $\|f_\mu\|_2^2=\mu^{1/2}\|f\|_2^2$. The identity proved by `transplantNorm` is consequently $\|\mu^{1/4}f_\mu\|_{H^1}^2=\|
abla f\|_2^2+\mu\|f\|_2^2$, under the stated support and smoothness conditions.

ns6.comparison-forcing.Breakdown.Periodic.heatDivFreeComparison: For $h=e^{t\Delta}\mathbb P\operatorname{div}F$ the Fourier coefficients of its periodization are exactly those of the periodic projected heat response. Hence the difference on $Q_L$ consists of the other copies of $h$, even though $F$ itself has no other copies meeting the cell. `heatDivFreeComparison` instead uses the corresponding integral and lattice sum in Fourier variables.

ns6.lemma-6-1.Breakdown.Periodic.heatDivFreeComparison: The bound in Lemma 6.1 holds for every $t>0$ with the same constant, since the other copies remain at positive distance. The normalized statement in Lean fixes the two ball radii, a lag window $[\varepsilon,\varepsilon^{-1}]$, and a tolerance $\delta$ before choosing the scale threshold $\mu_0$. It is uniform over all sources supported in the prescribed source ball, but does not compare arbitrarily small positive lags at once.

pdf-item-equation-6-2.Breakdown.Periodic.heatDivFreeComparison: On each lattice shell $|j|_\infty=n$ there are $O(n^2)$ terms, each bounded by $CL^{-4}n^{-4}\|F\|_1$ (or $CL^{-5}n^{-5}\|F\|_1$ for the gradient). Summing and taking the two norms on a cube of volume $L^3$ gives $L^{1/2}L^{-4}=L^{3/2}L^{-5}=L^{-7/2}$. The formal comparison has a different input and output: a supported $L^2$ vector source $A$ and a local error at most $\delta\|A\|_{3/2}$.

ns6.free-heat-comparison.Breakdown.Periodic.freeHeatComparison: In the divergence convention of §3.2, $\sum_m\partial_m(x_j f_m)=f_j+x_j\operatorname{div}f=f_j$. Thus (6.2) can also be used for the free datum; the Leray projection acts trivially on the solenoidal field and on its periodic copy. `freeHeatComparison` proves a direct comparison for a fixed compact test velocity, including zero lag.

pdf-item-equation-6-3.Breakdown.Periodic.freeHeatComparison: The factor $L$ lost from (6.2) bounds the first moment $\|x\otimes f\|_1$. For the cutoff datum $\bar u(0)$ this estimate gives $L^{-5/2}O(L^2)=O(L^{-1/2})$, while for $\gamma\in E$ it gives $O(L^{-5/2}\|\gamma\|_{\dot H^1})$ by the common support of $E$. The fixed-datum formal comparison is closer to the latter use.

ns6.cutoff-properties.Breakdown.Periodic.approxFieldProperties: Formula (5.1) also ensures that every mixed convection term involving $\bar u(t)$ is confined to the same ball, even when the perturbation is not compactly supported. The inner equality is used again at the end, for the comparison in (2.6). `approxFieldProperties_holds` gives the corresponding support, inner equality and solenoidality on a centered unit cell.

pdf-item-equation-6-4.Breakdown.Periodic.cutoffGradientClose: The cutoff error is uniformly bounded in the unweighted gradient norm: on the annulus its squared gradient integral is $O(L^{-4}L^3)$ and beyond it the tail is $O(L^{-1})$. In the comparison of the linearized equations this lets us use (4.21) with one bounded factor. `cutoffGradientClose` instead estimates the squared difference after pulling back to similarity coordinates, uniformly as the remaining time tends to zero.
pdf-item-equation-6-4.Breakdown.Periodic.cutoffMassBound: For the mass bound the relevant radial integral is $\int_0^{L/8}r^2r^{-2}\,dr=O(L)$, including the cutoff contribution by Lemma 5.1. The tensor $\bar u\otimes\bar u$ consequently has $L^1$ norm $O(L)$. In the formal estimate, with $h=T-t$, the similarity-coordinate mass squared is $O(h^{-1/2})$, and physical scaling supplies the compensating factor $h^{1/2}$.

ns6.cutoff-continuity.Breakdown.Periodic.approxLinks_holds: Fix $b<1$. All slices on $[0,b]$ are smooth and supported in the same ball, so continuity of the gradient in $L^2$ follows by dominated convergence. This is sufficient for membership in the space of continuous curves on $[0,1)$; no extension through the singular time is needed. `approxLinks_holds` also records the normalized endpoint relation.

ns6.approx-periodic.Breakdown.Periodic.approxPeriodic: Since the copies have disjoint supports, $(u^{\mathrm a}\cdot\nabla)u^{\mathrm a}=\Pi_L[(\bar u\cdot\nabla)\bar u]$ exactly. Thus the discrepancy between the two mild formulas below will come from the free and projected heat evolutions, not from a new convection term between different copies. `approxPeriodic` is the centered unit-cell version of the periodization.

ns6.periodic-continuity.Breakdown.Periodic.approxLinks_holds: Apply (6.1) to $\bar u(t)-\bar u(t_0)$ to get continuity of $u^{\mathrm a}$ without any comparison of heat flows. For `approxLinks_holds`, two consecutive pieces represent the same continuous physical curve at their common endpoint. The multiplier changes from $\mu_n^{1/4}$ to $\mu_{n+1}^{1/4}$, accounting for the factor $\lambda^{1/4}$.
ns6.periodic-continuity.Breakdown.Periodic.ApproxResidualSmall: The residual vanishes at zero just from its definition (4.16). In `ApproxResidualSmall` each interval has its own free term, initialized at the reference value at that interval’s left endpoint; its residual is therefore zero at every restart. These zero values will be used when imposing the datum and joining the corrected pieces.

pdf-item-theorem-6-2.Breakdown.Periodic.ApproxSizes: The size estimates compare the leading curve with the singular profile; the residual estimate compares it with the mild equation from its own datum. A small residual need not imply a large velocity, nor does a large velocity imply a small residual. `ApproxSizes` supplies the leading-field bounds, uniform on every normalized interval for sufficiently small $T$.
pdf-item-theorem-6-2.Breakdown.Periodic.TransplantNorm: The equality of gradient norms in (6.5) is exact, since $u^{\mathrm a}$ is one copy of the cutoff in each cell. The formal normalized $H^1$ identity contains a further nonnegative mass term. It can be dropped for the lower bound; the upper bound also needs the separate mass estimate.
pdf-item-theorem-6-2.Breakdown.Periodic.approxSizes: On interval $n$, let $\mu_n=T\lambda^n$ and $h=T-t=\mu_n(1-s)$, $0\le s\le1-\lambda$. If $f=\sqrt h\,\bar u_T(t,a+\sqrt h\,\cdot)$ is the cutoff in similarity coordinates, the normalized squared $H^1$ norm is $(\mu_n/h)^{1/2}\|\nabla f\|_2^2+(\mu_n h)^{1/2}\|f\|_2^2$. In `approxSizes`, $1\le(\mu_n/h)^{1/2}\le\lambda^{-1/2}$ and the last term is at most $K\sqrt{\mu_n}$. A sufficiently small gradient cutoff error therefore gives both bounds uniformly in $n$ and $s$.
pdf-item-theorem-6-2.Breakdown.Periodic.ApproxResidualSmall: For comparison of the two residual statements, write $\mu_n=T\lambda^n$ and $t=T-\mu_n+\mu_ns$, $0\le s\le1-\lambda$. Multiplication of a physical error by $\mu_n^{1/4}$ changes the weight $(T-t)^{\kappa-1/4}$ to $\mu_n^\kappa(1-s)^{\kappa-1/4}$, which is uniformly comparable to $T^\kappa(\lambda^\kappa)^n$. This explains the sequence weight $\theta^n$ in `ApproxResidualSmall`; it is a comparison of norms, not a deduction of its local residual bound from the paper’s global one.
pdf-item-theorem-6-2.Breakdown.Periodic.approxResidualSmall: The formal proof uses a different estimate. On a piece of physical length $\mu_n(1-\lambda)$ the differential force is bounded in $L^2$ by $C(\lambda\mu_n)^{-1/2}$. Integrating the $r^{-1/2}$ heat bound costs at most $2\sqrt{\mu_n}$, so the unnormalized mild discrepancy is bounded independently of $n$. The factor $\mu_n^{1/4}$ in the piece norm then gives $CT^{1/4}(\lambda^{1/4})^n\le CT^{1/4}\theta^n$.

pdf-item-equation-6-5.Breakdown.Periodic.ApproxSizes: After multiplying (6.4) by $(1-t)^{1/4}$, the cutoff contributes at most $CL^{-1/2}(1-t)^{1/4}$ to the error in the normalized profile norm. The estimate (6.5) replaces this by its maximum over time. In `ApproxSizes` the analogous bound is uniform over all normalized pieces.
pdf-item-equation-6-5.Breakdown.Periodic.TransplantNorm: No heat comparison is used for (6.5). It is an identity of instantaneous gradient norms before and after periodization, followed by comparison with $u^*$. `TransplantNorm` is the identity at scale $\mu$ on the unit torus, with the additional mass term $\mu\|f\|_2^2$ in the normalized squared norm.
pdf-item-equation-6-5.Breakdown.Periodic.approxSizes: `approxSizes` uses the norm at the fixed left-endpoint scale throughout each piece. At its right endpoint the remaining time has changed by the factor $\lambda$, so the squared gradient contribution is larger by at most $\lambda^{-1/2}$. The lower bound is unaffected because this factor is at least one, and the upper bound is independent of the piece index.

ns6.lemma-6-2-residual.Breakdown.Periodic.ApproxResidualSmall: The asserted bound for $F^{\mathrm a}$ is $CL^{-1/2}(1-t)^{\kappa-1/4}$; it does not assert uniform boundedness as $t\uparrow1$. This is the space of sources to which the right inverse of Lemma 6.3 will apply. In `ApproxResidualSmall` the local residuals belong to the corresponding divided sequence space: $\sup_n\theta^{-n}\|r_n\|\le KT^{1/4}$.
ns6.lemma-6-2-residual.Breakdown.Periodic.approxResidualSmall: The differential force used in Lean is $f=\partial_t\bar u+(\bar u\cdot\nabla)\bar u-\Delta\bar u+\nabla\bar p$, with a compactly cut off pressure. It vanishes in the inner ball, where the original equation holds, and outside the support ball. `approxResidualSmall` integrates its projected heat evolution from the left endpoint of each interval to obtain the mild residual. The latter need not be supported in the annulus.

ns6.residual-definition.Breakdown.Periodic.ApproxResidualSmall: Put $d=\bar u-u^*$. Subtracting the mild equation for $u^*$ gives $\bar F=d-e^{t\Delta}d(0)-\mathcal B(d,\bar u)-\mathcal B(u^*,d)$. In each product one factor is the bounded curve $d$, so (4.21) puts the residual in $C_\kappa$ for the same $\kappa$ as the inverse. Lean obtains a sequence residual by integrating a differential force instead.

ns6.residual-route.Breakdown.Periodic.ApproxResidualBound: One cannot periodize $\bar F$ using the compact-support construction of §6.1: the heat terms have spread outside the ball. The paper compares their compact inputs. In the formal differential route, `ApproxResidualBound` uses $\bar p=\eta(p^*-p^*(a_*))$ with a fixed annular point $a_*$. The subtraction makes the pressure term in the annulus controllable by the given pressure-gradient decay, regardless of the gauge of $p^*$.

ns6.residual-two-formulas.Breakdown.Periodic.ApproxResidualSmall: On $Q_L$ the first terms in the two displays agree exactly. Thus $F^{\mathrm a}-\bar F$ is the negative of the free heat difference plus the time integral of the projected convection difference. The sign of the latter is positive because $\mathcal B$ already contains a minus sign. `ApproxResidualSmall` uses this same residual convention on each piece.

ns6.residual-final.Breakdown.Periodic.ApproxResidualSmall: The estimate (6.3) costs $L^{-5/2}\|\bar u(0)\|_1\lesssim L^{-1/2}$, and (6.2) under the integral costs $L^{-7/2}\int_0^t\|\bar u(t\prime)\|_2^2dt\prime\lesssim L^{-5/2}$. Both errors are bounded before applying the time weight. Adding the $C_\kappa$ bound for $\bar F$ gives Lemma 6.2. The formal proof does not require either explicit comparison rate.

ns6.datum-map.Breakdown.Periodic.TorusLiftExists: The space of datum corrections is fixed by the whole-space problem. One transports its compact representatives, rather than finding a spectral subspace of the torus. `TorusLiftExists` produces $J_{\mathbb T}e=T^{1/4}\operatorname{toV}((\psi_e)_T)$, where $\psi_e$ is the linear test-field representative of $Je$ and $(\psi_e)_T$ its velocity transplant.

ns6.common-support.Breakdown.Periodic.TestLiftExists: It suffices to enclose the supports of a finite basis of $E$ in $\bar B_{r_E}$. Every output of the inverse then has that support, regardless of its coefficients. In particular Hölder and (3.1) give $\|\gamma\|_1\lesssim r_E^{5/2}\|\gamma\|_{\dot H^1}$, with $r_E$ fixed while $L$ increases. `TestLiftExists` supplies this common support for a linear family of compact representatives.

ns6.datum-norm.Breakdown.Periodic.TransplantNorm: The condition $L\ge8r_E$ makes $J=\Pi_L|_E$ an isometry by (6.1). It also ensures that the correction datum may be added to the cutoff before periodization. In `TransplantNorm` the corresponding normalized norm squared is $\|\nabla\gamma\|_2^2+T\|\gamma\|_2^2$ when $\sqrt T r_E\le1/8$; it is uniformly bounded on the unit ball of $E$.

pdf-item-equation-6-6.Breakdown.Periodic.torusOp: The term $e^{t\Delta}\Pi_L\gamma$ is part of the linear operator, since the datum is also an unknown. In `torusOp` this term is present on the first interval only; thereafter the free term propagates the previous endpoint, with the multiplier $\lambda^{1/4}/\theta$ for the divided correction. The mixed convection term is linear in $z$ on every interval.

ns6.candidate-inverse.Breakdown.Periodic.ShellInverseTransfer: A nonzero periodic right-hand side cannot be used as a whole-space $X$ field: its $L^6$ integral over all copies is infinite. But the mixed convection with $\bar u$ is determined by its restriction to the support ball. In (6.12) it is the whole-space heat response to that local convection, not the periodic right-hand side, that is supplied to $\mathcal R$. `ShellInverseTransfer` uses the same separation in the sequence setting.

ns6.local-norm.Breakdown.Periodic.ShellData: For fixed $L$ this is an equivalent norm on $H^1(B)$, but equivalence constants need not be uniform in $L$: recovering the $L^2$ norm from $L^6$ costs $|B|^{1/3}$. The gradient and $L^6$ terms are the ones needed in (6.8). `ShellData` uses the maximum of three $L^2$ derivative-entry norms and an $L^6$ value norm; arbitrary entries need not be the derivatives of the value field.

ns6.local-restriction.Breakdown.Periodic.restrictTorus: The notation $(g+v)|_B$ in (6.12) means the sum of the two restrictions, since the full fields have different domains. In `restrictTorus`, a piece velocity $z$ is pulled back by $x=a+\sqrt\mu y$: its value entry is $\mu^{1/4}z(x)$ and its derivative entries are $\mu^{3/4}\partial_j z(x)$, each cut to the comparison ball.

pdf-item-equation-6-7.Breakdown.Periodic.RestrictR3Bound: Restriction decreases the gradient integral, and $\|v\|_{L^6(B)}\le\|v\|_{L^6(\mathbb R^3)}\lesssim\|\nabla v\|_2$ by (3.1). Both constants are independent of the size of $B$. `RestrictR3Bound` gives the analogous uniform bound for the local values and derivatives.
pdf-item-equation-6-7.Breakdown.Periodic.restrictTorus: The uniform constant can be seen by dilating a mean-zero field to the unit cell: both the $L^6$ norm and the $L^2$ gradient norm acquire the same scaling factor. In `restrictTorus`, for the pullback by $x=a+\sqrt\mu y$, the value multiplier $\mu^{1/4}$ and derivative multiplier $\mu^{3/4}$ exactly cancel the Jacobian in their respective norms. The unit-cell inhomogeneous $H^1$ bound controls both.

ns6.restriction-continuity.Breakdown.Periodic.operatorNormBounds_ho: Bounded linear restriction preserves continuity of a curve in the ambient norm. Although the restricted fields are solenoidal on $B$, their traces need not vanish on $\partial B$. `operatorNormBounds_holds` supplies a bounded restriction into the larger formal local space, whose entries are extended by zero separately, without differentiating that zero extension.

ns6.local-curve.Breakdown.Periodic.ShellData: An $H^1$ extension of $\zeta$ across the boundary of $B$ is enough, even if that extension is not solenoidal outside $B$. Multiplication by $\bar u$ makes the extended product vanish outside $\bar B$; the divergence identity on $B$ uses only the given solenoidality there. In the formal local space the values and derivative entries are independent, so one forms the mixed convection directly.

ns6.local-forcing.Breakdown.Periodic.advectShell: If one extended $\zeta$ by zero before taking its derivative, a boundary distribution could appear. Here it is the tensor with factor $\bar u$ that is extended by zero. Its trace vanishes, and its divergence is the indicated $f_\zeta$ with integral zero. `advectShell` instead constructs a supported $L^2$ vector directly from the two sets of entries; it need not have zero mean for arbitrary shell data.

pdf-item-equation-6-8.Breakdown.Periodic.AdvectShellBounds: Hölder gives $1/(3/2)=1/6+1/2$, so there is no volume factor from the growing ball in either mixed term. In `AdvectShellBounds` the $L^{3/2}$ bound has the same form for independent value and derivative entries. The map `advectShell` also takes values in $L^2$ by compact support and smoothness of the background; the $L^{3/2}$ estimate is the one uniform in its gradient norm.

ns6.forcing-continuity.Breakdown.Periodic.advectShell: To prove continuity, subtract the two product expressions at times $t$ and $t_0$ and put the difference on one factor at a time. Hölder as in (6.8), with both remaining factors bounded near $t_0<1$, gives convergence in $L^{3/2}$. The local curve need not be differentiable in time. `advectShell` supplies the spatial linear map for a fixed background.

ns6.local-integrals.Breakdown.Periodic.r3Lambda: The output of $\mathcal A$ is a whole-space $X$ curve, generally with noncompact support. The map thus converts $g|_B$ into an admissible source for the existing inverse. In `r3Lambda` each background piece is a sum of compact test fields with continuous scalar coefficients; the response is the sum of their integrated mixed responses.
ns6.local-integrals.Breakdown.Periodic.torusLambda: The two integrals use the same local source; only the heat and Leray operators differ. In the sequence construction `torusLambda` integrates the source within one normalized interval, without propagating its contribution to later intervals. That propagation is supplied by the inverse of the free shift in `ComparisonSmall`.

ns6.integrand-bounds.Breakdown.Periodic.r3LambdaBound_holds: One spatial derivative of heat costs $(t-t\prime)^{-1/2}$; the $L^{3/2}$-to-$L^2$ gain costs $(t-t\prime)^{-1/4}$ in three dimensions. Their product is the integrable kernel $(t-t\prime)^{-3/4}$. `r3LambdaBound_holds` is the bound for the fixed-lag response to a shell source before integration in time.
ns6.integrand-bounds.Breakdown.Periodic.torusLambdaBound_hold: In the paper the periodic source has mean zero because it is the divergence of a compact tensor. The Leray projection itself does not discard the mean. The formal `V` includes the mean, so `torusLambdaBound_holds` instead estimates the full $H^1$ response for normalized lag $\tau>0$ with physical lag $\mu\tau\le1$.

ns6.integral-continuity.Breakdown.Periodic.r3Lambda: On a compact time interval ending before one, bound $\|f_\zeta(t\prime)\|_{3/2}$ by a constant. The last $\eta$ units of the integral then have norm at most $4C\eta^{1/4}$, uniformly for times in that interval. Away from the endpoint the integrand is continuous. This argument also gives continuity at zero, where the response vanishes; `r3Lambda` constructs the continuous pieces.
ns6.integral-continuity.Breakdown.Periodic.torusLambda: The same endpoint estimate applies in the periodic norm because the heat bound is uniform in $L$. In particular the response is continuous in the full space on the torus, before restricting to $B$. This is needed when $\mathcal A_{\mathbb T}$ is used to reconstruct $z$ in (6.12).

pdf-item-equation-6-9.Breakdown.Periodic.R3Factor: If two fields have the same restriction to $B$, their mixed convection with $\bar u$ is identical as a whole-space source. Applying the nonlocal projection and heat flow to that common source therefore gives the same response on all of $\mathbb R^3$. `R3Factor` proves the corresponding fixed-lag factorization, which can then be integrated.
pdf-item-equation-6-9.Breakdown.Periodic.TorusFactor: The factorization precedes the time integration. For the normalized unit-torus piece, the kernel in `TorusFactor` is $2\mu^{3/4}K_{\mathbb T}(\mu\tau)$. Indeed the change of integration time supplies $\mu$, the two input velocity normalizations supply $\mu^{-1/2}$ together, and the output normalization supplies $\mu^{1/4}$. This cancels the $\mu^{-3/4}$ in the smoothing bound.

ns6.weighted-local-integral.Breakdown.Periodic.operatorNormBounds_ho: From (6.8) the source size is bounded by $(1-t\prime)^{\kappa-1/2}\|\zeta\|_\kappa$. Substitution $t-t\prime=(1-t)r$ produces $(1-t)^{\kappa-1/4}$ times an integral of $r^{-3/4}(1+r)^{\kappa-1/2}$. Its integrability at infinity requires $\kappa<1/4$. The upper bound on the normalized response in the formal interval construction is obtained using the integrable short-lag kernel and the uniform bound for the background pieces.

pdf-item-equation-6-10.Breakdown.Periodic.operatorNormBounds_ho: Equation (6.10) controls each response on its full domain from input on the common ball, uniformly in $L$. The whole-space response goes into the right inverse, and the periodic response turns a discrepancy on the ball into a full periodic error. The paper uses a weighted norm on a continuous curve. The Lean statement gives uniform bounds for the localized Duhamel and restriction operators on sequences of interval pieces, along with bounds for the propagation operators.

pdf-item-equation-6-11.Breakdown.Periodic.ComparisonSmall: For (6.11) the source estimate is on $F_\zeta$, not on its divergence. Hölder costs $L$ to bound the local $L^2$ norm of $\zeta$ by its $L^6$ norm, and (6.4) costs $L^{1/2}$ for $\bar u$. The mass is therefore $O(L^{3/2}\|\zeta\|_B)$; (6.2) leaves $L^{-2}$ with no singularity in the time lag. In Lean the comparison is qualitative and also includes free propagation from preceding pieces.

pdf-item-equation-6-12.Breakdown.Periodic.ShellInverseTransfer: Write $z=g+h$ in (6.6). The equation for $h$ has right-hand side $\mathcal A_{\mathbb T}(g|_B)$, which has a whole-space counterpart $\mathcal A(g|_B)$. The inverse of Proposition 4.3 gives a compact datum correction $\gamma$ and a whole-space response $v$ to the latter. Use $g|_B+v|_B$ as the proposed local value of $z$ and reconstruct on the torus; $v$ itself is never periodized.

pdf-item-equation-6-13.Breakdown.Periodic.chainOp: In $\mathcal L(\gamma,z)-g$ the two heat curves of $\Pi_L\gamma$ cancel, leaving $\mathcal A_{\mathbb T}\zeta-\mathcal A_{\mathbb T}(z|_B)$. In particular (6.10) will give a global operator defect from a local estimate for $\zeta-z|_B$. In `chainOp` the interaction factors as $BR_r$ and the free shift and seed are separate linear maps.

ns6.local-agreement.Breakdown.Periodic.chainOp: The two local values agree at zero for every input: $v(0)=\gamma$ since $\mathcal A(g|_B)(0)=0$, and $z(0)=g(0)+\Pi_L\gamma$. Hence the defect in (6.13) has zero initial value. The remaining issue is the equality of the local values at positive time, not the matching of the prescribed datum.

pdf-item-equation-6-14.Breakdown.Periodic.r3Op: Equation (4.8) uses $u^*$ in the mixed term, whereas (6.9) uses $\bar u$. The identity $2\mathcal B(u^*,v)=\mathcal A(v|_B)-2\mathcal B(\bar u-u^*,v)$ gives (6.14) by linearity of $\mathcal A$. The last term is the sole error in the whole-space equation from changing the background; the periodic heat comparison has not yet entered.

ns6.lemma-6-3.Breakdown.Periodic.ShellInverseTransfer: The candidate inverse is bounded independently of $L$ and its composition with $\mathcal L$ tends to the identity in operator norm. The two estimates allow one to correct it without losing uniform boundedness. In the formal `ShellInverseTransfer` the perturbation is made on the reduced local operator, so the conclusion already gives an exact right inverse of the full periodic sequence operator.
ns6.lemma-6-3.Breakdown.Periodic.shellInverseTransfer: In `chainOp`, denote the free shift by $S$, the datum response by $G$, the local interaction response by $B$ and restriction by $R_r$. Put $D=(I-S)^{-1}$. If $(e,v)=R_f(Bw)$ for a local source $w$, then $v=D(Ge+B(w+R_rv))$. Thus $\zeta=w+R_rv$ solves $\zeta-R_rDB\zeta-R_rDGe=w$. After changing these two response maps to their periodic counterparts, take $w=R_t(I-S_t)^{-1}g$ and reconstruct $(I-S_t)^{-1}(g+G_te+B_t\zeta)$. This is the reduced equation implicit in (6.12), with the propagation included.
ns6.lemma-6-3.Breakdown.Periodic.ComparisonSmall: The paper compares with the cutoff on a ball whose physical radius grows with $L$. The formal argument first fixes compact test approximants to the reference pieces and the datum directions in a common ball in similarity coordinates. It transfers the inverse for those approximants as $T$ decreases, then perturbs to the actual periodic cutoff background. `ComparisonSmall` is the comparison step in the middle, with the radius and approximants fixed before the choice of $T$.

pdf-item-equation-6-15.Breakdown.Periodic.ComparisonSmall: In the reduced local equation only two maps change: the propagated interaction and the propagated datum response. `ComparisonSmall` bounds each difference by $\delta$; on the product space with its maximum norm the operator difference is at most $2\delta$. The local right-inverse bound is $K_{\rm loc}=1+K_f\|B\|(1+\|R_r\|)$, so $4\delta K_{\rm loc}\le1$ suffices for the Neumann correction.
pdf-item-equation-6-15.Breakdown.Periodic.ShellInverseTransfer: Writing $\mathcal R^{\mathrm a}g=(\gamma,z)$, (6.15) gives $\|\mathcal R^{\mathrm a}\|\le C$ and $\|I-\mathcal L\mathcal R^{\mathrm a}\|\le CL^{-1/2}$. These are estimates on different maps. The second gives a series on the right-hand-side space with norm at most two once $L$ is large; the first controls the reconstructed pair. `ShellInverseTransfer` includes this cost and the bounds $(1-q)^{-1}$, where $q=\lambda^{1/4}/\theta$, for eliminating the free shifts.

ns6.inverse-linearity.Breakdown.Periodic.ShellInverseTransfer: It is important that Proposition 4.3 gives a fixed linear right inverse. The existence of an admissible datum for each individual source would not by itself give a linear defect operator on which to use the series. All other maps in (6.12) are linear, including restriction and the transport of the datum.

ns6.inverse-input-bound.Breakdown.Periodic.operatorNormBounds_ho: Restriction by (6.7) followed by (6.10) gives $\|\mathcal A(g|_B)\|_\kappa\lesssim\|g\|_\kappa$. Both constants must be independent of $L$, since the cutoff ball grows. This gives an admissible source for the fixed whole-space inverse. The formal `operatorNormBounds_holds` supplies the separate bounds for the analogous restriction and response operators.

ns6.inverse-local-bound.Breakdown.Periodic.ShellInverseTransfer: The bound on $\zeta$ uses both domains: $\|g|_B\|_\kappa$ is controlled by the periodic Sobolev inequality, and $\|v|_B\|_\kappa$ by (3.1). Their sum is $O(\|g\|_\kappa)$. Thus (6.11) applies to the particular $L$-dependent source produced by the inverse, with the same constants as for an arbitrary local input.

ns6.inverse-output-bound.Breakdown.Periodic.ShellInverseTransfer: The reconstruction adds three bounded terms: the original periodic source, the periodic interaction of $\zeta$, and the heat curve of the compact datum. The last is bounded by $\|\gamma\|_{\dot H^1}$ because periodization is isometric on $E$. No smallness is needed here. In the sequence construction the corresponding reconstruction also includes $(I-S_t)^{-1}$, which sums the free shifts.

ns6.defect-decomposition.Breakdown.Periodic.chainOp: The difference $\zeta-z|_B$ can be computed without comparing $g$ on the two domains: its restriction cancels. What remains is a comparison of two interactions with the same local input, a comparison of the heat curves of the same datum, and the cost of changing $u^*$ to $\bar u$. The first two differences are estimated by the heat comparisons; the third uses the separate cutoff estimate (6.4).

ns6.defect-local-term.Breakdown.Periodic.ComparisonSmall: In the paper (6.11) applies to the output $\zeta$ of the candidate inverse, although it varies with $L$. In the sequence proof the comparison must be uniform also over the number of intervals. A contribution from piece $m$ to piece $m+j$ has a bound $Cq^j\|\zeta\|$, with $q=\lambda^{1/4}/\theta<1$. The terms with large $j$ have a uniformly small geometric sum. For bounded $j$ one compares the heat responses on bounded lag windows, with the short-lag part estimated separately. This gives the operator norm bound in `ComparisonSmall`.

ns6.defect-free-term.Breakdown.Periodic.freeHeatComparison: The support of every $\gamma\in E$ is inside the fixed ball $\bar B_{r_E}$. Therefore the right-hand side in (6.3) is $O(L^{-5/2}\|\gamma\|_{\dot H^1})$, unlike the cutoff datum in Lemma 6.2. In the formal seed comparison, the fixed-datum heat estimate is applied to a basis of the correction space; the finite basis and the geometric decay of the later propagated seeds give a uniform operator estimate.

ns6.defect-cutoff-term.Breakdown.Periodic.cutoffGradientClose: Use (4.21) with $\bar u-u^*$ as the bounded factor and $v$ as the factor in $C_0$. Its absolute supremum bound is $O(L^{-1/2})$ by (6.4), so the error in $C_\kappa$ is $O(L^{-1/2}\|v\|_0)$. The inequality $\|v\|_0\le\|v\|_\kappa$ then gives the desired bound. `cutoffGradientClose` is a normalized squared-gradient version of the cutoff estimate.

ns6.defect-final.Breakdown.Periodic.ComparisonSmall: The three bounds give $\|\zeta-z|_B\|_\kappa\lesssim (L^{-2}+L^{-5/2}+L^{-1/2})\|g\|_\kappa$. Equation (6.13) then applies $\mathcal A_{\mathbb T}$, whose full output norm is bounded by (6.10). Consequently the defect tends to zero in operator norm on the entire periodic source space. `ComparisonSmall` gives the propagated local response comparisons in Lean, not this global candidate-inverse estimate.
