ns6.uniform-smallness.Breakdown.Periodic.SeqPerturbation: The constants $C_1,C_2,\varepsilon_1$ must be fixed before increasing $L$. In particular $\varepsilon_1$ depends on the bilinear estimate and $\kappa$ but not on the approximate background. The period-independent constant of Lemma 3.7 is what makes the same nonlinear threshold available on each torus. `SeqPerturbation` likewise uses one kernel bound for all normalized pieces.

pdf-item-equation-6-16.Breakdown.Periodic.rightInversePerturb: Let $Q=I-\mathcal L\mathcal R^{\mathrm a}$. The first condition gives $\|Q\|\le1/2$, so $I-Q$ is invertible on the source space. The conclusion is surjectivity of $\mathcal L$; the series produces a right inverse without requiring injectivity. In `rightInversePerturb`, $AR=I$ and $\|A\prime-A\|K\le1/2$ give the same defect $Q=-(A\prime-A)R$.
pdf-item-equation-6-16.Breakdown.Periodic.SeqPerturbation: Put $a=\|F^{\mathrm a}\|_\kappa$ and $K=2C_2$. The quadratic map after applying the exact inverse has Lipschitz constant at most $4CK^2a$ on the ball of radius $2Ka$ by (4.19). The bound $K^2a\le\varepsilon_1=(8C)^{-1}$ therefore gives a contraction; the square of the inverse bound comes from the radius and from applying the inverse to a difference. `SeqPerturbation` uses a corresponding sufficient condition including the prescribed datum discrepancy $\xi$.
pdf-item-equation-6-16.Breakdown.Periodic.ApproxSizes: The last inequality in (6.16) reserves half the normalized lower bound $c_*$: $C_1L^{-1/2}$ is the loss from the cutoff and $4C_1C_2L^{-1/2}$ bounds the correction. This inequality is not used to solve the equation. The formal proof obtains a lower bound for the normalized leading field and needs only the decay of the normalized correction at late joining times to prove unboundedness.

ns6.inverse-neumann.Breakdown.Periodic.InverseAlgebra.Intern: The operator identity can be checked on a finite sum: $\mathcal L\mathcal R^{\mathrm a}\sum_{j=0}^NQ^jg=(I-Q^{N+1})g$. Letting $N\to\infty$ gives the right inverse, and the geometric norm sum is at most two. `sub_apply_inverse_one_sub` states the identity for the inverse of $I-Q$ in the Banach algebra of continuous linear maps.
ns6.inverse-neumann.Breakdown.Periodic.rightInversePerturb: Applying the candidate to $g$ leaves $Qg$ unmet; applying it to $Qg$ leaves $Q^2g$, and so forth. The repairs sum to $\mathcal R^{\mathrm a}(I-Q)^{-1}g$. This is also the construction in `rightInversePerturb`, where the candidate is a right inverse of the unperturbed operator and $Q$ measures its defect for the perturbed one.

ns6.global-inverse-hypothesis.Breakdown.Periodic.ShellInverseTransfer: The inverse is now exact on all of $C_\kappa$. Its bound is at most $2C_2$ for the pair, hence in particular for the trajectory as required by (4.22). In the nonlinear equation the source depends on the unknown correction; exact inversion must hold for that source as well as for the original residual. `ShellInverseTransfer` exports such an exact right inverse on the periodic sequence space.

ns6.small-residual-application.Breakdown.Periodic.ApproxResidualSmall: With $\chi=0$, the initial velocity of $u^{\mathrm a}$ is prescribed up to the unknown correction in $\Pi_LE$. Thus the first trial source is $-F^{\mathrm a}$, and the smallness bound is $(2C_2)^2\|F^{\mathrm a}\|_\kappa\le\varepsilon_1$. Lean uses $\rho=KT^{1/4}$ for the divided local residuals, and also allows a prescribed initial change $\xi$ to select a compact test approximation of the datum.

ns6.corrected-mild-solution.Breakdown.Periodic.SeqPerturbation: Expanding the mild residual of $u^{\mathrm a}+z$ with the corrected datum gives $F^{\mathrm a}+\mathcal L(\gamma,z)-\mathcal B_{\mathbb T}(z,z)$. The fixed-point equation makes this identically zero for all $0\le t<1$. Thus the small residual was an input to the construction, and there is no remaining external force. `SeqPerturbation` gives the exact mild equation on each piece and the matching of their endpoints.
ns6.corrected-mild-solution.Breakdown.Periodic.GlueMild: In `GlueMild`, $v_{n+1}(0)=\lambda^{1/4}v_n(1-\lambda)$ becomes equality of physical velocities upon division by the respective scales $\mu_{n+1}^{1/4}$ and $\mu_n^{1/4}$. For any $t<T$ there are only finitely many joins before $t$; the heat semigroup identity combines their local mild formulas into the mild equation from time zero.

pdf-item-equation-6-17.Breakdown.Periodic.SeqPerturbation: The value $z(0)=\Pi_L\gamma$ follows by evaluation of the exact correction equation at zero, since its residual and Duhamel terms vanish. Hence the initial datum is smooth by construction, although $z$ was found in a continuous energy-space norm. In Lean $z_0(0)=\xi+Je$; the prescribed $\xi$ replaces the initial cutoff by a compact approximation before the unknown datum correction is added.
pdf-item-equation-6-17.Breakdown.Periodic.TorusBlowup: Although the correction is constructed in a space of continuous energy-space curves, its datum is smooth: both $\bar u(0)$ and $\gamma$ are compact smooth solenoidal fields. The paper subsequently uses Lemma 2.3 to pass from the mild solution to a smooth one. `TorusBlowup` specifies smooth datum and an unbounded mild $H^1$ curve, without the quantitative rate.
pdf-item-equation-6-17.Breakdown.Periodic.seqPerturbation: On piece $n$ the actual normalized correction is $\theta^n z_n$. Division by $\theta^n$ makes the source $-\theta^{-n}r_n+\theta^n\mathcal B_n(z_n,z_n)$, with a prescribed free term on piece zero. The divided linear propagation uses $\lambda^{1/4}/\theta$. A bound on the sequence $z_n$ therefore gives a correction of vanishing relative size in the normalized pieces, even if its physical norm grows.

ns6.eq-6-18.Breakdown.Periodic.ApproxSizes: The reverse triangle inequality gives $(1-t)^{1/4}\|u(t)\|_{\dot H^1(\mathbb T_L^3)}\ge c_*-C_1L^{-1/2}-4C_1C_2L^{-1/2}(1-t)^\kappa$. The last condition of (6.16) bounds the two losses by $c_*/2$ for all times. `ApproxSizes` controls the normalized leading field, before the correction is subtracted.
ns6.eq-6-18.Breakdown.Periodic.glueUnbounded: At the joining times $t_n=T-\mu_n$, the physical $H^1$ norm is at least $\mu_n^{-1/4}(c_0-\theta^n Z)$, where $Z$ bounds the divided corrections. For large $n$ the parentheses are at least $c_0/2$ while $\mu_n^{-1/4}\to\infty$. This suffices for `glueUnbounded`; the paper proves the stronger two-sided bound at every time.

ns6.corrected-lower-bound.Breakdown.Periodic.glueUnbounded: The bound in (6.17) makes the correction small relative to the leading singular scale by the factor $L^{-1/2}(1-t)^\kappa$. Uniform smallness over all time gives (6.18), whereas convergence of the ratio to zero suffices for blow-up along a subsequence. `glueUnbounded` uses the latter with $\theta^n Z\to0$.

ns6.unit-torus-dilation.Breakdown.Periodic.transplantDilate: The Navier–Stokes dilation $u_{\mathrm{per}}(t,x)=Lu(L^2t,Lx)$ changes period $L$ to one and singular time one to $L^{-2}$. In Lean there is no final change of period: the cell is already of period one. `transplantDilate` is a composition identity for inserting compact fields at different scales in that cell, not a dilation theorem for arbitrary periodic solutions.

ns6.scaled-continuity.Breakdown.Periodic.TransplantNorm: The gradient norm gains $L^{1/2}$ under $D_{L^2}$: the gradient gains $L^2$ and the square root of the volume loses $L^{3/2}$. With $T=L^{-2}$ the identity $L^{1/2}(1-L^2t)^{-1/4}=(T-t)^{-1/4}$ preserves the rate. `TransplantNorm` instead concerns compact field transplants and includes the scaled mass contribution.

ns6.scaled-mild-equation.Breakdown.Periodic.GlueMild: The free term commutes with dilation as $D_{L^2}e^{L^2t\Delta}=e^{t\Delta}D_{L^2}$. For the quadratic integral the factor $L^2$ from $t\prime=L^2\tau$ is precisely the factor needed by the last identity of (3.21). Thus the mild equation itself is unchanged, not merely its norm estimates. `GlueMild` constructs the unit-torus mild curve instead by joining normalized pieces.

ns6.smooth-periodic-datum.Breakdown.Periodic.transplantSmooth: The two fields inside $\Pi_L(\bar u(0)+\gamma)$ are smooth, solenoidal and supported in $\bar B_{L/8}$. Dilation moves their support into $\bar B_{1/8}$, so the unit-period extension is smooth across the cell faces. The formal datum is likewise a sum of compact smooth transplants; the first field is a selected test approximation rather than the cutoff itself.

ns6.profile-scaling.Breakdown.Periodic.selfSimilar: The similarity phase is unchanged: $-\log(1-L^2t)=\log(T/(T-t))$. Also $L(1-L^2t)^{-1/2}=(T-t)^{-1/2}$, giving both the amplitude and spatial argument in $u_T^*$. The centered version is `selfSimilar`, with $x-a$ in place of $x$.

ns6.inner-ball-agreement.Breakdown.Periodic.approxFieldProperties: On $B_{L/16}$ the cutoff is identically one and only the central periodic copy is present. Hence $u-u^*=z$ there, as an equality of velocities and of their gradients. The local comparison consequently needs just the norm estimate on the correction, with no additional cutoff term. `approxFieldProperties_holds` establishes the leading-field equality.

ns6.inner-ball-rescaling.Breakdown.Periodic.transplantDilate: On $B_{1/16}$ the error equals $D_{L^2}z(L^2t)$. By the unit-cell norm equivalence (3.16) its local $H^1$ norm is bounded by a constant times the periodic gradient norm, which is at most $T^{-\kappa}(T-t)^{\kappa-1/4}\|z\|_\kappa$. The coefficient is $O(T^{1/4-\kappa})$ by (6.17). The linked compact-transplant identity is not a statement of this local estimate for the corrected trajectory.

ns6.proposition-2-2-conclusion.Breakdown.Periodic.TorusBlowup: Both estimates of (2.6) have now been obtained. In particular the error on $B_{1/16}$ divided by the singular scale $(T-t)^{-1/4}$ is $O(T^{1/4-\kappa}(T-t)^\kappa)$. `TorusBlowup` retains existence of smooth solenoidal datum and an unbounded mild $H^1$ curve but not the quantitative rate or this local comparison.
ns6.proposition-2-2-conclusion.Breakdown.Periodic.breakdownOnTorus_of_p: Proposition 2.2 is the mild localization result. To obtain the global nonexistence implication, the proof of Theorem 1.1 uses regularity and uniqueness, and the reduction to periodic pressure. `breakdownOnTorus_of_profile` gives that implication under its formal smooth-profile hypotheses. The existence of the required profile is a separate premise, addressed in Section 7.

ns7-data-s000.Breakdown.PeriodicSimilarityProfileExist: The input is a smooth nonzero solution in similarity variables, not initial data of compact support or finite energy. The formal proposition also includes decay of the second derivatives and pressure gradient. These are stronger displayed requirements than the velocity and first-derivative bounds in (1.3).

ns7-data-s001.Breakdown.extended_certificate_orbit_pro: The parameter selection in `extended_certificate_orbit_proved` uses the interval-and-ball geometry (7.29) and cancels the total auxiliary force. The conclusion records existence of an exact weak recurrent field; it does not state the quantitative estimate (7.38), the selected parameter, or the prescribed isometry. The passage to a smooth profile in Proposition 7.11 is a separate step.

ns7-data-s002.Breakdown.Cert.extendedHeldWeakEquationH: On adding (7.10) and (7.12) and expanding the convection of $W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}+v$, the two mixed terms form $\mathcal C_\alpha v$ and the two residual terms cancel. The remaining equation is $\mathcal T_S(W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}+v)+((W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}+v)\cdot\nabla)(W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}+v)\simeq-\sum_i(\beta_i^{\mathrm a}+\beta_i)b_i$. Thus solving for $v$ at a given $\alpha$ gives a forced solution; varying $\alpha$ is what removes the force.

ns7-data-s003.Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData: For example, a residual bound concerns the particular supplied field $F_\alpha^{\mathrm a}$, whereas the inverse bound concerns every perturbation, even one with harmonics or spatial dependence absent from the data. The finite description applies to the coefficients of the linearized problem, not to its unknowns. Appendix B estimates the omitted components as well as the represented ones. The data structure alone does not assert these estimates.

ns7-data-s004.Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.coercive: The estimate measures a solution of the constrained linear problem by two independent pieces of data: its right-hand side and the values of the constraints. It rules out nonzero homogeneous solutions with zero constraint values. To deduce the existence of a solution for every admissible pair of data one also uses compactness and the Fredholm alternative (Proposition 7.8). The finite cell conditions in Appendix B are sufficient for this estimate on the full perturbation space.
ns7-data-s004.Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.gap_tran: Set $D=W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}-W_\alpha^{\mathrm r}$. The change of the linearized right-hand side is $(D\cdot\nabla)v+(v\cdot\nabla)D$, and (7.19) controls it by $c_{\mathrm r}\|v\|_w$. The factor $c_1+c_0$ in (7.20) occurs because this new right-hand side is charged both in norm and in the finite row measurements.
ns7-data-s004.Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.adjoint_: For each adjoint direction the quadratic term enters through a scalar pairing. Unlike its full $\mathcal H$ norm in (7.49), the pairing in (7.32) is bounded by the square of the period norm alone. On the correction ball this gives the allowance $4\widetilde a_j\varepsilon^2$ for the coefficient estimate.

The purpose of (7.33) is to replace the pairing of the linearized equation with an adjoint field by $(Y\ell(v))_j$. Since the constraints prescribe $\ell(v)=\bar\ell(\alpha)$, this gives a known number plus an error bounded by $a_j\|v\|_w$. Subtracting the quadratic term then isolates a measurement of the auxiliary force.
ns7-data-s004.Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.frozen_f: The inverse estimate bounds the integral of the squared gradient norm over a period. The quadratic term requires its maximum in time as well. Pairing the equation with $-\Delta v$ makes the left side of (7.22) appear with a minus sign in the derivative of the gradient energy; its lower bound therefore limits the increase from a phase of small energy.

ns7-data-s006.Breakdown.sigmaSimilarityIntegrand: For a solenoidal test $\varphi$, integrating the time term by parts gives $-S^{-1}\langle W,\partial_\theta\varphi\rangle$. Since $\operatorname{div}y=3$, integrating the drift gives $-\frac12\langle W,(y\cdot\nabla)\varphi\rangle-\frac32\langle W,\varphi\rangle$. The term $\frac12W$ changes the last coefficient to $-1$, as in `sigmaSimilarityIntegrand`.

ns7-data-s007.Breakdown.IsTimePeriodic: Period one is in $\theta$ only: the spatial domain is still the whole $\mathbb R^3$. `IsTimePeriodic` specifies an equality at every time and point, whereas a Hilbert-space field is determined only almost everywhere. Compactly supported tests on the time line need not be periodic.

ns7-data-s008.Breakdown.IsPerturbation: The derivatives here need not be classical. For example, the combined time and dilation derivative is represented in Lean by a field $g$ whose pairing against a test $\varphi$ equals the pairing of $v$ against $-S^{-1}\partial_\theta\varphi-\varphi-\tfrac12(y\cdot\nabla)\varphi$. The coefficient $-1$ comes from the divergence of $y$ in three dimensions and the zeroth-order term $\tfrac12v$. The weak free operator is then represented by $g-\Delta v$.

ns7-data-s009.Breakdown.Cert.IsPeriodicField: The Hilbert space $\mathcal H$ is for the terms of the equation, not for the velocity. A velocity with a tail of order $|y|^{-1}$ may belong to $X$ without being in spatial $L^2$. Its Laplacian, linearized convection and the square-integrable combination of time and drift derivatives can nevertheless be elements of $\mathcal H$. This separation is used in the domain (7.4).
ns7-data-s009.Breakdown.periodPairing: In all the period pairings the integration is over one time circle and the whole spatial domain. In particular the constraint field is paired with $\nabla v$ in this space, rather than with a single time slice of $v$; the selected forcing measurements and adjoint measurements use the same scalar product on vector fields. This allows the residual estimates and the constraints to refer to the same linear problem.
ns7-data-s009.Breakdown.periodNorm: The time integral is an average in the original similarity time: for $F(\theta)=f(S\theta)$, $\|F\|_{\mathcal H}^2=S^{-1}\int_0^S\|f(s)\|_2^2\,ds$. Thus changing the period does not change the integration domain for the right-hand sides. In Lean `periodNorm` takes the square root after converting a nonnegative integral to a real number; the accompanying finiteness hypothesis is needed for this to represent an $L^2$ norm.
ns7-data-s009.Breakdown.matSq: For a derivative $G$, the three vectors $G e_j$ are its directional derivatives along the coordinate axes. Thus `matSq` sums $\sum_j|G e_j|^2$, the Frobenius norm squared used for $|\nabla v|^2$, rather than the squared operator norm.

ns7-data-s010.Breakdown.Cert.HH: The linked space `HH` corresponds to $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{div}}$, not to the unrestricted $\mathcal H$. It is the period-$L^2$ space with values in a Fourier realization of spatial solenoidal $L^2$. The divergence condition is spatial and imposes no restriction on the time harmonics. In Proposition 7.5 this is the range of $\mathcal T_S$.
ns7-data-s010.Breakdown.Cert.exists_projSpec: For any $F\in\mathcal H$, $F-\mathbb PF$ is orthogonal to $\mathcal H_{\rm div}$. The projection therefore preserves every solenoidal test pairing and decreases the $L^2$ norm. These facts let the free inverse act on $\mathbb PF$ while the numerical estimates are made on the supplied representative $F$; the extra row seminorm (7.17) need not decrease under projection.

ns7-data-s011.Breakdown.Cert.physToHH: For nonzero spatial frequency $\xi$, the symbol of the projection is $I-\xi\otimes\xi/|\xi|^2$. It removes the longitudinal part, leaving the two transverse components. The definition `physToHH` applies this projection at each time and passes to the time-circle $L^2$ class; it does not average over time.

ns7-data-s012.Breakdown.IsSpaceTimeTestField: Since $\operatorname{div}_y\varphi=0$, integration by parts gives $\langle\nabla q,\varphi\rangle=-\langle q,\operatorname{div}_y\varphi\rangle=0$. Compact support makes this valid for distributional pressure and permits integration by parts on the whole time line. The tests need not share the period or the symmetries of the unknown field.

ns7-data-s013.Breakdown.IsSpaceTimeTestField: The relation $F\simeq G$ tests $F-G$ against solenoidal fields; it requires only local integrability. This matters for the approximate equation (7.10), where the sum of terms on the left may not be globally square integrable even though it has an $L^2$ representative modulo gradients.
ns7-data-s013.Breakdown.sigmaSimilarityIntegrand: The weak form uses $\int (W\cdot\nabla)W\cdot\varphi=-\int\sum_i W_i W\cdot\partial_i\varphi$ for a solenoidal velocity $W$. Thus the quadratic term can be passed to a distributional limit through $W\otimes W$; locally strong $L^2$ convergence of velocities suffices. `sigmaSimilarityIntegrand` defines the integrand of this weak equation, with the time derivative and the drift integrated by parts as well.

ns7-data-s014.Breakdown.Cert.testPairingHolds_proof: Put $\varphi_{\rm per}(\theta,y)=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}\varphi(\theta+k,y)$. Splitting the integral over $\mathbb R$ into unit intervals and using the periodicity of $F$ gives $\int_{\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3}F\cdot\varphi=\langle F,\varphi_{\rm per}\rangle_{\mathcal H}$. The sum is locally finite and preserves zero divergence, so the pairing depends only on $\mathbb PF$.
ns7-data-s014.Breakdown.Cert.testDenseHolds_proof: If all compactly supported solenoidal test pairings of $F-G$ vanish, the periodization argument makes $F-G$ orthogonal to a dense subset of $\mathcal H_{\rm div}$. In particular it is orthogonal to $\mathbb P(F-G)$, and $\|\mathbb P(F-G)\|_{\mathcal H}^2=0$. This proves the converse without having to construct a scalar potential for $F-G$.

ns7-data-s015.Breakdown.Cert.periodize: The field $\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}\varphi(\theta+k,y)$ is periodic even though $\varphi$ has compact time support; for $\theta\in[0,1]$ the sum is finite. It is the test on the time circle corresponding to the full-line integral.
ns7-data-s015.Breakdown.Cert.testPairingHolds_proof: The periodization identity is a change of integration variables, not an integration by parts. On each interval $(k,k+1)$ translate time back to $(0,1)$ and use the period of $F$. The shifted tests then sum to a single periodic test, with no endpoint term.
ns7-data-s015.Breakdown.Cert.testDenseHolds_proof: Choose $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)$ with $\sum_k\chi(\theta+k)=1$. The periodization of $\chi(\theta)a(\theta)\psi(y)$ is precisely (7.3). For spatial density, first smooth a solenoidal $L^2$ field by the heat flow to obtain a solenoidal $H^1$ field, then use density of compactly supported solenoidal smooth fields in $H^1$. Density of smooth functions on the time circle gives density of the finite sums of products. Thus testing against full-line compactly supported fields suffices for the equality of the period-space projections.

ns7-data-s016.Breakdown.IsPerturbation: The space $X$ is the solenoidal homogeneous Sobolev space realized by $L^6$ fields with square-integrable gradient. Requiring the $L^6$ representative removes the additive constants: $\nabla v=0$ implies $v=0$. This is used in the injectivity arguments for both $\mathcal T_S$ and the constrained operator. The further conditions (7.4) concern the Laplacian and the free operator, not the $L^2$ norm of the velocity.

ns7-data-s017.Breakdown.IsPerturbation: For a field with a nonzero angular tail $r^{-1}A(y/r)$, the radial integrals for its sixth and second powers at infinity are proportional to $\int_1^\infty r^{-4}\,dr$ and $\int_1^\infty 1\,dr$, respectively. Thus a smooth cutoff of such a tail may have finite homogeneous $H^1$ norm without being in $L^2$. To belong to $\mathcal D_S$ it must in addition satisfy the transport condition in (7.4), as the following example illustrates.

ns7-data-s018.Breakdown.IsPerturbation: One can see the cancellation in an actual solenoidal field. Let $B$ be a nonzero skew-symmetric matrix, $r=|y|$, and outside a ball set $v(\theta,y)=r^{-2}A(2\log r-S\theta)By$ for a smooth nonconstant $S$-periodic $A$. It is solenoidal since $y\cdot By=0$ and $\operatorname{tr}B=0$. The time term is $-r^{-2}A'By$, and $\tfrac12(v+(y\cdot\nabla)v)=r^{-2}A'By$, so their sum vanishes. A smooth radial cutoff near the origin preserves zero divergence; the resulting field has $\nabla v=O(r^{-2})$, $\Delta v=O(r^{-3})$ and belongs to $\mathcal D_S$ although its separate time derivative is not in $\mathcal H$.

The energy identity requires values at individual phases, whereas $v\in L^2((0,1);X)$ initially determines a field only almost everywhere in time. The paper obtains a continuous representative by passing to Eulerian variables (7.40) and applying the Hilbert-space energy lemma there. In `exists_energyCurve` Lean instead approximates the free right-hand side $f$ by fields from a dense linear space: the estimate $\sup_\theta\|c_n(\theta)-c_m(\theta)\|_X\le\sqrt{4+6S}\,\|f_n-f_m\|_{\mathcal H}$ gives uniform convergence of the continuous periodic gradient states. The limit is an $X$-valued curve, not merely a continuous scalar energy.

ns7-data-s020.Breakdown.Symmetry: The condition can be written $v(\theta+\theta_0,Ry)=Rv(\theta,y)$: on advancing time by $\theta_0$, a velocity at the rotated point is the rotation of its former value. Neither the time shift nor the spatial action need fix the field on its own.

ns7-data-s021.Breakdown.Symmetry: The spatial part of a symmetry is a linear isometry, fixing the origin. Consequently the drift $y\cdot\nabla$ commutes with the induced action on velocities, as do the Laplacian and Leray projection. A spatial translation would introduce an extra term in the drift. No group axioms on the specified set of pairs are needed to impose these common fixed-point conditions.

ns7-data-s022.Breakdown.IsPerturbation.invariant: In Lean the relation is written with spatial argument $Ry$, so it becomes $v(\theta+\theta_0,Ry)=Rv(\theta,y)$. This is (7.5) after changing variables. For the weak perturbation the equality is almost everywhere.

ns7-data-s023.Breakdown.Cert.invariantHH: Each symmetry is represented by a bounded linear isometry $U$ on the period space. Its invariant fields form $\ker(U-I)$, a closed linear space; the intersection over $\Gamma$ is weakly closed as well. This matters when one takes a weak limit of right-hand sides in Proposition 7.10, without having pointwise convergence on the whole of space-time.
ns7-data-s023.Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.twist_me: When $(R,1/2)\in\Gamma$, the field at the next half-period may be different, but the gradient norm is unchanged under the orthogonal change of variables. It is the energy, not the velocity or the supplied residual representative, that can be followed for half a period in Proposition 7.9. Summing the energy increment over two translated intervals gives the improvement by $1/2$ in (7.55). Lean also allows the conservative choice $m=1$ in this case.

ns7-data-s024.Breakdown.Cert.invariantHH: Writing the time shift with a minus sign in the operator $\rho_{R,\theta_0}$ makes (7.5) precisely the fixed-point condition $\rho_{R,\theta_0}F=F$. Orthogonality of $R$ and translation invariance of the time-circle measure make this an isometry on $\mathcal H$.

ns7-data-s025.Breakdown.Cert.extendedInvarianceHolds_o: Under a rotation or reflection the derivative of $\rho_R G$ at $y$ is $R(DG)(R^{-1}y)R^{-1}$. Applying this derivative to $RF(R^{-1}y)$ gives $R((F\cdot\nabla)G)(R^{-1}y)$. The same identity holds with the common time shift. Hence convection of two invariant fields is invariant; in particular the nonlinear update preserves the symmetry class without projecting it back.

ns7-data-s026.Breakdown.Cert.invariantHH: The invariance of the domain of the free inverse follows from commutation and uniqueness: if $\rho_{R,\theta_0}f=f$, then $\mathcal T_S(\rho_{R,\theta_0}v)=f=\mathcal T_Sv$. Injectivity in Proposition 7.5 gives $\rho_{R,\theta_0}v=v$. Thus solving the free equation in the full space does not create any forbidden symmetry components.
ns7-data-s026.Breakdown.Cert.extendedInvarianceHolds_o: The residual need not itself be invariant. Nevertheless the other terms in (7.10) are invariant distributions and therefore have invariant pairings with solenoidal tests. Since (7.10) fixes the Leray projection of the residual, $\mathbb PF_\alpha^{\mathrm a}$ belongs to $\mathcal H_{\rm div}^\Gamma$. This is what allows the constrained solve to use the given residual.

ns7-data-s027.Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.params: The geometry of $K$ will be needed only to make the final parameter update admissible. At a fixed parameter the constrained inverse is constructed without using that geometry. The formal `params` already incorporates the scaled ball and intervals of (7.29).

ns7-data-s028.Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.profil: The family is chosen to make the eventual force cancellation possible, not merely to interpolate between numerical profiles. In Appendix C.4 the directions $W^i$, with changes in period and in forcing coefficients, are obtained by approximately solving linearized equations with prescribed constraint values. In (B.9) the family is affine in $\alpha$ inside the ball where the radial phase is fixed; outside it, a change of the period also changes the phase. This explains why the construction is not globally affine.
ns7-data-s028.Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.period: For fixed $\alpha$, $1/S(\alpha)$ is a given coefficient of $\partial_\theta$. A single normalized time circle therefore suffices for the family. The choice (B.9) makes $1/S(\alpha)$, rather than $S(\alpha)$, affine in $\alpha$; the same variation in the far-field radial phase is needed to cancel the leading transport term in the oscillatory tail (C.4). No derivative of the unknown exact period is needed in the trial equation.

ns7-data-s029.Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.period_c: Continuity of $S$ is used when a sequence of trial parameters converges: the operators in the free inverses are $\mathcal T_{S(\alpha_k)}$, and Proposition 7.5 gives local strong convergence of the corresponding velocities for weakly convergent right-hand sides. Together with positivity, continuity prevents a degenerate time rescaling in that limit.
ns7-data-s029.Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.period_p: The assumption is pointwise positivity on the compact set $K$, not a separate supplied lower bound for $S$. By continuity, $S$ has a positive minimum there. Consequently $1/S(\alpha_k)\to1/S(\alpha)$ whenever $\alpha_k\to\alpha$ in $K$, as needed when passing to the distributional limit of the normalized equations.
ns7-data-s029.Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.period_l: In (7.55) the factors $2S(\alpha)/m$ bound the growth of the slice energy over a period. Using the uniform $S_{\max}$ instead makes (7.27) a single sufficient inequality for all trial parameters.

ns7-data-s030.Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.profile_: In the limit of the equations (7.57), the two terms in $\mathcal C_\alpha v$ involve $W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}$ and $\nabla W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}$. Joint continuity makes these coefficients converge uniformly on the support of each test; the weak gradient and local strong velocity convergence then suffice. In (7.58) integration by parts similarly removes the need for continuity of the Hessian. Lean assumes a $C^1$ extension jointly in the ambient parameter, time and space, stronger than the stated continuity hypotheses.

ns7-data-s031.Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.profile_: The period-one identity belongs to the normalized field and holds independently of the candidate value of $S$. The formal hypothesis imposes it for all ambient parameter vectors, not only those in $K$ as in the paper.

The correction is constructed in a solenoidal space. Hence $\operatorname{div}(W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}+v)=\operatorname{div}W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}$, regardless of how small the momentum residual is. Zero divergence is therefore imposed on each approximate field before solving the correction equation.
ns7-data-s031.Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.profileS: No classical second derivative of $W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}$ is required in the paper: its spatial Hessian is a locally integrable distribution, whose trace gives the Laplacian. In Lean a weak Hessian is supplied on every time slice and has a pointwise decay bound. Neither formulation requires continuity of the Hessian in $\alpha$ for the parameter-limit argument, because the Laplacian can be integrated by parts against the test field.
ns7-data-s031.Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.profile_: Both convection and the free operator preserve the prescribed symmetry. Applied to (7.10), this makes the projected residual invariant, even if the chosen residual representative is not. Later, the same symmetry of the correction and approximate field gives (7.39) for their sum.

There are two steps in the compactness argument of Lemma 7.7. Outside $B_r$, the transport coefficient has supremum $O((1+r)^{-1})$ and the gradient coefficient has $L^3$ norm of the same order; Sobolev then gives a uniform small bound for the convection of a gradient-bounded perturbation. Inside $B_r$ the free inverse gives compactness of the velocities in $L^2$, and the bounded Laplacians give compactness of the gradients by integration by parts with a cutoff. Neither conclusion is compactness of the homogeneous Sobolev embedding on all of space. The formal decay hypothesis additionally bounds the weak Hessian of the approximate field.
ns7-data-s031.Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.actuator: The map $\beta\mapsto\sum_i\beta_i b_i$ has operator norm from Euclidean space to $\mathcal H$ at most $(\sum_i\|b_i\|_{\mathcal H}^2)^{1/2}\le b_*$. This estimate does not require orthogonality. In the energy estimate (7.55) the force therefore contributes at most $b_*|\beta|\|v\|_w$. Injectivity of the projected forcing map is a different matter: it follows from (7.18) by taking $v=0$ and $F=0$ if $\sum_i\beta_i b_i\simeq0$.
ns7-data-s031.Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.multipli: The force fields $b_i$ are fixed; continuity of $\beta^{\mathrm a}(\alpha)$ therefore gives strong continuity of the finite linear combination in $\mathcal H$. For the residual it will suffice to know continuity after testing modulo gradients, as shown in (7.58).
ns7-data-s031.Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.defect: The residual is a representative of the left side of (7.10) modulo gradients. In Lean `defect` chooses it by adding `pressureGrad` to the displayed momentum terms and the approximate forcing coefficients. This sum, not each of its terms, must be in $\mathcal H$. With the sign convention of (7.10), the force in the approximate momentum equation is $-\sum_i\beta_i^{\mathrm a}b_i$; the correction has to remove that force as well as the residual.

ns7-data-s032.Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.defect_l: For a fixed $\alpha$, a representative $F_\alpha^{\mathrm a}$ may include a gradient. Its full norm is the bound in (7.23) and in Lean's squared-integral hypothesis. Projection can decrease the norm, but a computation need not find the orthogonal representative in order to supply a sufficient upper bound.
ns7-data-s032.Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.pressure: The condition on `pressureGrad` is precisely what is needed for the residual pairing: its integral against every solenoidal test is zero. A pressure gradient may cancel non-square-integrable terms in the approximate equation before the residual is measured. The certificate need not supply a smooth scalar pressure, and does not require its gradient separately to belong to $\mathcal H$.

ns7-data-s033.Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.defect: A gradient in $\mathcal H$ can be added to $F_\alpha^{\mathrm a}$ without changing the solution of the constrained equation. But (7.24) is a bound for a chosen representative: the gradient may change both its norm and the additional row measurements. In contrast, the adjoint pairing in (7.34) is independent of this choice, since (7.33) with $v=0$ implies that $\psi_{\alpha,j}$ is solenoidal.
ns7-data-s033.Breakdown.Cert.extendedDataContinuityHol: For the linear solve it is enough that $\alpha\mapsto\mathbb PF_\alpha^{\mathrm a}$ be weakly continuous. Indeed, in a solenoidal test pairing one can replace the residual by (7.10) and move one derivative off the Laplacian; the remaining profile coefficients converge uniformly on the compact support of the test. By (7.23) the projected residuals are uniformly bounded in $\mathcal H$, so density of the periodized solenoidal tests upgrades the continuity of these pairings to weak continuity. There is no corresponding assertion of norm continuity, or even weak continuity, for an arbitrary choice of unprojected representatives.

ns7-data-s034.Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData: Use $f=\mathcal T_Sv$ as the unknown. On $\mathcal H_{\rm div}^\Gamma\times\mathbb R^n$ the bordered map then differs from the identity by $(\mathbb P\mathcal C_\alpha\mathcal T_S^{-1}f+\sum_i\beta_i\mathbb Pb_i,\,\ell(\mathcal T_S^{-1}f)-\beta)$. Its first velocity term is compact by Lemma 7.7 and the remaining terms are bounded and finite rank. Thus the map has index zero; (7.52) rules out a kernel and the Fredholm alternative gives a unique solution for every admissible right-hand side and constraint vector.

ns7-data-s035.Breakdown.pinValue:
The constraints measure the correction in directions of large response to the linearized equation. Indeed for constant $w$, if one could take $\Xi_i=
abla(wv_i-\Delta v_i)$ for such a response $v_i$, integration by parts would give $\ell_i(v)=w\langle
abla v,
abla v_iangle_{\mathcal H}+\langle\Delta v,\Delta v_iangle_{\mathcal H}$, the weighted inner product with $v_i$. In Appendix C.4 the gradients are approximated by cell polynomials, which need not themselves be gradients. Cauchy–Schwarz still gives a bounded functional of $v$, and the approximation error is accounted for in Appendix B.
ns7-data-s035.Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.target: The paper prescribes $\ell(v)=\bar\ell(\alpha)$, while Lean prescribes the value $t(\alpha)$ on the corrected profile. Since $\ell$ is linear, these formulations agree with $\bar\ell(\alpha)=t(\alpha)-\ell(W_\alpha^{\mathrm a})$, the quantity `targetGap`. In particular a target of substantial size need not cost much in (7.24) if it is already nearly attained by the approximate profile. When the parameter is fixed, this gap cancels upon subtracting two linear solves.
ns7-data-s035.Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.pin_fini: The gradient pairing is bounded on the period-$L^2$ space by Cauchy–Schwarz, so it passes to the limit under weak convergence of gradients. Lean requires measurability and finite square integral on the unit interval; it does not separately require the original representative of the pin field to be periodic.

ns7-data-s036.Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.IsHeld: At a fixed parameter the free inverse identifies $f=\mathcal T_Sv$ with $v$. The predicate `IsHeldSolution` states that the resulting velocity solves the nonlinear constrained equation and obeys the pair and slice-gradient bounds. It still allows a nonzero total force. Its finite-dimensional coefficient variable is normalized to $\omega\beta$, with the forcing fields divided by $\omega$.
ns7-data-s036.Breakdown.Cert.sliceConvection:
Expanding the convection of $W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}+v$ gives the approximate convection, the mixed terms $(W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}\cdot
abla)v+(v\cdot
abla)W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}$ and $(v\cdot
abla)v$. The first two mixed terms form the linear operator $\mathcal C_\alpha$ in (7.13), so the only unknown nonlinear right-hand side in a trial solve is $-(v\cdot
abla)v$.

ns7-data-s037.Breakdown.Cert.extendedHeldWeakEquationH: At each parameter the residual cancels on adding (7.10) and (7.12), but the force in the equation for $W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}+v$ is still $-\sum_i(\beta_i^{\mathrm a}+\beta_i)b_i$. Thus neither solving the correction equation nor finding a small $\beta$ gives an unforced profile. The last step must cancel the total coefficients, including those already present in the approximate equation.

ns7-data-s038.Breakdown.extended_certificate_orbit_pro: A solution of (7.12) at a prescribed parameter need not be a solution without force: its coefficient vector is still $\beta^{\mathrm a}(\alpha)+\beta$. The certificate first bounds the correction and then supplies conditions on that total vector. In the linked Lean proof a unique bounded constrained nonlinear solution is obtained at each parameter; continuity and the enclosure of its coefficient vector are used to find a zero. The paper obtains the parameter and the nonlinear solution together.

ns7-data-s039.Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData: The correction radius is independent of $\alpha$. This is needed to map the same set of trial quadratic fields into itself while the parameter changes. The residual estimate may still exploit the smaller values $\delta(\alpha),\delta_0(\alpha)$ at an individual parameter. In contrast, the energy estimate uses the common $\delta_{\max}$ and $S_{\max}$ to give one bound on the slice gradients.

ns7-data-s040.Breakdown.weightedEnergy: The norm is chosen for two different estimates. Control of $\Delta v$ and $\nabla v$ in the period integral gives $\|v(\theta)\|_\infty\le c_w|v(\theta)|_w$ almost everywhere in time. To integrate the product $|v||\nabla v|$ in $L^2$ one also needs a bound for the maximum of the gradient norm; controlling just the two period integrals would not give this product estimate. The latter bound comes from (7.22), not from (7.18) alone.

ns7-data-s041.Breakdown.Cert.IsAdmissibleWeight: With $0<w_*\le w\le\|w\|_\infty$, the norm $|u|_w^2$ lies between $\|\Delta u\|_2^2+w_*\|\nabla u\|_2^2$ and $\|\Delta u\|_2^2+\|w\|_\infty\|\nabla u\|_2^2$. Thus it is an equivalent norm on the intersection of the homogeneous first- and second-derivative spaces. The weight changes which perturbations are expensive, without changing the underlying class. Lean additionally requires invariance under the spatial parts of the prescribed symmetries.
ns7-data-s041.Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.multipli: The coefficient weight trades velocity allowance against force allowance in the same estimate. At a fixed pair radius, $\omega|\beta|\le2\varepsilon$ gives the crude force bound used outside $\mathcal J$. Increasing $\omega$ changes the inverse bound (7.18) that must be verified; it cannot be done merely to make (7.37) easier.
ns7-data-s041.Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.weightFn: The formal weight is invariant under every spatial part $R$ of a symmetry: $w(Ry)=w(y)$. Changing spatial variables then preserves the weighted gradient energy. The abstract paper does not impose this hypothesis; the constant weight in Appendix B satisfies it.

ns7-data-s042.Breakdown.weightedEnergy: The two terms of the weighted norm are used differently. The Laplacian is paired with the right-hand side in the energy identity, so $\|\Delta v\|_{\mathcal H}\le\|v\|_w$. The gradient term gives $\int_0^1\|\nabla v(\theta)\|_2^2\,d\theta\le\|v\|_w^2/w_*$, the bound for the minimum slice energy.
ns7-data-s042.Breakdown.stationaryEnergy: The form (7.22) is tested on a single spatial field, at a fixed phase of the approximate profile. Only symmetries $(R,0)\in\Gamma$ restrict that field: a symmetry involving a nonzero time shift relates different slices and need not hold on either slice alone. The lower bound $-c_3|u|_w^2$ allows instantaneous growth, but after setting $u=v(\theta)$ the growth term is integrable and costs at most $c_3\|v\|_w^2$ over one period.
ns7-data-s042.Breakdown.Cert.sizeZ: Set $\widehat\beta=\omega\beta$ and $\widehat b_i=b_i/\omega$. The force is unchanged, and the norm now has coefficient weight one. To preserve (7.30) one must also replace $\beta^{\mathrm a}$ by $\omega\beta^{\mathrm a}$ and $V_j$ by $V_j/\omega$. The bound $b_*$ scales by $1/\omega$, as does $\langle b,\psi_j\rangle-V_j$. Thus the normalization leaves both the physical forcing and the parameter enclosure unchanged.
ns7-data-s042.Breakdown.supBoundFactor: Xie's inequality bounds $\|u\|_\infty^2$ by $(2\pi)^{-1}\|\nabla u\|_2\|\Delta u\|_2$. Apply $2ab\le a^2+b^2$ with $a=\|\Delta u\|_2$, $b=\sqrt{w_*}\|\nabla u\|_2$: the resulting coefficient is $1/(4\pi\sqrt{w_*})=c_w^2$. This explains the square root in the definition of $c_w$.

ns7-data-s043.Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.coercive: The reference profile need not be an accurate approximate solution of the nonlinear equation. What is required of it is an inverse estimate and a small difference of its linearized convection from that of the approximate profile. In Appendix B one reference field is used for every parameter; this permits the same spatial coefficient description in the cell estimates while the periods and approximate profiles vary. The residual, however, is always that of $W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}$.

ns7-data-s044.Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.gap_tran:
Lemma B.9 separates the difference into $Z_0=W_0^{\mathrm a}-W^{\mathrm r}$ and $Z_1=W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}-W_0^{\mathrm a}$. The transport term is bounded by $(\|Z_0\|_\infty+\|Z_1\|_\infty)\|
abla u\|_2$ at each phase; for the other term use $\|u\|_\infty\|
abla Z_0\|_2$ and $\|u\|_6\|
abla Z_1\|_3$, with operator norms on the coefficient gradients. All three are bounded by constants times $|u|_w$. Squaring and integrating the resulting slice bound gives (7.19).

ns7-data-s045.Breakdown.Cert.sliceConvection: The map $W\mapsto\mathcal C_Wv$ is linear in $W$ at fixed $v$. Therefore replacing $W_\alpha^{\mathrm r}$ by $W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}$ adds $(D\cdot\nabla)v+(v\cdot\nabla)D$, where $D=W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}-W_\alpha^{\mathrm r}$. Both terms must be controlled in (7.19).

ns7-data-s046.Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.coercive: For fixed constraint values the right-hand side has two different costs. If $F$ is orthogonal to all the $e_k$, its cost in (7.18) is $c_1\|F\|_{\mathcal H}$; in the worst case it is $(c_1+c_0)\|F\|_{\mathcal H}$. Thus a large inverse response in a few directions need not impose that same large constant on every right-hand side. In Appendix B the additional measurements arise from a finite-dimensional estimate of the lower quadratic form; the error components not measured by the rows still have to be controlled.

ns7-data-s047.Breakdown.rowNorm: In Lean the row fields are orthonormal and carry weights $\tau_k\ge0$. The paper's fields $e_k$ correspond to $\sqrt{\tau_k}$ times these unit fields; hence $\tau_k\le c_0^2$ gives exactly the length bound in (7.17). A zero weight removes that row from the seminorm.
ns7-data-s047.Breakdown.Cert.rowNormHolds: Writing $e_k=\sqrt{\tau_k}\widehat e_k$ with unit, mutually orthogonal $\widehat e_k$, Bessel's inequality gives $[F]^2=\sum_k\tau_k|\langle F,\widehat e_k\rangle|^2\le c_0^2\|F\|_{\mathcal H}^2$. The triangle inequality is the ordinary Euclidean one for the vector of these weighted measurements. Zero rows of the paper can be discarded or assigned weight zero.

ns7-data-s048.Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.coercive: Lean assumes $c_2\ge0$ explicitly, while (7.18) allows real $c_2$. In fact, once Proposition 7.8 is proved and $n>0$, one may solve the transferred linear equation with $F=0$ and any nonzero constraint value. Inequality (7.52) then forces $c_2>0$. When $n=0$ the constraint term vanishes and its sign is immaterial.

ns7-data-s049.Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.coercive: The homogeneous constrained problem is the case $F=0$, $\ell(v)=0$, not necessarily a pointwise zero left-hand side: it may be a gradient. The estimate then implies $\beta=0$ and $\nabla v=0$, and the $L^6$ realization of $X$ excludes a nonzero spatial constant. After transfer to the approximate profile this gives injectivity. For existence, Proposition 7.8 uses the fact that in free-forcing coordinates the bordered operator is identity plus compact.

ns7-data-s050.Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.coercive: Projection decreases the norm of $F$ but not necessarily its row measurements. For example let $p$ be a unit solenoidal field, $q$ an orthogonal unit gradient, $F=p-q$ and $e_1=(p+q)/\sqrt2$. Then $[F]=0$ but $[\mathbb PF]=1/\sqrt2$. Thus the two terms of (7.18) should be evaluated for the same chosen representative; one cannot replace each independently by its projected value.
ns7-data-s050.Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.adjoint_: The inverse estimate may use the full representative $F$. The adjoint estimate has an additional consequence: putting $v=0$ in (7.33) makes every gradient $F\in\mathcal H$ invisible to $\psi_{\alpha,j}$. Consequently its pairing depends only on the projected residual, even when the finite row measurements in (7.17) do not.

ns7-data-s051.Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.gapSize_: The formal hypothesis bounds a square by $c_{\mathrm r}^2\|v\|_w^2$. The condition $c_{\mathrm r}\ge0$ allows its square root to be used in the absorption argument. It also ensures that the transfer loss $(c_1+c_0)c_{\mathrm r}$ is a nonnegative cost, rather than an apparent improvement of the inverse estimate.
ns7-data-s051.Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.coercive: The constant $c_L$ estimates a linear solve with zero constraint values, or the difference of two solves at the same parameter with equal constraint values. It need not estimate the entire response with prescribed nonzero constraints. This is why it controls the nonlinear iteration, whereas (7.24) uses $c_1$, $\delta_0$ and $c_2$ separately.

ns7-data-s052.Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.gap_tran: Keep $(v,\beta)$ fixed and put $G=(\mathcal C_\alpha-\mathcal C_\alpha^{\mathrm r})v$. If $F$ is a right-hand side at the approximate profile, then $F-G$ is one at the reference profile. The change therefore costs only the two right-hand-side terms of (7.18), with no new constraint term. Since the equations are modulo gradients, it is not necessary to project $G$ before applying that estimate.
ns7-data-s052.Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.transf: The triangle inequalities in the reference estimate give $c_1\|F-G\|+[F-G]\le c_1\|F\|+[F]+(c_1+c_0)\|G\|$. By (7.19), the last term is at most $\vartheta\|v\|_w$. The row bound $c_0$ is needed even if $[F]=0$, since the change of convection can have components in the row directions.
ns7-data-s052.Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.transfer: The right-hand side of (7.19) involves the unknown $v$, so the new term cannot be treated as an independently supplied small residual. It is at most $\vartheta\|v\|_w\le\vartheta\|(v,\beta)\|_{w,\omega}$. Absorbing it on the left is possible precisely with the strict margin $1-\vartheta>0$ in this argument. No smallness of the particular solution has been used.
ns7-data-s052.Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.coercive: With $\ell(v)=0$, (7.52) gives $\|(v,\beta)\|_{w,\omega}\le(c_1+c_0)\|F\|_{\mathcal H}/(1-\vartheta)\le c_L\|F\|_{\mathcal H}$. This is the estimate for a difference of two solves at the same parameter. For the residual itself it is better to retain the separate seminorm and prescribed constraint terms.
ns7-data-s052.Breakdown.Cert.Internal.AtProfile.coerci: There are two useful consequences of the same transferred estimate (7.52). Retaining all three terms gives the bound for the particular approximate residual and prescribed constraint gap in (7.24). For a difference of solves at fixed parameter the constraints cancel and the new right-hand side can be arbitrary; then use $[F]\le c_0\|F\|_{\mathcal H}$ to obtain the uniform constant $c_L$. Using the latter estimate for the residual as well could lose the benefit of small row measurements.

ns7-data-s053.Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.atProf: After transfer, the inverse bound has the same form as (7.18), with $c_1,c_2$ and the row seminorm divided by $1-\vartheta$. In the formal data this means dividing the row weights by $(1-\vartheta)^2$, since the seminorm takes a square root, and dividing both the row bound and the residual row allowance by $1-\vartheta$. The reference field is then set equal to the approximate field; the frozen-form bound is transferred separately.

ns7-data-s054.Breakdown.weightedEnergy: An integral bound alone can be compatible with very large values on a short interval. Let $E(\theta)=\|\nabla v(\theta)\|_2^2$. The bound $\min E\le\|v\|_w^2/w_*$ supplies a starting value, and (7.22) bounds the increase of $E$ from this value. Integrating the differential inequality, rather than estimating a time derivative separately, is what supplies the maximum needed in (7.49).
ns7-data-s054.Breakdown.Cert.ProductBoundHolds:
For different fields $v,z$, the pointwise inequality $|(v\cdot
abla)z|\le |v||
abla z|$ and (7.48) give $\|(v\cdot
abla)z\|_{\mathcal H}\le c_w\|v\|_w\sup_	heta\|
abla z(	heta)\|_2$. In particular the weighted norm always estimates the undifferentiated factor and the time supremum estimates the differentiated one. The same bound will be used on each of the two products in a difference of quadratic terms.

ns7-data-s055.Breakdown.Cert.Internal.ExtendedFrozenBr:
The positive gradient term in (7.22) comes from the similarity drift, not from an additional dissipation assumption. For a compactly supported smooth $u$, $
abla((y\cdot
abla)u)=

abla u\|_2^2$. Lemma 7.4 proves the interval identity on $\mathcal D_S$ without requiring the drift separately to be square integrable. The remaining contribution to the form is diffusion and the convection at the chosen phase.

ns7-data-s056.Breakdown.Cert.ExtendedSupBoundHolds: Write $E(\theta)=\|\nabla v(\theta)\|_2^2$ and $Q_\alpha(\theta,v)$ for the left side of (7.22). With right-hand side $F$ in the linear problem, (7.42) gives $E'/(2S)=-Q_\alpha(\theta,v)+\langle F-\sum_i\beta_i b_i,-\Delta v\rangle_{L^2}$. The upper bound on $E'$ is integrable even without control of the separate time derivative of $v$. Start at a minimum of $E$, bounded by $\|v\|_w^2/w_*$. Sum the increments over $m$ translates by $1/m$, which have the same energy increment but disjoint integration intervals. The bound over one period divided by $m$ gives (7.55), even for a residual representative without the shorter period.

ns7-data-s057.Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.IsHeld: The two bounds are on different quantities: the pair norm measures period-integrated spatial derivatives and the force coefficients, while $M$ bounds the slice gradient. They combine in the bilinear estimate (7.49), using the period norm for the undifferentiated factor and the supremum for the differentiated one. Lean's held-solution predicate records the normalized pair and an essential time supremum.

ns7-data-s058.Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData: The smallness of $F_\alpha^{\mathrm a}$ is used in two different norms of the solution. To bound the period-integrated correction, use the inverse estimate with its special row measurements and constraint term, as in (7.24). To bound a maximum in time, the energy identity pairs the forcing with $-\Delta v$, so only its full $\mathcal H$ norm is needed. The uniform bound $\delta_{\max}$ is used for this second purpose in (7.27).

ns7-data-s059.Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.defect_l: The quantity bounded by $\delta(\alpha)$ is $\|F_\alpha^{\mathrm a}\|_{\mathcal H}$ before projection. Lean states the squared integral inequality and separately imposes nonnegativity of the bound, so taking a square root gives (7.23).
ns7-data-s059.Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.defect_r: If the residual is nearly orthogonal to the selected rows, $\delta_0(\alpha)$ can be much less than $c_0\delta(\alpha)$. Equation (7.24) uses that smaller value directly, which can be decisive for a small correction radius.
ns7-data-s059.Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.defect_l: In the trial equation the right side is $-F_\alpha^{\mathrm a}-g$. Since $\|g\|_{\mathcal H}\le2c_w\varepsilon M$, the common bound $\delta_{\max}+2c_w\varepsilon M$ is available in (7.55) for every parameter and every trial $g$.
ns7-data-s059.Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.size: Let $L_\alpha^{-1}$ denote the constrained linear inverse of Proposition 7.8, with both forcing and constraint values as data. By linearity its response to $(-F_\alpha^{\mathrm a}-g,\bar\ell(\alpha))$ is the sum of the response to $(-F_\alpha^{\mathrm a},\bar\ell(\alpha))$ and that to $(-g,0)$. The former has norm at most $\varepsilon$ by (7.24); the latter has norm at most $c_L\|g\|_{\mathcal H}\le\varepsilon$ by (7.25) for the trial forcing ball. The factor two in the correction radius leaves room for the nonlinear term.
ns7-data-s059.Breakdown.Cert.ProductBoundHolds: The trial variable is an arbitrary invariant field $g$ of norm at most $2c_w\varepsilon M$. It is not required to have the form $(u\cdot\nabla)u$. The linear solve with this $g$ produces a $v$ satisfying the two bounds (7.59), so Lemma 7.6 gives $\|(v\cdot\nabla)v\|_{\mathcal H}\le c_w(2\varepsilon)M$. This proves that the quadratic-field update maps the ball into itself; equality with the trial field is obtained only at the fixed point.

ns7-data-s060.Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.small_fi: In the paper the inequality says that the linear response to a trial quadratic term of norm $2c_w\varepsilon M$ fits in the radius $\varepsilon$ left by the residual. Strictness is not needed for that inclusion alone. It matters for the formal fixed-parameter contraction: the difference of two quadratic terms has two products, and (7.26) controls the scaled gradient supremum of the output difference. The resulting contraction constant is $2c_Lc_wM$, not a constant involving the derivative of the parameter update.
ns7-data-s060.Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.small_se: Subtract two solves at the same parameter and let $h$ be the difference of their right-hand sides. The constraints and the approximate residual disappear, and the pair norm of the difference is at most $r=c_L\|h\|_{\mathcal H}$. Substitution in (7.55), with $|\beta_{\rm diff}|\le r/\omega$, gives $\sup E_{\rm diff}\le Ar^2$, where $A=1/w_*+(2S_{\max}/m)(c_3+b_*/\omega+1/c_L)$ is the bracket in (7.26). Hence $(2\varepsilon/M)\sup\|\nabla v_{\rm diff}\|_2\le r$. Lean needs this estimate to contract in both norms; the joint Schauder proof does not.
ns7-data-s060.Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.small_th: This inequality is for one solve rather than the difference of two. With $F=-F_\alpha^{\mathrm a}-g$ and the pair bound $2\varepsilon$, the right side of (7.55) is bounded by $4\varepsilon^2(1/w_*+2S_{\max}c_3/m)+(4S_{\max}\varepsilon/m)(\delta_{\max}+2c_w\varepsilon M+2\varepsilon b_*/\omega)$. Thus (7.27) supplies the slice-gradient bound $M$ for the output, including the effect of the approximate residual. This is distinct from the role of (7.26) for differences.

ns7-data-s061.Breakdown.Cert.extendedHeldContractsHold: In the fixed-parameter proof the constraint values stay fixed, so the difference of two linear solves costs at most $c_L$ times the forcing difference. That difference contains $((x-y)\cdot\nabla)x$ and $(y\cdot\nabla)(x-y)$; the period norm controls the undifferentiated factor and the slice maximum controls the differentiated one. The difference estimate (7.26) makes both output norms contract with factor $2c_Lc_wM$. Proposition 7.10 instead takes the quadratic field as an unknown and uses weak compactness.

ns7-data-s062.Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.nontrivi:
If the corrected field were zero, $
abla v=-
abla W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}$, and $w_*\|
abla W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}\|_{\mathcal H}^2=w_*\|
abla v\|_{\mathcal H}^2\le\|v\|_w^2\le4\varepsilon^2$. This contradicts (7.28). The lower bound is required throughout $K$ because the parameter will only be determined at the end.
ns7-data-s062.Breakdown.Cert.extendedHeldNonzeroHolds_: Nonvanishing is proved from the integrated gradient energy: an almost-everywhere zero corrected velocity would have zero weak gradient and would force the correction to cancel the approximate gradient. The strict inequality (7.28) excludes this. The formal conclusion is nonvanishing as a space-time field, not a claim that the velocity is nonzero at every point.

ns7-data-s063.Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.params: The shape of $K$ matches the estimates available for the next parameter. The adjoint bounds control the individual scaled changes $d_j\alpha'_j$ when $j\in\mathcal J$; the remaining estimate controls the Euclidean length of the vector $(d_j\alpha'_j)_{j\notin\mathcal J}$. Thus one requires the corresponding intervals and a single ball, rather than paying for a separate worst-case estimate of every remaining coordinate.
ns7-data-s063.Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.scale_ne: A nonzero scale $d_j$ allows the update to divide by it, and in the complementary ball one obtains $|\alpha_j|\le\varrho_*/|d_j|$. Either sign is allowed; its square determines the ball and its sign determines the direction of the update.

ns7-data-s064.Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.params: In scaled coordinates $d_j\alpha_j$ for $j\notin\mathcal J$, $K$ is a product of closed intervals and a closed ball. It is compact and convex even with zero radii. Thus the parameter step can use a compact-convex fixed-point theorem without requiring an interior.

ns7-data-s065.Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.frame_un: The columns $V_j$ are the directions in which the total coefficient vector is tested. They need not coincide with the forcing fields or be orthogonal. In particular $V_j$ can be chosen close to the vector of adjoint pairings (7.31). Their linear independence is needed at the end: if every tested component vanishes, then $V^{\mathsf T}(\beta^{\mathrm a}+\beta)=0$ implies $\beta^{\mathrm a}+\beta=0$.

ns7-data-s066.Breakdown.Held.testSetZero_of: Writing $D=\operatorname{diag}(d_j)$, the unprojected change is $-D^{-1}V^{\mathsf T}(\beta^{\mathrm a}+\beta)$. Since both matrices are invertible, the change is zero if and only if the total coefficient vector is zero. The linked theorem uses the same update with a continuous total coefficient map from the held nonlinear solves.

ns7-data-s067.Breakdown.Held.testSetZero_of: The matrix of the parameter step is an approximation to an inverse derivative, but its accuracy is not measured in a derivative norm. For a nonlinear correction at a given $\alpha$, write $B=\beta^{\mathrm a}(\alpha)+\beta$. The conditions instead estimate the values of $V^{\mathsf T}B-D\alpha$ throughout $K$, with $D=\operatorname{diag}(d_j)$. These are bounds on the deviation from the intended linear map, sufficient to place the update in $K$. Neither differentiability nor a contraction of the update is needed.

ns7-data-s068.Breakdown.Held.testSetZero_of: The condition required of a nonlinear solution at $\alpha$ is $\alpha'\in K$, not merely that its force be small. In one dimension, a projected update from $\alpha=1$ to $\alpha'=2$ on $K=[-1,1]$ has a fixed point at $1$, even though the change is nonzero. The enclosure inequalities exclude this possibility: at a fixed point the projection acts on a point already in $K$, hence $\alpha'=\alpha$.

ns7-data-s069.Breakdown.Cert.ExtendedAdjointEnclosureH: The two types of coordinate enclosure differ in what is known about the correction. The radius $2\varepsilon$ by itself gives only $|V_j\cdot\beta|\le 2\varepsilon|V_j|/\omega$. For $j\in\mathcal J$ the adjoint identity instead predicts the signed value of this component from the given residual and constraint values. An estimate of the error in this prediction can be much smaller than an estimate of the entire component.
ns7-data-s069.Breakdown.Cert.ExtendedStiffEnclosureHol: For the complementary coordinates no adjoint measurements are needed. Inequality (7.36) bounds the Euclidean length of $(V_j\cdot\beta)_{j\notin\mathcal J}$ by $a_*|\beta|\le2\varepsilon a_*/\omega$. This gives one enclosure for all these coordinates at once. The corresponding normalized Lean bound uses coefficient weight one.

ns7-data-s070.Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.adjoint_: The bound on $\psi_{\alpha,j}$ in Lean is a uniform slice $L^2$ bound, whereas the abstract paper asks only for membership in $\mathcal H$ and the pairing estimate (7.32). Lemma B.10 gives two sufficient ways of deriving the latter, one using a uniform slice $L^3$ bound and the other a uniform slice $L^2$ bound. The formal hypothesis selects the second type of slice control and also states (7.32) separately.
ns7-data-s070.Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.adjoin: The exact model for $\psi_{\alpha,j}$ is a row of the inverse of the constrained linear problem, not an adjoint eigenfunction. At fixed $\alpha$, the linear inverse sends $(\mathbb PF,\ell)$ to $(v,\beta)$; by (7.52) its coefficient functional $V_j\cdot\beta$ is bounded. Its Hilbert-space representation is $V_j\cdot\beta=\langle F,\psi_{\alpha,j}\rangle_{\mathcal H}-(Y\ell)_j$ with solenoidal $\psi_{\alpha,j}$. Testing first on $v=0$, then on $\beta=0$, gives the ideal forms of (7.31) and (7.33). The certificate uses approximate representatives of these rows and additionally requires control of their nonlinear pairings.
ns7-data-s070.Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.coupli: The $j$th row of $Y(\alpha)$ specifies the constraint functional that is to be represented by the adjoint of the linearized equation. Since $\ell(v)=\bar\ell(\alpha)$ is prescribed, its value is known before the velocity is found. Condition (7.33) bounds the difference between the two functionals in the dual of the weighted perturbation norm; no pointwise equation for the adjoint or differentiation of $Y$ in the parameter is required in Section 7.

ns7-data-s071.Breakdown.periodPairing: By linearity, $\langle\sum_i\beta_i b_i,\psi_{\alpha,j}\rangle_{\mathcal H}=\beta\cdot\langle b,\psi_{\alpha,j}\rangle_{\mathcal H}$. Thus one adjoint field gives a single scalar measurement of the entire coefficient vector. The vector (7.31) is the corresponding row of the measurement, written as a column to compare with $V_j$.
ns7-data-s071.Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.actuat: The measurement vector $\langle b,\psi_{\alpha,j}\rangle_{\mathcal H}$ can vary with $\alpha$, while $V_j$ in the parameter update is fixed. Define $E_j$ to be their difference. Replacing the measured scalar by $V_j\cdot\beta$ introduces $\beta\cdot E_j$, bounded by $|E_j|\,\omega|\beta|/\omega$ as in (7.35).

ns7-data-s072.Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.adjoint_: Here one needs only a scalar pairing, not the full $\mathcal H$ norm of the quadratic term. For example a uniform slice bound $\|\psi_{\alpha,j}(\theta)\|_2\le n_j$ gives $|\langle(v\cdot\nabla)v,\psi_{\alpha,j}\rangle_{\mathcal H}|\le n_jc_w\|v\|_w^2/\sqrt{w_*}$, by applying (7.48) and the gradient bound at each phase and then integrating. Lemma B.10 also gives an alternative using the slice $L^3$ norm. Neither estimate pays for the gradient supremum $M$, which is needed for the full norm of convection.

In (7.33) the representative $F$ corresponds to the linearized velocity equation alone, without forcing coefficients. Thus for a nonlinear correction one takes $F'=-F_\alpha^{\mathrm a}-(v\cdot\nabla)v-\sum_i\beta_i b_i$. Substitution gives a scalar equation involving $V_j\cdot\beta$, the known residual and constraint pairings, and the quadratic pairing. Its linear-functional error is bounded by $a_j\|v\|_w$; the replacement of the actual actuator pairings by $V_j$ is estimated separately.

The expression before $-d_j\alpha_j$ is a computable approximation to the total force coefficient in direction $V_j$ after correcting the profile. One wants this predicted coefficient to be near $d_j\alpha_j$, not near zero for every $\alpha$. For the represented certificate, the prescribed constraint gap is zero when $\mathcal J$ is nonempty. In the interior ball of Appendix B the residual has an exact quadratic expansion in the parameters (B.57); Lemma B.13 encloses the error in the intended slope and the other terms, including the exterior residual separately. The allowance $o_j$ is then independent of the unknown correction.

The tolerance in the scaled coordinate is $|d_j|\varrho_j$. The first term in (7.35) bounds the quadratic adjoint pairing on $\|v\|_w\le2\varepsilon$; the square-root term bounds the two linear errors together, using the full pair radius. Adding the known offset $o_j$ leaves at most $|d_j|\varrho_j$ for $|V_j\cdot(\beta^{\mathrm a}+\beta)-d_j\alpha_j|=|d_j\alpha'_j|$.
ns7-data-s072.Breakdown.Cert.extendedAdjointPairingHol: Apply (7.33) with $v=0$ and $F=(I-\mathbb P)\psi_{\alpha,j}$. Then $F\simeq0$ and $\ell(v)=0$, so $\langle F,\psi_{\alpha,j}\rangle=0$. By orthogonality the same pairing is $\|F\|_{\mathcal H}^2$, giving $\psi_{\alpha,j}\in\mathcal H_{\rm div}$. In particular the adjoint measurement of (7.12) is independent of the gradient representative of the residual.
ns7-data-s072.Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.adjust: At a given parameter the predicted correction coefficient is the negative of the residual pairing and the prescribed constraint pairing. Adding $V_j\cdot\beta^{\mathrm a}$ gives `adjustedMultiplier`, a known approximation to $V_j\cdot(\beta^{\mathrm a}+\beta)$. The prediction does not require that the residual itself be continuous as an unprojected field, or that the adjoint field vary continuously with the parameter. Continuity is needed for the actual update obtained from the solution, not for the separate pointwise enclosures of its error.

ns7-data-s073.Breakdown.Cert.ExtendedAdjointEnclosureH: Use $F'=-F_\alpha^{\mathrm a}-(v\cdot\nabla)v-\sum_i\beta_i b_i$ in (7.33), since $F'\simeq\mathcal T_Sv+\mathcal C_\alpha v$. Moving the residual and constraint terms to the left then gives $|\beta\cdot\langle b,\psi_{\alpha,j}\rangle+\langle F_\alpha^{\mathrm a},\psi_{\alpha,j}\rangle+(Y\bar\ell)_j|\le a_j\|v\|_w+\widetilde a_j\|v\|_w^2$. The formal enclosure also accounts for replacing the measured direction by $V_j$.

ns7-data-s074.Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.actuat: Set $E_j=\langle b,\psi_{\alpha,j}\rangle_{\mathcal H}-V_j$. The linear errors are bounded by $a_j\|v\|_w+(|E_j|/\omega)\omega|\beta|$. Cauchy–Schwarz in $\mathbb R^2$ gives $\sqrt{a_j^2+|E_j|^2/\omega^2}\|(v,\beta)\|_{w,\omega}$. This is sharper than separately replacing both components by $2\varepsilon$, since their squares share one radius.

ns7-data-s075.Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.adjoint_: Denote the computable prediction in (7.34) by $p_j$. To enclose the next parameter, write $-d_j\alpha'_j=(p_j-d_j\alpha_j)+(V_j\cdot(\beta^{\mathrm a}+\beta)-p_j)$. The first term is an error in the approximate family, bounded by (7.34) without solving for $v$. The second is the error in the adjoint prediction for the response of the constrained problem; its bound uses the radius of $(v,\beta)$. This separation is also the distinction between Lemmas B.13 and B.12.
ns7-data-s075.Breakdown.Cert.ExtendedAdjointEnclosureH: The enclosure is sharper than a separate estimate for each of $\|v\|_w$ and $\omega|\beta|$. The linear error uses $a_j\|v\|_w+|E_j||\beta|\le\sqrt{a_j^2+|E_j|^2/\omega^2}\|(v,\beta)\|_{w,\omega}$, and the quadratic one uses $\widetilde a_j\|v\|_w^2$. Only after these two estimates is the known offset $o_j$ added.

ns7-data-s076.Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.stiff_no: Let $A_*$ have rows $V_j^{\mathsf T}$ for $j\notin\mathcal J$. The first inequality of (7.36) says $\|A_*\|_{2\to2}\le a_*$. This controls the entire complementary coefficient vector by $a_*|\beta|$; using the sum of squared row norms would be sufficient but can give a larger value of $a_*$.
ns7-data-s076.Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.stiff_of: The second inequality in (7.36) compares two known vectors, $A_*\beta^{\mathrm a}(\alpha)$ and $(d_j\alpha_j)_{j\notin\mathcal J}$. It bounds the scaled parameter update that would result if the correction force were zero. The actual update differs by $A_*\beta$, which costs at most $2\varepsilon a_*/\omega$ in Euclidean norm.
ns7-data-s076.Breakdown.IsExtendedCertificate.stiff_in: For $j\notin\mathcal J$, $-d_j\alpha'_j=V_j\cdot\beta+(V_j\cdot\beta^{\mathrm a}-d_j\alpha_j)$. Taking the Euclidean norm of the vector of these identities gives at most $a_*|\beta|+o_*\le2\varepsilon a_*/\omega+o_*\le\varrho_*$. This is exactly the ball condition in (7.29), including the coordinate scalings.

ns7-data-s077.Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData.params: The proof needs compactness and convexity but not an open neighborhood of the origin. A zero interval radius fixes one coordinate exactly; a zero ball radius fixes all the complementary coordinates, since every $d_j\ne0$. The inclusion estimates must preserve these equalities. If $n=0$ the force and constraint vectors are empty, and only the nonlinear periodic equation remains.
ns7-data-s077.Breakdown.rowNorm: The integer $N$ counts the additional right-hand-side measurements, not the forcing fields. For $N=0$, $[F]=0$ for every $F$ and the inverse estimate has only its norm and constraint terms. One can have $N=0$ and $n>0$.

ns7-data-s078.Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData: There are two different problems: to prove that the inequalities of Subsection 7.3 imply existence, and to find fields satisfying those inequalities. The analytic proof below uses only the former hypothesis, not the polynomial representation of Appendix B. In the formal data a pressure-gradient representative is specified; changing it can change the residual norm and row pairings even when the projected equation is unchanged.

pdf-item-theorem-7-1.Breakdown.extended_certificate_orbit_pro: For $F(x)=x^2-2$ at $x=3/2$, the residual is $1/4$ and the linear correction is $-(1/4)/3=-1/12$. After that correction the residual is $1/144$, the square of the correction. The certificate controls those same three quantities for a periodic fluid profile. Theorem 7.1 must do more than find a small residual. It selects an $\alpha$ and gives an exact profile at that member's period, with the actual correction bounded by (7.38). The linked upstream theorem concludes only weak-profile existence; the quantitative identification and the prescribed symmetries are additional conclusions of the printed theorem. Neither asserts that a particular numerical certificate satisfies the conditions.
pdf-item-theorem-7-1.Breakdown.FarField.periodicLerayProfileE: The weighted derivative bound on the correction does not establish the pointwise decay of the sum. After the total auxiliary force has vanished, the weak-to-mild, regularity and spatial-decay arguments produce a profile of the class used in Theorem 1.1.
