sec7-nonlinear-049.Breakdown.FarField.lerayKernelBound_hold: A direct estimate of the integral in $L^\infty$ from (7.63) would use $u\otimes u\in L^3$ and the conjugate kernel norm $\|\nabla O_\tau\|_{3/2}\lesssim\tau^{-1}$. Its time integral diverges at zero. Passing first to a finite $L^q$ with $q>6$ costs $\tau^{-1+3/(2q)}$ for the nonlinear term, and the next step to $L^\infty$ costs $\tau^{-1/2-3/q}$. Both powers are integrable. The choice $q=12$ gives the exponents $-7/8$ and $-3/4$ below.

sec7-nonlinear-050.Breakdown.FarField.smoothFieldOfOrbit_ho: Put $r=1-t$. The $L^3$ tensor has norm $O(r^{-1/2})$ throughout $[t-r,t]$. To reach $L^{12}$, Young's inequality uses $1+1/12=3/4+1/3$, i.e. the $L^{4/3}$ kernel norm. The integral costs $r^{-1/2}\int_0^r\tau^{-7/8}d\tau=8r^{-3/8}$. The free term costs $r^{-1/8}r^{-1/4}=r^{-3/8}$ as well. The linked smooth-orbit theorem uses a different regularization, in Fourier variables.
sec7-nonlinear-050.Breakdown.FarField.lerayKernelBound_hold: The new $L^{12}$ estimate is available at every source time $t'$ in (7.64), giving $\|u(t')\otimes u(t')\|_6\lesssim r^{-3/4}$ for $r=1-t$. Convolution into $L^\infty$ uses the conjugate exponent $6/5$, costing $\tau^{-3/4}$. Its integral over $(0,r)$ is $4r^{1/4}$, giving $O(r^{-1/2})$ in (7.65). The free Gaussian now maps $L^{12}$ to $L^\infty$ with cost $r^{-1/8}$ and yields the same power.

sec7-nonlinear-051.Breakdown.FarField.kernelL1Bound_holds: On $[a,b]$, $b<1$, the bound (7.65) supplies a single $M$ bounding $\|u\|_\infty$. The spatial integral of the absolute value of the kernel times the tensor is bounded by $CM^2(t-t')^{-1/2}$, uniformly in the evaluation point. Integration gives $2CM^2\sqrt{t-a}$. This is absolute convergence of the iterated integral, not just existence of a Bochner integral in $X$.
sec7-nonlinear-051.Breakdown.FarField.kernelConvSup_holds: For a bounded representative of $u$ on $[a,b]$ with bound $M$, (7.65) and the $L^1$ kernel estimate give an absolute space-time pairing bound $2CM^2\sqrt{t-a}\|\psi\|_1$ for each compact smooth test $\psi$. Hence Fubini identifies the pointwise integral with the distribution represented by the Bochner integral in $X$. The two agree almost everywhere in space at each $t$; this suffices for the bounded-data Stokes formula.
sec7-nonlinear-051.Breakdown.FarField.smoothFieldOfOrbit_ho: The bounded-data regularity theorem [69, Proposition 4.1] can be applied on any interval $[a,b]$ with $b<1$ once (7.64) is read as the pointwise Stokes formula. It needs no $L^2$ bound for the ancient datum $u(a)$. `smoothFieldOfOrbit_holds` instead regularizes the whole-space mild orbit via homogeneous Fourier estimates; its hypothesis is a mild recurrent orbit, not the numerical bound (7.65) alone.

sec7-nonlinear-052.Breakdown.FarField.smoothFieldOfOrbit_ho: The derivative estimate of [69, Proposition 4.1] has weight $(t-a)^{k/2+l}$. To obtain an unweighted bound on a closed interior slab, start the mild formula strictly before its left endpoint. The smooth representative at every time is identified by continuity of the test pairings: equality almost everywhere in time extends to every time by the $X\hookrightarrow L^6$ embedding. The formal proof likewise works on an interior physical window: at time $1/2$ and phase offset $s-\log2$ the orbit has slice $D_2w(s)$, so local smoothing there gives smoothness near the arbitrary phase $s$.

sec7-nonlinear-053.Breakdown.FarField.IsVelocityOf: On each compact physical time interval the mild curve and its smooth representative determine the same element of $X$ at almost every time. Their continuity in $X$ extends the identity to all times. `IsVelocityOf` records this same phasewise property in similarity coordinates.

sec7-nonlinear-054.Breakdown.FarField.smoothFieldOfOrbit_ho: Write $G=\partial_tu-\Delta u+(u\cdot\nabla)u$. Testing with $\psi=\operatorname{curl}\varphi$ shows $\operatorname{curl}G=0$. For $p=-\int_0^1G(t,\sigma x)\cdot x\,d\sigma$, differentiating and using $\partial_iG_j=\partial_jG_i$ gives $\partial_i p=-\int_0^1\partial_\sigma(\sigma G_i(t,\sigma x))\,d\sigma=-G_i(t,x)$. Thus the missing term is a smooth pressure with the correct sign. The linked smoothing theorem proves existence of pressure by its own construction, not this particular primitive.

sec7-nonlinear-055.Breakdown.WeakProfile.physicalCurve: Put $\tau=t-1<0$ and $a=e^{S/2}$. One normalized return advances similarity time by $S$, giving $u(1+a^{-2}\tau,x)=a\,u(1+\tau,ax)$. Equivalently $u(1+\tau,x)=a\,u(1+a^2\tau,ax)$, the backward discrete scaling used in the next step. `physicalCurve` realizes the required change of variables in $X$.
sec7-nonlinear-055.Breakdown.FarField.IsSmoothOrbitField: Translate the singular time to zero by writing $\widetilde u(\tau,x)=u(1+\tau,x)$ for $\tau<0$. With $a=e^{S/2}$ the return becomes $\widetilde u(\tau,x)=a\widetilde u(a^2\tau,ax)$, the scaling of Chae–Wolf's theorem. In this proposition the isometry is $I$. The formal `IsSmoothOrbitField` records the return in similarity variables and permits any orthogonal twist.

sec7-nonlinear-056.Breakdown.FarField.farFieldDecay_holds: The paper uses Chae–Wolf with $p=6$. The formal proof starts instead from the integral equation of `IsRegularOrbitField`. A weighted estimate first gives $|W(s,y)|\lesssim(1+|y|)^{-3/4}$. Its square tensor then decays with exponent $3/2$; applying the profile integral operator gives exponent $\min(3/2,1)=1$. Differentiation of the integral equation and a separate pressure estimate complete the stronger formal decay bounds.
sec7-nonlinear-056.Breakdown.FarField.DecayBounds: With $t=1-e^{-s}$ and $x=e^{-s/2}y$, the denominator in (7.66) is $e^{-s/2}(1+|y|)$. Multiplication by $e^{-s/2}$ removes the physical velocity factor, giving the first bound of (1.3) for all phases with the same constant. `DecayBounds` additionally records the derivative and pressure-gradient estimates.

sec7-nonlinear-057.Breakdown.WeakProfile.physicalCurve: The inverse physical change of variables is $D_{e^{-s}}u(1-e^{-s})$. Since the normalized weak field was read at $\theta=-S^{-1}\log(1-t)$, this gives $W(s,\cdot)=\mathcal W(s/S)$ in $X$. Advancing $s$ by $S$ advances the normalized phase by exactly one. The pressure rescaling uses the square of the velocity amplitude.
sec7-nonlinear-057.Breakdown.FarField.IsVelocityOf: The inverse rescaling gives $D_{e^{-s}}u(1-e^{-s})=\mathcal W(s/S)$ in $X$ at every $s$. At $s+S$ the right side is the same element as at $s$. Therefore the two smooth velocity slices agree almost everywhere in $y$ and, by spatial continuity, everywhere. This is the passage from periodicity of the original weak field to the pointwise return law of the profile.
sec7-nonlinear-057.Breakdown.FarField.IsSmoothOrbitField: The inverse change of variables stays in the smooth region for every finite $s$, since $1-e^{-s}<1$. It gives the similarity equations and the return law pointwise. For `IsSmoothOrbitField` the smoothness and recurrence are supplemented by uniform spatial derivative bounds through order three, a uniformly vanishing velocity tail and a square-integrable pressure gradient. Weighted inverse-distance decay is proved in the next stage.

sec7-nonlinear-058.Breakdown.FarField.farFieldDecay_holds: The formal far-field proof also uses the whole-past integral equation. Put $\delta=1-t$ and $\tau=(t-t')/\delta$ in (7.64). The earlier similarity phase is $s-\log(1+\tau)$ and its spatial argument is $z/\sqrt{1+\tau}$ in the current spatial units. The squared velocity amplitude gives the factor $(1+\tau)^{-1}$ in `profileBilin`. Starting at $t-A(1-t)$, the rescaled heat term is bounded by $C(1+A)^{-1/2}$ because the heat kernel has mass one and the earlier velocity has smaller amplitude. It tends to zero as $A\to\infty$. Thus the profile is determined by the quadratic integral itself, to which the weighted decay estimates apply.
sec7-nonlinear-058.Breakdown.FarField.DecayBounds: The extra pressure-gradient bound in `DecayBounds` needs more than the velocity derivative estimates of Remark 1.2. The formal argument takes the divergence of (1.2), giving $-\Delta q=\sum_{i,j}\partial_i\partial_j(W_iW_j)$. In the Newton potential for $\nabla q$, away from the kernel singularity, two integrations by parts move the two derivatives onto the cut-off kernel. The second derivatives of this cut-off gradient kernel are bounded uniformly by $O(r^{-4})$, where $r=\max(1,|y|)$, and $\int_{|z|<2r}|W(z)|^2dz=O(r)$, giving $O(r^{-3})$ for this part. The complementary tail and the local source give the same bound; the square-integrability of $\nabla q$ is used to identify it with the Newton field.

sec7-nonlinear-059.Breakdown.FarField.periodicLerayProfileE: The field now has the nonzero return law and the decay required for Theorem 1.1. In the paper this is still the corrected field of Proposition 7.10. The upstream existential theorem gives a profile with the stronger formal decay assumptions, but does not retain the original field or its specified period and twist.

ac-001.Breakdown.VarConstIntegralInternal.conti: For $\tau$ near $\tau_0>0$, add and subtract $K(\tau)(z,z')$. The difference at the same lag is bounded by $\|K(\tau)\|(\|\chi-z\|\|\chi'\|+\|z\|\|\chi'-z'\|)$, tending to zero by local boundedness of the bilinear norms. The remaining difference tends to zero by continuity in $\tau$ for fixed inputs. This proves joint continuity without operator-norm continuity in the lag.

ac-002.Breakdown.VarConstIntegralInternal.conti: For a fixed $t$ the integrand is continuous on $[a,t)$ by the joint continuity just established. The one excluded point $t'=t$ is exactly where the lag vanishes. Its value can be assigned arbitrarily; the estimate in the next sentence controls convergence near it.

ac-003.Breakdown.VarConstIntegralInternal.norm_: With $M=\max\|u\|$ and $N=\max\|v\|$ on the full interval, the lag alone determines the majorant. The paper has $C_KMN(t-t')^{-3/4}$ for every positive lag. In the formal abstract setting the same bound holds for $t-t'\le1$, and heat contractivity gives $C_KMN$ beyond one. Both majorants have finite integrals on the interval.

ac-004.Breakdown.varConstIntegral: The improper endpoint costs at most $4C_K\|u\|_C\|v\|_C h^{1/4}$ on the last $h\le1$ units. Since the integrand is continuous away from that endpoint, its norm is integrable, giving the Bochner integral in the complete space $\mathcal X$. The value assigned at zero lag is immaterial.

ac-005.Breakdown.varConstIntegral: In the original time variable the singularity moves with $t$. The substitution $\tau=t-t'$ fixes it at zero. Extend the inputs by their endpoint values and insert the indicator $0<\tau<t-a$ on the fixed interval $(0,b-a)$. At a limiting $t$ the indicator converges except at the single point $t-a$, and the majorant from (3.12) is independent of $t$. Dominated convergence now applies in $\mathcal X$, also at $a$ where the integral vanishes.

ac-006.Breakdown.pieceOperator: The weighted norm is equivalent to the original supremum norm, with equivalence factors $e^{-\beta(b-a)}$ and one. In estimating the contribution of an input at $t'$, one extracts $e^{-\beta(t'-a)}\|h(t')\|$ and is left with $e^{-\beta(t-t')}$. Only the lag is discounted. Thus completeness is unchanged while the linear operator becomes small in the new norm.

ac-007.Breakdown.Freq.bilinShift_holds: For $t'<m$, the lag in the integrand at $m$ is $m-t'$. By the semigroup rule for $K$ it becomes $(t-m)+(m-t')=t-t'$ after applying $e^{(t-m)\Delta}$. The separate semigroup rule for the free heat term similarly replaces $m-a$ by $t-a$. The linked theorem supplies the bilinear rule for the whole-space frequency realization.

ac-008.Breakdown.restrict: No inverse of the heat operator is used. The contribution before $m$ is removed by forward heat evolution of the identity at $m$, followed by subtraction. Lemma 3.3 justifies the splitting of the Bochner integral at $m$. The result is `restrict` for the case $f=h=u$.

ac-009.Breakdown.mildUnique: The exact cancellation is $K(u,u)-K(v,v)=K(u+v,u-v)$, using symmetry. Thus for the difference one has the linear equation of Lemma 3.4 with coefficient $f=(u+v)/2$ and source zero. The initial values are equal, so there is no residual heat term.

ac-010.Breakdown.mildUnique: In the paper the bounded inverse sends $g=0$ to $h=0$. In the formal uniqueness proof, only the triviality of the kernel of the short-step operator $I-A$ is needed. On the next interval (3.13) gives zero initial difference again. This finite iteration establishes uniqueness without constructing an inverse for arbitrary continuous sources on the full interval.

ac-011.Breakdown.shift: Define $\widetilde u(s)=u(a+s)$. Then the fixed spatial test in (3.14) is unchanged and differentiation in $s$ is differentiation in $t=a+s$; the datum is now $\widetilde u(0)=u(a)$. The linked `shift` proves the analogous invariance of (2.4) by the substitution $t'=a+s'$, which leaves the lag unchanged. It concerns the mild identity rather than the weak equation translated here.

ac-012.Breakdown.Freq.weak_holds: For a moving test $\varphi(t)$, split the increment of $\int u(t)\cdot\varphi(t)$ into one at fixed test and one at fixed velocity. Apply (3.14) to the first and continuity in $L^6$ to the second. Integration gives the endpoint terms $\int u(m)\cdot\varphi(m)-\int u(0)\cdot\varphi(0)$, and the interior integral of $u\cdot(\partial_t+\Delta)\varphi+(u\otimes u):\nabla\varphi$. This is (NSW) in [46]. `weak_holds` uses a different integrated identity in $X$ against the fixed test $-\Delta\psi$.

ac-013.Breakdown.Freq.mild_holds: Dubois's integral is initially in $\mathcal S'$. Its integrand with the minus sign is $K(t-t')(u(t'),u(t'))$ since $\operatorname{div}(u\otimes u)=(u\cdot\nabla)u\in L^{3/2}$. By (3.7) and continuity of $u$ in $X$, this integrand has an integrable $X$ norm. Pairing its Bochner integral with Schwartz fields (bounded functionals by (3.1)) identifies it with the distributional integral. The datum is $u(0)$ by the continuous trace. Lean obtains the corresponding equality by heat testing instead.

ac-014.Breakdown.Freq.IsMildX: Dubois gives the identity before $b$. At $b$ the left side is continuous in $X$ by hypothesis, the free term by strong heat continuity, and the integral by Lemma 3.3. Hence the same equality holds at $b$; no further distributional endpoint condition is required. `IsMildX` explicitly includes this equality and integrability at each time of the closed interval.

ac-015.Breakdown.Periodic.heat_add: The projected evolution of a fixed mean-zero source has coefficients $e^{-4\pi^2\tau|k|^2}\mathbb P_k\hat f(k)$. Multiplication by the heat factor at $t$ gives the coefficient at $t+\tau$; there is no new estimate of a Fourier sum. The formal `heat_add` is the heat law on the inhomogeneous space at period one, including the zero mode.

ac-016.Breakdown.Periodic.heat_continuousOn: For a source in $L^{3/2}$ the value at lag zero need not be in the gradient space. To obtain continuity at a positive $\tau_0$, write $e^{\tau\Delta}Pf=e^{(\tau-\tau_0/2)\Delta}(e^{\tau_0\Delta/2}Pf)$ for $\tau$ near $\tau_0$. The inner field belongs to the space by (3.19), so strong continuity of heat suffices. The linked heat-continuity theorem concerns the inhomogeneous unit-period space.

ac-017.Breakdown.Periodic.kernelSharpBound_hold: The mean of $(u\cdot\nabla)v$ vanishes: as a periodic distribution it is $\operatorname{div}(v\otimes u)$, whose integral is its pairing with the constant test. Thus (3.19) applies to both advections in (3.17). Hölder with (3.18) bounds their $L^{3/2}$ norms by a constant times $\|u\|_{\dot H^1}\|v\|_{\dot H^1}$, independent of $L$. The linked bound is in the unit-torus inhomogeneous norm for lags at most one.

ac-018.Breakdown.mildUnique: It is the local competitor $\tilde u$ that is known to belong to $H^1$, by the local theory from $u_0$. Its continuous embedding into $X$ makes the two solutions comparable by Lemma 3.5. Once they agree there, the prescribed mild curve has the finite energy and smoothness of the competitor throughout the common interval.

ac-019.Breakdown.SmoothFlow.exists_symbolFlow_o: The formal continuation theorem needs an a priori bound for every partial symbol flow $F$ with the same initial symbol. By the mild uniqueness argument in `RegGlue.lean`, its physical velocity embeds as the given $u(t)$ on its own interval, so $\int|\xi|^2|F(t,\xi)|^2d\xi=(4\pi^2)^{-1}\|u(t)\|_X^2\le(4\pi^2)^{-1}\max_{[0,b]}\|u\|_X^2$. This one bound applies to all partial flows, irrespective of their duration. `exists_symbolFlow_of_homBound` converts it into existence through $b$.

ac-020.Breakdown.SmoothFlow.IsHsCurve: `IsHsCurve` gives continuity in the weighted Fourier norm with squared weight $(1+|\xi|^2)^m$. At $m=1$ this is equivalent to the full physical $H^1$ norm. The weight is bounded below by one even at low frequencies, unlike the homogeneous gradient weight $4\pi^2|\xi|^2$. This is the additional norm controlled in the local theory.

ac-021.Breakdown.varConstIntegral: After applying the bounded embedding $H^1_{\rm div}\to X$, the free term and the integrand of the local $H^1$ equation are the same as in (2.4). Lemma 3.3 gives continuity of the latter integral in $X$. Pairing with Schwartz tests identifies the integrals, and continuity of both sides in $X$ gives the equality at every time, as required by Lemma 3.5.

ac-022.Breakdown.mildUnique: The comparison is made on the common existence interval, but the bound obtained from it is on the fixed interval $[0,b]$: $\|\tilde u(t)\|_{\dot H^1}=\|u(t)\|_X\le\max_{[0,b]}\|u\|_X$. Thus the bound does not grow as the local interval approaches its maximal endpoint. The same comparison will be used with the energy bound to exclude blow-up in the full $H^1$ norm.

ac-023.Breakdown.SmoothFlow.isSolutionOn_physFi: If $A$ denotes the Fourier symbol of advection, the projected evolution reads $\partial_tF+4\pi^2|\xi|^2F=-\mathbb P_\xi A$. The pressure symbol in Lean gives $2\pi i\xi\widehat p=-(I-\mathbb P_\xi)A$; adding the full advection therefore recovers (1.1). The linked theorem realizes this identity as the smooth momentum equation at interior times of a closed slab.

ac-024.Breakdown.SmoothFlow.isHsCurve_of_flow: For a compact smooth datum the Fourier symbol has finite weighted $L^2$ norms of every order. `isHsCurve_of_flow` propagates each order from the same $H^3$ flow: for $m\le3$ use the weaker norm, and for $m\ge3$ use persistence of regularity. Spatial derivatives then follow from sufficiently high Sobolev orders; temporal derivatives and pressure use the evolution equation as well. The cited Tao theorem supplies the stronger explicit bounds of all space and time derivatives in $L^2$.

ac-025.Breakdown.mildRegular_realization: `mildRegular_realization` constructs a smooth velocity and pressure on a closed whole-space slab from a continuous mild curve with compact smooth solenoidal datum. The velocity represents that curve almost everywhere in space at each time; the momentum equation is stated at interior times. The linked theorem also supplies bounded energy and first spatial derivatives on the slab, rather than the entire set of derivative estimates quoted from [84].

ac-026.Breakdown.mildRegular_realization: The equality follows by integrating the equation against $\tilde u$. Solenoidality makes the pressure integral zero and writes the convection as the integral of $\operatorname{div}(\tilde u|\tilde u|^2/2)$; both vanish by the integrability of the smooth local solution. The diffusion term gives $-2\|\nabla\tilde u\|_2^2$ in the derivative of the squared energy. Hence $\|\tilde u(t)\|_2\le\|u_0\|_2$, with no dependence on the endpoint $b'$ of the local solution. `mildRegular_realization` asserts finite energy on a slab.

ac-027.Breakdown.SmoothFlow.exists_symbolFlow_o: Lean obtains a common higher-order bound before extending the local solution. Write $A=\int|\xi|^2|F|^2$, $B=\int|\xi|^4|F|^2$ and $w=\|F\|_1$ for its Fourier velocity symbol. Splitting at radius $R$ gives $w\lesssim R^{1/2}A^{1/2}+R^{-1/2}B^{1/2}$, so $w^4\lesssim AB$. The enstrophy estimate bounds $\int B$, using the prescribed bound on $A$, and hence $\int w^4$. For $n=(\int(1+|\xi|^2)^3|F|^2)^{1/2}$, the mild estimate is $n(t)\le n(0)+C\int_0^t(t-s)^{-1/2}w(s)n(s)ds$. Hölder with exponents $4/3,4$ bounds the integral to the fourth power by $27t\int_0^t w^4 n^4$. Grönwall therefore bounds $n$ on every partial interval by the same constant. The local construction then extends in steps of a common positive length.

ac-028.Breakdown.mildRegular_realization: The smooth velocity representatives on two slabs agree at every common time: they represent the same element of $X$ and are continuous in space. Their pressure gradients agree by (1.1), so their pressures differ by a function of time only; subtracting the value at $x=0$ gives a common gauge. Exhausting $[0,T)$ by slabs gives a single smooth pair there.

ac-029.Breakdown.mildRegular_realization: Each closed slab starts with the same datum, so the energy bound on every slab is $\|u_0\|_2$. In contrast the gradient bound used for continuation is $\max_{[0,b]}\|u\|_X$, which may grow with $b$. The uniform energy bound before $T$ follows from the printed energy identity, not from the slabwise definition `EnergyBoundedOn` alone.

ac-030.Breakdown.Periodic.mildUniqueness: At period one, $|k|\ge1$ for all nonzero Fourier modes, so for mean-zero velocities $\|\tilde u\|_2\le(2\pi)^{-1}\|\nabla\tilde u\|_2$. This makes the common gradient bound sufficient for the full $H^1$ continuation alternative, without an energy calculation. The formal `mildUniqueness` compares trajectories directly in the inhomogeneous unit-torus norm.

ac-031.Breakdown.Periodic.smoothPeriodicIsMild_: The direction of `smoothPeriodicIsMild_holds` is from a smooth periodic PDE solution to its integral equation. Together with `mildUniqueness` it is enough to rule out a hypothetical global smooth solution when an unbounded mild trajectory has been constructed. The paper proves more here: by the local $H^1$ theory and continuation it obtains smoothness of the prescribed trajectory itself.

b12-intro-estimates.Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.CellSystemCond: The six estimates form the input to the analytic proof: (7.18) and (7.19) give the transferred inverse bound, (7.22) controls the maximum in phase, and (7.32)–(7.34) give the selected-coordinate enclosure. Appendix B derives these estimates from conditions on the represented fields and on arbitrary perturbations. The linked `CellSystemCondition` specifies the common data and hypotheses; it does not produce a verified numerical instance.

b12-intro-weak.Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.pieceMultiplierDe: The domain of the multiplier inequality is independent of the representation (B.6). In the weak domain one supplies a spatial gradient and a weak Hessian, with the gradient and the trace of the Hessian in $\mathcal H$, and $v(\theta)\in L^6$ for almost every $\theta$. One also requires $g=S^{-1}\partial_\theta v+\frac12v+\frac12(y\cdot\nabla)v\in\mathcal H$ in distributions; the separate terms of $g$ need not be square integrable. The equation with right-hand side $F\in\mathcal H$ is imposed against solenoidal tests, so $F$ itself need not be solenoidal.

b12-intro-condition.Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.CellSystemCond: The conditions refer to a single choice of the fields, mesh, weights and matrices. In particular the cell inequalities must cover every perturbation in (7.18), not just the harmonics and polynomials used to represent the approximate profile. The linked structure includes the fifteen groups of conditions, including the further cell conditions named after B.14; it asserts no existence of data satisfying them.

b12-field-kinds.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.shapeInfoF: There are two different uses of the represented fields. The residual contains derivatives of $W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}$, and the multiplier and adjoint estimates use derivatives of the reference and adjoint fields. The forces are solenoidal fields with controlled derivatives and support. By contrast $\Xi_i$ and $e_k$ are used only in the integrals $\langle\nabla v,\Xi_i\rangle_{\mathcal H}$ and $\langle F,e_k\rangle_{\mathcal H}$. Their jumps across cell sides do not enter these integrals.

b12-cell-kind.Breakdown.CertCell.CellMatField.field: The indices of the printed coefficient $\Xi_{i,ab}^{Q,\iota}$ are the direction of differentiation $a$ and the component $b$. The Cartesian linear map in Lean has its indices in the opposite order: the term of `frameMap` with coefficient $x_{ab}$ sends $e_b$ to $x_{ab}e_a$. Thus the polynomial stored at `(b,a)` is the one multiplying $e_b\cdot(e_a\cdot\nabla)v$ in (B.10).
b12-cell-kind.Breakdown.CertCell.RowValues.rowFieldOf: The polynomials give the real generators $\tilde e_{k'}$. If $m_{k'}=\langle F,\tilde e_{k'}\rangle_{\mathcal H}$, the measurements against the unit rows are the components of $G^{-1/2}m$. The definition `rowFieldOf` forms these unit rows; (B.11) then multiplies each by $\sqrt{\tau_k}$, represented by a separate weight in the formal seminorm.

b12-constant-weight.Breakdown.CertCell.CellHypothesis:
For this choice, $\|v\|_w^2=\|\Delta v\|_{\mathcal H}^2+	frac{39}{50}\|
abla v\|_{\mathcal H}^2$. The term $
abla\lambda_p	imes\operatorname{curl}v$ in the multiplier is estimated using $\|
abla v\|_{\mathcal H}\le w_*^{-1/2}\|v\|_w$; this is the source of $w_*^{-1/2}$ in the constant of Proposition B.1.

b12-cylindrical-coordinate.Breakdown.CertCell.pointPlane: These are physical cylindrical coordinates, rather than the compactified coordinates of (B.3). The map to the meridian plane retains the sign of $z$; the cells introduced later use $(r,|z|)$ only because reflection is treated separately.

b12-angular-coordinate.Breakdown.CertCell.pointAngle: Only $e^{im\phi}$ for integer $m$ enters the scalar harmonics, so the branch of the angle is immaterial. Assigning an angle on the axis does not by itself make a field continuous there. The factors in (B.7) and the weighted polar and azimuthal vectors in (B.8) address this separately.

b12-cylindrical-frame.Breakdown.CertCell.frameUnit: If $u_r,u_\phi,u_z$ are the cylindrical components of a field, the angular column of its gradient in that frame is $r^{-1}(\partial_\phi u_r-u_\phi,\partial_\phi u_\phi+u_r,\partial_\phi u_z)$. The extra terms follow from $\partial_\phi e_r=e_\phi$ and $\partial_\phi e_\phi=-e_r$. In particular, the angular derivative of a mode acts on its components by $im$ plus a skew matrix, where $m$ is its angular Fourier integer. This distinction is used in the estimates of large angular frequencies.

b12-rotation-coordinate.Breakdown.axialRot: At $r>0$, the frame at $R_{\phi_0}y$ is the image under $R_{\phi_0}$ of the frame at $y$. Thus $R_{-\phi_0}v(\theta,R_{\phi_0}y)$ has the cylindrical components of $v$ at the shifted angle, expressed in the frame at $y$. This is the operation averaged in (B.12); averaging the Cartesian components without that rotation would give different mode labels.

b12-halfturn-coordinate.Breakdown.CertCell.flipPoint: The rotation $R_*$ sends $(r,\phi,z)$ to $(r,-\phi,-z)$. At the reflected point the radial basis vector is $R_*e_r$, whereas the other two basis vectors are $-R_*e_\phi$ and $-R_*e_z$. This is why the cell vectors below have two minus signs, and the cell tensors a minus sign exactly when one of their indices is radial.

b12-order.Breakdown.CertCell.CellHypothesis: The lower bound three is on the spacing of the angular Fourier lattice, not on the number of harmonics retained. In particular the first nonzero angular frequency has modulus at least three. In Lemma B.5, this makes both $|k|-1$ and $|k|-2$ positive for every nonaxisymmetric mode (where $k$ is that mode's angular Fourier integer).

b12-two-generators.Breakdown.CertCell.Bridge.IsModeClass: The mode-class predicate asks for these two particular group elements and an order at least one. This suffices to infer Fourier support and reflection of an invariant field. To apply the later certificate construction one also imposes order at least three and the generation condition, the latter being used to establish invariance of the represented data.
b12-two-generators.Breakdown.CertCell.Instance.GeneratedByC: To prove invariance of a represented field, it suffices to prove the identities for the two pairs in (B.1). The identity for a product follows by applying the two identities successively; period one accounts for the remaining integer time translation. This is the use of the generation condition, as opposed to membership of the two pairs, which is sufficient for restricting the modes of an already invariant perturbation.
b12-two-generators.Breakdown.CertCell.CellHypothesis: The restriction on $\Gamma$ ensures that the symmetry of the finite data and the symmetry assumed of the unknown perturbation are the same. Membership of the first pair also implies that the gradient energy has period $1/2$, by rotation invariance of the spatial integral. Thus the same choice of symmetries has a second use in Proposition 7.9, besides its use for the Fourier lattice here.

b12-allowed-symmetries.Breakdown.CertCell.Instance.GeneratedByC: A rotation through $a$ times the generating angle has time translation $a/2$ modulo integers. The reflection-type element with the same angle is obtained by composing it with $(R_*,0)$. These are exactly the products whose invariance follows from the two generator identities and period one.

pdf-item-equation-B-2.Breakdown.CertCell.labelPhase: The integer lattice may be read in terms of the two traveling phases of C.1: with $j=2\iota_2-\iota_1$ and $m$ the angular integer, the phase change under the combined shift is $\pi(j+m/k)=2\pi\iota_2$, where $k$ is the angular order. In particular a purely time-dependent mode has even $j$, but a mode with odd $m/k$ must have odd $j$.

b12-harmonic-parity.Breakdown.CertCell.labelPhase: The first generator imposes $e^{i\pi(j+j'/\varkappa)}=1$. Hence $\iota_1=j'/\varkappa$ and $\iota_2=(j+\iota_1)/2$ are integers, and (B.2) parametrizes all the allowed frequencies, including those with arbitrarily large integers.

b12-first-symmetry.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.fieldClass: The scalar components are unchanged under the combined shift, whereas the cylindrical frame rotates by the angle of the generator. Reassembling the components gives precisely the vector transformation in (7.5). The linked theorem proves it for the admissible fields (B.6), including points on the axis.

b12-label-reflection.Breakdown.CertCell.labelFlip: The time integer $2\iota_2-\iota_1$ is unchanged by $\iota^\flat$, whereas the angular integer is negated. In particular the two travelling families $\iota_2=0$ and $\iota_2=\iota_1$ of C.1 are exchanged. Applying the map twice gives the original label. Conjugation instead negates both integers (and, in (B.5), the radial index).

pdf-item-equation-B-3.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.chartCoord: The inverse relation is $R=\mathsf L\sigma/(1-\sigma)$, where $R=|y|$. Thus the endpoint $\sigma=1$ represents spatial infinity, and a zero of order $h$ there becomes decay of order $R^{-h}$. The last radial polynomial interval describes an unbounded region in physical space.
pdf-item-equation-B-3.Breakdown.CellCert.GivenFields.heightRat: Away from the origin $\eta$ is the cosine of the polar angle; the two endpoints correspond to the two halves of the axis. The formal value at $y=0$ is zero by the convention for division by zero. A field's limit at the origin must still be checked independently of that assigned coordinate.

pdf-item-equation-B-4.Breakdown.CellCert.GivenFields.polarVecQ: For $R=|y|>0$, $\mathbf p=\eta y/R-e_z$ is perpendicular to $y$ and has squared length $1-\eta^2$. It is minus the tangential projection of $e_z$ onto the sphere, and hence vanishes at both poles. One can therefore use $\mathbf p$ rather than the unit polar vector when writing a field with a regular axis. Its value at $y=0$ is immaterial to this calculation; the origin expansion is separate.
pdf-item-equation-B-4.Breakdown.CellCert.GivenFields.azimVecQ: The azimuthal vector is $e_z\times y/|y|$. In particular it is already multiplied by $r/|y|$, which removes the unit azimuthal vector's directional ambiguity on the nonzero axis. The total formal definition gives zero also at the origin.

b12-weighted-unit-vectors.Breakdown.CellCert.GivenFields.polarVecQ: Near a nonzero point of the axis, the factor $r/R$ in the length of $\mathbf p$ removes the singular unit polar vector. In (B.8) this allows the axisymmetric radial amplitude $u_0$ to be nonzero on the axis while the tangential amplitude contributes zero there. The nonaxisymmetric construction instead makes all three amplitudes vanish to fourth order in $r$.
b12-weighted-unit-vectors.Breakdown.CellCert.GivenFields.azimVecQ: Since $|e_z\times y|=r$, the length of $\mathbf a$ is $r/|y|=(1-\eta^2)^{1/2}$ away from zero. The amplitude multiplying it in (B.8) can therefore describe an axisymmetric swirl without a singular unit vector on the axis.

b12-phase-condition.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.IsRadialPh: For $R=|y|$, the first two radial derivatives of $f(R^2)$ are $2Rf'(R^2)$ and $2f'(R^2)+4R^2f''(R^2)$, of orders $R^{-1}$ and $R^{-2}$ at infinity; the third is of order $R^{-3}$. The third derivative is needed because (B.7) and (B.8) already differentiate the phase once in the velocity amplitudes, before the equation differentiates the velocity twice. A bound on the phase itself is unnecessary.

pdf-item-equation-B-5.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.keyPhase: For a fixed $\iota$, all the indices $l$ have the same factor $E_\iota(\theta,\phi)$. Their amplitudes, multiplied by $e^{ilf(R^2)}$, add before any norm of $\hat v_\iota$ is taken. The orthogonality used in B.2 is in $\iota$, not in the radial phase index $l$.
pdf-item-equation-B-5.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.shiftedSca: The scaled radial derivative $R\partial_R$ acts on $e^{ilf(R^2)}u$ by the product rule. On dividing out the exponential its two terms are $\sigma(1-\sigma)\partial_\sigma u$ and $2ilR^2f'(R^2)u$, namely $\mathcal V_l u$. Differentiating the amplitude alone would omit the second term, including in the divergence equation.

pdf-item-equation-B-6.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.shapeInfoF: The three terms are the radial, polar and azimuthal parts of a single velocity harmonic. Only two scalar splines are free: for a nonzero azimuthal frequency the third component is determined by divergence, whereas for zero frequency the first two are determined by a stream function.
pdf-item-equation-B-6.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.keyDiverge: The divergence calculation is performed on the complex summand, before taking its real part. In (B.7) the azimuthal derivative cancels the divergence of the meridian components; in (B.8) the meridian components already have zero divergence. Thus changing the coefficients within the admissible amplitude spaces preserves solenoidality without a further linear constraint in the numerical solve.
pdf-item-equation-B-6.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.IsTimeFiel: The finite list of keys and the two scalar splines for each key determine a field by (B.6)–(B.8). The data predicate imposes the further conditions on the exponents, joins, origin values and paired keys. It is these conditions, not the finite-sum formula alone, that give a periodic solenoidal $C^1$ field with the stated decay.

b12-finite-mode-data.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.shapeInfoF: For each nonzero angular integer the two free splines prescribe the radial and polar amplitudes, and the angular amplitude is obtained by dividing the meridian divergence by the angular derivative in (B.7). At angular integer zero this division is unavailable: one instead prescribes a stream function and a swirl, with the extra origin coefficient in the stream function. These are the independent coefficients of the velocity representation.
b12-finite-mode-data.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.keyDiverge: For each key $(\iota,l)$ the divergence identity holds before taking a real part or adding any other key. Thus the coefficients can be varied independently subject to the spline and symmetry conditions without solving a new equation for divergence. Finiteness is needed for the data representation, not for this cancellation.

b12-nonzero-exponents.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.IsTimeFiel: The factors have different jobs: near the origin $\sigma^{h_0}=O(R^{h_0})$, at infinity $(1-\sigma)^h=O(R^{-h})$, and near a nonzero point of the axis $(1-\eta^2)^2=r^4/R^4$. The last factor compensates for the angular derivatives, while $h_0\ge2$ ensures that the nonaxisymmetric summands have zero first derivative at the origin.

pdf-item-equation-B-7.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.reducedCom: With $R=|y|$, the three contributions to $R E_{\iota,l}^{-1}\operatorname{div}(E_{\iota,l}(u_0y/R+u_1\mathbf p+u_2\mathbf a))$ are $(\mathcal V_l+2)u_0$, $-\partial_\eta((1-\eta^2)u_1)$ and $i\varkappa\iota_1u_2$. The $2$ comes from differentiation of the spherical area factor $R^2$, and the minus sign from $\eta=\cos\vartheta$, where $\vartheta$ is the polar angle. Multiplication by $i\varkappa\iota_1$ in the last contribution cancels the first two by the factor $i/(\varkappa\iota_1)$ in (B.7).
pdf-item-equation-B-7.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.IsTimeFiel: The joins are imposed on the free splines, rather than separately on the three resulting amplitudes. In $u_2$ the radial derivative of $\mathsf A$ and the height derivative of $\mathsf B$ must themselves have continuous first derivatives. Thus $\mathsf A$ needs order two in $\sigma$ and order one in $\eta$, and $\mathsf B$ the reverse.

b12-zero-stream.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.reducedCom: For $\iota_1=0$ an azimuthal velocity has zero divergence regardless of its radial and height dependence, so it cannot be used to cancel the divergence of the other two components. Instead (B.8) imposes the cancellation between those components by a stream function, and leaves the swirl free.

pdf-item-equation-B-8.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.reducedCom: Let $b=\sigma(1-\sigma)^h\Psi$. Then $\mathsf u_0=-\partial_\eta((1-\eta^2)b)$ and $\mathsf u_1=-(\mathcal V_l+2)b$. The radial operator commutes with the height operator, so $(\mathcal V_l+2)\mathsf u_0-\partial_\eta((1-\eta^2)\mathsf u_1)=0$. The azimuthal component is unconstrained by divergence because its azimuthal frequency is zero.
pdf-item-equation-B-8.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.IsOriginPr: The coefficient $\gamma$ supplies the only possible nonzero first derivative at the origin. Indeed $\mathsf S,\mathsf T=O(\sigma)$ there, and the additional factor $\sigma$ makes their contributions $O(|y|^2)$. The leading $\gamma$ term is of order $|y|$ and yields the axisymmetric trace-free linear field described below.

b12-origin-function.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.IsOriginPr: At an interior join $\sigma_g$ the polynomial must have zero first and second derivatives, since it is followed by a constant. This ensures two derivatives of $g$ agree there: $u_1$ in (B.8) already contains one radial derivative of $g$.

b12-zero-divergence.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.keyDiverge: For (B.7) the last term cancels the first two by multiplication by $i$ twice. For (B.8) the two remaining operators commute because $\mathcal V_l$ involves only the radius. The linked theorem proves zero divergence even at the exceptional coordinate points under the field-data hypotheses.

b12-field-data-description.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.shapeInfoF: Changing $f$ leaves the spline data unchanged, but it changes two places in the field: the scalar factor $E_{\iota,l}$ and the radial derivative $\mathcal V_l$ used to construct the dependent amplitudes. The latter change is essential for retaining the divergence identity when the phase is varied in (B.9).

b12-joined-amplitudes.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.IsTimeFiel: Each differentiated amplitude needs one additional order of matching in the direction in which (B.7) or (B.8) differentiates it. Thus $\mathsf S$, which is differentiated in both directions, is joined through $(2,2)$, whereas the undifferentiated swirl needs only $(1,1)$. A shared partition is unnecessary for this argument.

b12-c1-periodic.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.FieldJoint: The $C^1$ assertion includes the axis and the origin, not only points at which the cylindrical coordinates are smooth. On the axis the explicit angular factors remove the singularity of the angular basis; at zero the axisymmetric $\gamma$ term supplies a Cartesian linear field and the other terms have vanishing first derivative. The joins give the same first derivatives on both sides of each sphere and cone.

b12-second-derivatives.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.FieldWeakH: The distributional derivative of $D_yW$ could have a surface term equal to its jump times the normal to an interface. The join conditions make this jump zero. Hence differentiating each column $D_yW\,e_j$ gives the ordinary second derivatives on the pieces, with no surface measure on a sphere or cone. Values assigned to the Hessian on those interfaces do not affect the weak identity.
b12-second-derivatives.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.fi: The decay estimate for the represented Hessian can be established using the formulas on the polynomial pieces. To use its trace as $\Delta W$ in a weak equation requires the distinct assertion that the represented Hessian is the weak derivative of $D_y W$. The latter follows from the matching first derivatives and is the content of `FieldWeakHessian`.

b12-conjugation.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.IsTimeFiel: Conjugation negates the radial index as well as the harmonic label, so that $\overline{\mathcal V_l u}=\mathcal V_{-l}\overline u$. In (B.7) the simultaneous negation of the azimuthal integer conjugates the purely imaginary prefactor of $u_2$ as well. The two constructed vector terms are thus conjugate, and a pair of distinct keys contributes twice the real part of one term.

b12-reflection-data.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.IsTimeFiel: Write $D_l=\mathcal V_l+2$ and $L_\eta u=\partial_\eta((1-\eta^2)u)$. Under the half-turn $u_0$ is reflected without a sign and $u_1$ with a minus sign, so $D_lu_0-L_\eta u_1$ is reflected without a sign. The angular integer changes sign, giving the required minus sign of $u_2$ in (B.7). In (B.8) the stream function and swirl are odd in $\eta$, which yields the same vector transformation.

b12-both-symmetries.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.fieldClass: The proof uses two different facts: the frequency lattice gives the half-period rotation and the reflected amplitudes give the half-turn at fixed time. Applying the first transformation twice also gives invariance under a spatial rotation by twice its angle, since the time period is one.

b12-gamma-invariant.Breakdown.CertCell.Instance.GeneratedByC: The generating transformations are invertible, so an identity $W(\theta+t,Ry)=RW(\theta,y)$ also gives the identity for the inverse pair. Iterating and using period one proves invariance for each product in the generation condition. No finiteness assumption on $\Gamma$ is needed for this argument.

b12-axis-factors.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.reducedCom: The factor in $u_1$ is $(1-\eta^2)^2$, so the height derivative in (B.7) differentiates a factor $(1-\eta^2)^3$ and leaves at least $(1-\eta^2)^2$. Thus the dependent amplitude has the same fourth-order vanishing in $r$ as the free amplitudes at a nonzero point of the axis. At the origin the common factor $\sigma^{h_0}$ persists as well, since $\mathcal V_l$ uses the scaled derivative $R\partial_R$.

b12-axis-zero-mode.Breakdown.CellCert.GivenFields.polarVecQ: Write $R=|y|$. Since $\sigma=R/\mathsf L+O(R^2)$, (B.8) gives $u_0=\gamma R(3\eta^2-1)/\mathsf L+O(R^2)$ and $u_1=-3\gamma R\eta/\mathsf L+O(R^2)$. Substitution of $\mathbf p=\eta y/R-e_z$ cancels the two terms proportional to $3\eta^2y$. The remaining vector is $-(\gamma/\mathsf L)(y_1,y_2,-2y_3)$, to be multiplied by the phase at zero. In particular the linear term is independent of the direction used to approach zero.
b12-axis-zero-mode.Breakdown.CellCert.GivenFields.azimVecQ: The swirl is a multiple of $e_z\times y/R$. On the nonzero axis this vector vanishes; at the origin the additional vanishing of $\mathsf T$ at $\sigma=0$ makes the entire swirl $O(R^2)$. Hence it does not contribute to the linear field at zero.

b12-decay-orders.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.fi: Near infinity put $s_1=1-\sigma=\mathsf L/(R+\mathsf L)$. The operator $R\partial_R=-\sigma s_1\partial_{s_1}$ preserves the factor $s_1^h$, as does multiplication by $2ilR^2f'(R^2)$, which is bounded. Thus even the dependent amplitudes retain their decay order. Ordinary spatial derivatives cost a further $R^{-1}$ each; time derivatives of a fixed harmonic merely multiply by its time frequency.

b12-decay-one.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.fi: The order-one tail is compatible with the homogeneous energy space: $R^{-1}\in L^6(R>1)$, $R^{-2}\in L^2(R>1)$ and $R^{-3}\in L^2(R>1)$. It need not be in $L^2$ itself. For the residual, the combination $S^{-1}\partial_\theta W+W/2+(y\cdot\nabla)W/2$ must also be in $\mathcal H$; order-one decay alone does not establish this. The phase choice in C.1 and C.4 cancels the leading transport of the oscillatory tail.

b12-profile-dependence.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.Pr: The field has two parameter dependences: the explicitly affine sum of coefficients and the common change of phase. For a key with radial index $l$ the latter gives a factor $e^{il(\mathsf k\cdot\alpha)f_*}$ and changes the dependent amplitude through $\mathcal V_l$. Both changes vanish on the cutoff ball. Outside, even the field indexed by $0$ depends on the parameter.

b12-phase-cutoff.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.st: The cutoff is identically zero near the lower endpoint of the integral, where $d\rho/\rho$ would be singular. Near infinity the integrand is exactly $d\rho/\rho$. The $C^2$ join of $\chi$ gives a $C^3$ radial phase, including at the transition radii, as required for differentiating (B.7) and (B.8) twice in space.

pdf-item-equation-B-9.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.Pr: The function $f_*$ allows the logarithmic slope of the radial phase at infinity to change while leaving the field on the interior ball unaffected by the phase change. Thus the same parameter can enter the interior residual polynomially and alter the leading similarity transport of an oscillating tail. The split between these two calculations is used in B.4.
pdf-item-equation-B-9.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.mo: Writing $a=\mathsf k\cdot\alpha$, the operation changes only the phase parameter from $f$ to $f+a f_*$. The compactification length and angular order stay fixed, so the same harmonic labels and amplitude meshes can be used for all trials.
pdf-item-equation-B-9.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.st: The integral is a function of squared radius, although it is integrated in the ordinary radius. If $R>0$, differentiation with respect to $R$ gives $R\partial_R f_*(R^2)=\chi(R/(R+\mathsf L))$. This explains both the interior agreement and the logarithmic tail.
pdf-item-equation-B-9.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.af: On the cutoff ball $f_*$ and its radial derivatives vanish, so the exponential and the differential construction of the amplitudes both agree with their values at $\alpha=0$. This gives an exact affine identity for the velocity, also for its first derivatives and almost everywhere its second derivatives. It is this identity on the ball that is used in the expansion (B.57).
pdf-item-equation-B-9.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.st: For $R\le r_\chi$, the whole interval $0\le\rho\le R$ in (B.9) has $\rho/(\rho+\mathsf L)\le\sigma_\chi$. Not only is the integral zero, but its radial derivatives vanish at the transition as well, to the orders implied by $\chi\in C^2$. This matters because $\mathcal V_l$ in the velocity formulas differentiates the phase.
pdf-item-equation-B-9.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.In: Beyond the last transition of $\chi$, the difference $f_*(R^2)-\log R$ has zero derivative in $R$. The resulting addition to the phase changes its logarithmic slope by $\mathsf k\cdot\alpha$, while leaving the power $(1-\sigma)^h$ unchanged. In the squared-radius variable the tail is $\tfrac12\log\rho+C$.

b12-independent-amplitudes.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.Pr: Each $W^i_\alpha$ has its own amplitude data; only the common phase varies. The formula therefore does not require identical spline meshes for the different fields. In particular a derivative with respect to $\alpha$ outside the cutoff ball also differentiates the radial phase.

b12-phase-vanishes.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.st: Inverting the compactification gives the cutoff radius $r_\chi=\mathsf L\sigma_\chi/(1-\sigma_\chi)$. On this entire ball the integrand has been zero, not merely zero at the upper limit. Hence $f_*$ vanishes there, including the boundary.

b12-phase-logtail.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.In: For $R$ beyond the transition of $\chi$, $\partial_R f_*(R^2)=1/R$. Hence the tail is $\log R+C$, or $\tfrac12\log\rho+C$ in the squared-radius argument $\rho=R^2$. The factor $1/2$ in the latter expression is needed when using $f_*'(\rho)$ in (B.5).

b12-profile-affine.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.af: On the matching ball write $U=\sum_i\alpha_iW_0^i$. Then the terms of degree two in the residual are $(U\cdot\nabla)U+(\varsigma\cdot\alpha)\partial_\theta U-\nabla(|U|^2/2)$, or equivalently the rotational form of the convection plus the period term. The pressure and force coefficients are affine there. This is an exact degree-two expansion as in (B.57), and the exterior is estimated separately; a gradient cannot simply be discarded in a pairing over the ball.

b12-phase-outside.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.mo: Outside the ball the coefficient combination alone no longer describes the parameter dependence. For key $(\iota,l)$ there is a new factor $\exp(il(\mathsf k\cdot\alpha) f_*(|y|^2))$; the radial operator differentiating that factor changes accordingly.
b12-phase-outside.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.shiftedSca: The change of phase alters the radial derivative even when the amplitude data are fixed. By $2R^2 f_*'(R^2)=\chi(\sigma)$, the new $\mathcal V_l$ differs by multiplication by $il(\mathsf k\cdot\alpha)\chi(\sigma)$. Retaining the old operator while changing the exponential would invalidate the divergence identity used in (B.7) and (B.8).

b12-joint-parameter-smooth.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.mo: Joint $C^1$ regularity is a local statement in $(\alpha,\theta,y)$. On differentiating the exterior phase in $\alpha_i$ one obtains the factor $il k_i f_*(R^2)$, which grows like $\log R$. Thus even though the velocity and spatial derivatives have the uniform decay of (7.8), the parameter derivative of a leading oscillatory term can be of order $R^{-1}\log R$. These are distinct assertions.

b12-uniform-parameter-decay.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.mo: For $\alpha$ in the bounded parameter box, $|\mathsf k\cdot\alpha|$ has one upper bound. Since $R\partial_R f_*(R^2)=\chi(\sigma)$, the scaled derivatives up to order three of $f_\alpha$ have common bounds, and the phase factors have modulus one. The finitely many amplitude splines then give uniform bounds in (7.8); there is no need for a uniform bound on $f_\alpha$ itself.

b12-period-affine.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.Is: The operator $\mathcal T_S$ contains $S^{-1}\partial_\theta$, so affine dependence of $S^{-1}$ makes this part of the interior residual a quadratic polynomial in $\alpha$. Affine dependence of $S$ itself would introduce a denominator. In the exterior the matching change of the logarithmic radial phase cancels the leading time and similarity transport terms as in C.4.

b12-forcing-affine.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.Is: The force coefficient of the approximate equation is prescribed by $\beta^{\mathrm a}(\alpha)$, whereas $\beta$ is solved for in the correction equation. The force of the corrected field is zero only when $\beta^{\mathrm a}(\alpha)+\beta=0$. This is the finite-dimensional equation addressed by the parameter bounds (7.35)–(7.37), after the linearized inverse has controlled $\beta$.

b12-pressure-residual.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.Is:
The left-hand side of (7.10) contains $(W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}\cdot
abla)W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}$. Using $(W\cdot
abla)W=\operatorname{curl}W	imes W+
abla(|W|^2/2)$, addition of $
abla(q_\alpha-|W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}|^2/2)$ leaves the rotational convection term and $
abla q_\alpha$. Thus $q_\alpha$ is the auxiliary total pressure of (C.1), not the pressure alone.
b12-pressure-residual.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.Pr: The stored pressure data are combined at the moved phase, just as the velocity data are. Their explicit coefficients are affine but their global fields need not be. The pressure formula supplies a scalar whose gradient can be added in forming the residual, not a solution of a pressure Poisson equation.

b12-pressure-terms.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.Is: The pressure data are used to select a representative of the residual modulo gradients. The advantage is that (7.23) measures the full norm of that representative, rather than requiring a computation of the Leray projection. The regularity conditions on the scalar ensure that its weak gradient is locally a function; they do not yet bound the residual in $\mathcal H$.

b12-pressure-exponents.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.Is: The exponent $h'$ belongs to the axis factor, not the radial factor $\sigma^{h_0}$. For a nonzero angular integer, $(1-\eta^2)^{h'}=(r/R)^{2h'}$ with $h'\ge1$ gives a bounded angular derivative divided by $r$ away from the origin. At the origin $h_0\ge1$ or a zero trace of $\mathsf P$ supplies order-$R$ vanishing. In the axisymmetric case $h'=0$ and a constant trace suffices if $h_0=0$. These are `axisOrder` and `lowOrder`, respectively; the pressure needs only a locally bounded weak gradient.

b12-pressure-symmetries.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.Is: Unlike the polar component of the velocity, a scalar pressure has no extra sign under the half-turn: only $\eta$ is reversed and the label replaced by $\iota^\flat$. Negating both the label and radial index gives the conjugate phase and requires conjugate coefficients.

b12-pressure-lipschitz.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.pr: The pressure field is continuous across its polynomial interfaces. Integrating its derivative on the two sides of an interface gives cancelling boundary terms because the values agree, even if the derivatives differ. Thus the weak gradient is represented by the piecewise classical gradient, locally bounded by the regularity theorem. This is sufficient for adding it to the residual.

b12-pressure-gradient.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.sc: Put $p_\alpha=q_\alpha-|W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}|^2/2$. Integration by parts against a compactly supported solenoidal test makes $\nabla p_\alpha$ disappear from the equation modulo gradients. It must nevertheless be included when computing $\|F_\alpha^{\mathrm a}\|_{\mathcal H}$ and $[F_\alpha^{\mathrm a}]$: the cell rows need not be globally solenoidal. The pressure is chosen to bound this particular representative, not just its action on solenoidal tests.

If the prescribed join order in one variable is $d$, identifying the endpoint derivatives through order $d$ gives equality of the corresponding traces on adjacent pieces. In a Hermite basis the free coefficients for higher endpoint derivatives and interior polynomials remain available to fit the field. For two variables the traces are themselves polynomials in the other variable, so their equality also supplies the necessary tangential derivative matches.

b12-forcing-data.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.IsCompactT: Multiplying an arbitrary solenoidal field by a scalar cutoff would produce the extra divergence $\nabla\chi\cdot b$. Here support is imposed instead on the free amplitude splines before (B.7) and (B.8) construct the dependent components. With the zero origin coefficient the field is compactly supported and the divergence cancellation is unchanged.

b12-forcing-smooth.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.FieldJoint: The support is imposed on the free splines, not by multiplying the resulting field by a discontinuous characteristic function. At the last support sphere their joined traces also vanish to the orders required in (B.7) and (B.8). This is consistent with the global $C^1$ assertion for $b_i$ even at that sphere.

b12-forcing-divergence.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.keyDiverge: No projection is needed to make the represented force divergence-free: each harmonic is constructed by (B.7) or (B.8), and the divergence of each term vanishes under the shape hypotheses. The cutoff is built into the amplitudes, rather than applied afterwards to a solenoidal vector field.
b12-forcing-divergence.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.fieldClass: The force uses its own length and radial phase, but the same angular order and reflection rules. Since these are precisely the hypotheses for generator invariance of the represented fields, each force respects the common symmetries. Full $\Gamma$-invariance additionally uses the generation condition.

b12-forcing-support.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.compactFie: The last possible nonzero radial coordinate is $\sigma_i$, whose inverse image is the sphere of radius $\mathsf L_i\sigma_i/(1-\sigma_i)$. All terms, including the origin term, are zero beyond it: the free polynomials vanish there, and $\gamma=0$. The meridian square in B.3 encloses this ball, so no forcing term is omitted in treating the complement.

b12-adjoint-data.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.Is: The choice $h\ge3$ makes $\psi_j$ itself square integrable over the period, since its square is $O(R^{-6})$, and $y\cdot\nabla\psi_j$ has the same decay. pdf-item-equation-B-21.Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.RowRestClause: The right side of (B.21) supplies precisely the quantities absent from (B.20): the positive coefficient energy $c\omega^2|\beta|^2$ and the opposite of the linear actuator term, with $c=3/50$. Once the inequalities are combined, the only other costs are the measured components of $F$ and the constraint values. This is an estimate for the bordered problem, not for the velocity operator alone.
pdf-item-equation-B-21.Breakdown.CertCell.rowRestClause_closed: Proposition B.8 supplies this inequality for arbitrary admissible $v,\beta,F$, not just their retained coefficients. The finite vector in B.3 records certain measurements of these fields; the omitted coefficients, omitted harmonics and the complement of the cells all have lower estimates. The linked theorem assumes the complete cell, region and tree conditions, and proves (B.21) together with finiteness of $\mathcal I^-$. It does not assert that those conditions have been verified for numerical data.

b12-density-from-cells.Breakdown.CertCell.rowRestClause_closed: In (B.44) the measured coordinates $x_{\rm p}$ are fixed by the perturbation and forcing, but the auxiliary coordinates $x_{\rm f}$ can still be chosen. The right side is at most the difference in (B.21), for every choice, since $2\zeta\cdot\ell(v)-|\zeta|^2/1000\le1000|\ell(v)|^2$. Thus one only needs a single extension $(x_{\rm p},x_{\rm f})$ on which the tree form is nonnegative. The dimension argument after Lemma B.7 provides it; positivity on all auxiliary vectors is neither required nor expected.

pdf-item-equation-B-22.Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.extendedCoerciveC: Set $c=3/50$ and $t=1000$. The scalar estimate gives $\sqrt c\|(v,\beta)\|_{w,\omega}\le c_{\mathsf M}\|F\|_{\mathcal H}+\sqrt c[F]+\sqrt t|\ell(v)|$. Dividing by $\sqrt c$ explains the first two comparisons in (B.22), and the coefficient of the row seminorm is exactly one.
pdf-item-equation-B-22.Breakdown.CertCell.Instance.IsRowInstanc: The first two inequalities of (B.22) normalize the multiplier and pin estimates in Lemma B.2. The third concerns the row space independently: $c\tau_k\le400(1+2^{-18})$ and $\tau_k=\|e_k\|_{\mathcal H}^2$, where $c=3/50$. Together with orthogonality this gives $[F]\le c_0\|F\|_{\mathcal H}$, needed when the right-hand side changes in Section 7.

b12-row-norm-budget.Breakdown.CertCell.Instance.IsRowInstanc: The cap on $c\tau_k$ and orthonormality of the unweighted rows give $\|e_k\|_{\mathcal H}^2=\tau_k\le c_0^2$. It is a uniform bound per row. The formal row instance imposes the weight budget, while the Gram normalization theorem supplies the unit norms.

b12-lemma-b2.Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.extendedCoerciveC: Lemma B.2 establishes the reference estimate (7.18). For the approximate profile put $G=(\mathcal C_\alpha-\mathcal C_\alpha^{\mathrm r})v$; the reference equation has right side $F-G$ with the same pins and force coefficients. The cost of $G$ in the two forcing terms is at most $(c_1+c_0)c_r\|v\|_w$. Absorption gives (7.52), with the factor $1-\vartheta$ on the left. For zero pins this gives $c_L$ by (7.21); existence for every datum still uses Proposition 7.8.
b12-lemma-b2.Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.rowMultiplierIneq: Let $I=\mathcal I^+-\mathcal I^-$ and $A=\sum_i\beta_i\langle b_i,\mathsf Mv\rangle$. Then (B.20) says $I+A\le\langle F,\mathsf Mv\rangle-c\|v\|_w^2-c_\mu\|v\|_\mu^2$, while (B.21) says $I+A\ge c\omega^2|\beta|^2-c[F]^2-1000|\ell(v)|^2$, with $c=3/50$. Comparing the bounds eliminates both $I$ and $A$ and leaves the squared norm of the pair with the extra frequency energy.
b12-lemma-b2.Breakdown.le_add_of_sq_le: For $P,a,Q\ge0$, suppose $P>a+Q$. Then $P>Q$ and $P-a>Q$, so $P(P-a)>Q^2$, contrary to $P^2\le aP+Q^2$. The simple bound $P\le a+Q$ keeps the right-hand-side and constraint contributions separate without having to estimate a quadratic root.
b12-lemma-b2.Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.extendedCoerciveC: The linked theorem abstracts the last step: once the row-multiplier inequality is available, the specific harmonic, cell and tree expressions are no longer needed. A positive reserve $c$ for the joint norm and a pin penalty $t$ produce the constants $c_{\mathsf M}/\sqrt c$ and $\sqrt{t/c}$, while the factor $c$ on the squared row seminorm gives coefficient one. Here $c=3/50$ and $t=1000$.

b12-lemma-finite.Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.pieceMultiplierDe: The multiplier theorem gives a finite $\mu$ seminorm even before assuming the density bound. The lemma additionally assumes $\mathcal I^-<\infty$, which makes $\mathcal I^+$ finite by the extended inequality. Only then is the real subtraction in (B.20) legitimate.

b12-lemma-addition.Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.rowMultiplierIneq: The two inequalities bound the same sum $I+\sum_i\beta_i\langle b_i,\mathsf Mv\rangle$ from above and below. Comparing the bounds moves $c\omega^2|\beta|^2$ next to $c\|v\|_w^2$, so their sum is exactly $c\|(v,\beta)\|_{w,\omega}^2$. The row and constraint terms move to the right with positive signs.

b12-lemma-cauchy.Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.extendedCoerciveC: The multiplier norm bound involves $c\|v\|_w^2+c_\mu\|v\|_\mu^2$, which is at most $P^2$ because $P^2$ also contains the nonnegative coefficient energy. Thus $\langle F,\mathsf Mv\rangle\le c_{\mathsf M}\|F\|_{\mathcal H}P$. No separate estimate of $\beta$ is required before this step.

b12-lemma-quadratic.Breakdown.le_add_of_sq_le: Since $P,Q,a\ge0$, the completed-square inequality implies $P-a/2\le Q+a/2$, regardless of the sign of $P-a/2$. Thus $P\le a+Q$. The further estimate $Q\le\sqrt{3/50}[F]+\sqrt{1000}|\ell(v)|$ separates the two data terms in the desired linear estimate.

b12-lemma-division.Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.extendedCoerciveC: Using $P\le a+Q$ and $Q\le\sqrt c[F]+\sqrt t|\ell(v)|$, drop the nonnegative frequency energy from $P^2$ and divide by $\sqrt c$. The coefficient of $[F]$ becomes one by construction; the others become $c_{\mathsf M}/\sqrt c$ and $\sqrt{t/c}$. This is the normalization in (7.18).

b12-uniform-coercivity.Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.extendedCoerciveC: For all $\alpha$ the same expression $c_{\mathsf M}^2=(1+n_\lambda+n_{\nabla\lambda}/\sqrt{w_*})^2/(3/50)+n_\mu/c_\mu$ bounds the multiplier in the two reserved energies. The mode sets and frequencies may yield different energies for the same $v$ at different parameters. After the scalar estimate eliminates the extra energy, the resulting $c_1,c_2$ no longer involve those frequencies.

ns-b3-purpose.Breakdown.CertCell.rowRestClause_closed: The integral in (B.21) measures what is left after the positive energies in (B.20) have been reserved. A lower bound for it is needed, not a bound on its absolute value. The forcing-field pairing has opposite signs in (B.20) and (B.21); its cancellation leaves an estimate for both $v$ and $\beta$, not just for $v$.

ns-b3-perturbation-class.Breakdown.CertCell.rowRestClause_closed: Fix $\alpha$ and a solution $(v,\beta)$ of the reference linearized equation with right-hand side $F$. No size restriction or truncation of $v$ is made. The finite vector used below consists of measurements of this solution; the inequalities for the remaining parts are what allow the resulting estimate to hold on the full domain.

ns-b3-quarter-plane.Breakdown.CertCell.modeDensityBridge_clo: Although each $\mathcal I_\iota$ is independent of time and angle, $J$ contains products of different harmonics and must first be averaged. The reduction to $(r,z)$ is exact. In particular neither the Fourier coefficients nor the integrals in (B.23) are values at discretization nodes.

ns-b3-modal-meridian-values.Breakdown.CertCell.modeDensityBridge_clo: By (B.13), moving from $(0,(r,0,z))$ to $(\theta,R_\phi(r,0,z))$ multiplies a mode by a phase and rotates its vector components. The gradient transforms by the rotation on both indices and the Hessian on all three. The Euclidean norms in (B.16) are therefore unchanged.

ns-b3-mean.Breakdown.CertCell.CellLayerData.meanStr: The mean is normalized by $1/(2\pi)$, the period in $\theta$ having length one. It is the mean of the entire expression $J$, not the expression obtained by substituting the means of its factors. The latter would miss the couplings between perturbation harmonics of different labels.

pdf-item-theorem-B-3.Breakdown.CertCell.modeDensityBridge_clo: The change of variables is applied separately to the positive and negative parts of the terms, including $J$. Tonelli's theorem then permits the sum over the whole harmonic lattice. Finiteness of the negative integral is enough to subtract the two identities, even if the result is $+\infty$.

ns-b3-b3-hypotheses.Breakdown.CertCell.modeDensityBridge_clo: Reflection at $z=0$ changes the harmonic label as in (B.24). The symmetry (B.17) is needed for the coefficients of the five squares to change in the same way. Thus the sum over labels has the required symmetry even if a single modal density does not.

pdf-item-equation-B-23.Breakdown.CertCell.modeDensityBridge_clo: The cylindrical change of variables gives $2\pi r\,dr\,dz$, since the time interval has length one. The second factor of two follows by (B.24), after summation over the reflected labels. This accounts for the factor $4\pi$ relating the integrals over the cells to the integral in (B.21).

ns-b3-b3-integrability.Breakdown.CertCell.DensityIdentity: One has $(\bar J)^-\le\overline{J^-}$, and the inequality can be strict: a nonzero sign-changing $J$ with mean zero has $(\bar J)^-=0$. The equality of sign integrals uses the expression on the right, not the negative part taken after averaging.

ns-b3-cylindrical-factor.Breakdown.CertCell.Bridge.halfPlaneReduc: The Jacobian of $y=(r\cos\phi,r\sin\phi,z)$ is $r$. Integration over $0<\phi<2\pi$ therefore gives $2\pi r\,dr\,dz$; averaging over $0<\theta<1$ introduces no additional factor. The passage from the full meridian to $z>0$ is a separate use of symmetry.

ns-b3-reflection-change-of-variable.Breakdown.CertCell.Bridge.modeFlip: In the two Fourier integers of (B.2), the transformation is $(j,k)\mapsto(j,-k)$. Since $j=2\iota_2-\iota_1$, changing the sign of $\iota_1$ while keeping $j$ fixed requires changing $\iota_2$ to $\iota_2-\iota_1$. This gives $\iota^\flat$, which is not the conjugate label $-\iota$.

pdf-item-equation-B-24.Breakdown.CertCell.Bridge.modeFlip: At $(r,0,0)$, $R_*y=y$ and $R_*$ has signs $(1,-1,-1)$ on the cylindrical frame. For a fixed label ($\iota_1=0$) the azimuthal and axial velocity traces therefore vanish on $z=0$. For a nonfixed label, the axial trace is instead the negative of that of $\iota^\flat$. The rectangles below exploit the latter identity.

ns-b3-reflect-density.Breakdown.CertCell.Bridge.halfPlaneReduc: For the integrals over $z<0$ change variables to $-z>0$, then replace the summation label by $\iota^\flat$. Since $(\iota^\flat)^\flat=\iota$, this is a bijection of the harmonic lattice. It is the full sum that is even in $z$; a single $I_\iota$ need not be.

ns-b3-reflect-stretch.Breakdown.CertCell.modeDensityBridge_clo: The rotation $R_*$ is the half-turn about the first coordinate axis and has determinant one. In particular $(R_*a)\times(R_*b)=R_*(a\times b)$, and curl transforms by $R_*$ as well. This is why all three contractions in (B.18) are unchanged; an orientation-reversing reflection would require different curl signs.

ns-b3-positive-negative.Breakdown.CertCell.modeDensityBridge_clo: The equality for each sign precedes the averaging of the signed stretching density. By Tonelli one may sum the nonnegative integrals over all labels even without absolute convergence. Once the negative integral is finite, subtraction yields (B.23).

ns-b3-stretch-bounded.Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.exteriorPoin: On the complement there will be no matrix entries for interactions between different harmonics. We bound the whole negative contribution of $J$ by a sum of losses depending on one harmonic at a time. This permits the use of scalar tests (B.29)–(B.30), including on infinitely many harmonics, rather than a matrix test there.

ns-b3-b25.Breakdown.CellCert.CellAnalysis.supremum: The mean $\bar{\mathbb V}$ is taken in the rotating frame, in which its two Fourier integers are zero. The terms with this coefficient pair equal labels. For the fluctuation use $2|\nabla v||v|\le \mathsf h|\nabla v|^2+|v|^2/\mathsf h$ on the full field before averaging; Parseval then separates the squares. The choice of $\mathsf h(r,z)$ trades a gradient loss for a velocity loss.

ns-b3-curl-matrix.Breakdown.CellCert.CellAnalysis.supremum: The curl depends only on the antisymmetric part of the gradient: $|\operatorname{curl}G|^2=2|(G-G^{\mathsf T})/2|^2$. The bound by $2|G|^2$ is used when a curl-square coefficient is negative. If that coefficient is nonnegative, it can instead be discarded in a lower bound; this gives the minimum with zero in $\mathsf f_1^*$.

ns-b3-stretch-coefficients.Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.IsRegionChar: The sign of the first term of (B.18) matters: one needs only an upper bound on the largest eigenvalue of the symmetric strain, not on the magnitudes of its negative eigenvalues. The last two terms are estimated in absolute value; hence the bounds $\mathsf s_2$ and $\mathsf s_3$ are on operator norms. The mean defining $\mathsf s_2$ is taken in the cylindrical frame.

ns-b3-stretch-signs.Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.IsRegionChar: The strain $\mathbb S$ is symmetric with trace $\operatorname{div}W^{\mathrm r}=0$. Its largest eigenvalue is therefore nonnegative, so every upper bound for its quadratic form on unit vectors is nonnegative. The two other bounds are on operator norms.

ns-b3-three-harmonic-sets.Breakdown.CertCell.IsCellMesh: The three sets have different uses. Resolved harmonics contribute polynomial coordinates; only the subset with triples $\varphi$ gives explicit tests of the equation. Eliminated harmonics contribute to those estimates without contributing coordinates: their velocity can be expressed through an angular derivative. They, like the other unresolved harmonics, must still pass the residual test after the charges in (B.28) have been deducted.

ns-b3-axis-modes.Breakdown.CertCell.IsCellMesh: Off the axis the polynomial norm is unweighted, so one can use $r\ge r_1>0$ to compare it with the physical norm. At the axis this would give a zero lower bound; the radial Jacobi basis instead includes the weight $r$ in its orthogonality. The resolved harmonics there have zero angular frequency but may have nonzero time frequency.

ns-b3-degrees.Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.IsCellMo: The degree $\mathsf d_0$ bounds the tests of the equation. The larger degree $\mathsf d$ bounds the measured gradient, and $\mathsf d-1$ the measured velocity. These are two projections of the actual field and its actual gradient; one is not obtained by differentiating the other. In particular the derivative of a velocity polynomial of the first omitted degree can still be measured. Its contribution to the error is the reason for $\mathsf T_{\mathsf Q}$.
ns-b3-degrees.Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.IsTestOf: For a harmonic of angular frequency $k$, the divergence equation of a test is $\partial_r(r\varphi_r)+ik\varphi_\phi+r\partial_z\varphi_z=0$. The three component degree bounds place this entire expression in the space of bidegree at most $(\mathsf d_0,\mathsf d_0)$. One can therefore enforce zero divergence by a finite set of linear equations on the polynomial coefficients. `IsTestOfShape` specifies the degrees, not the vanishing of that expression.

ns-b3-polynomial-models.Breakdown.CertCell.ModelPolys: The models are for the coefficients of the linearized equation, not for the unknown perturbation. The two models $W^{\rm r}$ and $\operatorname{curl}W^{\rm r}$ enter the linearization of $(\operatorname{curl}W)\times W$, while $\mathbb S$ and $\mathbb V$ enter the stretching form (B.18). Their errors are bounded before choosing the perturbation.

ns-b3-inverse-period-model.Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.IsPeriod: The time derivative on the mode contributes $2\pi i(2\iota_2-\iota_1)/S(\alpha)$. Replacing $1/S(\alpha)$ by a number with error at most $\varepsilon$ changes this multiplier by at most $2\pi|2\iota_2-\iota_1|\varepsilon$. The bound is required on the whole parameter set $\mathcal K$, since the same cell certificate is used in every linear solve there.

ns-b3-cell-data.Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.IsCellMo: The side and corner data permit integration by parts without recovering the whole field from its polynomial coefficients. For instance, on $[a,b]$, $(b-a)u(a)=\int_a^b(u-(b-r)u_r)\,dr$. Applying this identity in both directions gives the corner velocity in terms of volume integrals of $u,u_r,u_z,u_{rz}$, which also define it for the weak perturbations used in Lean.

ns-b3-additional-unknowns.Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.IsCellFo: The coefficients $\beta$ are part of the given equation; they belong to the prescribed coordinates. By contrast $\zeta$ is introduced to write $1000|\ell(v)|^2$ as the maximum of $2\zeta\cdot\ell(v)-|\zeta|^2/1000$. The inequality is valid for every $\zeta$, which lets the tree choose it along with the other free coordinates.

ns-b3-global-unknowns.Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.InRowRange: For instance the moments of the normal velocity on a side shared by two cells arise from the same trace of $v$. If outward fluxes are used, the two moments have opposite signs. Expressing the two cell vectors through one real vector imposes this relation exactly, rather than requiring a matrix inequality on two independent copies of the same trace.

ns-b3-determined-free.Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.TreeRowCondi: The perturbation determines $x_{\rm p}$ once, before any of the matrix bounds is used. The inequalities (B.33) and (B.34) are then required for every $x_{\rm f}$ with this same $x_{\rm p}$. In the formal state this is the role of `freeMap_zero`: varying the auxiliary coordinates does not alter the prescribed measurements.

ns-b3-global-relations.Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.TreeRowCondi: On a radial side $r=a>0$, divergence gives $\partial_r u_r=-(u_r+ik u_\phi)/a-\partial_z u_z$. Multiplication by a side polynomial and integration by parts in $z$ expresses the normal derivative moment in terms of velocity moments and endpoint values of $u_z$. Thus the side relations eliminate more coordinates than mere continuity across the cell interface would.

ns-b3-complex-forms.Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.TreeStateInt: For a real global vector $x$, the local form is $\operatorname{Re}((X_Qx)^*A_QX_Qx)$. It is therefore the real symmetric form with matrix $\operatorname{Re}(X_Q^*(A_Q+A_Q^*)X_Q/2)$. This is how a complex cell matrix contributes to the real form $N$ in (B.38).

ns-b3-leaf-matrix.Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.IsLeafVa: There are two matrices here. The $12\times12$ matrix at $(r,z)$ acts on the nine gradient components and the three velocity components of one harmonic. Integrating its entries against products of basis polynomials supplies part of the energy matrix. The cell matrix $\mathsf A_{\mathsf Q}$ acts on the much larger vector containing polynomial coefficients, side and corner data, and auxiliary unknowns.

ns-b3-leaf-coefficients.Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.IsLeafVa: The lower bounds $\mathsf I_2>0$ and $\mathsf I'_2\ge0$ apply to different second-derivative squares. A positive Hessian floor supplies the principal reserve in (B.27). If there is also a curl-gradient reserve, it first pays the cost involving the curl of the omitted part; only the excess curl cost has to be paid from the Hessian reserve.

ns-b3-leaf-upper-lower.Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.IsLeafVa: The first comparison makes $A^{\mathsf Q,\iota}$ a lower model for the three lower-order terms of $\mathcal I_\iota$, after allowance for coefficient errors. The second ensures that its contribution on the omitted polynomial part can pay the stretching and other losses, up to costs assigned to the derivative reserve. Neither comparison asserts positivity of $\mathsf A_{\mathsf Q}$.

ns-b3-b26-admitted-vectors.Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.InRowRange: The comparison need not hold on arbitrary independent values of all the moments. It holds on vectors consistent with the prescribed row relations, for example the divergence relation on a side. `InRowRange` also permits the stated gauge and pressure-head directions; a moment marked unused is not constrained by its row equality.

pdf-item-equation-B-26.Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.EliminationC: The direction of (B.26) is dictated by (B.33): we seek a lower bound for the density integral, so the form of $\mathsf A_{\mathsf Q}$ must be no greater than the sum of the forms obtained from that integral and the permitted pairings. The subtraction of $\mathsf T_{\mathsf Q}$ is essential; it has already spent part of the measured gradient energy on the velocity tail. `residual_value_le` imposes the comparison only on the admitted local vectors.

ns-b3-cell-energy-form.Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.IsLeafVa: For example, if $P=\sum c_{jl}P_j(r)Q_l(z)$ is a retained component on an off-axis cell, then $\int |P|^2\,dr\,dz=\sum |c_{jl}|^2$. A variable coefficient $a$ in the physical integral instead gives matrix entries $\int aP_jQ_l\overline{P_{j\prime}Q_{l\prime}}r\,dr\,dz$. The matrix is thus determined by the coefficient field and the basis, not by point evaluations of the perturbation.
