ns-b3-cell-potential-pairing-top.Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.EliminationC: The form $\mathsf P_{\mathsf Q}$ concerns the stretching products and $\mathsf B_{\mathsf Q}$ the signed pairings with $\nabla b_i$ and $\Xi_i$. The deduction $\mathsf T_{\mathsf Q}$ is needed even when the gradient tail is small: the velocity is retained one degree less than the gradient. An omitted velocity coefficient can be controlled by gradient coefficients near the cutoff which are still among the unknowns, and their cost has to be included in the finite form.

ns-b3-cell-eliminated-rows.Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.EliminationC: For one gradient coordinate of an eliminated mode, denote its weight by $w>0$, its combined source by $s$, and the proposed linear approximation by $b$. Expand $w|g|^2-2\operatorname{Re}(\bar g s)$ about $g=b$. The constant term is $w|b|^2-2\operatorname{Re}(\bar b s)$; Young's inequality bounds the mixed remainder below by $-|s-wb|^2/(w\delta)-\delta w|g-b|^2$. This gives `bandEliminated` and leaves $(1-\delta)w|g-b|^2$ for the forcing-row errors. Here $0<\delta<1$; at $\delta=0$ the source must equal $wb$.

ns-b3-b27.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.hessTailGain: An omitted gradient coefficient has degree at least $\mathsf d+1$ in at least one variable, so the derivative gain is bounded below by the smaller of the two eigenvalues. Off the axis it is multiplied by $r_1$. The angular derivative of a gradient has two rotation indices; for angular integer $k$ its gain is $(|k|-2)_+^2$. Its measure is $r\,dr\,dz/r^2$, giving the additional coefficient $(|k|-2)_+^2/r_2$. These gains come from distinct parts of the Hessian square.
ns-b3-b27.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.TailBudget.H: Divide the costs by the squared gradient remainder. A curl cost already paid by the curl-gradient reserve need not be counted again; the positive excess costs at most twice as much in gradient units, by $|\operatorname{curl}G|^2\le2|G|^2$. The velocity remainder costs its nonnegative charge divided by the smaller eigenvalue at degree $\mathsf d$, in addition to the form $\mathsf T_{\mathsf Q}$ on measured coefficients. `TailBudget.Holds` compares the resulting sum with the Hessian reserve at degree $\mathsf d+1$.

If $r_1>0$, the unweighted radial and axial derivative estimates gain the factor $r_1$ on passing to $r\,dr\,dz$. On the axis this comparison would give zero. Instead the Jacobi radial basis uses $r\,dr$ from the outset, and the axial estimate uses this same weight as a parameter. The factor in the tail gain is then $1$.

ns-b3-polynomial-eigenvalues.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.hessTailGain: For example on $[-1,1]$ a Legendre polynomial satisfies $-[(1-x^2)P_j']'=j(j+1)P_j$. Integrating by parts gives a derivative form with coefficient $1-x^2\le1$, whose eigenvalues bound the omitted coefficients. With the radial weight $1+x$ on an axis cell the Jacobi derivative form gives $j(j+2)$ instead. The derivative weight vanishes at the endpoints; no zero boundary values of the perturbation are required.

ns-b3-unresolved-charges.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.offModeDensi: The quantities $\mathsf a'_1,\mathsf a_1,\mathsf a_0$ account for the curl, gradient and velocity squares left out of the finite cell form. Inside a cell these are signed coefficient allowances: for instance the velocity allowance contains the cost of the reflected trace in (B.34). On the complement there is no cell form to return a credit, and the three allowances are required to be nonnegative. This ensures $\mathcal I_\iota-\mathcal L\ge\mathcal I_\iota^\circ$ there.

ns-b3-b28.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.offModeDensi: The left side of (B.33) consists of the finite matrix form, the error term and the sum of these residual integrals for the modes with no resolved polynomial. The aim is to show that the latter sum can be dropped from a lower bound. This requires an estimate for the actual modes of $v$, including their couplings to the polynomials, not a Fourier truncation of $v$.

ns-b3-modified-stretch-constant.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.PointCoef.wi: In (B.25) the factor $\sqrt{7/2}$ multiplies the mean-gradient product $\mathsf s_2|G||u|$ and the two Young terms with $\mathsf s_3$. Replacing it by $\mathsf c^*$ leaves the curl-square cost $\mathsf s_1$ alone. The larger constant is therefore allowed at the expense of a smaller lower bound for the unresolved density.

ns-b3-rectangle-region.Breakdown.CertCell.Bridge.IsCreditPatch: The rectangle does not introduce a second copy of the trace. Its vector consists of selected axial trace moments already present in the cells along $z=0$. The energy for their estimate comes from the reflected harmonic, which is neither resolved nor eliminated, so that it can be reserved in its velocity charge in (B.28).

ns-b3-rectangle-harmonic.Breakdown.CertCell.creditLeavesBound_clo: At $z=0$ the axial component changes sign under $R_*$. Hence $\hat v_{\iota^\flat}\cdot e_z=-\hat v_\iota\cdot e_z$ on that plane. One can use the energy of the absent reflected harmonic to control the resolved trace moments without introducing any new trace coordinates.

ns-b3-rectangle-test.Breakdown.CertCell.Bridge.IsCreditPatch: For a combination $\psi_c$ of the rectangle tests, divergence of the reflected mode $u$ gives the bottom trace pairing (up to sign) as $\int_\Pi u\cdot\overline{\nabla\psi_c}\,r\,dr\,dz$, where the gradient includes the angular derivative. With the positive reserved weight $a$, put $E=\int_\Pi a|u|^2r\,dr\,dz$. Weighted Cauchy–Schwarz and the Dirichlet matrix bound give $|c^*m|^2\le E c^*Mc$ for the vector $m$ of these trace pairings. Taking $c=M^{-1}m$ gives $m^*M^{-1}m\le E$, including the trivial case $m=0$. The credit is bounded by this inverse form.

ns-b3-regional-test.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.IsOffModeCon: The polynomial comparison (B.26) acts on finitely many coordinates. For a mode not resolved in a cell we instead estimate a quadratic form on its five derivative norms. The angular relations (B.35) reduce this comparison to two norms, $|\nabla u|$ and $|u|$, with $u=\hat v_\iota$. One scalar test can then cover every perturbation and many harmonic labels at once.

ns-b3-region-coefficient-data.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.IsOffModeCon: The labels in a regional set must share the enclosures for the multiplier pieces. Membership in $N_p$ and lower bounds on $|\Omega_p(\iota)|$ determine the contributions from (B.14)–(B.16); $|\varkappa\iota_1|\ge k_0$ supplies a separate angular derivative bound. In particular a mode with $\iota_1=0$ and large $|\iota_2|$ can benefit from the multiplier but not from a positive angular gain in (B.35).
ns-b3-region-coefficient-data.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.IsExteriorCo: At infinity the four numbers replace the pointwise choice of $\mathsf t$, not the bounds on the original five coefficients. We still need the lower Hessian coefficient and the charged coefficients throughout the region. The additional bounds compare the effective gradient term with losses of orders $\rho^{-2}|u|^2$ and $\rho^{-1}|\nabla u||u|$, where $\rho=|(r,z)|$.

ns-b3-regional-cover.Breakdown.CertCell.rowRestClause_closed: For a fixed label $\iota$, a finite cover of a cell suffices: the conclusions there hold almost everywhere, and are preserved on the union. On the complement the exterior inequality concerns an integral over an entire region. Summing inequalities for overlapping regions would count some parts of the density more than once, so the cover there is a partition up to null sets.

ns-b3-charged-coefficients.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.PointCoef.wi: Subtract (B.25) with $\mathsf c^*$ and the three charges in (B.28) from the five lower coefficients of (B.16). No term being subtracted contains a second derivative of the mode, so $\mathsf f_2$ and $\mathsf f'_2$ are unchanged. The sixth coefficient $\mathsf f_{01}$ bounds a loss, not a square, which is why it is an upper bound and enters (B.36) with a minus sign.

ns-b3-effective-coefficients.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.PointCoef.gr: Let $b=\mathsf f'_1+\mathsf f'_2(k_0-1)_+^2/r^2$. If $b<0$, the cost of the curl terms is at most $2|b||\nabla u|^2$; if $b\ge0$, their lower bound is zero. The Hessian term supplies $\mathsf f_2(k_0-2)_+^2/r^2$ to the gradient coefficient. Thus $\mathsf f_1^*$ includes the angular gains from the second derivatives, but not yet the gain from the first derivative of $u$.
ns-b3-effective-coefficients.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.PointCoef.ve: Put $q=(k_0-1)_+^2/r^2$. For $\mathsf t\ge0$, $\mathsf t|\nabla u|^2\ge q\mathsf t|u|^2$. Transferring this part of the gradient coefficient increases the velocity coefficient by $q\mathsf t$. Taking too much would leave too little of $\mathsf f_1^*$ to bound the mixed term in (B.29).

ns-b3-b29.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.PointCoef.Pa: With $A=\mathsf f_1^*-\mathsf t$, $B=\mathsf f_0^*$ and $c=\mathsf f_{01}$, the last inequality says that the matrix with diagonal entries $A,B$ and off-diagonal entries $-c/2$ is positive semidefinite. Equivalently, $4A(Ax^2+B y^2-cxy)=(2Ax-cy)^2+(4AB-c^2)y^2$ when $A>0$. If $A=0$, the condition forces $c=0$. Both cases give a nonnegative residual for $x=|\nabla u|$, $y=|u|$.

ns-b3-exterior-shapes.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.IsExteriorCo: The square exterior is a ray exterior with inner radius $a/\max(r/\rho,z/\rho)$ in the direction $(r,z)/\rho$. Its separate condition exploits the component symmetries of the zero angular mode. The constant $2$ in place of $1/4$ in (B.31) reduces the velocity cost in (B.30) by a factor of eight and the mixed cost by $\sqrt8$.
ns-b3-exterior-shapes.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.IsDirectionR: Fixing a direction fixes a single inner radius. The proof of (B.37) uses the interval from this radius to infinity, and differentiates only along the ray; no regularity of an angular boundary derivative is used. The formal condition requires a measurable radius with uniform positive lower and finite upper bounds, constant along each ray.

ns-b3-exterior-integrated-test.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.IsExteriorCo: At a label with zero angular wave number, (B.29) cannot repair a negative $\mathsf f_0$, because $(k_0-1)_+=0$. In the exterior, (B.31) gives control of $|u|/\rho$ even for such a mode. This permits a negative velocity coefficient decaying as $\rho^{-2}$, provided the integrated gradient term pays for it and the mixed term.

ns-b3-exterior-coefficient-bounds.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.IsExteriorCo: The factors $\rho^2$ and $\rho$ remove precisely the powers of radius controlled by (B.31). The velocity loss is bounded by a constant times the integral of $|u/\rho|^2$; the mixed loss is bounded by a constant times the integral of $|\nabla u||u/\rho|$. Any faster decay of the adverse coefficients can be incorporated into smaller upper bounds on the chosen exterior.

pdf-item-equation-B-30.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.IsExteriorCo: Use measure $r\,dr\,dz$ on $Z$, and put $D=\int_Z|\nabla u|^2r\,dr\,dz$, $V=\int_Z|u|^2\rho^{-2}r\,dr\,dz$. By (B.31), $V\le D/\Lambda_0$, and Cauchy–Schwarz bounds the mixed integral by $\sqrt{DV}$. Substitution into (B.36) gives a lower bound of $(\mathsf f_1^\infty-\mathsf f_0^\infty/\Lambda_0-\mathsf f_{01}^\infty/\sqrt{\Lambda_0})D$. Equation (B.30) makes this nonnegative.

ns-b3-b31.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.modeRayInver: One cannot add two estimates each using the whole gradient square. The ray estimate uses the derivative in direction $(r\mathbf e_r+z\mathbf e_z)/\rho$, and the angular estimate uses the derivative in direction $\mathbf e_\phi$. These directions are orthogonal, so the two energies occur separately in $|\nabla u|^2$. Since $r\le\rho$, both estimates can be written with weight $\rho^{-2}$.
ns-b3-b31.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.modeSquareIn: For the zero angular wave number the cylindrical coefficients are independent of $\phi$, but $\partial_\phi\mathbf e_r=\mathbf e_\phi$ and $\partial_\phi\mathbf e_\phi=-\mathbf e_r$. Consequently the gradient square still contains $(|u_r|^2+|u_\phi|^2)/r^2$. This is the term needed in the square-exterior estimate for the two transverse components.

pdf-item-theorem-B-4.Breakdown.CertCell.formNegFinite: The first conclusion of B.4 precedes any calculation with the finite matrix: it ensures that the density integral can be defined as $\mathcal I^+-\mathcal I^-$. Only in the finite-positive case are the real-valued cell bounds (B.33) and (B.34) needed. The linked theorem establishes the negative-part assertion.

ns-b3-b4-finite.Breakdown.CertCell.formNegFinite: The conclusion concerns the sum of the negative parts of the modal and stretching terms. It is not merely finiteness of the negative part after summing them, which could conceal cancellation. Once this is known, the signed density integral is meaningful even if its positive part is infinite.

ns-b3-b32.Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.exteriorPoin: For each $(r,z)$ the stretching bound gives $\bar J\ge-\sum_\iota\mathcal L_\iota$, so that the density is bounded below by a sum of single-mode terms $\mathcal I_\iota-\mathcal L_\iota$. On the complement there are no finite cell forms to compute, and it is this sum to which the scalar region estimates are applied.

ns-b3-b4-global-state.Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.TreeRowCondi: The condition $x_p=0$ at $v=\beta=F=0$ is essential, even though we are interested in nonzero perturbations. Applied to (B.44) it says that the assembled form is nonpositive on the full free-coordinate subspace. That subspace will therefore meet the strictly positive column kernel of Lemma B.7 only at zero.

ns-b3-b33-error-quantifiers.Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.IsCellFo: The numbers $\mathsf r_{\mathsf Q,j}$ are witnesses to an inequality for the chosen extension $x_{\rm g}$, not new certificate constants required to work for all perturbations. Only their signed combination, $\mathsf r_{\mathsf Q,1}+\mathsf r_{\mathsf Q,2}+\mathsf r_{\mathsf Q,3}|\beta|^2-\mathsf r_{\mathsf Q,0}$, must obey the common bound (B.34). Keeping this combination avoids charging the same error twice.

pdf-item-equation-B-33.Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.IsCellFo: There are two operations still to perform on (B.33): drop the unresolved residual integrals using (B.29), and move $\mathsf r_{\mathsf Q,0}$ to the right. The resulting signed error is exactly the one in (B.34), which also accounts for the rectangle forms. Neither operation requires the cell form itself to be nonnegative.

ns-b3-b33-absolute-convergence.Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.IsCellFo: The complement of the resolved set is taken separately in each cell. Absolute convergence is asserted for the sum of its residual integrals, not obtained merely by knowing each integral exists. This justifies discarding their nonnegative sum after (B.29), even though infinitely many harmonics have no coordinates.

ns-b3-b34.Breakdown.CertCell.rowSharesOfInstance: Put $f_k=e_k/\sqrt{\tau_k}$. By (B.11) the $f_k$ are orthonormal, whereas $[F]^2=\sum_k\tau_k|\langle F,f_k\rangle_{\mathcal H}|^2$. The weights are therefore part of the row calculation in (B.34); replacing it by an unweighted projection norm would in general change the coercive estimate.
ns-b3-b34.Breakdown.CertCell.InstancePair.pairShar: The actuator term in (B.34) is a gradient pairing. Indeed the modes of $b_i$ have $\operatorname{sgn}_p(\iota)=0$ for all the skew multipliers by the condition in B.2, so $\langle b_i,\mathsf Mv\rangle_{\mathcal H}=\langle\nabla b_i,\nabla v\rangle_{\mathcal H}$. The other pairing, $2\zeta\cdot\ell(v)$, has the gradient representation (B.10). Thus both can be estimated by the polynomial gradient data and errors in the cells.
ns-b3-b34.Breakdown.CertCell.creditLeavesBound_clo: One trace estimate uses the charged velocity square of $\iota^\flat$. The estimate for the conjugate label $-\iota^\flat$ gives the same real form because the underlying perturbation is real. This accounts for the factor $2$ in (B.34); it is not the factor of two from the reduction of the meridian to the quarter plane.

ns-b3-square-final-claim.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.modeSquareIn: For $\iota_1=0$ the reflected label is the original one. At $z=0$ the axial component changes sign in (B.24), so its trace is zero. On the axis, a smooth axisymmetric vector must be fixed by all axial rotations, hence its transverse components vanish. These are the boundary conditions on the coordinate planes; none is imposed on the two inner sides of the square exterior.

ns-b3-negative-finite-proof.Breakdown.CertCell.formNegFinite: One need not first prove that the full signed density is integrable. The lower bounds for the coefficients of (B.16) control only its possible negative contributions, using the regularity of the perturbation; for $J$ the derivative bounds on $W^{\rm r}$ and Hardy control the mixed velocity-gradient terms. This establishes $\mathcal I^-<\infty$ independently of the sign of the finite form.

ns-b3-parseval-coupling.Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.meanStretchT: With the conjugated factor of label $\jmath$, a coefficient of label $\eta$ contributes through $E_\eta E_\iota\overline{E_\jmath}$. The mean vanishes unless $\jmath=\eta+\iota$. In particular a nonzero coefficient label gives an off-diagonal coupling, not a term which vanishes merely because that coefficient has mean zero.

ns-b3-strain-first-term.Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.IsRegionChar: The strain term of (B.18) is $-\langle\mathbb S\operatorname{curl}v,\operatorname{curl}v\rangle$. The assumption $\mathbb S\le s_1 I$ gives the lower bound $-s_1|\operatorname{curl}v|^2$. Since $s_1$ is independent of time and angle, Parseval now gives the sum of the corresponding modal lower bounds.

ns-b3-trace-free-contraction.Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.exteriorPoin: The two mixed terms in (B.18) must be estimated together: the matrix $\mathbb V$ has trace zero because $\operatorname{div}\operatorname{curl}W^{\rm r}=0$. The contraction estimate quoted here uses this restriction to obtain the constant $\sqrt{7/2}$. Since both the mean and the fluctuation have trace zero, the same estimate is available for the diagonal modal pairing and the full fluctuation pairing.

ns-b3-local-data-modulo-gauge.Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.InRowRange: A spatially constant pressure can be added at each time without changing the equation. More generally the row representation permits the gauge and pressure-head directions in `InRowRange`. The represented local vector need only agree with the actual measurements modulo the allowed directions (and unused rows); the form comparison is imposed on that set, not on arbitrary complex arrays.
ns-b3-local-data-modulo-gauge.Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.TreeRowCondi: It is not necessary for $\mathsf X_{\mathsf Q}x_{\rm g}$ to agree with every chosen pressure representative as a vector. It suffices that their difference lies in directions on which the cell form does not depend. In particular `head_kernel` requires annihilation by the cell matrix and its adjoint, so that adding a pressure-head vector introduces neither a square nor a cross term in the form.

ns-b3-resolved-splitting.Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.IsCellMo: For the polynomial projection $P_j$ the two remainders are $(1-P_{\mathsf d})\nabla u$ and $(1-P_{\mathsf d-1})u$. Orthogonality cancels cross terms only in the measure of the polynomial basis; for example $\int P\bar R\,dr\,dz=0$ does not imply $\int aP\bar R\,r\,dr\,dz=0$. The matrix bounds and charges must account for such products.

ns-b3-resolved-energy-bound.Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.IsLeafVa: A lower bound with constant Hessian coefficient allows the portion recovered from the retained gradient coefficients to be separated from a derivative remainder. The remainder is what pays the charges for the missing polynomial coefficients. The lower-order matrix comparison alone would not supply that reserve.

ns-b3-coupling-label-rule.Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.meanStretchT: The rule for the blocks is addition of the two labels: a coefficient of label $\eta$ multiplying a mode of label $\iota$ can pair with the conjugate of a mode of label $\iota+\eta$. In particular a finite harmonic model of the coefficient supplies only finitely many label differences, even though the perturbation has infinitely many harmonics.

ns-b3-resolved-model-coupling.Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.EliminationC: The actual cross term between retained polynomials $P_1,P_2$ and a coefficient $a$ differs from the modeled one by at most $2\varepsilon\int_Q |P_1P_2|r\,dr\,dz$ if $|a-a_{\rm mod}|\le\varepsilon$. Young's inequality charges this to the two diagonal squares. The error bound must hold on the entire cell, not just at points used to fit the coefficient.

ns-b3-eliminated-mode.Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.EliminationC: In the cylindrical frame the angular derivative is $r(e_\phi\cdot\nabla)u=(ikI+e_z\times)u$. On the axial and the two circular transverse components the eigenvalues are $ik,i(k+1),i(k-1)$. Since nonzero angular frequencies here have $|k|\ge3$, the map is invertible. All pairings with the velocity of an eliminated harmonic can thus be included in pairings with its gradient, on which a positive square has been reserved.

ns-b3-unresolved-absorption.Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.IsLeafVa: After computing the resolved-polynomial couplings and treating the eliminated band, the remaining products contain at least one factor not measured by the cell vector. For a resolved harmonic their costs must be absorbed by the lower pointwise comparison for $A^{\mathsf Q,\iota}$ and the derivative-tail bounds. For an unresolved harmonic the costs are deducted from $\mathcal I_\iota$ in defining $\mathcal I_\iota^\circ$.
ns-b3-unresolved-absorption.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.offModeDensi: The residual in (B.28) is not the original energy of an unresolved mode. The stretching loss and the three extra charges have already been deducted from it. Its nonnegativity therefore leaves the deducted energy available to pay for the products and measurements assigned to that harmonic.

ns-b3-forcing-rows.Breakdown.CertCell.rowSharesOfInstance: A triple $\varphi$ is divergence-free inside the cell; its extension by zero need not be divergence-free across a side. In the integral of $\nabla p_\iota\cdot\bar\varphi$, the interior term after integration by parts vanishes, but the boundary term $\int_{\partial Q}r p_\iota\overline{\varphi\cdot n}\,ds$ remains. This is why pressure must be measured even though the full-space equation is tested modulo gradients.

ns-b3-row-and-pairing-errors.Breakdown.CertCell.rowSharesOfInstance: The forcing term $\mathsf r_{\mathsf Q,1}$ is a form of the squared test pairings; $\mathsf r_{\mathsf Q,2}$ contains the signed actuator and pinning pairings. The latter sign is essential. Replacing that pairing by its absolute value would not recover the cancellation with the multiplier inequality and the pinning expression in (B.44).
ns-b3-row-and-pairing-errors.Breakdown.CertCell.InstancePair.pairShar: For an actuator-gradient error $e_i$, a mixed term of the form $\beta_i\langle e_i,\nabla v\rangle$ can be estimated by a positive multiple of the gradient square plus a coefficient of $|\beta_i|^2$ proportional to the weighted square of $e_i$. The former spends energy in the cell and the latter contributes to $n_b$. This explains why (B.43) deducts $n_b|\beta|^2$ from the global leaf.

ns-b3-remainder-budget.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.TailBudget.H: There are two parts to the velocity-tail bound. A coefficient outside degree $\mathsf d-1$ is controlled by the derivative in a variable in which its degree is at least $\mathsf d$. That derivative may have a measured component near the top degree, giving $T$, as well as an unmeasured component. In the polynomial norm the bound is $V\le T+G/\min(\Lambda^r_{\mathsf d},\Lambda^z_{\mathsf d})$, where $V,G$ are the squared velocity and gradient remainders. The first cost is included in (B.26), the second in (B.27).

ns-b3-rectangle-absorption.Breakdown.CertCell.creditLeavesBound_clo: The bottom normal trace of the absent reflected harmonic equals, up to sign, the measured axial trace of the resolved harmonic. The rectangle bound therefore uses a velocity energy that was already reserved in $a_0$ of the absent harmonic. The conjugate reflected harmonic supplies the same estimate, yielding the coefficient two in front of $\mathsf C_\Pi$.

ns-b3-b34-sum.Breakdown.CertCell.rowSharesOfInstance: For each cell and harmonic group, the pairings with the given triples are normalized by the inverse square root of the Gram matrix in (B.11), then weighted by $\tau_k$ in the squared norm. The groups have disjoint supports or orthogonal harmonics. Adding their contributions gives $[F]^2$; the normalization of (B.33) requires the factor $(3/50)/(4\pi)$.
ns-b3-b34-sum.Breakdown.CertCell.InstancePair.pairShar: The actuator and pinning pairings reassemble to the global pairings once their cellwise profile errors are included. In particular $n_b|\beta|^2$ bounds the remaining actuator error rather than multiplying the forcing measurement. The $4\pi$ factor is the conversion from the quarter-plane form to the original space-time integral.
ns-b3-b34-sum.Breakdown.CertCell.creditLeavesBound_clo: Add the rectangle forms to the sum of the cell forms, moving $\mathsf r_{\mathsf Q,0}$ to the right in (B.33). The resulting right-hand side contains precisely the left-hand side of (B.34), which is bounded by the global row and pairing terms. This is why the rectangle forms are added in (B.38), although they are paid for by energy deducted from unresolved harmonics.

ns-b3-square-component-argument.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.squareExteri: Write $\rho^2=r^2+z^2$ and $L=\partial_r^2+r^{-1}\partial_r+\partial_z^2$. The positive functions $h=z/\rho^2$ and $h=r/\rho^2$ satisfy $-Lh=2h/\rho^2$ and $(-L+r^{-2})h=2h/\rho^2$, respectively. Writing the scalar component as $g=hq$ and integrating by parts leaves $\int_Z h^2|\nabla q|^2r\,dr\,dz$ after subtracting the inverse-square term, together with the nonnegative inner boundary term. This gives the constant $2$.
ns-b3-square-component-argument.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.modeSquareIn: The additional term $|g|^2/r^2$ in the estimate for a transverse component is its share of the azimuthal derivative energy. Apply the scalar inequalities to the real and imaginary parts of all three components and add them. The symmetry-preserving approximation then gives the estimate for weak modes, with the full vector gradient on the right.

pdf-item-theorem-B-5.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.angularModeB: These derivative inequalities use the spatial transformation law (B.13), at fixed $\theta$. In particular their frequency is the angular wave number, independent of the rates $\nu_p(\alpha)$ used in (B.15). They apply to all the harmonics of $v$, including those not chosen in a cell or acted on by a skew multiplier.

ns-b3-b35.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.angularModeB:
For the example in C.1 the angular order is $19$. The first nonzero angular wave number already gives $|
abla u|^2\ge324|u|^2/r^2$ and $|
abla^2u|^2\ge289|
abla u|^2/r^2$. The zero angular modes have neither gain, irrespective of their time frequency. The lemma also applies to the smaller orders allowed by (B.1).

ns-b3-b36-hypotheses.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.pointwiseQua: Two different sign hypotheses are needed to turn the second-derivative energies into first-derivative energies. In the Hessian term it is the lower coefficient $\mathsf f_2$ that must be nonnegative. In the curl-gradient term it is the actual coefficient $\mathsf I'_{2,\iota}$, nonnegative by admissibility. A negative enclosure $\mathsf f'_2$ is therefore allowed, even though multiplying the angular inequality directly by that enclosure would reverse its sign.

pdf-item-equation-B-36.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.PointCoef.gr: Equation (B.36) retains all the Hessian gain in $\mathsf f_1^*$ while discarding any positive remainder in the curl square. It has not yet used the bound for $|u|$ in terms of $|\nabla u|$. That last step can be taken pointwise by (B.29) or, on the exterior, in the integrated form (B.31).
pdf-item-equation-B-36.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.Internal.Ext: In `quad_lower` the exterior expression $\mathsf f_1^\infty|\nabla u|^2-\mathsf f_0^\infty|u|^2/\rho^2-\mathsf f_{01}^\infty|\nabla u||u|/\rho$ is subtracted from the actual form. By the exterior coefficient bounds the resulting lower form has nonnegative effective gradient and velocity coefficients and zero mixed coefficient. It passes the same scalar test with $\mathsf t=0$. This yields the pointwise lower bound used in B.6, without requiring pointwise nonnegativity of the exterior density.

ns-b3-b5-conclusion.Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.offModeCondi: The regional test is independent of the unknown field. To apply it, the actual mode must satisfy the derivative inequalities, which hold almost everywhere for the weak perturbation. Thus the conclusion is almost-everywhere nonnegativity for each $\iota$ in the region's set, including on its intersection with the cell when the region is larger than that cell.

ns-b3-curl-differences.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.AngularRelat: For each pair of indices $j<l$, the estimate $|\partial_ju_l-\partial_lu_j|^2\le2(|\partial_ju_l|^2+|\partial_lu_j|^2)$ holds also for complex components. Summing over the three pairs gives the first inequality of (B.35). The upper estimate is used precisely when the combined coefficient of the curl square is negative.

ns-b3-angular-derivative.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.angularModeB: Let $Jx=\mathbf e_z\times x$. The angular derivative acts on a vector as $ikI+J$, rather than $ikI$: on the axial and circular transverse components its eigenvalues are $ik,i(k+1),i(k-1)$. Each transverse component can lose at most one unit of $|k|$. Keeping the directional derivative in this estimate will also give the extra term in (B.31).

ns-b3-gradient-commutator.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.angularModeB:
With $G=
abla u$ in Cartesian coordinates, differentiating the two rotations of $G$ gives $r(\mathbf e_\phi\cdot
abla)G=ikG+JG-GJ$, where $Jx=\mathbf e_z	imes x$. In the Frobenius norm, $|JG|,|GJ|\le|G|$. Hence $r|
abla^2u|\ge(|k|-2)_+|G|$. The second loss of one comes from rotating the differentiating direction.

ns-b3-curl-angular.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.angularModeB: The antisymmetric derivative represented by curl transforms as a vector under $R_\phi$ because the rotation preserves cross products. Its gradient therefore has the same lower bound with $(|k|-1)_+$ as the gradient of $u$. Treating curl as a general matrix of derivatives would unnecessarily lose another unit of wave number.

ns-b3-lower-coefficients.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.pointwiseQua: The five square coefficients of the actual mode dominate the corresponding lower enclosures. For the product $|\nabla u||u|$ the comparison goes the other way, since its coefficient is subtracted. This one-sided comparison is sufficient even when some of the regional bounds are negative; the extra sign hypotheses are used only when replacing a derivative norm by an angular lower bound.

ns-b3-negative-lower-coefficient.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.pointwiseQua: If $\mathsf f'_2\ge0$, multiplication of the last squared inequality in (B.35) by this coefficient preserves its direction. If $\mathsf f'_2<0$, the proposed lower bound is nonpositive while the actual curl-gradient term is nonnegative by admissibility. This proves the same bound in either case.

ns-b3-intermediate-curl-gain.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.pointwiseQua: The curl-gradient term can be used before charging the curl square to the gradient. If $\mathsf f'_1<0$ and $\mathsf f'_2>0$, the curl loss is absorbed wherever $\mathsf f'_2(k_0-1)_+^2/r^2\ge-\mathsf f'_1$. Only the remaining negative part of the combined coefficient needs the estimate $|\operatorname{curl}u|^2\le2|\nabla u|^2$.

ns-b3-scalar-minimum.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.pointwiseQua: The upper bound for the curl square must be used with a nonpositive multiplier. Writing $b=\mathsf f'_1+\mathsf f'_2(k_0-1)_+^2/r^2$, we have $b|\operatorname{curl}u|^2\ge\min(b,0)|\operatorname{curl}u|^2\ge2\min(b,0)|\nabla u|^2$. This proves the curl contribution to $\mathsf f_1^*$ in one inequality.

ns-b3-discriminant.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.pointwiseQua: One can choose $\mathsf t$ independently of the perturbation. With $q=(k_0-1)_+^2/r^2$, $F=\mathsf f_1^*$, $B=\mathsf f_0$, maximize the concave quadratic $(F-t)(B+qt)$ on $[\max(0,-B/q),F]$ when $q>0$ and this interval is nonempty. The maximizer is $(qF-B)/(2q)$ if it lies in the interval, otherwise the nearer endpoint. For $q=0$, $t=0$ maximizes the product whenever the diagonal conditions are feasible.

pdf-item-theorem-B-6.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.modeRayInver: The first assertion of B.6 is an inverse-square inequality for the ray geometry and the angular mode, with no multiplier coefficients in it. The second requires such an inequality and the exterior coefficient test. This separation permits the constant from Proposition B.4 for the square exterior to be used in the same argument.
pdf-item-theorem-B-6.Breakdown.CertCell.exteriorConditionSoun: We first need to know that the signed integral of $\mathcal I_\iota^\circ$ is defined, even if its positive part is infinite. A lower bound consisting only of the finite gradient and inverse-square integrals ensures that its negative part is finite. The formal conclusion is a comparison of the nonnegative integrals of the two sign parts, which is the form used in the subsequent assembly.

ns-b3-b6-ray-claim.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.modeRayInver: The inner boundary of the ray integral may vary from ray to ray, but on each ray the boundary term is $-a|U(a)|^2$ and has the same sign. Combining the radial and angular estimates gives $1/4+(|k|-1)_+^2$ for the given mode. A smaller common constant $\Lambda_0$ can therefore be used for all the harmonics of a region.

ns-b3-b6-integrated-claim.Breakdown.CertCell.exteriorConditionSoun: After (B.31) is available, the shape of $Z$ no longer enters the coefficient calculation. The total negative contribution is bounded by the gradient energy times $\mathsf f_0^\infty/\Lambda_0+\mathsf f_{01}^\infty/\sqrt{\Lambda_0}$. This also explains why the exterior cover must be assembled by integrals, rather than by testing individual points.

ns-b3-ray-density-class.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.radialRay: The harmonic projection (B.12) is an average of time translates and spatial rotations with factors of modulus one. Its gradient norm is bounded by the mean of the gradient norms of the slices, since rotation preserves this norm. Thus the projected field belongs to the homogeneous gradient completion, even when it has no finite $L^2$ velocity norm. Equation (B.13) then reduces the full spatial integrals of the squared norms to $2\pi$ times the corresponding meridian integrals.

ns-b3-b37.Breakdown.CellCert.Exterior.rayLine: Integrating $(\rho|U|^2)'$ from $a$ to infinity gives the boundary contribution $-a|U(a)|^2\le0$. Discard it and put $I=\int_a^\infty|U|^2\,d\rho$ and $D=\int_a^\infty\rho^2|U'|^2\,d\rho$; Cauchy–Schwarz gives $I\le2\sqrt{ID}$. If $I>0$ divide by $\sqrt I$, and if $I=0$ the result is immediate. No boundary condition at $a$ is needed.

ns-b3-radial-approximation.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.radialRay: Approximate the real and imaginary parts in the homogeneous gradient norm. Sobolev gives convergence in $L^6$, hence a subsequence converging almost everywhere. Fatou bounds the inverse-square integral of the limit, whereas the radial derivatives converge strongly in $L^2$ on the lifted exterior. No trace on its inner surface is needed for the weak inequality.

ns-b3-angular-radial-combination.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.modeRayInver: At a point off the axis the radial unit vector is $(r\mathbf e_r+z\mathbf e_z)/\rho$, perpendicular to $\mathbf e_\phi$. Thus $|\partial_\rho u|^2+|\mathbf e_\phi\cdot\nabla u|^2\le|\nabla u|^2$. The angular estimate has the weight $r^{-2}$, which is at least $\rho^{-2}$; after this weakening it has the same weight as the radial estimate and the constants add.

ns-b3-exterior-coefficient-signs.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.Internal.Ext: Set $s=\sqrt{\Lambda_0}$, $G=\mathsf f_1^\infty-\mathsf f_{01}^\infty/(2s)$ and $A=\mathsf f_0^\infty+s\mathsf f_{01}^\infty/2$. Equation (B.30) is equivalent to $\Lambda_0G\ge A$; as $A\ge0$, also $G\ge0$. This sign is needed to multiply the gradient lower bound in (B.31) by $G$.

ns-b3-exterior-lower-bound.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.Internal.Ext: The lower bound from `quad_lower` contains only $|\nabla u|^2$, $|u|^2/\rho^2$ and their geometric mean. The first integral is finite by the perturbation hypothesis and the second by (B.31); Cauchy–Schwarz then gives finiteness of the mixed integral. This is sufficient even if some of the original higher-derivative terms have infinite positive integral.

Young's inequality with a free parameter $s>0$ gives a cost of at most $\mathsf f_{01}^\infty(1/(2s)+s/(2\Lambda_0))$ in units of the gradient integral. The minimum is at $s=\sqrt{\Lambda_0}$, the choice in the proof. It agrees with the constant obtained by applying Cauchy–Schwarz directly to the two integrals.

ns-b3-exterior-integrability-sign.Breakdown.CertCell.exteriorConditionSoun: Both terms in the lower bound are integrable with measure $r\,dr\,dz$: the gradient energy is finite and (B.31) bounds the inverse-square integral. If $L$ denotes this lower bound, then $(\mathcal I_\iota^\circ)_-\le L_-$. Thus the signed integral is defined before its nonnegativity is established, including when its positive part is infinite.
ns-b3-exterior-integrability-sign.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.Internal.Ext: With $G,A$ the two coefficients after Young’s inequality, (B.31) gives $\int_Z\mathcal I_\iota^\circ r\,dr\,dz\ge(G-A/\Lambda_0)\int_Z|\nabla u|^2r\,dr\,dz$. Expanding the coefficient gives exactly $\mathsf f_1^\infty-\mathsf f_{01}^\infty/\sqrt{\Lambda_0}-\mathsf f_0^\infty/\Lambda_0$, nonnegative by (B.30).

ns-b3-tree-data.Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.signedTre: The tree works with the sum of the forms attached at a node and the forms supplied by its children. A node keeps its own outgoing form, records positive pivot squares and records negative column squares. The signs of the outgoing forms are immaterial except at the root. Their intermediate contributions cancel when the node estimates are added.

ns-b3-attached-matrices.Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.TreeStateInt: Partitioning a cell matrix into blocks does not partition its coordinates into independent problems. Off-diagonal blocks join two coordinate groups, and a block and its adjoint must be kept together to account for the real cross term. The additional matrices attached at two nodes with opposite signs are permitted because their sum in (B.38) is zero.

ns-b3-b38.Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.TreeStateInt: This identity is a sum of the attached forms, not a new inequality: every cell block is included, the rectangle forms have their factor two, the global form occurs once and the auxiliary pairs cancel. Thus the later tree estimates are estimates of exactly the form used in (B.44).

ns-b3-node-data.Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.PassesRea: Let $S_\xi=\mathsf N_\xi+\sum_{\xi'}\mathsf V_{\xi'}$. The node need only certify a lower bound for $S_\xi-\mathsf V_\xi$. The simpler matrices $\mathsf H_\xi$ and $\mathsf K_\xi$ approximate its two terms from opposite sides, with separate allowances for errors. They need not be equal to the incoming and outgoing matrices.

ns-b3-b39.Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.PassesRea: Put $S_\xi=N_\xi+\sum_{\xi\prime}V_{\xi\prime}$. Subtracting (B.39) gives a lower bound on $S_\xi-V_\xi$ consisting of $H_\xi-K_\xi$, the positive nonpivot charges, and the negative error form $-(H^\prime_\xi+K^\prime_\xi)$ on $|x|$. The nonpivot charges are exactly those needed to cancel the corresponding diagonal error in (B.40).

ns-b3-b40.Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.PassesRea: Write $C=|B|+\mathsf H^\prime+\mathsf K^\prime$ for the entrywise error bound in (B.40) and put $a_j=1/\mathsf w_j$. The row test is $(Ca)_i\le m_i a_i$. By symmetry and $2|x_i x_j|\le (a_j/a_i)x_i^2+(a_i/a_j)x_j^2$, it gives $|x|^{\mathsf T}C|x|\le\sum_i m_i x_i^2$. The positive weights redistribute the required diagonal margins: for an error joining only two coordinates, making one margin smaller makes the other larger.

ns-b3-pivot-diagonal-and-slack.Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.PassesRea: At a pivot the error allowance must be paid out of the proposed positive diagonal: $p_j-m_j\ge p_{\xi,j}>0$. At a nonpivot it is paid by deducting $m_jx_j^2$ from the outgoing form, as in (B.39). Thus a variable need not have a positive margin at every node where it appears; the sum of the node estimates will require one positive pivot somewhere.

ns-b3-complex-coordinates.Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.PassesCom: At a complex pivot, $z_l=x_j\pm ix_{j\prime}$ with $j\ne j\prime$ when both components occur. Hence $|z_l|^2=x_j^2+x_{j\prime}^2$; if one component is absent, only its remaining square is present. After multiplying by $t_\xi$, each such coordinate contributes the stated amount to the real pivot coefficients. Nonpivot coordinates need not have this normalization.

ns-b3-complex-matrices.Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.PassesCom: The Hermitian residual need not be nonnegative: entrywise modulus gives $|z^*Bz|\le\sum_{l,m}|B_{lm}||z_l||z_m|$. This is a real symmetric error form in the moduli, so the weighted row bound applies exactly as for a real node. No order comparison between the complex entries themselves is used.

ns-b3-complex-node-enclosures.Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.PassesCom: Apply the two enclosures at $z=X_\xi x$ and subtract. Since $t_\xi\ge0$, the weighted row error estimate still applies after multiplication by $t_\xi$. The outgoing nonpivot deduction cancels the nonpivot part of this error, leaving scaled complex pivot and column squares, which are then expressed in the real coordinates.

ns-b3-complex-residual.Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.PassesCom: The complex analogue of a real column square is the Hermitian form $yy^*$, whose value is $|y^*z|^2$. Thus $Y^\prime Y^{\prime *}$ contributes nonnegative squares and $-YY^*$ contributes negative squares. The residual, after removing these and the proposed pivot diagonal, is estimated entrywise by moduli in (B.40).

ns-b3-complex-pivot-transfer.Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.PassesCom: For a complex column $y$ write $a+ib=\sqrt{t_\xi}\mathsf X_\xi^*y$, with $a,b$ real. Since the global vector $x$ is real, $t_\xi|y^*\mathsf X_\xi x|^2=(a^{\mathsf T}x)^2+(b^{\mathsf T}x)^2$. Killing a complex pairing generally requires two real equations. Both columns must be included in the count used to bound the codimension in Proposition B.8.

ns-b3-pivot-coverage.Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.PassesPiv: The root condition allows the root form to be dropped from the telescoping lower bound. Coverage by strictly positive pivots makes that lower bound positive on the common column kernel. The column count is a different condition: it ensures that the kernel has dimension at least the number of prescribed coordinates. None of these conditions requires positivity on the whole space.

pdf-item-theorem-B-7.Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.signedTre: This is a signed lower bound, not an assertion that $\mathsf N$ is positive definite. The negative column squares are kept explicitly. The hypothesis on the tree is arranged so that when they vanish, every nonzero global vector has a strictly positive pivot contribution.
pdf-item-theorem-B-7.Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.pivotCoun: The column-count condition and the pivot condition are used for different conclusions. If there are $f$ free coordinates, the common kernel of the real negative-column pairings has codimension at most $f$. The positive pivot coefficients make the root lower form strictly positive there, and the signed-tree bound transfers this to the total form. B.8 supplies the additional fact that the kernel meets the free-coordinate subspace only at zero.

ns-b3-b41.Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.signedTre: With $D$ the diagonal of the accumulated positive pivots and $Y$ the matrix of negative columns, (B.41) reads $x^{\mathsf T}\mathsf N x\ge x^{\mathsf T}D x-|Y^{\mathsf T}x|^2$. In particular on any subspace orthogonal to the columns, $\mathsf N$ is strictly positive away from zero. This is the lower bound to be combined with the zero-perturbation test in Proposition B.8.

ns-b3-column-kernel-positive.Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.pivotCoun: For a vector in the common kernel the only surviving terms in (B.41) are the positive pivot squares. Each coordinate has at least one strictly positive coefficient, so the sum can vanish only at zero. The formal positivity assertion is for the root lower form, which bounds the total form from below by the preceding lemma.

ns-b3-residual-matrix-identity.Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.signedSla: The definition of the residual gives an exact decomposition of $H-K$ into the proposed pivot diagonal, $Y^\prime(Y^\prime)^{\mathsf T}$, $-YY^{\mathsf T}$ and $B$. The positive column squares may be dropped in a lower bound; the negative ones must be retained. Rather than assigning a sign to $B$, the proof bounds its loss by the diagonal row allowances.

ns-b3-weighted-row-proof.Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.signedSla: The row-sum argument controls the residual $B$ and the two enclosure errors together. Their combined contribution to the lower estimate is at least $-|x|^{\mathsf T}(|B|+\mathsf H^\prime+\mathsf K^\prime)|x|$, hence at least $-\sum_jm_j x_j^2$ by (B.40). It is not necessary for either enclosure-error matrix to be positive semidefinite; their entries are nonnegative and the estimate is on $|x|$.

ns-b3-b42.Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.realNodeE: The row estimate costs $m_jx_j^2$ at every coordinate. On nonpivots the outgoing comparison already subtracts this term, so it cancels there. On pivots it lowers $p_j$ to $p_j-m_j\ge p_{\xi,j}$. Dropping the positive $Y^\prime$ squares then gives (B.42) with the negative $Y$ squares retained.
ns-b3-b42.Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.complexNo: After subtraction in complex coordinates the uncanceled diagonal terms are $t_\xi(p_l-m_l)|z_l|^2$ on the pivots, together with the negative column terms $-t_\xi|y^*z|^2$. Use the coordinate and column correspondences to express both in $x$. The resulting inequality is (B.42), the same one as at a real node.

ns-b3-complex-pivot-proof.Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.complexNo: The pullback of a complex squared column pairing is $t_\xi|y^*X_\xi x|^2=|a^{\mathsf T}x|^2+|b^{\mathsf T}x|^2$, with $a+ib=\sqrt{t_\xi}X_\xi^*y$. At pivots the real and imaginary parts are distinct real coordinates with coefficients of modulus one, so the squared modulus also splits into the required real pivot squares. This is why the same real tree inequality applies.

ns-b3-tree-cancellation.Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.signedTre: When the inequalities (B.42) are added, a nonroot $\mathsf V_\xi$ occurs on the right at its own node and on the left at its unique parent. Only the root form remains on the right; dropping it uses its nonnegativity. The sum of all the $\mathsf N_\xi$ is the assembled form (B.38), not the matrix of a single cell.

ns-b3-strict-positivity-proof.Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.pivotCoun: On the column kernel the lower bound is a sum of positive multiples of coordinate squares, and every coordinate has a pivot at some node. A nonzero vector therefore gives a strictly positive term. Strict positivity, not just nonnegativity, is needed below to exclude a nonzero free vector from the kernel.

ns-b3-b43.Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.TreeRowCondi: The normalization of the global leaf is the same as that of the cell inequalities. The coefficient $-\mathsf n_b$ on $|\beta|^2$ cancels the allowance of (B.34), while the remaining two penalties become $-3\omega^2|\beta|^2/50$ and $-|\zeta|^2/1000$ on multiplication by $4\pi$. The inequality for $\mathsf A_0$ must hold on every extension of the prescribed vector.
ns-b3-b43.Breakdown.CertCell.globalForm: `globalForm` is the scalar penalty $-(c\omega^2/(4\pi)+e)|\beta|^2-|\zeta|^2/(4\pi t)$, giving (B.43) for $c=3/50$, $e=n_b$, $t=1000$. Its definition fixes the signs and normalization. The inequality that the actual global leaf is no greater than this penalty is a separate condition.

ns-b3-error-budget.Breakdown.CertCell.InstancePair.pairShar: The error from replacing $\nabla b_i$ by a surrogate is paired with the actual perturbation gradient and multiplied by $\beta_i$. Young’s inequality bounds such a product by a derivative-energy cost and a squared surrogate-error integral times $|\beta|^2$. The latter integrals, with their specified weights and the other nonnegative allowances, form the lower bound required of $\mathsf n_b$. They need not be evaluated on the perturbation.

pdf-item-theorem-B-8.Breakdown.CertCell.rowRestClause_closed: Proposition B.8 is the passage from finitely represented data and their inequalities to a bound on every admissible perturbation. It supplies (B.21), not yet (7.18); the latter follows by Lemma B.2 together with (B.20). The Lean implication has the cell, region, tree and field-data conditions as hypotheses. Neither the statement nor its proof is an enclosure of the numerical matrices of a particular certificate.

ns-b3-b8.Breakdown.CertCell.rowRestClause_closed: Fix any $\alpha\in\mathcal K$. The same supplied conditions give the lower density bound for every solution of the reference linearized equation at that parameter. Lemma B.2 combines this with the multiplier estimate to obtain (7.18); only afterwards are the bounds (7.19)–(7.21) used to transfer the estimate to the approximate profile.

ns-b3-b8-finiteness-proof.Breakdown.CertCell.rowRestClause_closed: The negative integral is finite by B.4. If the positive integral is infinite, the left side of (B.21) is $+\infty$ while its right side is finite for the given $v,\beta,F$. It is therefore enough to prove the remaining inequalities in the case where both contributions are finite.

ns-b3-finite-signed-integrals.Breakdown.CertCell.modeDensityBridge_clo: Finiteness of both sign integrals implies summability of the absolute modal integrals and integrability of the stretching term. In particular the quarter-plane expression in (B.23) can now be restricted to the cells and their complement and added back as an ordinary integral. This is the reason for disposing of the infinite-positive case first.

ns-b3-free-state-choice.Breakdown.CertCell.stateEnclosureCertifi: At this point the same prescribed vector $x_{\rm p}$ is held fixed throughout the calculation. Keeping $x_{\rm f}$ arbitrary proves (B.44) on the entire affine space of extensions. Only after this uniform bound is available will the tree select an extension; choosing the pinning variable or other free coordinates beforehand would restrict the space available to that argument.

ns-b3-cell-off-modes.Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.offModeCondi: The finite cover makes the negative-part integral of the unresolved density zero for each unresolved label. The formal cover can use larger regional curl, gradient and velocity charges, with the same stretching constant, than those subtracted in the cell: this only decreases the tested form. The sum of unresolved negative-part integrals is therefore zero (`OffModesVanish`), which leaves the absolutely convergent nonnegative remainder in (B.33).

ns-b3-exterior-loss-comparison.Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.offModeDensi: The original stretching loss uses $\sqrt{7/2}$; (B.28) enlarges it to $\mathsf c^*\ge\sqrt{7/2}$ and subtracts further nonnegative charges on the complement. Consequently $\mathcal I_\iota-\mathcal L_\iota\ge\mathcal I_\iota^\circ$. On bounded regions the latter is nonnegative pointwise by (B.29), whereas on unbounded regions only its integral need be nonnegative. Either estimate suffices to show that the exterior makes no negative contribution after summing the modal integrals.

ns-b3-exterior-sum-positive.Breakdown.CertCell.exteriorConditionSoun: For a fixed label, sum the regional inequalities over the partition of the complement. Since $\mathsf c^*\ge\sqrt{7/2}$ and the three exterior charges are nonnegative, (B.28) is no greater than $\mathcal I_\iota-\mathcal L(\nabla\hat v_\iota,\hat v_\iota)$. It follows that the integral of $\mathcal I_\iota$ pays for the integral of the stretching majorant for this label.
ns-b3-exterior-sum-positive.Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.exteriorPoin: We are now in the case $\mathcal I^+<\infty$ and $\mathcal I^-<\infty$. By B.3, the sum of the integrals of $|\mathcal I_\iota|$ is finite. The nonnegative $\mathcal L_\iota$ on the complement has integral at most that of $\mathcal I_\iota$ for each $\iota$, so its sum is integrable as well. This permits (B.32) to be integrated and gives the nonnegative exterior contribution to (B.21).

ns-b3-sum-before-b44.Breakdown.CertCell.initialState_closed: After dropping the nonnegative unresolved residuals, add the cell bounds and move the four error terms to the right. Add the rectangle forms; (B.34) bounds the resulting error by the forcing rows, actuator and pin pairings, and $\mathsf n_b|\beta|^2$. The last term cancels with (B.43). Multiplication by $4\pi$ now puts both the density and the pairings back in their original normalization. The exterior can be included because its integral is nonnegative.

pdf-item-equation-B-44.Breakdown.CertCell.initialState_closed: Put $D$ equal to the left side of (B.21) minus its right side. By completing the square, (B.44) reads $4\pi\langle\mathsf N x_{\rm g},x_{\rm g}\rangle\le D-|\zeta-1000\ell(v)|^2/1000\le D$. It is enough to find one extension of the prescribed vector on which the form is nonnegative. The bound is available on all extensions, which is crucial for the following dimension argument.
pdf-item-equation-B-44.Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.TreeStateInt: By (B.38) the cell forms, twice the rectangle forms and the global form constitute the same real quadratic form that is bounded by Lemma B.7. The auxiliary matrices used in the tree have zero total contribution. Thus no further matrix approximation is needed between the analytic inequality (B.44) and the signed tree bound.

ns-b3-completed-square.Breakdown.CertCell.initialState_closed: The pinning expression has the exact form $1000|\ell(v)|^2-|\zeta-1000\ell(v)|^2/1000$. Its maximum provides the term in (B.21), but we do not choose $\zeta$ to attain it. Any $\zeta$ gives a sufficient upper bound, including the one selected by the tree argument.

ns-b3-find-free-coordinate.Breakdown.CertCell.stateEnclosureCertifi: The remaining step concerns the affine set $(x_{\rm p},0)+\{(0,x_{\rm f})\}$, not all global vectors at once. We seek a point of this set orthogonal to every negative column. The tree gives positivity on their common kernel; what remains is to show that this kernel meets every such affine set.

ns-b3-column-kernel.Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.pivotCoun: Let $Y$ have as its columns all the real columns $\mathsf Y_\xi$. Then $\mathcal Y^\perp=\ker Y^{\mathsf T}$. Its codimension is the rank of $Y$, which is at most the number of columns, whether or not the columns are independent. Lemma B.7 gives positivity on this particular kernel.

ns-b3-zero-perturbation.Breakdown.CertCell.stateEnclosureCertifi: Set $v=\beta=F=0$, so $x_{\rm p}=0$, and keep all the free entries arbitrary, including $\zeta$. Inequality (B.44) gives $4\pi\langle\mathsf N(0,x_{\rm f}),(0,x_{\rm f})\rangle\le-|\zeta|^2/1000\le0$. This is a sign condition on the whole free-coordinate subspace, not merely on its zero vector. Strict negativity is not needed.

ns-b3-kernel-free-intersection.Breakdown.CertCell.stateEnclosureCertifi: If two vectors in $\mathcal Y^\perp$ have the same prescribed coordinates, their difference is purely free. Its form is nonpositive by the zero-input estimate and strictly positive by B.7 unless the difference vanishes. This proves injectivity of projection onto prescribed coordinates and explains the need for strictly positive pivots.

ns-b3-dimension-count.Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.pivotCoun: If there are $p$ prescribed and $f$ free coordinates and $m\le f$ columns, then $\dim\mathcal Y^\perp=p+f-\operatorname{rank}Y\ge p$. Projection onto the $p$ prescribed coordinates has zero kernel on $\mathcal Y^\perp$ by the preceding argument. The dimensions therefore agree, and the projection is an isomorphism. In particular equality forces $\operatorname{rank}Y=m=f$.
ns-b3-dimension-count.Breakdown.CertCell.stateEnclosureCertifi: The same argument can be written as the linear system $Y_{\rm f}^{\mathsf T}x_{\rm f}=-Y_{\rm p}^{\mathsf T}x_{\rm p}$, with the rows of $Y$ divided into prescribed and free coordinates. A vector in the homogeneous kernel would be a nonzero purely free vector in $\mathcal Y^\perp$, which is impossible. The column count makes the system square and invertible. In particular there is no need to invert a block of $\mathsf N$, which need not be positive definite.

ns-b3-final-nonnegativity.Breakdown.CertCell.stateEnclosureCertifi: Take the extension in $\mathcal Y^\perp$ with the prescribed $x_{\rm p}$. Its form is nonnegative by (B.41), and by (B.44) the gap in (B.21) is at least $4\pi$ times this form. The extension changed no measured quantity of $v,\beta,F$. Since these were arbitrary and their omitted parts were included in the estimates, (B.21) holds on the full perturbation class.

ns-b4-001.Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.CellSystemCond: Unlike the estimate of B.3, the estimates below do not require a cellwise representation of the unknown perturbation. The quadratic and linear adjoint pairings are bounded by a multiple of $\|v\|_w^2$ and of $\|v\|_w$, respectively. It is the known fields in those pairings whose norms must be enclosed. The last estimate, (7.34), involves only the given approximate family.

pdf-item-equation-B-45.Breakdown.sixthPowerGradientBound_four_t: The coefficient in the linked inequality is $4/3$ because (B.45) has been squared. For a vector, $\|u\|_6^2=\|\sum_i|u_i|^2\|_3\le\sum_i\|u_i\|_6^2\le(4/3)\sum_i\|\nabla u_i\|_2^2$. Thus summing the scalar estimates introduces no dimension factor.

pdf-item-equation-B-46.Breakdown.CertReduction.energyBoundsHold: Put $a=\|\Delta u\|_{L^2}$ and $b=\sqrt{w_*}\|\nabla u\|_{L^2}$. The mixed product is bounded by $(a^2+b^2)/2\le |u|_w^2/2$, which gives the third bound. Together with (7.48) it also gives $\|u\|_{L^\infty}^2\le (4\pi\sqrt{w_*})^{-1}|u|_w^2$. The linked result uses the constant weight of Appendix B.

pdf-item-theorem-B-9.Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.ShiftNumbersBo: There are two fields associated with the centre of the parameter set: $W_0^{\mathrm a}$ is the member used in (B.9), while $W^{\mathrm r}$ is the field used to prove the inverse estimate in B.2–B.3. The latter can be chosen for ease of certification and need not be a member of the approximate family. Its difference from the centre is estimated once, and the additional variation from the centre is estimated uniformly on $\mathcal K$.
pdf-item-theorem-B-9.Breakdown.CertReduction.FrozenFormBounde: There are two contributions to the reference convection form. The one in which $W^{\mathrm r}$ differentiates $u$ reduces by incompressibility to a quadratic form in $\nabla u$ with the strain as coefficient. Only its lower bound is needed. The term in which $u$ differentiates $W^{\mathrm r}$ is bounded in absolute value with the $L^3$ norm of the full reference gradient.
pdf-item-theorem-B-9.Breakdown.CertReduction.gapTransferBridg: In (7.52) the use of the reference estimate costs $(c_1+c_0)c_{\mathrm r}\|v\|_w$ because the change of forcing is measured in both the norm and the seminorm (7.17). Thus $c_{\mathrm r}<1/(c_1+c_0)$ is needed when $c_1+c_0>0$. The inverse constant for zero constraints is then bounded by $(c_1+c_0)/(1-(c_1+c_0)c_{\mathrm r})$. The first bound of (B.48) must be sufficiently small for the chosen $c_L$ in (7.21).
pdf-item-theorem-B-9.Breakdown.CertReduction.formShiftBridgeH: A bound for the period norm in (7.19) by itself gives no bound on the supremum of the gradient energy over time. For the latter, Proposition 7.9 uses the energy identity and integrates from a phase of minimum energy. The spatial form (7.22) controls the increase between phases, so its estimate is required for each $\theta$, before time integration.
pdf-item-theorem-B-9.Breakdown.CertReduction.frozenFormBridge: The reference-form bound applies to the given model field before using any of the difference estimates. The formal statement permits the reference field to depend on the parameter; its strain and $L^3$ gradient bounds must then hold uniformly. Appendix B makes that field fixed, and a separate estimate bounds the cost of replacing it by $W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}$.

pdf-item-equation-B-47.Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.ShiftNumbersBo: Both differences enter the transport term through their supremum norms. For the derivative term the two alternatives are $\|u\|_\infty\||\nabla Z|_{\rm op}\|_2$ and $\|u\|_6\||\nabla Z|_{\rm op}\|_3$. The paper uses the first for the fixed centre error and the second for the family variation. The choice concerns the products after the Sobolev constants are included, not a comparison of the two unweighted gradient norms.
pdf-item-equation-B-47.Breakdown.CertReduction.FrozenFormBounde: The condition $\mathbb S\ge-\mathsf s_- I$ is a lower bound for a quadratic form, not an absolute bound on its entries. In the transport pairing it is exactly the condition on the derivative of the reference field acting twice on the same vector. A bound on the full gradient in $L^3$ is required for the other pairing, with two different vectors $u$ and $\Delta u$.

ns-b4-006.Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.ShiftNumbersBo: The supremum in $\theta$ of the spatial norm is taken separately for each parameter, and the same bound must hold for all parameters in $\mathcal K$. It cannot be replaced by an $L^3$ norm in space-time: the product involving $u$ is to be estimated also for a single time slice in (7.22). For the fixed centre error the parameter quantifier is redundant.
ns-b4-006.Breakdown.CertReduction.FrozenFormBounde: For a real vector $g$, $g\cdot(\nabla W^{\mathrm r})g=g\cdot\mathbb Sg$, since the skew part has zero quadratic form. Consequently $\mathbb S\ge-\mathsf s_- I$ gives exactly the derivative form bound required in the formal reference certificate. An upper bound on the strain is unnecessary for this part of the estimate.

pdf-item-equation-B-48.Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.ShiftNumbersBo: Group the first budget as $A+B$, where $A=c_w\mathsf n_0^{(2)}$ and $B=(\mathsf n_0^\infty+\mathsf n_1^\infty+2\mathsf n_1^{(3)}/\sqrt3)/\sqrt{w_*}$. The third budget is $A+B/2$. Its terms multiplying $\|\nabla u\|_2\|\Delta u\|_2$ gain the factor $1/2$ from (B.46); the term $\|u\|_\infty\|\Delta u\|_2$ has already used the mixed product in the derivation of $c_w$ and is bounded by $c_w|u|_w^2$.
pdf-item-equation-B-48.Breakdown.CertReduction.FrozenFormBounde: The middle budget concerns only $W^{\mathrm r}$. The strain loss is at most $\mathsf s_-\|\nabla u\|_{L^2}^2\le(\mathsf s_-/w_*)|u|_w^2$. The remaining convection term has one gradient and one Laplacian norm, so (B.45) and the product estimate in (B.46) give the coefficient $\mathsf n_{\mathrm r}^{(3)}/\sqrt{3w_*}$.

ns-b4-008.Breakdown.CertReduction.gapTransferBridg: At fixed $\alpha$, the reference equation and the approximate-field equation use the same $S(\alpha)$, constraints and forcing fields. Hence the change in the equation is exactly the two convection terms with $W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}-W^{\mathrm r}$. There is no estimate of a time derivative of this difference in (7.19).
ns-b4-008.Breakdown.CertReduction.formShiftBridgeH: The form (7.22) is obtained after the contribution of the free operator has been evaluated. Its diffusion and dilation terms have the same coefficients for either convection field. Subtracting the forms thus leaves only the pairing with $-\Delta u$ of the change of convection, which can be bounded in absolute value.
ns-b4-008.Breakdown.CertReduction.frozenFormBridge: The middle inequality of (B.48) is a bound at $W^{\mathrm r}$ alone. The first and last inequalities involve the difference of the profiles, whereas this middle one requires a bound on the strain and on the full $L^3$ gradient of the reference. It is not necessary for $W^{\mathrm r}$ itself to be small.

ns-b4-009.Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.ShiftNumbersBo: Here both profiles are evaluated at the same $\theta=s/S(\alpha)$ in period-one coordinates. The centre error $Z_0$ is fixed as a function of these coordinates. By (B.9), $Z_1$ is affine in $\alpha$ inside $B_{r_\chi}$ (and vanishes at $\alpha=0$); outside the ball the radial phase varies as well. The gradient norm in (B.47) must enclose the derivative of that phase, not just the affine coefficient variation.

pdf-item-equation-B-49.Breakdown.CertReduction.gapSupTermHolds_: For the transport part of the difference the pointwise bound is $|(Z\cdot\nabla)u|\le |Z||\nabla u|$. The supremum bounds on $Z_0,Z_1$ give a coefficient $(\mathsf n_0^\infty+\mathsf n_1^\infty)/\sqrt{w_*}$ in units of $|u|_w$. In the formal period estimate this coefficient is squared along with the norm.
pdf-item-equation-B-49.Breakdown.CertReduction.gapGradTermHolds: In the second inequality of (B.49), the prescribed $L^2$ gradient is multiplied by a perturbation bounded in $L^\infty$; in the third, the prescribed $L^3$ gradient is multiplied by a perturbation in $L^6$. These are the two cases of `gapGradCoeff`. The former uses both spatial derivative norms in $|u|_w$, while the latter uses only its gradient term.
pdf-item-equation-B-49.Breakdown.CertReduction.cubicWeightProdu: To obtain the squared norm bound, apply Hölder to $|\nabla Z_1|_{\mathrm{op}}^2|u|^2$ with exponents $3/2$ and $3$. The resulting factors are $\||\nabla Z_1|_{\mathrm{op}}\|_{L^3}^2$ and $\|u\|_{L^6}^2$, respectively. The latter gives the constant $4/3$ by (B.45), which becomes $2/\sqrt3$ in (B.49).

ns-b4-011.Breakdown.CertReduction.gapTransferBridg: Use the triangle inequality in $L^2$ before squaring. In particular there is no orthogonality between the centre and family variation terms; the square of the sum of the three constants is the available coefficient of $|u|_w^2$.

ns-b4-012.Breakdown.CertReduction.gapTransferBridg: The bound is for the unprojected difference of the two convection fields. Squaring and integrating over the normalized period gives $\|G\|_{\mathcal H}^2\le c_{\mathrm r}^2\|v\|_w^2$ for $G=(C_\alpha-C_\alpha^{\mathrm r})v$. This also proves $G\in\mathcal H$, so that the reference right-hand side $F-G$ in (7.52) is admissible before any projection onto solenoidal fields.

ns-b4-013.Breakdown.CertReduction.frozenFormBridge:
The transport term $(W\cdot
abla)u$ would give a bound involving $\|W\|_\infty$ by Cauchy–Schwarz. Instead integration by parts with $-\Delta u$ reduces it to the strain acting on $
abla u$, since $W\cdot
abla|
abla u|^2$ integrates to zero. This is why (B.47) asks for a lower strain bound for the reference field rather than a further small velocity bound.

ns-b4-014.Breakdown.CertReduction.convectionIdenti: For a component $u_i$, the product rule applied to $W\cdot g$, $g=\nabla u_i$, gives the two terms $(\partial_kW_j)g_jg_k$ and $W_j(\partial_k g_j)g_k$. The equality $\partial_k g_j=\partial_jg_k$ changes the second to $\tfrac12 W_j\partial_j|g|^2$ after summation in $k$. This uses that $g$ is a gradient, and remains valid for its weak derivatives.

ns-b4-015.Breakdown.CertReduction.convectionIdenti:
Since $g,
abla g\in L^2$, the product rule gives $|g|^2\in W^{1,1}$, with $\|
abla |g|^2\|_1\le2\|g\|_2\|
abla g\|_2$. Integrating against $W$ with a cutoff at radius $R$, the divergence-free identity leaves only the cutoff derivative, bounded by $C\|W\|_\infty R^{-1}\int_{R<|y|<2R}|g|^2dy$. It tends to zero, so the cancellation holds for the whole-space weak field.
ns-b4-015.Breakdown.CertReduction.FrozenFormBounde:
For each $i$ the remaining integral is at least $-\mathsf s_-\|
abla u_i\|_{L^2}^2$. Summation over the three components gives $-\mathsf s_-\|
abla u\|_{L^2}^2$. Since the skew part of $
abla W$ has zero quadratic form on $g$, no estimate on that part is needed for this pairing.

ns-b4-016.Breakdown.CertReduction.frozenFormBridge: The first bound is a signed estimate: positive strain in the transport pairing can be retained, and only the negative eigenvalues need a bound. The second is an absolute estimate because $(u\cdot\nabla)W$ is paired with $\Delta u$, not with $u$. It requires the full operator norm of the gradient in $L^3$.
ns-b4-016.Breakdown.CertReduction.shiftGradTermHol: Hölder bounds the second pairing in magnitude by $\mathsf n_{\mathrm r}^{(3)}\|u\|_{L^6}\|\Delta u\|_{L^2}$. Use (B.45), then $2\sqrt{w_*}\|\nabla u\|_{L^2}\|\Delta u\|_{L^2}\le|u|_w^2$. Its cost is thus at most $\mathsf n_{\mathrm r}^{(3)}|u|_w^2/\sqrt{3w_*}$.

ns-b4-017.Breakdown.CertReduction.frozenFormBridge: In (7.22) we may discard $\|\Delta u\|_2^2+\|\nabla u\|_2^2/4$ when obtaining a lower bound. The remaining two terms are the strain contribution and the term estimated by Sobolev. The resulting bound may be negative; Proposition 7.9 controls the increase of the energy over an interval, without requiring the form to be coercive at every phase.

ns-b4-018.Breakdown.CertReduction.shiftSupTermHold: The supremum terms of (B.49), paired with $\Delta u$, give $(\mathsf n_0^\infty+\mathsf n_1^\infty)\|\nabla u\|_{L^2}\|\Delta u\|_{L^2}$. The third inequality of (B.46) gives the coefficient $(\mathsf n_0^\infty+\mathsf n_1^\infty)/(2\sqrt{w_*})$ in the form-shift estimate.
ns-b4-018.Breakdown.CertReduction.shiftGradTermHol: The $L^2$ gradient error is bounded using $\|u\|_{L^\infty}\|\Delta u\|_{L^2}\le c_w|u|_w^2$. For the $L^3$ error, apply (B.45) and the third inequality of (B.46) to get $\|u\|_{L^6}\|\Delta u\|_{L^2}\le |u|_w^2/\sqrt{3w_*}$. These give the remaining two terms in the third budget of (B.48).
ns-b4-018.Breakdown.CertReduction.formShiftBridgeH: Pairing the operator-norm bound (7.19) with $-\Delta u$ at the slice level would give the first budget of (B.48) as a sufficient coefficient. The proof instead keeps the separate terms in (B.49) until multiplying by $\|\Delta u\|_2$. It thereby gains a factor of two in the costs of transport and of the $L^3$ gradient error, but not the $L^2$ gradient error.

ns-b4-019.Breakdown.CertReduction.formShiftBridgeH: For each $u$ and $\theta$ the form at the reference is at least $-c'_3|u|_w^2$, and the change to $W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}$ is at least $-c''_3|u|_w^2$. Adding proves (7.22). In Lean the two assertions are combined in `ExtendedFrozenBridge.profile_form`, using the inequality for the declared total form bound.
ns-b4-019.Breakdown.CertReduction.frozenFormBridge: In (7.55), the total $c_3\ge c'_3+c''_3$ contributes $(2S(\alpha)/m)c_3\|v\|_w^2$ to the bound for the squared gradient supremum. At $\|v\|_w\le2\varepsilon$, the cost is at most $8S_{\max}c_3\varepsilon^2/m$, which appears in (7.27). The bound on $c_{\mathrm r}$ is used earlier, to obtain the joint norm estimate in (7.52).

ns-b4-020.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AdjointDefectBou: An exact adjoint field would recover the linear functional $(Y(\alpha)\ell(v))_j$ by testing the linearized velocity equation. Thus the unknown field would enter this measurement only through the prescribed constraint values. B.12 quantifies the error of this replacement; it is distinct from the bound on the nonlinear pairing and the offset of the approximate family.

ns-b4-021.Breakdown.CertReduction.AdjointQuadratic: To estimate $(v\cdot\nabla)v$ in $\mathcal H$ one needs the separate supremum in time from (7.27). To estimate its pairing with $\psi_j$ it suffices to control the product of the two velocity factors at each time by $|v|_w^2$. This is why Lemma B.10 uses a spatial norm of the given test field uniformly in time.

pdf-item-theorem-B-10.Breakdown.CertReduction.AdjointQuadratic: For each $j$ one may choose whichever of the two products $2n_\psi/(\sqrt3 w_*)$ and $c_wn_\psi/\sqrt{w_*}$ is smaller, with $n_\psi$ bounding the appropriate norm.
