pdf-item-theorem-B-10.Breakdown.CertReduction.adjointQuadratic: The bridge first bounds the integral of $|(v\cdot\nabla)v|\,|\psi_j|$ on the period. This is sufficient both to define the pairing and to bound its absolute value by $\tilde a_j\|v\|_w^2$. In contrast to B.11 below, the estimate does not use cancellation between angular or temporal modes.

ns-b4-023.Breakdown.CertReduction.adjointQuadratic: There is no smallness hypothesis on $v$ in B.10. Its coefficient is computed before solving (7.12); only when (7.32) is used in (7.35) does the radius $2\varepsilon$ give a quadratic error of size $4\tilde a_j\varepsilon^2$.

ns-b4-024.Breakdown.CertReduction.adjointQuadTerm_: The useful pointwise bound is $|(v\cdot\nabla)v\cdot\psi_j|\le |v||\nabla v||\psi_j|$. Hölder applies with reciprocal exponents $(1/6,1/2,1/3)$ or $(0,1/2,1/2)$. No derivative falls on $\psi_j$ in either estimate, and both bound the absolute integrand.

ns-b4-025.Breakdown.CertReduction.adjointQuadTerm_: The spatial bound is obtained for almost every $\theta$, with a coefficient independent of $\theta$. Its integral is $\tilde a_j\int_0^1|v(\theta)|_w^2\,d\theta=\tilde a_j\|v\|_w^2$. In particular the estimate does not require a bound for $\sup_\theta|v(\theta)|_w$.
ns-b4-025.Breakdown.CertReduction.adjointQuadratic: Compare Lemma 7.6: the square of the full $L^2$ norm of the quadratic forcing involves the product $\|v(\theta)\|_\infty^2\|\nabla v(\theta)\|_2^2$, for which a supremum bound is needed. Here the pairing is integrated without squaring the spatial estimate. The energy over one period therefore suffices, and the coefficient in (7.35) is $4\tilde a_j\varepsilon^2$.

ns-b4-026.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.periodInnerInteg: All of the pairings are taken in the normalized time $\theta=s/S$. Thus $\iint v\cdot\mathsf R$ uses a period of length one for every $\alpha$; the factor $1/S$ belongs in the time derivative of the operator, not in this pairing.

ns-b4-027.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.DualBounded: The quantity controlled is a functional of the homogeneous gradient norm, not of the $L^2$ norm of the velocity. For example, even $\mathsf R$ of finite $L^2$ norm would not suffice by Cauchy–Schwarz if $v\notin L^2$. The factor $|y|$ in the norm of the ordinary remainder supplies the missing weight through Hardy; a known angular expansion permits a smaller bound for the other part.

ns-b4-028.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.RemainderBounded: Write $v\cdot\mathsf R'=(v/|y|)\cdot(|y|\mathsf R')$. The first factor has norm at most $2\|\nabla v\|_{\mathcal H}$ by Hardy; thus the data need to bound twice the weighted norm of the second. This is the part of the dual bound that requires no information about angular frequencies.

ns-b4-029.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AzimuthalBounded: Here $k$ is the wave number of a scalar Cartesian component, not the label $\iota_1$ in (B.2). Indeed a cylindrical mode of angular number $m$ has $u_1\pm iu_2=e^{\pm i\phi}(u_r\pm iu_\phi)$, hence scalar wave numbers $m\pm1$, and its third component has number $m$. It is these scalar numbers that enter $(|k|+1/2)^{-2}$. For $|k|=1$ the resulting dual norm coefficient is $2/3$ instead of $2$.

pdf-item-theorem-B-11.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.weightedPairingI: Although the modal estimate uses a smaller weighted sum, every term in that finite sum has a strictly positive coefficient. Consequently each $|y|g$ is in $L^2$, and ordinary Hardy makes the pairing integrable. The angular gain applies to the spatially integrated pairing, not to $\iint|v\cdot\mathsf R|$ with the same constant.
pdf-item-theorem-B-11.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.dualBoundedBound: For a given decomposition the cost is $\mathsf n'+\mathsf n''$. Orthogonality is available within the represented modal field but need not hold between that field and the ordinary remainder. The linked bound in fact tests arbitrary weak-gradient slices in $L^6$ with finite period gradient energy, without a solenoidality hypothesis.

ns-b4-031.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.dualBoundedBound: An adjoint residual with dual bound $\mathsf n$ contributes at most $\mathsf n\|\nabla v\|_{\mathcal H}\le (\mathsf n/\sqrt{w_*})\|v\|_w$. This is the estimate used not only for $\mathsf R_{j,\alpha}$ in (B.56) but also for the transposed stretching and time-derivative terms. No $L^2$ bound for $v$ is needed.

ns-b4-032.Breakdown.CertCell.Internal.slice_invers: In the ray integral, the volume factor $\rho^2$ cancels the inverse-square weight, so (B.37) with $a=0$ gives $\int |U|^2/|y|^2\le4\int|\partial_\rho U|^2$. The radial energy is only part of the full gradient energy; the remaining angular part is what will improve this bound for a nonzero wave number.

ns-b4-033.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.weightedPairingI: Before averaging or interchanging integrals, the proof obtains $|y|\mathsf R',|y|\mathsf R''\in\mathcal H$. Thus $\iint |v\cdot\mathsf R|\le\|v/|y|\|_{\mathcal H}\||y|\mathsf R\|_{\mathcal H}<\infty$. The constant obtained here need not be the small constant $\mathsf n$; that is the object of the remaining angular calculation.
ns-b4-033.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.remainderPlainHo: Hardy gives $\|v/|y|\|_{\mathcal H}\le2\|\nabla v\|_{\mathcal H}$, while the hypothesis gives $\||y|\mathsf R'\|_{\mathcal H}\le\mathsf n'/2$. Multiplying the two bounds gives the coefficient $\mathsf n'$ without a further constant.

pdf-item-equation-B-50.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AzimuthalParts.s: Put $m=|k|$. The radial contribution is $1/4$; the angular one is $m(m+1)$ rather than just $m^2$. To see the extra $m$, expand the last square: its cross term is $m\eta\partial_\eta|U|^2$, whose integral is $-m\int_{-1}^1|U|^2\,d\eta$ since $U$ vanishes at the poles. The linked theorem applies this estimate to the $k$th projection of the complex horizontal component of a smooth test, without requiring the original test itself to be a single mode.
pdf-item-equation-B-50.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AzimuthalParts.m: The paper passes (B.50) to a weak function of a prescribed angular number. Lean instead proves the summed estimate $\sum_k (|k|+1/2)^2\|P_k U/|y|\|_2^2\le\|\nabla U\|_2^2$, encoding a complex $U$ as two real components. This follows by passing each projected estimate to the limit and bounding the sum of the projected gradient energies. It will allow a test against several angular modes at once.

ns-b4-035.Breakdown.CertCell.Internal.slice_invers: At $k=0$ the coefficient in (B.50) is $1/4$, giving $\|U/|y|\|_2\le2\|\nabla U\|_2$. The argument for $k\ne0$ uses the vanishing of a smooth mode on the axis; that vanishing is not available for $k=0$ and is not needed.

ns-b4-036.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AzimuthalParts.w: There is no requirement of convergence in unweighted $L^2(\mathbb R^3)$. For the cutoff error in the gradient use $\|U\nabla\chi_R\|_2\le\|U\|_{L^6(R<|y|<2R)}\|\nabla\chi_R\|_3\to0$; the latter factor is bounded independently of $R$. `WeakClassApproxHolds` supplies convergence of the gradients on all of space and convergence in $L^2$ on each fixed ball, which suffice to pass the projected inequalities to the limit.

ns-b4-037.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AzimuthalParts.m: Averaging a smooth approximant against $e^{-ik\phi'}$ preserves compact support in a ball and contracts the gradient norm. In the paper this gives approximants to a function of fixed wave number. In `modeInverseSquareWeak_of` local $L^2$ convergence gives a lower limit for the weighted norm of each projection, while convergence of the gradients gives the limit of the right side; the resulting inequalities are then summed.

ns-b4-038.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AzimuthalParts.g: Orthogonality is with respect to the gradient inner product, so finite $L^2$ mass of the velocity is not required. In Lean `gradientModeTotal` is the spatial Bessel inequality, for the angular projections of the derivative matrix on a slice. It bounds the sum of all angular gradient contributions by the gradient energy; time integration is carried out separately.
ns-b4-038.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AzimuthalParts.t: The paper projects the test in time as well as angle. Lean uses temporal orthogonality on the given field instead: for a fixed component and angular number, put $B_k(\theta,y)=\sum_{k'}e^{2\pi ik'\theta}g_{k',k}(y)$. Integrating $\||y|B_k(\theta)\|_2^2$ over one period gives the sum of $\||y|g_{k',k}\|_2^2$ by distinctness of the time integers. This is the estimate in `timeModeSum`; it requires no time derivative of the test.

ns-b4-039.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AzimuthalParts.m: In the paper the two averages select $u_{k',k}$; only this projection pairs with $e^{2\pi ik'\theta}g$. The linked `modePairing` works at a fixed time: for a scalar amplitude $B$ of angular number $k$, rotation gives the pairing with $P_ku$, which is bounded by $\|P_ku/|y|\|_2\||y|B\|_2$. Time-dependent amplitudes of the same angular number are grouped before applying this estimate.

ns-b4-040.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.remainderAzimuth: The paper applies Cauchy–Schwarz to the gradient norms of the double projections and the weighted norms of their partners. In Lean, at time $\theta$, let $E(\theta)$ be the gradient energy and $A(\theta)$ the weighted sum of squared norms of the grouped angular amplitudes. The spatial estimate bounds the absolute spatial pairing by $\sqrt{E(\theta)A(\theta)}$. A second Cauchy–Schwarz in time uses $\int_0^1 A\le(\mathsf n'')^2$ from temporal orthogonality. The constant is the same.

ns-b4-041.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AzimuthalParts.I: The complex components are a redundant representation of a real vector. The sum of $(v_1+i v_2)\overline{(R_1+iR_2)}$ and $(v_1-i v_2)\overline{(R_1-iR_2)}$ is $2(v_1R_1+v_2R_2)$. Half of this sum, plus $v_3R_3$, is the original pairing. No imaginary part remains.

For either sign, $|
abla(v_1\pm i v_2)|^2=|
abla v_1|^2+|
abla v_2|^2$. Thus assigning weight $1/2$ to each horizontal component and 1 to the vertical one recovers precisely the original gradient energy. The same weights must occur in the squared modal budget.

ns-b4-042.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.remainderAzimuth: The half weights on the two horizontal complex components are needed on both sides of Cauchy–Schwarz: their weighted gradient energies sum to the horizontal gradient energy of $v$. The formal proof first does this on each slice, then integrates the absolute value of the spatial pairing. In particular it proves $\int_0^1|\int v\cdot\mathsf R''\,dy|\,d\theta\le\mathsf n''\|\nabla v\|_{\mathcal H}$, which implies the required bound.

ns-b4-043.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.IsAdjointField: For the adjoint transport terms, $\psi_j$, $\partial_\theta\psi_j$ and $y\cdot\nabla\psi_j$ decay at the same rate. To pair them with an $L^6$ velocity one needs exponent $h>5/2$ so that they are in $L^{6/5}$. The represented fields have $h\ge3$. The general formal `IsAdjointField` uses an exponent $\gamma>5/2$ and weak spatial second derivatives; its bound for the latter only uses exponent $\gamma$, not $\gamma+2$.

ns-b4-044.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.IsPotentialData: The auxiliary fields are a way of representing a functional of the perturbation in norms already present in (7.14). A term $\Delta\mathsf G_j$ can be paired with $\Delta v$ by moving two derivatives, whereas $\Delta\mathsf U_j$ can be paired through the gradients by moving one. Thus a potential of size $O(|y|^{-1})$ is allowed for $\mathsf U_j$, even though it need not have finite $L^2$ norm. The remaining defect is measured by B.11.

pdf-item-equation-B-51.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.IsPotentialData: The bounds $O((1+|y|)^{-2})$ on $\mathsf G_j,\nabla\mathsf U_j,\mathsf F_j,q_j$ give square integrability in space. The common bound on their indicated derivatives is in $L^{6/5}$, both near zero and at infinity, as required in (B.55). The linked condition also bounds $\mathsf U_j=O((1+|y|)^{-1})$ and gives the stronger separate decay estimates for $\Delta\mathsf G_j$ and $\Delta\mathsf U_j$ of orders $-4$ and $-3$. These are regularity requirements, not the smallness requirements in (B.53).

pdf-item-equation-B-52.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.remainderField: The sign of the constraint source follows from $\langle v,-\Delta\tilde\Phi_l\rangle=\langle\nabla v,\nabla\tilde\Phi_l\rangle$. Thus the desired adjoint equation has right side $-\sum_lY_{jl}\Delta\tilde\Phi_l$, and moving it to the left gives the plus sign in (B.52). The three auxiliary terms may reduce the dual norm of the remainder, but their own costs must be included in (B.53).
pdf-item-equation-B-52.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.adjointTransport: `adjointTransport` is the zero- and first-order part of the adjoint, with the time derivative taken on the test field. The diffusion is kept in divergence form: $-\Delta\psi_j$ is $-\operatorname{div}(\nabla\psi_j)^{\mathsf T}$, combined in `pinFlux` with the constraint generators. This permits testing using the weak gradient of $v$.
pdf-item-equation-B-52.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AdjointDefectEnt:
Write $A_l=
abla	ilde\Phi_l-(
abla	ilde\Phi_l)^{\mathsf T}$ in the paper's matrix convention. Its transposed divergence is $\Delta	ilde\Phi_l-
abla\operatorname{div}	ilde\Phi_l=\Delta	ilde\Phi_l$. The formal flux is $
abla\psi_j-\sum_lY_{jl}A_l$; taking the negative transposed divergence gives precisely the diffusion and constraint-source terms of (B.52).

ns-b4-047.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.adjointTransport:
There are two different transpositions. Since $\operatorname{div}W_\alpha^0=0$, the transport operator $W_\alpha^0\cdot
abla$ is skew under the pairing. The other convection term is multiplication by $
abla W_\alpha^0$ and is transposed as a matrix, with no change of sign. This gives $\sum_k\psi_{j,k}
abla W_{\alpha,k}^0$.

ns-b4-048.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.remainderField: The adjoint is chosen to reproduce a constraint, not to be in the kernel of the transposed operator. The advantage is that at the corrected solution the constraint has a prescribed value. Because the matrix field $\Xi_l$ is not generally a gradient, (B.52) uses a divergence-free replacement generator and (B.56) restores the difference from the true constraint.

ns-b4-049.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.PotentialNorms: The decay of $\mathsf G_j$ gives an $L^2$ bound for the field itself, but for $\mathsf U_j$ (B.51) supplies only the corresponding bound on its gradient. After integration by parts their costs are therefore $\mathsf n_{\mathsf G}\|\Delta v\|_{\mathcal H}$ and $w_*\mathsf n_{\mathsf U}\|\nabla v\|_{\mathcal H}$. The matrix term is also paired with $\nabla v$. This explains the grouping in the first square root of (B.53).
ns-b4-049.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AdjointDefectBou: Although the test and the potentials are fixed, the residual of (B.52) varies with $\alpha$ through $W_\alpha^0$. Its dual bound must be verified throughout $\mathcal K$. In the general formal data one can fit auxiliary potentials also to individual tangent defects; the represented cell instance has no such directions, by `fitted_empty`.

ns-b4-050.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AdjointDefectBou: The weights $\varpi_i$ are auxiliary positive numbers, not the energy weight $w_*$. They allow large and small tangent fields to be charged differently: the coefficient vector is divided by $\sqrt{\varpi_i}$ and the field or dual norm multiplied by it. Common rescaling of all $\varpi_i$ leaves the product of the resulting bounds unchanged (with the norm enclosures rescaled accordingly). Only the relative weights can improve it.

pdf-item-theorem-B-12.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.adjointDefectBri: Lemma B.12 gives a bound for the difference between two linear functionals of $v$, before the constraints are imposed. In (B.56) the first line is the adjoint equation defect with its auxiliary terms, the second changes the operator to the one at the actual parameter, and the third changes the represented constraint back to (7.11). Each is bounded by a multiple of the same energy norm.
pdf-item-theorem-B-12.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AdjointDefectEnt: The two operator-related costs in (B.53) make up `defectSum`: the first covers the residual of the adjoint about $W_\alpha^0$ with period $S(0)$, and the second covers the remaining changes in the operator. The formal definition also has a sum for individually fitted tangent defects; it is empty for the represented family. The pin error is a separate charge.

The two replacements have different costs. For $\Xi_l-\nabla\Phi_l$ one needs a matrix norm, since $\Xi_l$ is a rounded cell polynomial and not necessarily a gradient. For $\Phi_l-\tilde\Phi_l$ integration by parts moves the derivative to $v$, allowing a norm of the vector field itself. The solenoidal $\tilde\Phi_l$ is the one used in the adjoint source and its skew flux.
pdf-item-theorem-B-12.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AdjointDefectBou: Smallness of the remainder alone would be meaningless if the added auxiliary terms were large. The first term of (B.53) accounts for both; the next two terms then restore the parameter-dependent operator and the original constraints. The resulting estimate controls the adjoint of the full linearized operator, not only the residual of (B.52).
pdf-item-theorem-B-12.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.Ad: To use the general adjoint bound, its data must describe the same operator and constraint as (7.33). The links set the adjoint field to the represented $\psi_j$, the coupling coefficients to the row $Y_{jl}$, and the base and tangent fields to $W_\alpha^0,W_\alpha^i$. They also identify the rates in $1/S(\alpha)$ and set the fitted set empty.

pdf-item-equation-B-53.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AdjointDefectEnt: All three errors $w_*\mathsf n_{\mathsf U}$, $\mathsf n_{\mathsf F}$ and $\mathsf n_{\mathsf R}$ act on the same gradient of the perturbation; they have to be added before using Cauchy–Schwarz with the Laplacian term. Treating their squares as independent would not give a justified bound. The extra terms in `defectSum` account for changes in the operator, not these same gradient errors a second time.

The last two summands have different powers of the weight because their test fields are different. The error in the potential is multiplied by $\|\Delta v\|_{\mathcal H}$, whereas the error of the rounded constraint matrices is multiplied by $\|\nabla v\|_{\mathcal H}$. Hence only the latter coefficient, $\mathsf n_Yc_\Xi$, is divided by $\sqrt{w_*}$.
pdf-item-equation-B-53.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AdjointDefectBou: The number $a_j$ is an upper bound for an operator norm on the perturbation space, uniform over $\alpha\in\mathcal K$. For example, the first square root alone is not sufficient if the inverse period or the tangent fields change appreciably. The other terms in (B.53) restore the full operator and the actual constraint, respectively.
pdf-item-equation-B-53.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.Ad: The expression in (B.53) is recovered from the general formal budget by substituting the links of this represented instance. In particular, no tangent direction is fitted by a separate potential, so the sum over fitted directions is zero and the free-direction sum runs over all coordinates. The row of coupling coefficients is the one used in the constraints.

ns-b4-053.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.IsAdjointField: Although $F$ is only specified modulo gradients, its pairing with the divergence-free $\psi$ is independent of the representative: $\langle F,\psi\rangle_{\mathcal H}=\langle PF,\psi\rangle_{\mathcal H}$. This is why the pressure of the unknown correction is absent from (B.54)–(B.56). The statement still assumes $F\in\mathcal H$.

ns-b4-054.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.representationHo: The domain requires the combined expression $S^{-1}\partial_\theta v+v/2+(y\cdot\nabla)v/2-\Delta v$ to be in $\mathcal H$, not separate bounds on the time and dilation derivatives. Transposition in the weak equation avoids those additional requirements. Lean first uses a smooth compactly supported time window with translates summing to one: integrating its derivative against a periodic integrand gives zero, leaving the period pairing (B.54).

ns-b4-056.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.adjointTransport: The dilation adjoint contains $-\tfrac32$ in addition to $-\tfrac12 y\cdot\nabla$, since the dimension is three. Adding the original zeroth-order coefficient $\tfrac12$ gives $-1-\tfrac12y\cdot\nabla$; the period derivative transposes with a minus sign.

ns-b4-057.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.testFieldDensity: Cutting off $\psi$ itself can destroy solenoidality, so for the weak solenoidal equation the formal proof uses a curl potential $A$ and takes $\operatorname{curl}(\chi A)=\chi\psi+\nabla\chi\times A$. The latter term is supported on the cutoff annulus. The decay assumptions allow convergence of the test and its gradient as well as of its time derivative and radial derivative in the norms needed for (B.54); smoothing gives admissible compact tests.

pdf-item-equation-B-55.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.Internal.Potenti: Both sides of (B.55) extend from compact tests in the gradient norm. The matrix pairing uses $A\in L^2$ and the velocity pairing uses $\operatorname{div}A^{\mathsf T}\in L^{6/5}$ with Sobolev. The linked weak pairing instead uses $|y|\operatorname{div}A^{\mathsf T}\in L^2$ with Hardy, together with local integrability and the weak divergence identity. Neither argument requires $v\in L^2$.

The formal `pair_flux` verifies the hypotheses of the weak pairing from decay: if $A$ and $|y|\operatorname{div}A^{\mathsf T}$ are bounded by $B(1+|y|)^{-a}$ with $2a>3$, both are in $L^2$. The condition concerns the divergence with one factor of $|y|$, not its unweighted $L^2$ norm. This allows the indicated singularity at the origin.

ns-b4-059.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.Internal.Potenti: For $A=q_j I$, the right side of (B.55) is $-\int q_j\operatorname{div}v=0$. This removes the auxiliary pressure from the defect bound, not from the definition of the strong residual. In B.13 the pairing will instead be restricted to a ball, where the same cancellation cannot be made without a boundary condition.

ns-b4-060.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.Internal.transpo: The decomposition does not expand the radial phase in powers of $\alpha$. It is exact at the current phase: $W_\alpha^{\rm a}-W_\alpha^0=\sum_i\alpha_iW_\alpha^i$. Hence the difference from the operator in (B.52) consists only of this convection change and the inverse-period change $\varsigma\cdot\alpha$. No term involving $W_\alpha^0-W_0^0$ has to be added to (B.56).
ns-b4-060.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.Ad: The base and tangent fields in the adjoint equation and in the offset calculation must come from the same represented family. `centre_eq` and `free_eq` use the phase at $\alpha$; `centrePeriod_eq` and `periodRate_eq` identify the reciprocal period and its affine coefficients with those in B.13. The matching-ball restriction in B.13, not these links, is what permits evaluating the fields at $\alpha=0$.

ns-b4-061.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.Internal.Potenti: Solve (B.52) for the first line. The three auxiliary terms to be paired with $v$ are then $-\Delta\mathsf G_j$, $-w_*\Delta\mathsf U_j$ and $+\operatorname{div}\mathsf F_j^{\mathsf T}$. Moving two, one and one spatial derivatives respectively gives the signs $-,+,-$ in the first line of (B.56); the pressure pairing vanishes. The linked slice identity formalizes this part of the calculation.
ns-b4-061.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.Internal.transpo: The inverse-period change contributes $-(\varsigma\cdot\alpha)\iint v\cdot\partial_\theta\psi$ because it is the adjoint of the time derivative. The convection change contributes $\sum_i\alpha_i[(W_\alpha^i\cdot\nabla)v\cdot\psi+v\cdot\sum_k\psi_k\nabla W_{\alpha,k}^i]$ under the integral. These are exact differences of linear operators; there are no products of two direction fields as in (B.57).
ns-b4-061.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.pinChargeHolds_p:
Subtract the original constraint after adding and subtracting $
abla\Phi_l$. Then $\langle
abla v,
abla	ilde\Phi_l-
abla\Phi_langle=\langle\Delta v,\Phi_l-	ilde\Phi_langle$, while $\langle

ns-b4-062.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.adjointDefectBri: The three estimates use no norm of the time derivative of $v$. Even the period-change term now pairs $v$ with a derivative of the known field, to which B.11 applies. Hence the bound for the defect is in $\|v\|_w$, the norm provided by the inverse estimate, rather than the full graph norm of the similarity operator.

ns-b4-063.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.potentialBoundHo: Put $B=w_*\mathsf n_{\mathsf U}+\mathsf n_{\mathsf F}+\mathsf n_{\mathsf R}$. The bound $\mathsf n_{\mathsf G}\|\Delta v\|_{\mathcal H}+B\|\nabla v\|_{\mathcal H}$ is the dot product of $(\mathsf n_{\mathsf G},B/\sqrt{w_*})$ with $(\|\Delta v\|_{\mathcal H},\sqrt{w_*}\|\nabla v\|_{\mathcal H})$. Cauchy–Schwarz gives the square root in (B.53), rather than the larger sum $\mathsf n_{\mathsf G}+B/\sqrt{w_*}$.

ns-b4-064.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.freeShiftBoundHo: At fixed $\alpha$, Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|\sum_i\alpha_i W_\alpha^i|\le(\sum_i\bar\varrho_i^2/\varpi_i)^{1/2}(\sum_i\varpi_i|W_\alpha^i|^2)^{1/2}$. Pair the latter factor times $|\psi|$ with $|\nabla v|$. For the transposed stretching term use B.11 first, then the same weighted Cauchy–Schwarz on $\sum_i|\alpha_i|\mathsf n_i$. Thus the common radius factor multiplies $\mathsf n_{\rm v}+\mathsf n_{\rm d}$.

ns-b4-066.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.pinChargeHolds_p: It is the norm of the map $x\mapsto\sum_lx_l(\Xi_l-\nabla\Phi_l)$ that is bounded by $c_\Xi$. Inserting the row $(Y_{jl})_l$ in this bound gives $\mathsf n_Yc_\Xi$ in one step. There is no need to sum the norms of the individual errors, which would discard possible cancellations in that row.

ns-b4-067.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.adjointDefectBri: The final inequality has the form $|\langle F,\psi\rangle_{\mathcal H}-(Y(\alpha)\ell(v))_j|\le a_j\|v\|_w$. It has been established for any $v\in\mathcal D_{S(\alpha)}$ with the indicated $F$, not just for a perturbation of size $2\varepsilon$. The size restriction enters only when the inequality is used for the parameter update.

ns-b4-068.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.of: One could try to expand $F_\alpha^{\rm a}$ on the whole space, but a change of period changes the logarithmic radial phase at infinity (C.4). The phase correction vanishes on $B_{r_\chi}$, where the velocity and inverse period are affine. Therefore the coefficient calculation on that ball is exact and the exterior needs just a norm enclosure, not bounds on the parameter derivatives of the phase.

pdf-item-equation-B-57.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.qu: The second-order part of the interior residual comes only from multiplying the affine inverse period by $\partial_\theta W_\alpha^{\rm a}$, from convection, and from the gradient of the kinetic energy. For an ordered pair $(i,i')$ its coefficient is $\varsigma_i\partial_\theta W_0^{i'}+(W_0^i\cdot\nabla)W_0^{i'}-\frac12\nabla(W_0^i\cdot W_0^{i'})$. This is `quadraticDefect`; the force and the pressure potential $q_\alpha$ contribute only at degrees zero and one.
pdf-item-equation-B-57.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.Of: Collecting the ordered coefficients gives $F^{(ii)}$ once, and gives $F^{(ii')}$ as the sum of the two orders for $i<i'$. For example, the gradient contribution from $\alpha_i\alpha_{i'}$ is then $-\nabla(W_0^i\cdot W_0^{i'})$, not half of it. The resulting coefficient is used once in (B.58) and (B.59).
pdf-item-equation-B-57.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.ce: The constant coefficient of the ball response is $V_j\cdot\beta^0-\langle F^{(0)},\psi_j\rangle_\chi$. It includes the centre's prescribed force as well as its residual, even though the desired diagonal response vanishes at $\alpha=0$. The corresponding whole-space constant differs by the exterior pairing, bounded later in B.13.
pdf-item-equation-B-57.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.li: On the ball this coefficient is the first variation of the actual residual with respect to $\alpha_i$. Differentiating the factor $S(\alpha)^{-1}$ gives $\varsigma_i\partial_\theta W_0^0$ in addition to $S(0)^{-1}\partial_\theta W_0^i$. The pressure variation and $-\nabla(W_0^0\cdot W_0^i)$ must be kept because the coefficient will be paired on the ball, not modulo gradients.

ns-b4-072.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.ba: Solenoidality removes a gradient from a pairing on all of space under the indicated integrability hypotheses. On the ball, however, $\int_{B_{r_\chi}}\nabla p\cdot\psi_j=\int_{\partial B_{r_\chi}}p\,\psi_j\cdot\nu$ for smooth fields, and there is no zero-normal condition on $\psi_j$ there. Thus the pressure and kinetic-energy gradients in (B.57) are retained in (B.58). Lean integrates on the closed ball; the sphere has measure zero.

pdf-item-theorem-B-13.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.Is: The intervals in (B.58) enclose coefficients of the signed scalar response, not of the norm of the residual. In particular the centre and linear coefficients subtract the residual pairing from the corresponding force coefficient. For the quadratic part the force is affine, so its coefficient is just $-\langle F^{(ii')},\psi_j\rangle_\chi$.
pdf-item-theorem-B-13.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.of: The target polynomial has no constant or quadratic terms, and its linear coefficients vanish except for $d_j$ at $i=j$. Hence if the centre of the diagonal interval is exactly $d_j$, its contribution to the error is still $\tilde{\mathsf C}^1_{jj}\hat\varrho_j$. It is the displacement from the target interval, not the size of the original coefficient, that enters the bound.
pdf-item-theorem-B-13.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.co: The monomial estimates use an enclosing box of the parameter set. For distinct $i,i'\notin\mathcal J$ one could use $|d_i d_{i'}\alpha_i\alpha_{i'}|\le\varrho_*^2/2$ from the sum of their two squares; (B.59) instead uses the simpler product of the individual radii. Thus the budget is sufficient, not necessarily the supremum of the response error on $\mathcal K$.
pdf-item-theorem-B-13.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.of: Write the ball response as $P_j(\alpha)=V_j\cdot\beta^{\rm a}(\alpha)-\langle F_\alpha^{\rm a},\psi_j\rangle_\chi$. Then the quantity to bound in (7.34) is $P_j(\alpha)-d_j\alpha_j-\langle F_\alpha^{\rm a}\mathbf1_{|y|>r_\chi},\psi_j\mathbf1_{|y|>r_\chi}\rangle_{\mathcal H}$, since $\bar\ell=0$. The polynomial enclosures are used only for the first difference.

ns-b4-074.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.Is: The exterior residual is the actual $F_\alpha^{\rm a}$, including the pressure-gradient representative and the parameter-dependent phase. Its restricted $\mathcal H$ norm must be bounded for all parameters. The other factor is the exterior norm of the fixed test $\psi_j$, so a large residual where the adjoint is small may still give a small exterior pairing.

pdf-item-equation-B-59.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.of: A bound on the absolute response itself would also charge the term $d_j\alpha_j$ needed for the Newton update. Instead the diagonal linear coefficient is centered at $d_j$ and the other coefficients at zero. The sum in (B.59) encloses the remainder after these subtractions, which is the approximate-family part of $-d_j\alpha'_j$ in (7.35).

ns-b4-076.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.co: On the selected coordinates, (7.29) gives the individual radii $\varrho_i$. On the other coordinates it bounds the Euclidean norm of $(d_i\alpha_i)_{i\notin\mathcal J}$, hence also each $|d_i\alpha_i|$ by $\varrho_*$. Dividing by $|d_i|$ gives the second radius; it is essential that $d_i\ne0$. The formal definition writes $|\varrho_*|$, equal to $\varrho_*$ under the sign assumption.

ns-b4-077.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.of: Equation (7.34) is an enclosure of the approximate-family contribution to the new scaled coordinate, not the whole coordinate. In (7.35) one still needs the quadratic pairing, the linear adjoint defect, and the difference of the force pairings from $V_j$. The coordinates outside $\mathcal J$ are estimated by (7.36)–(7.37), without the ball polynomial for an adjoint row.

ns-b4-078.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.ba: On the open ball the correction to the radial phase is identically zero, so its derivatives vanish there as well. One may freeze the phase before taking derivatives in the residual. The boundary sphere has measure zero in the ball pairing, so no expansion across the transition of the radial phase is needed.

ns-b4-079.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.ba: The representation uses the phase in both the factors $E_{\iota,l}$ and the differential operators $\mathcal V_l$. Equality of the phases with their derivatives consequently gives equality of the represented velocity, gradient, second derivatives, pressure and pressure gradient. These are all needed to substitute into the residual; agreement only of the velocity values would not suffice.

ns-b4-080.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.In: Because $S(\alpha)^{-1}$, not $S(\alpha)$, is affine, all terms of the residual after substitution have degree at most two: the time coefficient multiplies an affine time derivative, and the convection and kinetic energy multiply affine velocities. Spatial differentiation does not change the degree. This is an exact polynomial on the matching ball, with no neglected third-order term.

ns-b4-081.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.of: Subtract $d_j\alpha_j$ from the ball response, and then subtract the exterior residual pairing. In the resulting polynomial the coefficient of $\alpha_i$ is $V_j\cdot\beta^i-\langle F^{(i)},\psi_j\rangle_\chi-d_j\mathbf1_{i=j}$, and all degree-two coefficients are negative residual pairings. The exterior term is not part of the polynomial.

ns-b4-082.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.In: The enclosure radius for the linear coefficient does not change when the target is subtracted. If $L_{ji}=V_j\cdot\beta^i-\langle F^{(i)},\psi_j\rangle_\chi$, then $|L_{ji}-d_j\mathbf1_{i=j}|\le |\mathsf C^1_{ji}-d_j\mathbf1_{i=j}|+\tilde{\mathsf C}^1_{ji}$. Multiply this by $\hat\varrho_i$ for the contribution to (B.59).

The difference of the full pairing and the ball pairing is the integral over $|y|>r_\chi$ (the boundary has measure zero). Its absolute value is at most $\|F_\alpha^{\rm a}\mathbf1_{|y|>r_\chi}\|_{\mathcal H}\|\psi_j\mathbf1_{|y|>r_\chi}\|_{\mathcal H}$. No polynomial expansion or cancellation is used outside.

ns-b4-083.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.In: Retain the $i$th summand in the nonnegative sum $\sum_{l\notin\mathcal J}d_l^2\alpha_l^2\le\varrho_*^2$. Taking the square root gives $|d_i||\alpha_i|\le\varrho_*$; division gives the individual coordinate bound. This is sufficient for the monomial-by-monomial estimate, even though the simultaneous ellipsoid constraint can be sharper.

ns-b4-084.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.of: The adjoint pairing predicts the force with the additional term $-(Y(\alpha)\bar\ell(\alpha))_j$ in (7.34). In B.1 the constraints for the correction have value zero, so the entire offset is the one just estimated. If nonzero constraints were prescribed, their known contribution would have to be included before testing the parameter inclusion.

ns-b4-085.Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.CertificateCla: The remaining inequalities close the analytic argument. In (7.24) the given residual fits the correction budget; (7.25) and (7.27) permit the quadratic correction map to preserve the energy and supremum bounds. The paper imposes (7.26) but does not use it in the proof. Finally, (7.28) ensures nontriviality: if $v=-W_\alpha^{\rm a}$ then $w_*\|\nabla W_\alpha^{\rm a}\|_{\mathcal H}^2\le\|v\|_w^2\le4\varepsilon^2$, contradicting the strict inequality.

b4-prop-b14.Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.isExtendedCert: Proposition B.14 replaces the analytic estimates of Section 7 by conditions on represented fields and cell data. It does not construct a new approximation: the same fields, force coefficients and parameter set are used in the analytic certificate. The linked theorem returns an `IsExtendedCertificate` for those data with a decay constant obtained from their representation; existence of admissible numerical data is not its conclusion.
b4-prop-b14.Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.CellSystemCond: The conditions must hold for one common choice of fields and numbers. For instance, `offset_expansion` encloses the residual of the profile whose base and tangent fields occur in `adjoint_links`, and the same constraints occur in the coercivity and adjoint inequalities. This prevents combining individually valid estimates for different approximate families.

ns-b4-087.Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.isExtendedCert: The conclusion supplies the hypotheses of Theorem 7.1, not its solution. The theorem will solve the constrained correction problem with the certified inverse estimate, choose the parameter using the adjoint and stiff-coordinate enclosures, and use (7.28) to exclude the zero profile. The formal assembly likewise establishes the certificate predicate; the profile construction is a subsequent theorem.

ns-b4-088.Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.isExtendedCert: Properties such as the allowed harmonics, the symmetries and zero divergence come from the represented form in B.1 and its compatibility conditions. Bounds such as the size of the residual and coercivity do not follow just from this form. This is why the statement of B.14 needs both the representation and the inequalities.

ns-b4-089.Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.CertificateCla: The required residual is the unprojected representative supplied in B.1. In (7.23) one measures its full $\mathcal H$ norm and the weighted row pairings of (7.17), not just the Leray projection. Although its gradient part disappears from the whole-space solenoidal adjoint pairings, changing the representative can affect both bounds used in (7.24).

ns-b4-090.Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.isExtendedCert: B.8 and B.2 give the a priori estimate at the reference field, while B.9 bounds its change to the approximate field and the growth of the slice gradient energy. B.10–B.13 supply the three adjoint bounds for the parameter update. Conditions such as invertibility of $V$, the residual size, and the scalar inclusions (7.35) and (7.37) remain direct hypotheses; they are not consequences of the cell coercivity estimate.

ns-b4-091.Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.breakdownOnSpa: The conclusion in the paper proceeds through the exact smooth profile of Theorem 7.1 and then its localization. The linked formal theorem proves the two global nonexistence statements from the cell-system hypothesis, via a weak recurrent profile and the formal localization implications. It does not assert the quantitative tracking conclusions of Theorem 1.1. In particular no certificate data satisfying the cell-system hypothesis are constructed here.

ns-b4-092.Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.CellSystemCond: Local pressure variables have a free additive constant, since their derivatives alone enter the equation. The cell quadratic form must be invariant under this change of constant, and the passage from the global unknowns to the local ones must respect that invariance. These conditions ensure that the summed cell estimate is an estimate for the global perturbation, not one that depends on arbitrary pressure normalizations.

ns-b4-093.Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.CellSystemCond: Checking the finite matrices alone is insufficient. Their entries must enclose the intended integrals, the polynomial identities must match the global-to-cell map, and the coefficient inequalities must hold throughout the relevant cells and regions. The positive forms are then tested on all allowed coefficient vectors, with the omitted modes controlled by the estimates of B.3.

ns-b4-094.Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.CellSystemCond: The numerical thresholds at the end of B.4 are restrictions on any admissible data, not the achieved sizes of the computed error. For example (7.25) bounds $M$ by $(2c_Lc_w)^{-1}$; dropping nonnegative terms in (7.27) gives $2\varepsilon/\sqrt{w_*}\le M$. Combining the two gives the stated restriction on $\varepsilon$. The formal unresolved-mode and exterior estimates permit a stretching constant at least $\sqrt{7/2}$.

ac-032.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.shapeInfoF: The computed period is $\bar S$ in similarity time $s$. Normalizing by $\theta=s/\bar S$ allows the same integer frequency lattice to be used regardless of the value of $\bar S$. The form of (B.6) specifies the fields in terms of supplied coefficients; the computed coefficient values are additional data.

ac-033.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.af: The correction directions may have the same logarithmic tail dependence as the base field, but the phase change in (B.9) is turned off on a ball. There one may form the trial profile and its derivatives by ordinary affine combinations of fixed fields, which is useful for bounding the residual as a function of the parameter.

ac-034.Breakdown.CertCell.labelPhase: Since every azimuthal Fourier integer is $19\iota_1$, pure rotation through $2\pi/19$ preserves each scalar component in the rotating frame. The half-period rotation in (B.1) is a stronger relation between time and angle: it permits a rotation through half that angle if time also advances by half a period.

ac-047.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.fieldClass: The two spatial symmetries follow from different parts of the representation: the angular frequency is a multiple of nineteen, and the reflected amplitudes give the half-turn. The theorem establishes both for any admissible data; its application to $\bar W$ requires identification with those data.

ac-048.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.fieldClass: Writing $W(\theta,y)=\bar W(\bar S\theta,y)$, the generator identity reads $W(\theta+1/2,R_{\pi/19}y)=R_{\pi/19}W(\theta,y)$. Replacing $y$ by $R_{-\pi/19}y$ and returning to $s=\bar S\theta$ gives the half-period relation in the paper. Thus the sign of the rotation in the argument is fixed by the vector symmetry, not by the sense of either individual travelling pattern.

ac-035.Breakdown.CertCell.labelPhase: The two lines $\iota_2=0$ and $\iota_2=\iota_1$ are characterized by phases $\iota_1(19\phi\mp2\pi\theta)$. In similarity time $s=\bar S\theta$ the corresponding angular velocities are $\pm2\pi/(19\bar S)$. Thus in the frame of either pattern its own harmonics have zero frequency. The useful high-frequency test in C.4 uses the other frame for these harmonics, rather than assuming that every large angular integer oscillates rapidly in either frame.

ac-052.Breakdown.CertCell.labelPhase: The identity $(\iota_1,\iota_2)=(\iota_1-\iota_2,0)+(\iota_2,\iota_2)$ gives the factorization of $E_\iota$. The meridian amplitudes are still independent functions; the factorization concerns only the two angle variables. In the linearized equation, products add these lattice labels, including products of modes belonging to different patterns.

ac-050.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.fi: The plot rescales the field and the derivatives by $(1+|y|)^{1+j}$ for derivative order $j$. The representation gives boundedness of these rescaled functions under its shape hypotheses, including bounded piecewise second derivatives. It does not determine their supremum from the exponents alone: the magnitude of the spline coefficients and the radial phase bounds enter the constant.

ac-051.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.fi: Order-one decay means $|\bar W(s,y)|\le C(1+|y|)^{-1}$, not that a nonzero leading coefficient has been established in each direction. The derivative bounds decay one power faster per derivative. A nonzero $R^{-1}$ oscillatory leading term is used to explain the phase choice below; its existence is not asserted by the decay theorem.

ac-049.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.logPhaseIs: For $f(\rho)=A\log(1+\rho/r_c^2)$ one has $\rho^j|f^{(j)}(\rho)|=|A|(j-1)!(\rho/(r_c^2+\rho))^j$ for $j=1,2,3$. These are bounded by $|A|(j-1)!$ since $r_c>0$. Thus the phase grows logarithmically but meets exactly the derivative conditions of B.1.

ac-036.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.keyPhase: The integer $l$ is minus the ordinary time Fourier integer $j=2\iota_2-\iota_1$. With $f(R^2)=(2\pi/\bar S)\log(1+R^2/r_c^2)$ this combines the time and radial exponentials into a phase proportional to $\log(1+R^2/r_c^2)-s$. The general representation (B.5) does not require this relation between the radial and time indices.

ac-037.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.keyPhase: At fixed $x\ne0$, substitute $y=x/\sqrt{T-t}$ and $s=\log(T/(T-t))$ into the square brackets. They become $\log((T-t)+|x|^2/r_c^2)-\log T$, which has a finite limit as $t\to T$. The prefactor of a leading $R^{-1}$ term becomes $|x|^{-1}$ in Eulerian velocity. Thus the logarithmic radial phase compensates the time oscillation for the specified leading coefficient.

ac-038.Breakdown.SimilarityResidual: For a solenoidal smooth field, $-\Delta W=\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}W$. Also $(W\cdot\nabla)W=(\operatorname{curl}W)\times W+\nabla(|W|^2/2)$. Substituting both identities into (1.2) gives the curl formulation, with the kinetic-energy gradient absorbed into $H$. `SimilarityResidual` uses the original advection and diffusion form.
ac-038.Breakdown.Coercive.Internal.TestDensityP: For any smooth vector field, $\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}W=\nabla\operatorname{div}W-\Delta W$. In (C.1) the second displayed equation sets the first term on the right to zero. The linked lemma is the solenoidal specialization of this identity; it explains why the diffusion term in the residual of (C.1) is the positive double curl.

ac-039.Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.Internal.Rem: At a fixed point set $M=DW(y)$ and $x=W(y)$. The linked identity, tested against every vector $\psi$, is $Mx-(\operatorname{curl}W)\times x=M^Tx$. The chain rule gives $M^Tx=\nabla(|W|^2/2)$. Hence the pressure in the curl formulation is $q+|W|^2/2$, with the plus sign.

ac-041.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.IsTimeFiel: The specified exponents are the smallest allowed by the general nonzero-azimuthal amplitude construction. They give second-order vanishing at the origin and order-one decay at infinity. The linked predicate permits other exponents and additionally requires the spline joins and symmetries; it does not supply the computed choice.

ac-053.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.shapeInfoF: For a nonzero azimuthal mode the two splines determine the third amplitude via (B.7); for an axisymmetric mode the stream function and swirl determine the velocity via (B.8). The numerical unknowns therefore consist of the independent scalar coefficients and the origin coefficients, with one additional unknown for the period. No separate divergence equation for three independent velocity components is necessary.

ac-054.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.IsTimeFiel: A common partition lets every retained harmonic use the same radial rings and height intervals in quadrature and Newton's method. The general representation does not require this: each spline may have its own partition, provided its own traces agree to the orders in B.1.

ac-055.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.IsTimeFiel: The join conditions are built into the polynomial basis used for the unknowns. For example $\mathsf A$ needs an extra radial derivative and $\mathsf B$ an extra height derivative because of their contributions to $u_2$ in (B.7); $\mathsf S$ needs both because of the two derivatives in (B.8). The resulting velocity has continuous first derivatives, although its second derivatives in the residual are only piecewise continuous.

ac-056.Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.keyDiverge: The identity is structural: every admissible velocity summand has zero divergence by the formulas for its components. Hence a finite linear combination of the corresponding basis fields is solenoidal without an additional divergence equation in the discretized solve. The theorem does not establish that the reported numerical coefficient data meet all its hypotheses.

ac-057.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.sc: The term $\nabla H$ in (C.1) drops out of the weak equations because the tests are solenoidal. For a compactly supported test the identity is immediate by integration by parts; the represented tests in the computation have decay rather than compact support, so removal of a spatial cutoff uses their decay. This pressure elimination does not mean the residual before subtracting a gradient is small.

ac-043.Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.IsStrong: The differential expression in (C.2) is the linearization at the current profile. The formal strong right-hand side also allows the actuator forcing and the gradient of pressure: its diffusion term is minus the Hessian trace, using solenoidality to replace $\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}v$ by $-\Delta v$. In Appendix C the expression is tested in a finite space to find an approximate field; in Appendix B its cellwise pairings are estimated for arbitrary perturbations of the reference field.
ac-043.Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.coupling: Writing $\omega=\operatorname{curl}W$ and $\delta\omega=\operatorname{curl}v$, the first variation of $\omega\times W$ is $\delta\omega\times W+\omega\times v$. These are the two terms of `couplingField` once the supplied gradient is identified with $\nabla v$. Both are needed in the momentum rows of the linearized equation.

On solenoidal smooth fields the divergence term vanishes, so the diffusion is $-\Delta v$. The formal identity is proved for smooth fields without imposing solenoidality; that additional restriction is what gives the expression here.

The equation $F^{(i)}\simeq0$ is the target of that solve, not an exact identity of the represented fields. Even a small first variation modulo gradients does not by itself bound its ball pairing; (B.58) uses the actual residual representative and the adjoint field. The phase is changed only outside the matching ball so that this first variation and the quadratic terms are exact interior coefficients.

ac-046.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.af: For a leading term with time integer $j$ and radial index $l=-j$, the change $S^{-1}\mapsto S^{-1}+\varsigma\cdot\alpha$ adds $2\pi i j(\varsigma\cdot\alpha)$ to its similarity transport multiplier. Without such cancellation, the change produces an order-$R^{-1}$ term for a nonzero leading oscillatory coefficient, whose square is not integrable at infinity. The cutoff allows the change to be made only in the exterior.

Excluding them from all selected sets ensures that both skew pairings vanish on every force; it does not constrain the radial or height resolution of the force fields.
